News.title: Iran opens criminal probe after actress rests head against actor’s chest during play in latest crackdown by evil regime
News.content:
Next

IRANIAN prosecutors have opened a criminal case against a theatre company after a female actress rested her head on a male actor on stage.

Lackeys of Tehran’s savage mullahs claim the behaviour violates the country’s standard of public decency and was a “violation of social norms.”



An audience members shared footage of popular play Tehran Paris Tehran, being staged at Book Garden, showing Fatemeh Masoudifar leaning her head toward Mehrdad Sedighian’s chest.

Mehrdad places his hand over her head as she appears to tightly embrace him.



Due to strong religious rules in the Islamic Republic, physical contact between unrelated or unmarried men and women in public is strictly prohibited.

Fars News Agency, affiliated with the Revolutionary Guards, scrutinised the scene, saying it was indicative of what it described as “the gradual erosion of the boundaries governing artistic freedom and public conduct”.

They wrote: “It seems there is no supervision over theater stages.”

The production company responded to the controversy saying it was all a misunderstanding as the angle of the video misconstrues the true distance between the actors.



Moreover, the moment depicts a brother and sister interacting during a “moment of crisis”, meaning they have not broken or offended any Islamic laws.

They added that they have since changed the actors’ positions in the scene to avoid further misunderstanding.

Tehran Paris Tehran follows Sara, a young girl who embarks on a journey from Iran to France and back to avenge her father’s murder.

It comes after recent backlash in Iran for its response to violations of the Islamic Republic’s social and religious restrictions.

Authorities have increasingly handed out severe punishments such as women facing flogging sentences for singing without compulsory hijabs alongside male musicians.



Singer Parastoo Ahmadi and seven others involved in a concert at the historic Caravanserai were each sentenced to 74 lashes, a two-year ban on audiovisual and musical activity and a two-year travel ban.

An appeals court in Qom on Friday has upheld a ruling against the defendants, confirming that the performance violated religious, legal, and public morality standards.

In August, Iran’s parliament approved the general framework of a new bill that increases punishments for citizens who interact with foreign media, individuals, or organisations.

This would include foreign embassies or institutions, domestically or internationally.

According to state media, any Iranian person convicted of violating the bill could serve up to two years in prison unless they first obtain explicit written permission from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.



Iran already heavily restricts sharing information with exiled or Western-backed networks like Iran International, BBC Farsi, and VOA Farsi.

Additionally, the bill outlaws all educational and research activities tied to foreign institutions.

Violators could face up to 10 years in prison if their work is deemed “incompatible with Iranian culture.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Since the 1979 revolution, Iran’s leadership has been deeply concerned with stopping “foreign infiltration.”

This concern primarily targets the United States and Israel, which Tehran views as its main adversaries.

News.title: Four rushed to hospital after smoke enters plane forcing passengers to use oxygen masks as pilot makes emergency landing
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

MID-AIR CHAOS Four rushed to hospital after smoke enters plane forcing passengers to use oxygen masks as pilot makes emergency landing







Next

FOUR passengers have been rushed to hospital after a plane was forced to make an emergency landing in Portugal due to smoke in the cabin.

Fourteen people were treated for smoke inhalation in total after alarms were sounded mid-flight.



The plane was en route to Boston, US, when it was forced to make an emergency landing in Porto on Saturday afternoon.

Twelve people on board the Airbus A330 had to be given oxygen mid-air, according to the Portuguese press.



As the aircraft was about to cross the Atlantic Ocean, it made a sudden u-turn and flew south-easterly.

The crew then declared an emergency using squawk code 7700 and diverted landing to Porto’s Sá Carneiro Airport.



A level two alert was sounded around 5.30pm to warn emergency teams of the aircraft’s arrival.

Firefighters, police, and ambulances were mobilised on the tarmac to prepare for the plane’s unscheduled landing.



Air traffic in the area was momentarily suspended to allow for a safe touchdown.

In total, four passengers were rushed to hospital, with two men admitted to Sao Joao Hospital’s A&E suffering from smoke inhalation.

A spokesman said both had “mild” respiratory symptoms and were in a stable condition.

The remaining 282 uninjured passengers were evacuated and placed on an alternative flight scheduled for this afternoon.

The plane had taken off from Barcelona’s El Prat airport around 3.40pm local time and landed around 3 hours later.



Disruptions to the airport’s operations were understood to have been brief.

Popular flight tracking sites, such as FlightRadar24, monitored the whole ordeal for aviation fanatics to follow.

News.title: Elderly man, 84, rams car into wife & kills her during botched parking attempt before causing £80K damage in crash spree
News.content:
OAP HORROR Elderly man, 84, rams car into wife & kills her during botched parking attempt before causing £80K damage in crash spree







Next

AN ELDERLY man rammed into his wife and killed her during a failed parking attempt in Germany, police said.

The 84-year-old man was reversing his car when he smashed into a parked vehicle before accelerating forwards and fatally crashing into his unaware partner.



His wife was standing in front of the car in Niedernhausen at the time, police said.

Cops are continuing to investigate her tragic death.



After striking his wife, the man reportedly continued to race down the road at a terrifying speed.

He collided with several garden fences, two parked cars and a camper van.



His car later came to a halt after making it just 500ft, police said.

Initial estimates put the damage at more than £86,000.

The wife tragically died at the scene while her husband was taken to hospital with serious injuries.

It remains unknown why the man sped from the scene where his wife.was dying



A police probe into the incident continues.

It comes after another terrifying incident that saw a driver launch his car into the air during a high-speed chase with cops in America.

The jaw dropping scene unfolded as the man fled the scene of a traffic stop.

In shocking dashcam footage, police were seen pursuing the man in a white car as the chaos unfolded.

The driver suddenly swerved his vehicle to the right as it sped down the I-41 at Military Road in Wisconsin.



Careening the car across two lanes, the vehicle then ploughed straight off the road.

It crossed the grass bank between two intersections, then sped up the small road-side ditch.

In a hair-raising second, the vehicle became airborne as it flew over another car.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The vehicle then crashed down on the other side of the road and ground to a halt.

Abandoning the crashed car, the driver attempted to flee across an empty field on foot but was quickly accosted and arrested by police.

News.title: First Strictly live show had its messy moments – but it reminded us of some important truths about the show
News.content:
Next

FIRST we had the silences from Josh Widdecombe missing his cues, then the maelstrom of Johannes Radebe trying to speak amid the cheers of the Clauditorium.

Finally a third sound – Strictly producers frantically ringing round agents to see if Mick Fleetwood and Sam Fox were still available.



A bit harsh, I know.

After all The Brits is a big beast to harness and Mick and Sam didn’t have Emma Willis there to save them, either.



She was, once again, absolute perfection amid the messier moments of Saturday night’s first live show.

But overall, it really wasn’t that bad at all.



Strictly is always greater than the sum of it’s not insubstantial parts and perhaps we’re all over scrutinising the presenters?

Let’s not forget Tess Daly was nicknamed the Tess-bot by some unkind viewers and Claudia Winkleman was initially greeted with some scepticism when she first started.

But in the end they bedded in nicely as a duo.

In fact Saturday night’s episode was a reminder of some important truths about Strictly.



Nothing, and no one, is bigger than the show.

Also, the fame of the competing stars really doesn’t matter as much as the performances, and the judges – particularly the consistently hilarious Craig Revel Horwood – are actually more important than the hosts.

Which is just as well.

If all else fails we can, obviously, rely on Katya Jones doing something with one of the male celebrities that will keep us distracted until Christmas.



Sometimes it’s dancing.

News.title: Three people rushed to hospital after being cut free from two mangled cars following serious crash
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

CRASH PANIC Three people rushed to hospital after being cut free from two mangled cars following serious crash







Next

THREE people have been rushed to hospital after being cut free from two mangled cars following a horror crash.

Emergency services rushed to Blackrod Bypass in Bolton, Greater Manchester at at around 4.20pm on Sunday.

Fire crews quickly arrived on the scene as they pulled out three people trapped in the wreckage.

They were treated at the scene by emergency medics before being raced to hospital for further treatment.





The circumstances around the shocking crash currently remain unclear.

Cops have closed the A6 in both directions as crews continue to clear the area of debris with no indication of when the road will reopen.

The fire services were at the scene for around 90 minutes before leaving.

A spokesperson for Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service (GMFRS) said: “At around 4:20pm this afternoon (Sunday, 27th September), firefighters were called to reports of a crash on Blackrod Bypass in Blackrod, Bolton.

“Two fire engines from Horwich and Hindley fire stations, along with the Enhanced Rescue from Leigh fire station, quickly arrived at the scene which involved a collision between two cars.

“Firefighters extricated three casualties who were trapped inside the vehicles.

“All casualties were treated by colleagues from the North West Ambulance Service and conveyed to hospital.

“Greater Manchester Police closed the road in both directions while crews worked to clear the roadway and make the area safe.



“Crews were in attendance for approximately 90 minutes.”

The Sun has contacted Greater Manchester Police and North West Ambulance Service for comment.

News.title: Starving Ukrainians left for dead in besieged city by Putin & forced to eat only weeds as ‘Russians shoot down supplies’
News.content:
VLAD'S BARBARITY Starving Ukrainians left for dead in besieged city by Putin & forced to eat only weeds as ‘Russians shoot down supplies’







Next

STARVING Ukrainian civilians have been left for dead with Vladimir Putin’s brutal forces accused of shooting down and stealing aid drops.

The Russian-occupied city of Oleshky was once brimming with life before it was captured by Putin’s ruthless troops with terrified residents now forced to survive on just weeds.



Home to 24,000 people in 2022, Oleshky now serves as a desperate hideout for an estimated 6,000 people – including 200 malnourished children.

Tetiana Hasanenko, Head of Oleshky City Military Administration, said food was last officially delivered on May 26.



With the constant fear of prowling Russian drones, bodies of the dead are left to be eaten by dogs in the streets.

The population is living under a “full blockade” by Russian forces, according to Ukraine‘s Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha.

Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to put pressure on Russia to allow humanitarian aid into the city.

He warned of a coming “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”.



Over the weekend, the Ukrainian military used large drones to carry out the first airdrop of emergency food, water and medical supplies in months.

The military governor’s office said four tonnes of food were dispatched to 100 locations.

But it was unclear how much made it to ground before it was intercepted by patrolling Russian troops.



It came after Moscow reportedly rejected a ceasefire to evacuate civilians again.

Ukraine’s successful drone campaign targeting Russian supply lines has resulted in Putin’s desperate troops stealing what little food Ukrainians have left.

In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they survived on one meal of soup made from courgette and weeds a day.

“We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer.

“Come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying.”



The city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka dam was attacked three years previously.

Earlier this week the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced “a critical situation” and “problems with supplies of food and medicine”.

But the regime said it was working to resolve the issues and instead blamed Kyiv.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ukrainian officials believe Russia is preventing evacuation of the remaining civilians to try and ward off a Ukrainian counterattack.

Hasanenko said: “The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields.”

News.title: Labour’s disastrous stampede down Benefits Street will never end – so does spendaholic Burnham have courage to stop it?
News.content:
Next

ON this day 50 years ago, Labour Chancellor Denis Healey was nursing a VIP gin and tonic at Heathrow ahead of a flight to an International Monetary Fund summit.

The global economy was under threat from a Middle East oil crisis and the IMF was on standby as a last-resort cashpoint to save poor countries from going broke.



As Healey waited for his plane, a shock collapse in the Pound turned Britain into one of those countries.

The Chancellor was forced to go cap-in-hand for a multi- billion dollar IMF loan to bail out his own Treasury crisis.



With a threatened currency, soaring inflation and sky-high oil prices — an echo of events today — a humiliated UK became The Story.

“Britain is bust,” trumpeted The Economist.



“Goodbye, Great Britain,” chorused the Wall Street Journal.

Half a century later, we face a mirror image of the crippling debt crisis that brought this once-great nation to its knees.

And we have another Chancellor Healey — ex-Defence supremo John Healey — whose task is to save us from going bust.

The September 28, 1976, fiasco coincided then as it does today with the annual Labour conference, then in Blackpool.



PM Jim Callaghan told sullen trade union bosses: “We used to think you could spend your way out of a recession.

“I tell you in all candour, that option no longer exists.”

Instead of seeing sense, the comrades stepped up their “wildcat” strikes, paralysing the NHS and state-run car, coal, steel and railway industries.

It was the beginning of the infamous Winter of Discontent.

Today the warning signs are flashing again from friends and critics of this spendaholic Labour regime.



Does Labour PM Andy Burnham have the courage this week to tell welfare-hooked socialist MPs that their bloated £330BILLION benefits bill is “no longer an option”?

Will he listen to Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden, who moans that every Cabinet big-spender asks: “Who can we tax to pay for benefits”?

Does the PM understand UK taxpayers cannot for ever carry the £3TRILLION burden of national debt?



Or pay the £110billion- a-year interest due to the bond market he blames?

Burnham cannot pretend he doesn’t know.

Nor can he resort to blaming the Tories — even Liz Truss.

His pal, Labour economic guru Lord Jim O’Neill, warns Britain’s debt-interest costs are “increasingly crazy”.

Labour fan and ex-Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane says: “The Achilles heel of this Government has been its unwillingness or inability to cut public spending.”



In 1979, as hospital admissions were vetted by striking health workers and rubbish piled up in the streets, Jim Callaghan asked: “Crisis? What crisis?”

It was his defining moment as PM.

Today the IMF itself fears a replay unless Labour slashes its monstrous debt and cuts handouts.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva says: “It’s impossible to stress strongly enough how critical it is to take the steps necessary.”

These warnings will fall on deaf ears in Liverpool this week.



Labour MPs have already toppled one prime minister over the two-child benefit cap.

They will not vote to slow the stampede down Benefits Street.

Chancellor Healey Mk2 might try in his October 28 budget to seem prudent.



As they say, you can put ­lipstick on a pig. But it’s still a pig.

Burnham himself shows no sign of grasping the lesson.

He thinks the Seventies were Britain’s Golden Age.

Yet the 1976 meltdown led to almost two decades of Tory rule, neutered trade union militants and Britain’s revival from “Sick Man of Europe” to world-beating economy.

The union militants have not gone away.



They have simply moved to the public sector — Whitehall, local government, the judiciary and the police.

They run our shroud-waving charities and multi-billion pound quangos.

Under the pro-Gaza flag, they now control the Home Office, Border Force and immigration tribunals.



Spiteful socialists despise everything that once made Britain great . . . free speech, a free Press and the rule of law.

They loathe the capitalist system which uses those freedoms to create prosperity instead of forcing us to rely on state handouts.

It is strange but true that Labour MPs love mass immigration and open borders.

So-called asylum seekers are mostly frauds but the issue divides society usefully.

It fuels public anger over the huge cost of migrant health care, and the unfairness of housing and education, at the expense of the citizens who foot the bill.



Ministers will do nothing this week to stop it.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

At some point, voters will decide enough is enough.

And that will be the end of Andy Burnham’s butterfly reign as Prime Minister.

News.title: Man, 44, charged with murder after beloved mum, 44, found dead in flat above city pub
News.content:
MURDER CHARGE Man, 44, charged with murder after beloved mum, 44, found dead in flat above city pub







Next

A MAN has been charged with murder after a beloved mum was found dead in a flat above a city pub.

Leanne Park, 44, was pronounced dead inside a flat over The Greyhound on Parkgate in Darlington, Durham at around 9.15pm on September 23.



Andrew Bell, of Darlington, has now been charged with murder and remanded in police custody, Durham Police said.

The 44-year-old will appear at Newton Aycliffe Magistrates’ Court on Monday.



A 27-year-old man arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender has been released on bail, the force added.

Leanne’s family paid a heartbreaking tribute to her as “the best mam, nana, daughter, and friend we could wish for” on Saturday.



They said: “She was loved by everyone and would do anything for anyone.

“She was the life and soul of the party and loved to dance.



“We love her so much and miss her more than words can describe. We are completely devastated. Her death has ripped the heart out of our family.

“We are grateful for all the kind messages and the support since her death.

“We ask that everyone remembers her for the kind-hearted woman she was.”

Emergency services had been called to the pub at around 9.15pm on Wednesday, September 23.

Tragically, despite the best efforts of medics, Leanne was pronounced dead at the scene.



Durham Police said a cordon will remain in place for some time.

The force said specialist crime scene investigators continue to work at the scene.

Leanne’s death has sparked an outpouring of tributes, including with bouquets of flowers which have been left outside the pub.

One tribute read: “Always in our hearts, taken too soon. Heaven has gained a beautiful angel”.

Another said: “RIP our beautiful Auntie. You are so loved and going to be a huge miss, love you always”.



Her colleagues at the Ventress Hall care home in Darlington previously said she would “do anything for anybody”.

In a Facebook post the home, said: “I can’t actually believe I am writing this, but it is with a heavy heart that I say we have lost our friend and work colleague, Leanne.

“Leanne was always so kind and would do anything for anybody, especially our residents.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The world is beyond cruel and you have been taken too soon. We love you much Leanne. Love all your Ventress Work Family. You will never be forgotten. Our condolences to all Leanne’s family.”

A spokesperson from Durham Police said: “Anyone with any information is asked to call Durham Constabulary on 101, quoting incident number 521 of September 23.”

News.title: Protesters disperse in Northern Ireland after ‘process’ announced to address Drumcree stand-off
News.content:
Protesters disperse in Northern Ireland after ‘process’ announced to address Drumcree stand-off

A tense stand-off erupted on Sunday after the Orange Order assembled to walk the Drumcree parade route in Northern Ireland, but they have now dispersed

View 3 Images The stand off in Northern Ireland on Sunday (Image: Getty Images)

Protesters who blockaded a road in Portadown to stop a contentious loyal order parade have mostly dispersed after being told by a community leader that a fresh process to address the dispute was being initiated.

‌



At the height of the blockade, thousands of people gathered on the Garvaghy Road throughout Sunday (September 27) to prevent the Orange Order parade from nearby Drumcree Church from passing along the route.

‌



The mass gathering, which was illegal under parading legislation in Northern Ireland, involved senior Sinn Féin politicians, including Stormont’s First Minister Michelle O’Neill.

‌



It was organised after Orangemen managed to overturn a long ban on them parading down the predominantly nationalist road. The blockade continued through the day and late into the night, as Orangemen assembled at Drumcree Church around a mile from the road waited to commence their parade.

Around midnight, Breandán Mac Cionnaith from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, told protesters they had secured a “victory”. He said he would meet Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant and Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher on Monday morning for talks on the Drumcree parade.

View 3 Images It was the first time in 30 years the parade was allowed (Image: Peter Morrison/PA Wire)

‌



Mr Mac Cionnaith said he had received “commitments” that the parade would not be proceeding down the Garvaghy Road overnight. He asked for 20 to 30 volunteers to remain on the road to ensure those commitments were not broken.

“We’ve stopped them once. The process now is to ensure we stop them permanently,” he said. On his planned meetings on Monday, he added: “That process starts tomorrow when we go in and meet the chief constable and we’ll meet the secretary of state.

‌



“We’re not going in to do deals with them, or to take half measures with them. We said the other day, and we said yesterday, and the day before – we’re not going back, we’re not turning the clock back. We’re putting the clock forward.”

Ms O’Neill also said the Garvaghy Road community had won a “victory”.

“This community do not want this, they do not want this march,” she told reporters before leaving the area shortly after midnight on Monday morning. “And tonight, I believe, is another victory for this community in standing steadfast for the right to live free from sectarian harassment and intimidation.”

‌



View 3 Images (Image: Peter Morrison/PA Wire)

Earlier, the Northern Ireland Secretary appealed for calm and urged political and community leaders to reach for compromise to resolve the deepening dispute over the Drumcree parade. He held talks with political leaders on Sunday night, but no resolution emerged.

Article continues below

The presence of Ms O’Neill and other senior Sinn Féin figures at the blockade prompted accusations of law breaking from unionists.

Under parading legislation in the region, protests against parades must be notified and approved by the Parades Commission adjudication body. The blockade on the Garvaghy Road was an unnotified gathering.

News.title: Green shoots show new beginnings at site Sycamore Gap tree - three years after it was illegally felled
News.content:
Green shoots show new beginnings at site Sycamore Gap tree - three years after it was illegally felled

The National Trust has showcased new growth at the UNESCO heritage site on the three year anniversary of the shock felling in 2023 by Daniel Graham and Adam Carruthers

View 4 Images The National Trust has shared growth at the Sycamore Gap site (Image: Annapurna Mellor/National Trust Images/PA Wire)

Three years since the tree at Sycamore Gap was felled, the National Trust has shared images of a thick ring of new shoots around its stump.

‌



New growth at the site at Hadrian's Wall in Northumberland stands two to three feet tall and show the benefit of keeping the area fenced off, the conservation charity has said. The tree was illegally felled on September 28 2023 by Daniel Graham and Adam Carruthers who travelled from their homes in Cumbria to cut down the much-loved sycamore during a storm.

‌



The destruction caused a national outcry and international headlines when the pair were jailed for criminal damage to the tree and the ancient wall.

‌



Robin Hood hiding place Major Oak declared dead after hordes of 'loving' visitors smothered tree READ MORE :

View 4 Images The National Trust has said the new shoots are 'really encouraging' (Image: Annapurna Mellor/National Trust Images/PA Wire)

In a bid to see if the stump would recover, the remains of the tree were fenced off. Andrew Poad, general manager for the National Trust at Hadrian's Wall said: "These flourishing shoots are really encouraging and show that the special measures we've taken, including reducing soil compaction around the roots and limiting human disturbance, are paying off.

"We're grateful to all the visitors who, through the care they are taking, are supporting our efforts to protect the tree and give it the best possible chance to thrive.

‌



"We're monitoring the tree closely and, over time, our rangers will manage it depending on how it develops. But for now, we're filled with hope by the way nature is taking its course." Saplings have been grown from seeds found at the site and arts projects have been launched to show the importance of nature in the modern world.

View 4 Images The original tree was felled by Daniel Graham and Adam Carruthers in 2023 (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

In July last year two men who chopped down the "irreplaceable" Sycamore Gap tree in an act of "sheer bravado" were each jailed for four years and three months.

‌



Daniel Michael Graham 39, and Adam Carruthers, 32, both from Cumbria, were convicted of criminal damage after filming themselves using a chainsaw to illegally fell the landmark tree by Hadrian's Wall in Northumberland. Sentencing them at Newcastle Crown Court, Mrs Justice Lambert rejected a claim of "drunken stupidity" and said, while a full motive was not clear, felling the tree and the ensuing outrage gave the men "some sort of thrill".

The National Trust, which owned the more than 100-year-old tree, said the landmark could "never be replaced". The pair, whose friendship imploded in the aftermath as the public revulsion became clear to them, drove to the site under the cover of darkness in the early hours of 28 September 2023.

View 4 Images The National Trust said the original Sycamore Gap tree can 'never be replaced' (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



They used the winds of Storm Agnes to help them topple the tree on to the Unesco World Heritage Site wall, the court heard.

The value of the tree was disputed with prosecutors saying it was worth about £458,000 and Graham's team claiming it to be about £150,000, but Mrs Justice Lambert said the exact financial price did not really matter. The judge said the tree was a landmark of Northumberland and "symbol of the untamed beauty" of the landscape around Hadrian's Wall.

It was a place of "peace and tranquillity" which people returned to year after year, the judge said, adding it held great personal significance to many. She said Carruthers used spray paint and a chainsaw to mark and then cut a wedge out of the tree, while Graham filmed it on his mobile phone.

Article continues below

Mrs Justice Lambert said a full motive was not clear, but she was "confident a major factor was sheer bravado," adding the action of felling the tree and the outrage it caused gave the men "some sort of thrill". The men then "revelled in [their] notoriety" in the aftermath, the judge said.

News.title: John Healey sets sights on jobless youngsters with 'generation hope' pledge
News.content:
John Healey sets sights on jobless youngsters with 'generation hope' pledge

EXCLUSIVE: John Healey is expected to say that 'the best thing we can offer a young person isn't a benefit. It's a first job with training and a wage' in his conference speech

View 2 Images Chancellor John Healey will give a major speech to Labour conference on Monday (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

John Healey will set his sights on getting young people back into the work with a pledge to transform them from "generation jeopardy to generation hope.”

‌



In a speech to Labour’s annual conference today, the Chancellor is expected to weigh in on the crisis facing nearly a million youngsters out of employment, education and training (Neets). The latest figures, published in August, estimated there were 981,000 Neets in April to June.

‌



Mr Healey is expected to say: “The best thing we can offer a young person isn't a benefit. It's a first job. With training. And a wage.

‌



"Our determination to help matched by their determination to hope. Because conference, I believe this generation has the potential to be a great generation. From Generation Jeopardy to Generation Hope.”

Andy Burnham vows to fight next election with NHS-style social care plan READ MORE :

View 2 Images John Healey said he wants to get young people back into work (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

Mr Healey will use the high-stakes moment to introduce himself to the country after taking over one of the toughest jobs in Government. He is facing a battle to balance the books in next month's Budget amid a gloomy picture as the Iran war continues to wreak havoc on the global economy.

‌



But the Chancellor is understood to be deeply concerned about youth unemployment, and is closely involved in a hotly anticipated review by former Health Secretary Alan Milburn into the challenges facing jobless youngsters.

A source close to the Chancellor told the Mirror: "John’s politics were forged in the industrial heartlands of South Yorkshire, where youth unemployment skyrocketed in the 80s and the 2010s when the Tories deindustrialised Britain.

"He was part of the last Labour Government who brought hope back to young people and now he’s determined to do the same again."

‌



Mr Healey is also preparing to bring back a £15 million-a-year fund to help workers gain new skills. Staff in union-led workplaces will be given training to help them build essential skills and adapt to changes like AI.

The Mirror understands he plans to restore the Union Learning Fund from next year, which will allow workers to avoid fees for courses ranging from essential English, maths and digital skills, to training for jobs in growing industries, such as advanced manufacturing.

The previous fund, established in 1998 but closed by the Tories in 2021, supported around 200,000 employees each year.

‌



In his speech to Labour faithful, Mr Healey, a former Defence Secretary, is also expected to pledge “new age of industrialisation” with a multi-billion pound investment in British shipyards. Three new floating docks for the Royal Navy's Scottish submarine base at Faslane will be built in Britain through a UK-only competition for contracts.

Known as Programme Euston, plans for the new docks were first set out in 2023 and are expected to upgrade HM Naval Base Clyde's facilities by the 2030s for the next generation of nuclear submarines.

Mr Healey will argue that the UK cannot return to the coal mines of the past as he sets out his vision for firing up British industry. He will say: “Our coal mines are not coming back. But this is how Britain’s industrial past is being remade now for the modern world. This is the new age of industrialisation. A new confidence in Britain.”

‌



It follows a £115m commitment by Louise Haigh, the First Secretary of State, to commission a new marine research vessel, which will also come into service in the early 2030s.

On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told conference that getting people into work and off benefits was "the cause of our times". He said: "We don’t just owe people an income. We owe them a future too and that is what the system should be built around."

Mr McFadden laid down the gauntlet to Labour MPs, who rebelled on Keir Starmer's botched welfare reforms, saying: "I want us to change the question that the system asks from “what benefit are you entitled to”, to “how do we help you live the fullest life?”

Article continues below

He confirmed plans, first reported by the Mirror, that firms taking on young disabled people under a new government scheme will see 100% of wage costs covered for the first six months.

Meanwhile, Andy Burnham met Norwegian counterpart Jonas Store for talks on European security while in Liverpool. The Prime Minister said the two countries had a “warm friendship that goes back for so many years”, but now faced “new challenges” together on defence and security.

The football-mad PM also joked that Norway’s close ties with the UK included Manchester City’s star striker Erling Haaland.

News.title: UK weather: Brits face flood warnings as coastal gales and downpours loom — see full list
News.content:
UK weather: Brits face flood warnings as coastal gales and downpours loom — see full list

The Met Office forecasts "coastal gales and heavy, blustery rain" in the coming days, especially for regions in the west, and so authorities have told Brits to prepare for floods

View 3 Images Take care on the roads this week as some may suffer flooding (Image: PA)

This weather map shows several points along the British coastline at risk of flooding — as downpours loom.

‌



Bands of low pressure are to sweep in from the Atlantic in the coming days and it is expected to be turn windy, particularly along the west coast of the UK. This will lead to unsettled weather, including heavy bursts of rain which will make parts of the UK vulnerable to floods.

‌



These areas include sections of the North Sea coast, such as between Easington and Kilnsea in Humberside and between Staithes and Whitby in North Yorkshire. The Environment Agency says the concern for the section in Humberside, near Hull, is greatest because high tides, strong winds and large waves will combine from Monday morning.

‌



Caravan parks there, and elsewhere, are especially vulnerable. Authorities have warned people in areas below at risk of flooding to avoid walking, cycling or driving through floodwater.

Met Office weather maps turn blue as Brits brace for 830-mile downpours on Sunday READ MORE :

View 3 Images Many of the flood alerts are along the east coast of England (Image: GOV.UK)

Sunday has been particularly wet across parts of western Scotland, Cumbria, Lancashire and north Wales. These areas could be vulnerable to flooding if further rain, next due in all these parts on Tuesday night and into Wednesday, hit saturated ground.

‌



But the Environment Agency's main areas of concern at the moment centre on the east coast, though there is worry in Somerset and West Sussex. There are two separate alerts for parts of Norfolk, including along the coast between East Cley and Kelling Hard, including Salthouse.

High tides today may lead to flooding at Porlock Weir in Somerset, and flooding is possible at Shoreham Harbour in West Sussex. In relation to the latter, the Environment Agency says: "We are closely monitoring the situation. Avoid beaches and coastal promenades, which may be flooded."

View 3 Images The forecast this week is wet and windy (Image: James Linsell Clark / SWNS)

‌



While Tuesday will be balmy, the next band of significant rain is expected then. The Met Office says: "Turning warm and windy on Tuesday with coastal gales and heavy, blustery rain in the west."

These showers will push west during the course of the day, and will be heaviest across Northern Ireland and western Scotland. There are no flood alerts or warnings currently in force in Scotland, though, the Scottish Environmental Protection Agency says.

And authorities in Northern Ireland and Wales are, as yet, not concerned enough to issue any flood alerts. But the new band of rain could become heavy on Wednesday, particularly across south Wales.

‌



Below the Mirror has listed all the warnings and alerts the Environment Agency currently has in place. Warnings are more severe than alerts, the authority says.

News.title: Mum of man who fell to his death at Pete Doherty party calls on police to get to the truth
News.content:
Mum of man who fell to his death at Pete Doherty party calls on police to get to the truth

Mark Blanco, 30, died during a drug-fuelled gathering with the Babyshambles star Pete Doherty in December 2006 and the case has never been resolved despite his mum Sheila's relentless fight for justice

View 4 Images Sheila Blanco outside Scotland Yard following her meeting last week (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

The mother of a man who fell to his death at a party with Pete Doherty has implored police to get justice for her son as they review the case twenty years on.

‌



Mark Blanco, 30, died during a drug-fuelled gathering with the Babyshambles star in December 2006 and the case has never been resolved despite his mum Sheila's relentless fight for justice.

‌



She had previously called for an outside force to be brought in to examine the Metropolitan Police's handling of the investigation but none could be found. Sheila had a meeting with two senior officers to discuss her Victims' Right to Review last week.

‌



View 4 Images Mark and Sheila Blanco (Image: Channel 4)

Speaking outside Scotland Yard she told the Daily Mirror: "In this year, the twentieth anniversary of Mark's tragic death, I implore the police to consult all the necessary experts and use the means available to them to secure justice for Mark.

"Mark was generous in life and in death, saving the lives of three men by organ donation. I have been trying for the last 20 years to get the police to classify my son's death as murder."

‌



Sheila's lawyer Mike Schwarz, of Hodge Jones & Allen, said: "We hope that the police will review the statements and accounts given by suspects and reinterview them where necessary and decide whether that provides sufficient further evidence to reopen the case and if appropriate charge those responsible. The police could, and should, ask everyone at the flat what took place."

It comes three years after a Channel 4 documentary Pete Doherty, Who Killed My Son? suggested Mark had been murdered after an FBI expert claimed he was thrown to his death.

View 4 Images Sheila with her lawyer Mike Schwarz (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

‌



A 2007 inquest heard Mark had been kicked out of the London "crack den" during a row with Doherty, his literary agent Paul Roundhill and minder Johnny "Headlock" Jeannevol.

Mark returned two minutes later before somehow falling to his death from a balcony.

Police investigated and suggested the Cambridge graduate's death was suicide, which a coroner rejected and called for them to reopen the case.

‌



The inquest heard that Jeannevol had confessed to police that he pushed Mark off but retracted it, saying he was high on cocaine when he made it, and was released without charge.

Doherty has previously denied any knowledge of how Mark died but admitted running away from the scene to avoid the police because he had drugs.

View 4 Images Pete Doherty has denied any knowledge of how Mark died (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



FBI instructor Grant Fredericks told the Channel 4 film that his belief after analysis of CCTV was that Mark was "thrown over the balcony".

Sheila said: "There was a confession to his murder and the police seemed to look the other way. Throughout the 20 years, there has been nothing but apathy by the police and above all, I would like to know why.

"It's been an ongoing battle. We know that Mark was beaten up. We know that he was punched in the face several times by Roundhill and we know that his clothes were torn. I think he was thrown over, maybe conscious, maybe not conscious. The first investigation underpins the whole thing and it was laughable."

‌



Roundhill told the inquest that he punched Mark repeatedly on the evening he died.

In October 2023, a month after the Channel Four documentary aired, Doherty said that he needed to get in touch with Sheila because “she believes that I killed her son” and the story is “just not going to go away”. He admitted there was "a bit of friction between us", adding: "We all had an altercation with Marco Blanco. There was pushing and shoving. The next thing he's on the floor and his skull's cracked open."

Asked if she was confident the police would get to the bottom of the case, Sheila said: "They were understanding, we will wait and see."

‌



A Met Police spokesperson said: “Following the conclusion of the latest police investigation into Mark’s death, his family requested a victim’s right to review process.

“Detectives will now review aspects of the investigations previously carried out to ensure certain lines of enquiry have been explored to their full conclusion.

“We hope this will help provide Mark’s family with answers to their concerns.

Article continues below

“Our thoughts remain with them, and they will be kept fully updated on our progress.”

News.title: RAF Fairford 'terror plot': Woman who called 999 warned neighbours on WhatsApp over 'men in balaclavas'
News.content:
RAF Fairford 'terror plot': Woman who called 999 warned neighbours on WhatsApp over 'men in balaclavas'

The five suspects were arrested after police foiled a suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire — counter-terrorism officers are investigating possible links to Iran

View 8 Images A dramatic picture shows five shirtless men being held at gunpoint by armed police

A hero farmer warned her neighbours to lock their doors — after witnessing men "hanging around" on a country lane — moments before five suspects were arrested amid a suspected terror plot.

Police foiled the feared plot on an RAF base used by the United States air force today after the farmer called 999 with the information. She also told neighbours to keep doors and windows closed.

Counter-terrorism police are investigating whether they have links to Iran. They were caught after a hero member of public called 999 at 12.45am when they spotted three suspicious vans near RAF Fairford. But President Donald Trump has claimed: “They were looking to do big damage. We had them under view for a long time, and we got them.”

Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the incident as “deeply concerning”. There were dramatic pictures of five shirtless men being held near the Gloucestershire base.

Aerial footage also showed a bomb disposal robot circling three white vans, two of which had open rear doors. Large black barrels were seen scattered outside.

Have you been affected by this story? Contact webnews@mirror.co.uk

View 8 Images Armed police man a roadblock while posted at an entrance to RAF Fairford (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

RAF base on alert amid Iran tensions

The base is at the centre of protests over the government’s decision to allow the US to use it to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards issued a chilling warning to Britain back in July not to allow US bombers to fly from the base.

It is understood all other US bases have been put on Delta alert, the highest threat level that can be issued by Washington's Department of Defence.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said they were in the "early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody".

She said Counter Terrorism officers are "working closely" with partners to "understand the circumstances of the incident.” She added: "We continue to work with Gloucestershire Police to keep the community safe as we work to gather evidence from the scene."

View 8 Images Emergency services on the scene around RAF Fairford (Image: SWNS)

Residents evacuated as police probe ‘suspicious vans’

She said a 400m cordon was in place around the vehicles while the Army's Explosive Ordinance Disposal unit carried out examinations, and 85 households were evacuated. Those residents are unable to return to their homes tonight.

Cops even ferried family pets left behind during the evacuation to their owners in a nearby leisure centre.

Gloucestershire Police Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone said armed officers arrested five men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act.

Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in the nearby village of Whelford for 30 years, said a resident had reported three "suspicious vans" in the village.

He said: “Evidently, they phoned the airbase police, who didn't answer the phone. It just rang out so she dialled 999."

He said he was evacuated at around 7am, adding: "The police were then banging on the door, so I went downstairs in my dressing gown.

"There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there's been a major incident, said he couldn't elaborate."

View 8 Images Cops declared a major incident early on Sunday (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Hero neighbour’s 999 call sparks arrests

The woman who made the call saw the men “hanging around“ two vans that appeared to belong to them and phoned 999 to report what she had seen.

The villager, driving home from a party in the early hours, reportedly spotted abandoned vehicles on a quiet country road. She said she quickly drove away before calling police and warning a local WhatsApp group to lock their doors.

The five men were arrested less than 25 minutes later, with footage showing them handcuffed in the road. The woman said she felt “quite lucky”, given what might have happened had the men tried to stop her.

‌



One other local, who asked not to be named, said: “Thank goodness this woman in the village saw what she saw and had the wit to call the cops out quickly. She may well have saved a lot of lives.

“She saw that these guys hanging around the two vans and said they were acting suspiciously and did not appear to be locals.”

The man who took the photos said: “I couldn't tell what was being shouted but as I got nearer the window, I could see the road was being lit up by blue flashing lights from police vehicles.

‌



View 8 Images President Donald Trump speaks with reporters upon arriving at Chicago O'Hare International Airport (Image: AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

“On one side of the road, officers had five men lined up. They all had their shirts removed They were instructed to sit down. They were patted down by the officers and then had their shoes and socks removed.

“I think they must have been there for about half an hour. The suspects were then told to get up and were walked round the corner.

‌



“I lost sight of them after that but I presumed they were put in police vans and led away. This all happened just outside the perimeter of RAF Fairford.

“The police are investigating three work vans parked a few hundred yards from my house. We've not been told much, we were just asked to evacuate our homes early this morning.”

Meanwhile another woman living on the base's perimeter described an apparent increase in military security in recent days.

‌



View 8 Images A bomb disposal robot (top right) has been used at the scene of the incident in the village of Whelford (Image: Sky News)

Iran warning resurfaces

She said: ”In the prior few weeks they have put heavy, very heavy, vehicles across all gates."

She described them as "very big tractors and things like that" parked behind crash-gates into the base, adding: "Obviously they're taking security seriously."

‌



The Iranian Revolutionary Guards issued a warning to the UK against allowing the US to operate bombers from RAF Fairford.

In a statement shared by Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency, they said: “Any base that is used to invade Iran's territory is our legitimate goal.” adding that the US had "switched to using B1 planes flying from Fairford Air Base, England."

View 8 Images A military vehicle at RAF Fairford (Image: Ben Birchall/PA Wire)

‌



Burnham said: “I know today's incident near RAF Fairford will be deeply concerning for local residents and for many people following developments across the country.

"My thanks go to Gloucestershire Police, Counter Terrorism Policing, our Armed Forces and all those working to keep the public safe.

"The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts." Donald Trump praised the arrests of the five men as "fantastic".

‌



The US president added that the men were “looking to do big damage” and “we had them under view for a long time”.

View 8 Images Armed police man a roadblock while posted at an entrance to the base (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Trump hails arrests

Trump praised the UK police response as “amazing” and said that Washington and London had been working together.

‌



He said: “It was fantastic. Working with Britain, it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They, they were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great. It may have been Scotland Yard, I don’t know. We worked with a lot of them.

“We had them under view for a long time, and we got them. Thank you.” The incident will raise fresh questions over the difficult ecisions to be made on defence by Burnham and his Chancellor John Healey at the Budget next month.

Burnham's predecessor Keir Starmer initially refused to permit US bombers to use British bases after the outbreak of the Iran war in February, drawing the fury of President Donald Trump, who said the former Labour leader was 'no Winston Churchill'.

But he later relented and gave the US permission in March for the 'specific and limited defensive purpose' of destroying Iranian missiles 'at source'.

Anyone arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000 can be detained for up to 14 days without charge. That's different to the usual 24-hour limit for standard arrests without an extension application.

The five men were arrested under the act - meaning any hypothetical charge could come as late as 11 October.

News.title: Lisa Nandy issues warning over far-right agitators - 'something has changed'
News.content:
Lisa Nandy issues warning over far-right agitators - 'something has changed'

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told a fringe event at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool that otherwise decent people have been joining far-right violence as she called on Britons to disagree respectfully

View 3 Images Lisa Nandy has warned about the dangers of far-right agitators preying on otherwise decent people (Image: Andrew Stenning/Daily Mirror)

Lisa Nandy has warned "something has changed" as she described otherwise decent people being preyed on by the far-right.

‌



The Culture Secretary told an event hosted by The Mirror at the Labour Party Conference that while her Wigan constituency has fought off fascists in the past, people from there have become vulnerable to racist agitators.

‌



She joined calls for people to disagree in a respectful way, backing this newspaper’s Britain Talks campaign. Brendan Cox, whose Labour MP wife Jo was murdered by a far-right terrorist in 2016, said Britons should be "less relaxed" about the way hatred is taking hold in our streets.

‌



Cabinet member Ms Nandy said that while she believes most people are decent, far-right influences have spiralled in the last 15 years. The frontbencher told delegates that Andy Burnham is alive to the dangers, but said good people must "fight for the country we believe in".

Blow for Nigel Farage as poll finds more than half of voters dislike him READ MORE :

View 3 Images Tracy Brabin described the online hatred she faces (Image: Andrew Stenning/Daily Mirror)

She said: "We are a working-class town where for over 100 years we've always been targeted by the far right.

‌



"It's a very white working-class town predominantly, where people are warm and welcoming, and where working-class, white, British people have fought off the fascists over and over again every time they've tried to get a foothold in our town.

"So I know that people are decent, because I see it every day with my own eyes. But something has changed, because a couple of years ago when we had the riots in Southport, a lot of my constituents were down there in Southport out on the streets.

"People who 10 years ago, 15 years ago, when I first became the MP, would never have gone near a demonstration like that. And it worries me, because they're not the same as the racist thugs who've always come to towns like mine and try to cause trouble. They're people who don't see themselves heard in our national story.

‌



"They don't see their contribution is recognised or valued.” She described this year's conference as "probably the most important of modern times", telling delegates: "Thank goodness for all of these people on the panel who've been fighting for that country that we believe in, the better country that we know that we are, who've been fighting for it to be heard.

View 3 Images Brendan Cox said people should be 'less relaxed' about the state of the country (Image: Andrew Stenning/Daily Mirror)

"It's the country that George Orwell once said lies beneath the surface and must be heard, because we are a better country than the one we've been led to believe in, and we're a better country than the one that's been on display."

‌



Mr Cox told the fringe event: "There's something fundamentally gone wrong in our country when we have blackshirt paramilitaries on our streets in balaclavas, when Jewish people are too scared to identify themselves as Jewish in case they are attacked in the street, when our Muslim friends face not just hostility from extremists, but increasingly from mainstream politicians who even question whether they should be able to pray. When you are responding to awful events like the killings in Southport and the response to that is to try to burn asylum seekers and refugees to death in a hotel.

"When you're seeing on the streets of Belfast people going street to street and burning down the houses of those people with a different skin colour.

"I think you do take a moment and think that is the country that we now live in, I think it does require a more fundamental response. I think we need to be less sanguine, less relaxed."

Article continues below

And Mayor of West Yorkshire Tracy Brabin, a former Coronation Street actress, said she is inundated by online hatred. But in a message of defiance, she told the event: "If we are afraid, they win.

"We have to find a way to mock and diminish. I know that the majority of the hate I get online is bots. The rest of it is losers in their Y-fronts in their mum's back bedroom eating Pot Noodles. You know, they would never say that to my face."

News.title: Five arrested as counter-terror police investigate major incident near RAF Fairford
News.content:
Five men have been arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act and explosive offences after three "suspicious vehicles" were reported travelling towards an RAF base, police have said.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire were evacuated following the report at about 00:45 BST on Sunday.

An Army explosive ordnance disposal team has been examining vehicles near the base, which is used by the United States Air Force (USAF), as counter-terror police lead the investigation.

Residents evacuated from the nearby village of Whelford have been told they will not be able to return home overnight, but officials say they believe the incident is contained.

Aerial pictures showed a remote-controlled robot approaching stationary white vans in a wooded area, though its use has not been confirmed by police.

A 400m cordon has been placed around the area, where a hazardous area response team was deployed as part of a major emergency service response.

News.title: Protesters disperse after blocking contentious Orange Order parade
News.content:
Hundreds of protesters blocked a road in Portadown, County Armagh on Sunday, preventing a contentious Orange Order march from taking place.

The Drumcree parade, which in the 1990s sparked some of the most serious disorder in Northern Ireland's history, was due to go ahead for the first time in 30 years following a series of late legal challenges.

Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill joined the protesters, while members of the Orange Order and Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) politicians gathered about a mile away, waiting for the road to clear.

Most of the protesters have since dispersed, but some members of the Order remain and still intend to try and march.

Since 1998, the Order had been banned from completing its Drumcree march - and until this year had been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route by the Parades Commission, which was set up to adjudicate disputes.

The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation, while the area where it wants to walk - specifically along the Garvaghy Road - is largely Catholic and predominantly inhabited by pro-Irish nationalists.

Many Catholics see the marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, Catholic or nationalist areas.

News.title: Watch: BBC reports from the front-line of an escalating war in Yemen
News.content:
In rare access to Yemen's conflict zone, the BBC has travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where the Houthi control ends and no man's land begins.

Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war.

From the front-line a drone is heard above, which a soldier accompanying the crew in south-western Yemen said is usually followed by an attack.

Within about 10 minutes, after the crew had driven away, the loud thuds of strikes followed, senior international investigations correspondent Nawal Al-Maghafi reports.

News.title: My hometown shows that high streets have to change or die
News.content:
The empty building that used to be the home of Marks & Spencer in Aberdeen is one of the first things you see when you arrive off the train and come into the city centre. The sign has gone, though the shape of the lettering can still be made out; the windows are blacked out and the doors boarded up.

This is my hometown. As a teenager, I spent hours on Union Street, its main thoroughfare, nicknamed the Granite Mile after the local silver-grey stone. It was the place to try on all the latest fashions from the likes of Clockhouse and Chelsea Girl.

The street used to be packed with shoppers from across the north-east of Scotland.

Now, it's pockmarked with empty shops.

"I come to Union Street to take a bus somewhere else... there's nothing to shop for nowâ¦ it's horrendous," complains Marie Sim, a lifelong Aberdeen resident.

It's a similar story across the country: High Streets, once bursting with shops, hit first by the rise of out-of-town retail centres and then by online commerce.

But Aberdeen is in the thick of an ambitious turnaround plan. The port city has essentially declared war on its empty shop problem, taking an unusually hands-on approach to filling vacant units and bringing long-neglected upper floors of buildings into use.

News.title: Republic of Ireland 'raised awareness worldwide' in Israel game
News.content:
The Republic of Ireland players were jeered by the small number of Israel fans in attendance when they emerged for their pre-game warm-up.

While the FAI confirmed no tickets would be sold to Republic of Ireland supporters, a handful of fans were spotted inside the stadium.

Hallgrimsson confirmed Bazunu would be included in the squad for Thursday's game against Austria in Dublin, but not for the second match against Israel.

"I think he is very happy that we have won the game," said Hallgrimsson.

"Nobody was questioning his decision. It was only the timing that was difficult for us to kind of react to it, but none of us were asking him not to take his stand and now he's flying back with us on the plane."

When asked if player's opinions regarding the fixture were taken into account when selecting his team for Sunday's game, Hallgrimsson said: "Absolutely not.

"This team selection was about who we thought could make the best performance for Ireland."

During a dramatic day on Saturday, doubts emerged over whether the game would take place after the Republic of Ireland's pre-match news conference was postponed because of the squad meeting.

When the news conference commenced at 14:30 BST on Saturday - more than five hours later than planned - Courell said a players' vote on whether to play the game passed by a "significant majority".

Courell added that the Republic of Ireland would not engage in pre-match formalities such as handshakes.

In 2024, the Ireland women's basketball team chose not to shake hands with Israel players or stand on court for the anthems before a EuroBasket qualifier in Riga, but the teams did exchange handshakes when they met again last year.

The Republic of Ireland have faced calls to boycott the matches since the Nations League draw in February.

Last November, the FAI approved a motion calling for Uefa to suspend Israel from Uefa competitions.

In May, the team's friendly against Qatar was interrupted after fans threw tennis balls featuring the Palestinian flag on to the pitch.

In June, the FAI confirmed their home fixture would be played behind closed doors in Backa Topola instead of Dublin's Aviva Stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil".

At an extraordinary general meeting in July, delegates backed an FAI motion to proceed with the games amid concerns that boycotting the fixtures would cause "significant and lasting harm" for the association.

Calls for the Republic of Ireland to boycott the games have intensified in recent weeks. Earlier this week, more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by Irish Sport for Palestine group urging the team not to play.

Courell also said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the Republic of Ireland and Israel to be kept apart in future competition draws.

Tensions between the teams were raised this week when the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity" after the coach said, "we're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide".

Speaking on Saturday, Hallgrimsson said it was "a wrong word for me to use", while Israel FA head of communications Shlomi Barzel said he would not apologise for his association's response but said he would "take back the word stupidity".

The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

Israel has repeatedly denied that it has committed genocide, as well as war crimes and crimes against humanity. It says its military operations in Gaza have been conducted in self-defence and in accordance with international law.

News.title: Healey to promise 'new age of industrialisation' for UK in conference speech
News.content:
John Healey will promise "a new age of industrialisation" for the UK, when he delivers his first Labour conference speech as chancellor on Monday.

Healey will tell delegates "our coal mines are not coming back", but that Labour will remake Britain's industrial past "for the modern age" by backing advanced manufacturing.

He will also announce plans to boost Britain's shipbuilding industry, with new orders for Royal Navy floating docks and a maritime research vessel.

With just a month to go until his first Budget, the chancellor is under pressure to cut spending or raise taxes to tackle the ballooning cost of government borrowing.

But he is not expected to reveal any details about his Budget plans in his speech at Labour's annual conference in Liverpool.

Instead, he will attempt to set out a positive vision for the future of British industry, based around what he will call a "new confidence in Britain".

The former defence secretary will announce that three new floating docks at HM Royal Naval Base Clyde, at Faslane, will be built in the UK, rather than put out to international tender.

Plans for the new docks were first set out in 2023 and are expected to upgrade Faslane's facilities for the next generation of British submarines.

The docks form part of a wider Â£15bn upgrade programme for the Royal Navy's shipyards and are expected to come into service in the early 2030s.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh said in a speech on Sunday that the government would also commission a new marine research vessel as part of plans for a "new era of reindustrialisation".

The chancellor is expected to announce Â£115m in funding for the ship, which is also set to come into service in the early 2030s.

Ahead of his speech, Healey said: "By backing British shipyards, we are not only boosting national security but also securing resilience in the industries that will drive growth today while building the capabilities the country needs for the future."

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the plans were "reheated announcements" with "no clarity on where the money is coming from".

He added: "Labour are running scared of making the tough choices needed to pay for Britain's defence.

"All they can offer is reannounced docks and more hot air from Healey. Only the Conservatives will cut the welfare bill to fund defence."

Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, national secretary of the GMB union, which has campaigned for the move, said it would be a "massive boost" for the UK's shipbuilding sector.

"For too long juicy contracts have been sent to overseas - often subsidised - yards.

"This policy could reinvigorate UK yards and the communities that depend on them," he added.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who is due to deliver his big conference speech on Tuesday - has previously spoken about his ambition to "reindustrialise" Britain, including in talks last week with US President Donald Trump.

But in a survey to be published on Monday, the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) will highlight falling economic activity across key sectors such as retail and services in the three months to September, with manufacturing declining more moderately.

CBI deputy chief economist Alpesh Paleja said rising energy and employment costs combined with weak demand were continuing to put pressure on profit margins.

He added: "Uncertainty ahead of next month's Budget is also holding back activity in some sectors.

"Against the backdrop of renewed fiscal pressures, the Budget must draw a clear red line under any more rises in the cost of hiring, investing and doing business."

The chancellor is also under pressure from some of Labour's trade union backers to do more to tackle the cost of living.

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, has called on Healey to "do something for workers and the working class" in his Budget.

She urged him to unfreeze income tax thresholds "to put money back into people's pockets" and take further action on energy bills.

In his conference speech, Healey will also announce plans to bring back a training scheme run by trade unions, to help workers in England gain new skills and adapt as technology, including AI, changes the workplace.

The Union Learning Fund will get Â£15m in taxpayers' money, taken from existing government budgets.

Employees do not need to be union members to benefit, with support options ranging from essential English, maths and digital skills, to training for jobs in growing industries, such as advanced manufacturing.

News.title: More questions than answers after major incident near RAF Fairford
News.content:
But some eyes, too, have turned to Moscow.

Danish intelligence warned last week Russia could in the coming months launch a limited military attack on a Nato country.

Germany has already formally accused Russia of using a drone carrying explosives in an attempted attack on Leipzig in August.

Over the summer, the Russian embassy in London warned the UK against allowing Ukraine to use British drones deep inside Russian territory: "The deeper [the UK's] involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv's terrorist machinery, the higher price it will pay."

That, too, was seen as a direct threat.

There are also possibilities of some kind of Islamist attack, or even an incident of direct action by a group opposed to both the US-Israeli war on Iran or the use of UK bases to launch strikes.

One central question is whether the authorities were prepared for such an attack.

The US handles security within the base; the UK is responsible all threats outside the perimeter. What did the authorities know?

President Trump said the suspects had been under investigation "for a long time".

But there are also suggestions the incident was foiled only because a passing driver reported strange vans to the police.

At the time of the explicit Iranian threat against the UK, a spokesman for the Ministry of Defence said: "Our armed forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it's on our soil or from abroad. The UK stands ready 24/7 to defend itself."

So for now, there remain more questions that facts.

Was a hostile foreign state involved, or were proxies acting on its behalf? What was intended and what was the potential risk to local people?

One thing is clear: the threat from conflicts involving the UK will not always stay overseas.

News.title: Late September warmth before wind and rain returns this week
News.content:
A vast area of low pressure in the Atlantic is set to draw warm south to south-easterly winds across the UK early this week, but for some rain will not be far behind.

Tuesday looks as if it will be the warmest day and after that temperatures will generally return closer to the September average.

Much of the UK can also expect a spell of wetter and windier weather from the approaching depression, with the most unsettled conditions likely to affect Scotland, Northern Ireland and western parts of England and Wales.

However, many central, southern and eastern areas of England, which have been affected by drought, may see far less rain.

News.title: Burnham proposes NHS-style social care system for England
News.content:
Andy Burnham wants to offer access to free social care services to everyone in England, and will put his plans before voters at the next general election.

The prime minister told the BBC that it would be a system in which "everyone contributes, everyone is covered". He did not rule out tax rises, acknowledging it may be "difficult or unpopular" with some.

Burnham said he wants to set out his "vision" on Tuesday and Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey, who is conducting a review, will advise on the "best way of doing it".

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the PM was suggesting Labour wanted "more tax rises" to pay for the reforms, adding the Conservatives would not support this.

Burnham has made reforming social care one of his flagship policies and has spoken of the experience of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's and died earlier this month.

While he has been clear on his ambition to make changes to the system, he has yet to explain how any changes would be funded.

Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than Â£23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the prime minister said: "I am talking about a system that works on NHS principles because that is the only way you can make it work.

"There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same and it's not something we're going to rush."

Personal care offered in Scotland is available to all adults who are assessed as needing help with tasks including eating and bathing.

News.title: Ten NHS staff removed over Noah Woods data breach
News.content:
Ten NHS staff have been removed from duty or suspended after a data breach involving the digital medical records of three-year-old Noah Woods.

Launching an "urgent" investigation, Dr Martin Mansfield, deputy chief medical officer at East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust, said that any unauthorised access of patient data was "completely unacceptable".

The trust has apologised "unreservedly" to Noah's family and said disciplinary action would be taken if needed.

A major search for Noah was carried out in the village of Brantham, Suffolk, after the child went missing on 15 September. His body was found the next day in a nearby pond by police divers.

A spokesperson for the trust said 10 employees had been "removed from active duty or suspended whilst investigations are concluded".

It comes after Sir Jim Mackey, the chief executive of NHS England, wrote to every trust on Friday, ordering stronger measures to tackle data breaches.

"We have seen too many cases of people abusing that trust, and enough is enough," said Sir Jim.

"Anyone who thinks they can satisfy their curiosity by looking at a patient's record should know this: they will be found out, they may lose their career and could end up with a criminal record."

News.title: More than 50 arrested at Palestine Action support rally
News.content:
Merseyside Police said more than 50 people had so far been detained at the Defend Our Juries event and that officers were in the process of making arrests on suspicion of wearing/carrying an article supporting a proscribed organisation.

A force spokesperson said it respected everyone's rights to protest lawfully while also aiming to keep the peace and ensure public safety.

The force said it made "detailed and co-ordinated plans ahead of such events to ensure it can apply this consistently, fairly and proportionately".

The spokesperson said not everyone present at the protest had been committing a criminal offence.

The arrests were criticised by Amnesty International, which called them a "shameful attack on freedom of speech".

One of those detained was human rights barrister Margaret Owen, 94.

A spokesperson for Defend Our Juries said: "We had hoped the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, would do the sensible thing and bin the ban on Palestine Action given the weight of public pressure to do so and the escalating amount of resources required in enforcing it.

"Continuing the charade of the proscription of Palestine Action is illogical, unsustainable and immoral."

News.title: Thousands affected and roads closed after burst pipe
News.content:
Thousands of homes in parts of West Sussex have water supply issues and a number of roads have flooded after what police are describing as a "significant" leak.

Roads around the Southgate Roundabout in Crawley have been closed on Sunday morning due to the burst water pipe, Sussex Police said.

Southern Water said about 9,000 customers were impacted, but as of 19:45 BST, most customers had seen their supplies restored.

A company spokesperson said: "Our teams are on site and working as quickly and safely as possible to repair the burst and restore supplies."

The company said customers were experiencing a loss of water supply or low pressure in the following areas - Woolborough Road, Holmcroft, Southgate, Tilgate and Furnace Green.

It first reported at 12:00 that supplies had returned to some homes.

Southern Water said its teams were still carrying out repairs but the damaged section of pipe had been removed and its replacement installed.

"We apologise for this disruption and would like to thank customers for their patience while we complete the repair," it added.

John Boulton, who is 82, and his partner were without water earlier.

He said: "It's pretty disgusting, really - we pay so much for the water supply."

Boulton said he had just paid Â£22 for bottled water in a shop.

News.title: Murder probe as cyclist dies following moped crash
News.content:
A murder inquiry has begun after an e-bike cyclist died following a collision with a moped in west London.

Emergency services were called to North Pole Road, North Kensington, at about 01:20 BST on Friday where the seriously injured 24-year-old man was found. He was pronounced dead at the scene shortly after.

Police said the investigation was at an early stage but it was believed the moped had been pursuing the e-bike cyclist prior to the crash.

Dt Ch Insp Neil John said detectives were "pursuing a number of lines of inquiry, including efforts to identify and trace the rider of the moped".

"Our thoughts are with the victim's family at what is a very difficult time," he added.

"We have launched a full investigation and are working hard to get answers and establish exactly what happened.

"As part of this, we're urging anyone who was in the area at the time and may have seen the e-bike or the moped to get in touch with us as soon as possible. If you have any information that could help, please come forward."
