World.title: Colombia breaks diplomatic ties with Iran
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had broken diplomatic ties with Iran and designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.

The foreign ministry made the announcements in two separate statements that were published in its website.

In the first statement, the government claimed that the decision claimed to defend “national and hemispheric security, and the fight against transnational crime.”

According to the foreign ministry, the Iranian government has “alleged ties to international terrorist groups and other narco-terrorist groups that threaten [Colombia’s] security.”

Colombia also took into account the documented human rights violations committed by the Iranian government on its territory, the verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities’ obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran’s nuclear program. Foreign Ministry

In regards to the IRGC, the foreign ministry claimed that the Iranian armed force “poses a serious threat to international peace and security” through “covert operations beyond Iran’s borders.”

“Colombia will strengthen its control and security measures to prevent individuals associated with the IRGC from entering its territory,” said the foreign ministry in a second statement.

In his 2017 book “Watch Your Backyard,” Foreign Minister Omar Bula claimed that “Iran and Islamic extremist groups such a Hezbollah and Al Qaeda have profusely penetrated Latin America.”

As part of his foreign policy, President Abelardo de la Espriella has renewed ties with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

In a response, the Iranian government said that the accusations of the De la Espriella government go “against the principles of mutual respect” and damage both countries’ “interests and benefits.”

“It is clear that none of the arguments put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical, and that this measure was adopted solely under the influence of the Zionist regime and the United States,” said Iran’s foreign ministry.

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Colombia withdraws support for ICJ genocide case against Israel
World.content:
Colombia has withdrawn its participation in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Tuesday.

In a statement, the court in The Hague said that Colombia’s government “decided to withdraw the Declaration of intervention that it had filed… on 5 April 2024 in the case concerning Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip.”

The decision of the administration of President Abelardo De la Espriella is part of a wider attempt to restore ties with Israel and its main sponsor, the United States, and appease its Evangelical Christian support base.

In response to the ongoing genocide in Palestine, former President Gustavo Petro took a leading role in diplomatic efforts that sought to isolate Israel and seek justice for Israel’s victims through the world court.

In a response, the US Government put Petro on a blacklist and actively campaigned for the election of De la Espriella to prevent another leftist victory in elections earlier this year.

The new president, who took office in August, immediately restored diplomatic ties to Israel and lifted a ban on coal exports to the country in West Asia.

World.title: ACSN crime group shuts down parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast
World.content:
Santa Marta-based crime group ACSN shut down parts of the city and the surrounding region after Colombia’s armed forces killed one of their commanders.

Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” and six of his comrades were killed during an offensive on Monday.

The son of Fredy Castillo, a.k.a. “Pinocho,” who is one of the alleged bosses of the crime group, was reportedly among those killed during the operation.

Shortly after, a pamphlet that was signed by the ACSN ordered an “armed strike” of 48 hours because of the “the fierce attacks that the government has been launching against our organization in the Sierra Nevada since this afternoon.”

Multiple buses were incinerated in the region around Santa Marta.

We hereby declare a 48-hour armed strike throughout the province of Magdalena, particularly along the Troncal del Caribe highway, in the city of Santa Marta, and in the banana-growing region. We do not want any businesses to remain open for a period of 48 hours. ACSN

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who traveled to the city, “they are trying to intimidate the public by promoting an armed strike.”

“I will not allow any criminal organization to subjugate citizens through threats and terror,” the president added.

Notwithstanding, multiple shop owners in Santa Marta and along the highway kept their shops closed on Tuesday, afraid to challenge the authority of the local crime bosses.

The district government closed public schools in neighborhoods where the ACSN is believed to have a strong presence. Public transport was suspended as videos of armed men opening fire on shops that failed to close voluntarily were posted on social media.

The ACSN control much of drug trafficking to the port of Santa Marta and to the coastline of the neighboring La Guajira province.

De la Espriella ended attempts to negotiate the group’s surrender and ordered a military approach after taking office in August.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: Court imposes strict conditions on Colombia’s military air strikes if minors are present
World.content:
A Bogota court imposed strict conditions on Colombia’s military authorities if they want to carry out air strikes on illegal armed groups in places where victims of forced recruitment are present.

The ruling of Bogota’s 34th Family Court lifted a suspension on the strikes that had been imposed earlier this month in response to a lawsuit.

The court imposed the following conditions on air strikes to evade violating International Humanitarian Law, which prioritizes the rights of child victims of forced recruitment over the success of military operations.

Don’t assume minors are legitimate targets because they form part of an illegal armed group

Intensify the verification and cross-checking of available information on the possible presence of minors at potential targets

Explicitly include this assessment to the legal and operational assessment of the attack

Assess the foreseeable risk of an attack on the lives and integrity of the minors

Examine the existence of less harmful means, methods, timing or operational alternatives that would allow the achievement of a comparable military advantage

Rigorously apply the principles of distinction, precaution, and proportionality before authorizing and executing the operation

The court additionally ordered family welfare institute ICBF to be integrated into military operations and strengthen the pathways for disengagement, restoration of rights, comprehensive care, and reintegration of children and adolescents who are victims of recruitment, with a differentiated and territorial approach.

The court asked the Ombudsman and the Inspector General’s Office to monitor compliance of the orders issued to maximize the protection of children’s rights.

The lawsuit had been filed in a successful attempt to protect children against the violence President Abelardo de la Espriella sought to unleash on illegal armed groups that refused to demobilize.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: Brazil reaches the election with its top court under suspicion and the candidates tied
World.content:
Brazil reaches the election with its top court under suspicion and the candidates tied

27th Sunday, September 2026 - 12:26 UTC Full article

Flávio Bolsonaro has said that, if he wins, his priorities will be to grant his father an amnesty and to bring Brazil into the security alliance Trump is promoting in the region

Brazil votes next Sunday in a presidential election that arrives with the Supreme Federal Court mired in its worst institutional crisis since the return to democracy, the right's candidate formally under investigation in the same case, and the two leading contenders tied within the margin of error in every poll.

The Banco Master case, in which the bank's former owner, Daniel Vorcaro, was arrested on Supreme Court orders over an alleged fraud of up to 12 billion reais, has reached both Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and several justices of the court itself. The Liberal Party candidate has been formally under investigation since July for alleged money laundering, currency evasion and corruption, focused on his contacts with Vorcaro and on the financing of “Dark Horse”, a film about his father. There is no formal indictment or conviction. In February, a Brasília judge ordered the removal of false online content claiming an arrest warrant existed against him.

The institutional dimension came later. The law firm of Justice Alexandre de Moraes's wife held a contract with the bank, and a police report revealed around a hundred messages between Vorcaro and the justice three weeks before his arrest. Justice André Mendonça, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro and responsible for a central part of the investigation, acknowledged receiving Vorcaro once and defended the lawfulness of his conduct. The court's president, Edson Fachin, ordered the case files unsealed. No irregularity has been established regarding any of the justices. Flávio Bolsonaro called at a São Paulo rally for Moraes's removal and demanded that other cases also be made public, including one involving a son of Lula.

Polling remains stable. The latest Datafolha survey, conducted last Tuesday and Wednesday among 2,002 voters with a two-point margin, gave Lula 40% and Bolsonaro 36% in the first round, and 47% to 45% in a prospective October 25 runoff. Earlier surveys by Quaest, BTG/Nexus and AtlasIntel produced different results, all within their margins. Neither man approaches the 50% plus one needed to win outright.

Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was sentenced on September 11, 2025 to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup and four other offences, alongside seven allies of what the court called the plot's core group. He is barred from office and is under house arrest with an electronic tag, granted in March on humanitarian grounds after pneumonia. In May a law was enacted allowing applications for sentence reductions, which are not automatic. He designated as his successor his eldest son, a senator for Rio de Janeiro after 16 years as a city councillor, despite establishment preferences for a candidate without the family name.

Researchers quoted by the Brazilian press attribute Bolsonarismo's electoral resilience to the combination of a discourse centred on moral questions with the growth of evangelical churches in urban peripheries. “Bolsonaro did not create moral conservatism. He did not bring broad evangelical sectors into politics, nor did he create the Brazilian far right. What he did was assemble those elements very effectively around a candidacy,” says political anthropologist Mercia Alves, of the Centro Brasileiro de Análise e Planejamento. David Magalhães, of the Observatório da Extrema Direita, says suspicions surrounding the court feed the idea that the former president is “a victim of a system”.

Flávio Bolsonaro has said that, if he wins, his priorities will be to grant his father an amnesty and to bring Brazil into the security alliance Trump is promoting in the region, from which the country was left out after Lula rejected the designation of the PCC and Comando Vermelho as terrorist organisations.

World.title: De la Espriella announces the reopening of oil exploration in Colombia, including fracking
World.content:
De la Espriella announces the reopening of oil exploration in Colombia, including fracking

26th Saturday, September 2026 - 11:06 UTC Full article

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Friday that his government will “fully” reopen hydrocarbon exploration and the signing of new contracts, including hydraulic fracturing, during the swearing-in of businessman Joaquín Gutiérrez as president of Ecopetrol, the country's largest company.

“My government is fully reopening the path of exploration and the signing of new contracts, including fracking, whatever it takes, as I said during the campaign, with absolutely every criterion of environmental responsibility,” the president said, adding a call to “drop the environmental hysteria”. He criticised the policy of his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, who reduced the signing of new exploration contracts as part of an energy transition strategy: “That is not energy transition but energy dependence, which is what no policy of this government will accept. In the era of the Tiger we will have energy sovereignty.” He also backed environment ministry measures to speed up licensing procedures.

The announcement does not in itself change the existing framework. Reactivating fracking in Colombia would require reversing the cancellation of the pilot projects ordered under the previous government and navigating regulatory and judicial restrictions whose precise status the executive has not detailed. The technique faces objections over its impact on water resources and the risk of induced seismicity. No environmental or opposition voices took part in the event.

The ceremony was held at the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino in Santa Marta, the estate where Simón Bolívar died. Gutiérrez said his arrival opens “a new era” and that the company should “be reborn to fulfil its true mission”, with the aim of aspiring to “the places of glory among the world's leading oil companies”.

The new president also announced that Ecopetrol will have a second headquarters in Barranquilla, set out plans for a “more austere and efficient” company with higher productivity, less centralised and with a greater regional presence, and said it would be “a depoliticised Ecopetrol”. He said the company would carry out “responsible fracking”, that it would reach its highest ever value under his tenure and that his legacy would be to leave it “with reserves for decades”. He also said there would be complaints over the previous administration's management; no irregularity has been established to date.

Gutiérrez is a business administrator, takes up the post with no previous experience in the hydrocarbons sector and managed De la Espriella's presidential campaign. His appointment was announced on Thursday by Ecopetrol's board, whose members had been renewed by shareholders on September 15. The company is listed on the Colombian Stock Exchange and in New York, with the Colombian state as majority shareholder.

De la Espriella took office on August 7. In these weeks his government has aligned its foreign policy with the United States and Israel, saw Colombia kept on Washington's list of countries it deems to have failed demonstrably to combat drug trafficking — with explicit praise for the new president — and delegated the country's address to the UN General Assembly to his vice president.

World.title: Falklands Assembly responds to Argentina's campaign: “This Assembly remains calm”
World.content:
Falklands Assembly responds to Argentina's campaign: “This Assembly remains calm”

25th Friday, September 2026 - 23:26 UTC Full article

Ford thanked the British prime minister, the foreign secretary, the minister for the Overseas Territories and figures “right across the UK political spectrum” for their support

The chair of the Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly, Jack Ford, said on Thursday during a sitting of the body that there is “nothing new” in the claims made this week, and that the institution “remains calm” and steadfast in defending the right of the archipelago's residents to determine their own future.

“Claims of this kind have been made against the Falkland Islands many times over many years, and throughout all of them these Islands have continued to grow, to develop, and to thrive. We will go on doing exactly that,” said Ford, who alongside chairing the assembly holds the Corporate Services portfolio and has represented the Camp constituency since last December's general election.

The statement came after a week in which Argentine President Javier Milei called on the UN General Assembly on Wednesday to act over what he described as unilateral British actions, arguing that the principle of self-determination does not apply to the archipelago because, in his government's view, its population was implanted. The United Kingdom responded with a written statement entered into the organisation's official record.

Ford thanked the British prime minister, the foreign secretary, the minister for the Overseas Territories and figures “right across the UK political spectrum” for their support, saying Westminster had shown “unwavering commitment” to the right of self-determination and to developing the archipelago's natural resources. He cited the extension of offshore hydrocarbon production licences announced this month with British backing, calling it “a clear mark of confidence in our future”.

The central nuance of his remarks came next. “Our confidence does not rest on the support of others alone, welcome as it is. It rests on our own democratic choice, made clearly and repeatedly by the people who live here,” he said, citing the 2013 referendum, in which on a 92% turnout 99.8% voted to remain a self-governing British Overseas Territory, a result he described as “independently monitored and beyond dispute”.

Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago, does not recognise the validity of licences granted by the local government and maintains that the referendum does not settle the question. It has 60 administrative proceedings open with no penalty applied and three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors, and last week sent Congress a sovereignty bill extending prohibitions to all natural resources on the continental shelf. None of the allegations has been proven.

It is the third public intervention by an assembly member in ten days. On September 17, Lewis Clifton, who holds the Emergency Services and Island Security portfolio, said the archipelago's defences are adequate; on September 21, Cheryl Roberts, responsible for Trade, Industry and Mineral Resources, announced the extension of the oil licences.

World.title: The Falklands economic development agency appoints Josh Smith as managing director
World.content:
The Falklands economic development agency appoints Josh Smith as managing director

25th Friday, September 2026 - 21:35 UTC Full article

According to FIDC, Smith has built an international career over two decades, holding senior leadership positions in the UK Civil Service and previously working in Canada, Taiwan and Saudi Arabia

The Falkland Islands Development Corporation, the archipelago's economic development agency, announced on Friday the appointment of Josh Smith as its new managing director, subject to final relocation arrangements. He will succeed Zachary Franklin, who will conclude his tenure in December.

The corporation did not give a start date for the incoming director and said details on the transition would be announced in due course. Franklin took up the post in September 2022, after more than twelve years living and working in the Asia-Pacific region, meaning he will have served just over four years at the head of the organisation.

According to FIDC, Smith has built an international career over two decades, holding senior leadership positions in the UK Civil Service and previously working in Canada, Taiwan and Saudi Arabia across economic development, trade, innovation and public policy. Those details come from the corporation's statement and have not been independently verified.

“Following a highly competitive recruitment process, the Board is delighted to appoint Josh as Managing Director of FIDC,” said the organisation's chair, Michael Poole, highlighting his “strong combination of leadership, commercial experience and strategic vision”. Poole was a member of the Legislative Assembly between 2013 and 2017 and joined the corporation as development manager in August 2018. The board also thanked Franklin for his contribution, saying his leadership had “helped guide the organisation through an important period”.

Smith said he looked forward to working “with the Board, staff, government, businesses and the wider community”, and that the corporation “has an important role in supporting sustainable economic growth”.

Established in 1984 and largely self-funding, FIDC provides loans and grants and promotes economic diversification, investment and entrepreneurship across the archipelago. Its recent activity includes an internal artificial intelligence pilot project, leading a group of local businesses at the first trade expo held by the International Association of Antarctica Tour Operators in Maryland in April, efforts to expand shipping links with a Valparaíso-based shipping group, and a feasibility study for a marina.

The handover comes as Argentina maintains 60 administrative proceedings open, with no penalty applied, and three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors over hydrocarbon exploration in waters near the archipelago. None of the allegations has been proven. FIDC's statement makes no reference to that situation.

World.title: Milei and Netanyahu discussed the Falklands in his only bilateral in New York
World.content:
Milei and Netanyahu discussed the Falklands in his only bilateral in New York

25th Friday, September 2026 - 21:28 UTC Full article

Asked by Argentine reporters whether the subject had come up, Quirno said “yes”, and “fine” when asked how that part of the conversation had gone

Argentine President Javier Milei met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for about twenty minutes on Thursday at United Nations headquarters, in what was his only bilateral meeting with a head of state or government during his trip to New York. Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno confirmed they discussed the Falklands.

Asked by Argentine reporters whether the subject had come up, Quirno said “yes”, and “fine” when asked how that part of the conversation had gone. He did not specify whether they addressed the judicial and administrative actions Argentina is pursuing against Navitas Petroleum, the Israeli company operating the Sea Lion project alongside Britain's Rockhopper Exploration. Milei was also accompanied by Economy Minister Luis Caputo.

What was said is known almost entirely from the statement issued by Netanyahu's office; the Argentine government released a photograph. According to that text, the prime minister thanked Milei for his “steadfast and unconditional support” for the State of Israel and congratulated him on receiving the “Defender of Israel” award from Yeshiva Darchei Torah. The two are said to have discussed bilateral cooperation and the possible expansion of the so-called “Isaac Accords”, an initiative the statement attributes to Milei to deepen security and economic cooperation between Israel and Latin American countries, and for whose content and status no independent documentation is available.

The praise was mutual. “President Milei is one of the great leaders of our time,” Netanyahu said according to the same statement, adding that what he has done with Argentina's economy “is masterful”. Milei replied that it was an honour to receive such words “from you, one of the greatest leaders in all of world history”. Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, posted that “Latin America clearly hasn't heard about Israel's diplomatic isolation”.

The meeting came hours after dozens of delegations walked out of the General Assembly hall during Netanyahu's speech, in which he called those who left “moral cowards” and described genocide allegations over Gaza as “the biggest lie of the century”. Netanyahu also held no formal meeting with US President Donald Trump during the week. On the walkout, Milei said earlier at the Economic Club of New York that “focusing on the number of people in the assembly is a twenty-fifth-order matter” and that “what matters is the message”. He repeated that his support for Israel “is unconditional”.

The International Criminal Court has an outstanding arrest warrant against Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity. Argentina is a state party to the Rome Statute.

The meeting came amid Argentina's campaign against companies operating hydrocarbons in waters near the archipelago. Buenos Aires has 60 administrative proceedings open with no penalty applied and three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors; federal prosecutor Carlos Stornelli expanded the charges last week. None of the allegations has been proven. Netanyahu has taken no public position on the dispute. His son Yair, who holds no post in the Israeli government, has backed Argentina's claim on X.

World.title: “The UN has more reason to exist every day”, Uruguay's president said two days after Milei
World.content:
“The UN has more reason to exist every day”, Uruguay's president said two days after Milei

25th Friday, September 2026 - 10:41 UTC Full article

“The UN has more reason to exist every day,” Orsi said, while calling for multilateral institutions that are “more effective, more representative” and closer to people's needs

Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi defended the United Nations' relevance and condemned the economic embargo on Cuba before the General Assembly on Thursday, in an address of just under twenty minutes that contrasted with that of his Argentine counterpart, Javier Milei, two days earlier from the same podium.

“The UN has more reason to exist every day,” Orsi said, while calling for multilateral institutions that are “more effective, more representative” and closer to people's needs. “We cannot go on being hostages to the will of a handful of countries that can be counted on the fingers of one hand,” he said, referring to the workings of the Security Council. Milei, on Tuesday, had described the organisation as a fossilised institution and questioned the point of resolutions that go unenforced.

Orsi speaks from a dual regional position: he holds the pro tempore presidency of Mercosur since July 1 and that of the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States since March 21. It was his second address to the assembly since taking office on March 1, 2025.

The passage with the greatest domestic political impact concerned Cuba. “We cannot be indifferent to the pain of an endless state of war, the fear and pain generated by organised crime, the permanent threat of terrorism, the repression that arises from tyranny, or the suffering caused by a tight economic blockade such as the one the Cuban people endure,” he said. Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had already denounced the embargo on Tuesday.

The speech opened with a greeting to the American people on the 250th anniversary of their independence, marked in July, and a reference to that country's founding values: that people hold rights, that life, liberty and happiness should guide every government, and that the governed decide who governs them, principles he said were inherited in South America half a century later.

AHORA | HABLA EL PRESIDENTE ORSI EN LA ONU



“Ninguna nación tiene el monopolio de las soluciones; ningún pueblo debería ser condenado a elegir entre modelos impuestos desde afuera”



“Hoy vivimos un tiempo particularmente difícil” con “desigualdad extrema”, “pobreza” y ”las… pic.twitter.com/MZ7Z5cEK0Z — Telemundo (@TelemundoUY) September 24, 2026

Orsi described Uruguay as a country “of great convictions” rather than “great stridency”, championed humility in international relations — “nobody is more than anybody”, “no country owns the absolute truth” — and said no people should be forced to choose between models imposed from outside. He reaffirmed Uruguay's participation in UN peacekeeping missions and argued that peace is not “simply the absence of war”. He closed with the phrase “we are and we transform ourselves together”.

The president avoided taking sides in ongoing conflicts and did not mention Gaza or the Middle East. “We do not believe that taking one side or the other in a war, a confrontation or a dispute necessarily helps resolve it. Often, on the contrary, it deepens those divisions,” he said. In another passage, without naming any country, he said: “We know well that this is not about good guys and bad guys. Often the good become bad very quickly, or those we condemned harshly yesterday magically become reference points in our alliance for good.” Executive sources cited by the Uruguayan daily El País read that passage as distancing from US policy towards Venezuela; the president made no reference to that country.

Figures from the National Party, unnamed in that same coverage, called the speech “vague” and said the president had acted as “a spokesman for the Cuban regime”. Reception within the governing coalition was favourable, including among sectors that have voiced differences with the government's foreign policy: Socialist senator Gustavo González highlighted the reference to the embargo as “a humanitarian situation that must be addressed”.

World.title: Poverty in Argentina rises to 32.3%, ending two years of decline
World.content:
Poverty in Argentina rises to 32.3%, ending two years of decline

25th Friday, September 2026 - 10:26 UTC Full article

The measurement covers the 31 urban agglomerations surveyed by the Permanent Household Survey, where 9,729,000 people fell below the poverty line and 2,249,000 below the extreme poverty line

Poverty in Argentina reached 32.3% of people in the first half of 2026, an increase of 4.1 percentage points on the second half of 2025, the National Institute of Statistics and Census reported on Thursday. The figure interrupts the downward path the indicator had followed since mid-2024. Extreme poverty rose 1.2 points, from 6.3% to 7.5%.

The measurement covers the 31 urban agglomerations surveyed by the Permanent Household Survey, where 9,729,000 people fell below the poverty line and 2,249,000 below the extreme poverty line. Projected to the country as a whole, estimates published by Argentine media place the figure at between 15.4 and 15.5 million people in poverty and around 3.6 million in extreme poverty. In household terms, 24.4% fell below the poverty line and 5.6% below the extreme poverty line.

The year-on-year comparison gives a different result. Against the first half of 2025, when poverty stood at 31.6% and extreme poverty at 6.9%, the increases are 0.7 and 0.6 points respectively. The second-half 2025 reading of 28.2% had been the lowest since 2018, when it closed at 27.3%.

In Argentina poverty is measured by income: the cost of a basic basket is compared with each household's available resources, making the indicator sensitive to inflation. In June, a family of four needed 1,531,473 pesos to stay above the poverty line and 689,853 to avoid extreme poverty.

Figures by age show a higher incidence among children: 44.5% of those under 14 live in households below the poverty line, against 36.9% among those aged 15 to 29 and 28.8% among those aged 30 to 64. Geographical differences are also pronounced. Concordia recorded the highest level, at 56.2%, followed by Gran Resistencia at 48.6% and Posadas at 42.2%. In the Buenos Aires metropolitan area, the surrounding districts reached 36.9% against 11.1% in the City of Buenos Aires. Agglomerations of fewer than 500,000 inhabitants recorded a 4.9-point rise, greater than the 3.9 points in larger centres.

Leopoldo Tornarolli, a researcher at the Centre for Distributive, Labour and Social Studies at the National University of La Plata, said the result “is not a surprise” and confirms a trend already visible between the third and fourth quarters of last year, though the scale of the rise was larger than expected. He attributed it to two factors: the increase in inflation between May 2025 and March 2026, and weak dynamism in the formal labour market. He said the slowdown in prices in recent months has probably already halted the rise, but warned that returning to a sustained path of reduction requires “a more dynamic labour market”.

The agency simultaneously released economic activity data showing a 2.9% fall in July compared with June. Economy Minister Luis Caputo attributed it to “transitory shocks”: lower gas availability for industry, exceptional rain and snowfall, and fewer hours worked in some sectors because of the football World Cup. On poverty, he said on X that both rates “recorded a sharp fall relative to the first half of 2024”.

In that half, the first of Javier Milei's administration, poverty had reached 52.9% and extreme poverty 18.1%, following the devaluation of more than 110% and the price corrections implemented in December 2023. Hours before the report was released, Milei had told business figures at Citi's headquarters in New York that his administration had lifted “14 million people out of poverty” and that “we are the ones who have done the most for the most vulnerable sectors”.

World.title: Trump and Xi end the state visit with the trade truce extended and no substantive deals
World.content:
Trump and Xi end the state visit with the trade truce extended and no substantive deals

25th Friday, September 2026 - 09:37 UTC Full article

Artificial intelligence was the clearest point of declared agreement

Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to Washington ended on Thursday with a two-month extension of the bilateral trade truce, agreed before the meeting itself, and no progress on the central issues dividing the two powers: tariffs, rare earths, agricultural purchases, Taiwan and export restrictions on advanced chips.

The extension was settled on Wednesday night, after an unscheduled meeting between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng. It runs to January 10 an agreement that was due to expire on November 10 and which had lowered US tariffs and suspended Chinese export controls on rare earths and critical minerals. Those same talks produced a commitment to explore a communication mechanism for artificial intelligence incidents affecting national security.

Each side arrived with a request that went unanswered. Washington wants Beijing to use its influence over Tehran to end a war approaching its seventh month. Xi is seeking a permanent halt to arms sales to Taiwan and an easing of restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports. According to Chinese state agency Xinhua, he urged the United States to “adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence and handle the Taiwan issue with prudence”, one of his most explicit statements on the matter. After May's summit in Beijing, the US administration postponed a US$14 billion arms sale to Taipei; Trump has described such sales as “a very good negotiating tool” in dealing with China.

Artificial intelligence was the clearest point of declared agreement. Xi said both countries “have the capacity and the responsibility to develop and manage AI effectively, ensuring its development remains under human control”. Trump had written before the meeting that he wanted to leave it “exactly as it is”, attributing the same position to China.

It is the first state visit by a Chinese leader to the United States since 2015, though Xi was in the country in 2023 for the APEC summit in San Francisco. The three-day visit began with his arrival on Wednesday evening at Joint Base Andrews, where Trump met him at the foot of the aircraft steps, and continued with a Thursday ceremony featuring a military review, gift exchange and flyover. Trump spoke of a “truly great friendship” built on “mutual respect and the vital interests of our people”.

The day closed with a state banquet for 134 guests in the White House East Room, decorated in red and gold. Neither the speeches nor the toast referred to bilateral tensions. Trump said he and Xi had “never” got on “better” and presented a carving of a bald eagle as a gift. Xi called on both countries to act “as responsible major powers” and to “explore a new path” for cooperation. The menu combined American ingredients with Chinese influence and opened with the same wine shared by Richard Nixon and Zhou Enlai during the visit that restored relations between the two countries.

Guests included Elon Musk, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, AMD's Lisa Su, Alphabet co-founder Sergey Brin and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman. The Chinese delegation included no business figures, an early sign the summit would not produce concrete results.

The two will meet twice more before the end of the year: in November in Shenzhen, at the APEC summit, and in December in Miami, at the G-20, both after the US midterm elections.

World.title: How to conjugate Spanish verbs and impress your friends
World.content:
Are you at that point in your language learning where conjugating Spanish verbs — or constructing “doing” words such as running, swimming and cooking — is causing you headaches? Have you realized that, in this respect, English is a relatively simpler language?

In Spanish, you must conjugate the verb depending on who you are speaking to. In English, you often don’t.

When my Italian boyfriend started learning Spanish, I noticed that he learned some easy verb combinations. It was a simple way for him to make progress, without racking his brain.

In these combinations, you only have to remember the pattern and then add the verb you intend to actually use. Here are some examples.

To express the future, an intention or a plan

VOY A (going to)

Voy a comer (I am going to eat)

Voy a leer (I am going to read)

¿Vas a venir? (Are you coming)

Vamos a bailar (We are going to dance)

To talk about something you have to do

TENER QUE (have to)

Tengo que descansar (I have to rest)

Tienes que comprar leche (You have to buy milk)

Tenemos que manejar (We have to drive)

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mexico News Daily (@mexiconewsdaily)

To talk about something you have just finished

ACABO DE (I just)

Acabo de llegar (I just arrived)

¿Acabas de comer? (Did you just eat?)

Acabamos de terminar (We have just finished)

To express that you are about to do something

ESTAR POR (To be about to)

Estoy por llegar (I am about to arrive)

Estoy por comer (I am about to eat)

Estamos por terminar (We are about to finish)

To express you need something

NECESITO (I need)

Necesito dormir (I need to sleep)

¿Necesitas comprar más? (Do you need to buy more)

Necesitamos empezar ya (We need to start now)

These are some examples of verb combinations that can help you start speaking faster. My recommendation would be to learn one or two of them and start practising whenever you have the chance. It is all about finding the pattern, getting used to it and start using it as soon as you can!

Paulina Gerez is a translator-interpreter, content creator, and founder of Crack The Code, a series of online courses focused on languages. Through her social media, she helps people see learning a language from another perspective through her fun experiences. Instagram: paulinagerezm / Tiktok: paugerez3 / YT: paulina gerez

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico City residents express civic pride in having the ‘world’s worst traffic’
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — After briefly ceding the top spot to Barranquilla, Colombia, Mexico City has officially reclaimed its title as the most congested city on Earth, prompting widespread civic celebration across a gridlocked metropolis that refused to accept second-best.

According to the latest TomTom Traffic Index, capital motorists averaged a staggering 75.9% congestion level, successfully re-establishing dominance over rival logjams in Bengaluru, India, and Dublin, Ireland. The news was met with enthusiastic horn-honking across the Viaducto, where commuters celebrated by advancing three meters over the course of forty-five minutes.

“We lost our edge there for a moment, and frankly, it was embarrassing,” said local driver Eduardo Ramos, speaking through a rolled-down window while idling near Insurgentes. “When Barranquilla took the crown, people started moving at reasonable speeds. It felt like we were losing our cultural identity. But today, standing entirely still on a Tuesday afternoon, I have never been prouder to be a chilango.”

City officials held a formal press conference to honor the milestone, though several key speakers arrived two hours late due to a localized standstill near the Zócalo. Transportation authorities praised the collective dedication of millions of daily drivers who consistently chose to get behind the wheel during peak hours, ensuring that an average 10-kilometer trip once again required a heroic 34 minutes and 29 seconds.

The report highlighted Wednesday, May 28, as the city’s finest hour of the year, when congestion spiked to an unprecedented 117%. Commemorative plaques are reportedly planned for the Periférico overpass to mark the historic afternoon when an estimated two million vehicles successfully converted six lanes of highway into an outdoor parking lot.

“Other cities try to compete, but they simply lack the stamina,” noted urban mobility analyst Sofía Mendoza. “In places like London or Athens, drivers get frustrated when traffic slows down. In Mexico City, we treat a stationary commute as a contemplative space for personal growth, breakfast and running a small business out of the glove compartment.”

At press time, traffic on the Circuito Interior had come to a complete, triumphant halt, with thousands of motorists joining in a synchronized, ceremonial revving of engines to ensure Colombia would not challenge the title again anytime soon.

World.title: The Monobloc chair: The plastic throne that rules Mexico
World.content:
I grew up on a chair.

Not literally. That would have been weird.

Instead, I come from an Italian family where chairs were everywhere. Sitting was merely one of their many functions.

On a good day, you sat in them and observed the family theatrics. On a bad day, they became climbing rigs for reaching my cousin’s secret stash of Nutella. They made glorious goalposts too and, when the mood was ripe, even served as Hulk Hogan-style wrestling weapons.

So perhaps it was inevitable that, when we arrived in Mexico, my attention was drawn to chairs.

Not just any chairs. Plastic ones, branded and unbranded. Stacked outside shops, scattered around taco stands and lined up for parties.

I soon realized something important: The Mexican plastic throne is bona fide everyday infrastructure.

This, of course, raised questions. Where do they come from? Who makes them and, most crucially, who tests them? Is there a government-appointed Chair Inspector whose career involves dropping heavy tíos onto spindly legs and taking notes? “Load tolerance: not bad. Man: slightly sweaty. Chair: 100% unbreakable.”

Is there a Ministry of Seating with a maximum permissible wobble? And who decides the colors?

I began to suspect a secret council: 12 people in a windowless room, surrounded by polypropylene, debating whether next year’s official hue should be turquoise or something more adventurous. Perhaps they never sit, preferring to stand and nod, secretly longing for a bar stool.

The superhero of street seating

There could even be a Mexican chair superhero, but not the sort who fights crime; Mexico has enough people for that. His superpower is knowing exactly how many chairs the perfect quinceañera requires.

He arrives at the venue, surveys the courtyard, then whispers, “148 … 84 green, 36 red and 28 fuchsia.”

Nobody asks how he knows; they just start stacking.

His other powers remain classified, although rumors suggest he can identify a broken chair from 900 yards away and appear instantly whenever somebody says, “We’re going to need more chairs, dude.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dastaangoi (@dastaangoi)

I might be digressing.

To understand how a single injection-molded object achieved near-mythological status, I did what any self-respecting journalist would do when confronted with patio furniture: watched an unhealthy amount of completely irrelevant TikTok videos, nearly polished off a whole jar of spreadable Dulce De La Rosa Marzipan and, with the deadline looming, contacted Mexico’s academics.

First, I spent an afternoon at a taquería near my house.

One taquero used a single chair as a stepladder, cash stand and footrest in under four minutes. It didn’t flinch. It simply creaked around its torn backrest, as if puffing out its plastic chest, and muttered: “Is that all you got, hermano?”

Fascinating.

Defining community through cheap plastic

Dr. Armando Cisneros, a sociologist at UAM-Azcapotzalco, took the question considerably more seriously than I did.

“Objects don’t just serve communities,” he told me. “They define them. The chair’s petroleum-born virtues — dirt-cheap and stubbornly durable — don’t just suit street life; they help shape it.”

Cisneros elegantly calls it a “culture of rest,” a nationwide understanding that wherever commerce or conversation happens, a place to sit will follow.

If Cisneros explained the chair’s DNA, Dr. Mario Ortiz Murillo, a sociologist at UNAM, deftly mapped its territory.

“It serves rich and poor alike, because everyone gets tired,” Ortiz Murillo told me.

But in Mexico, he explained, it does more than hold weight. It holds space.

“Tied to a lamppost, it claims a curb. Stacked in a pickup, it’s a pop-up taquería.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by 𝙋𝙖𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙚 𝘾𝙡𝙪𝙗 (@gio_palace)

“The plastic chair,” Ortiz Murillo said, “is how Mexicans move through and confidently claim the city.”

And claim it they do.

I asked Rosa, who runs my neighborhood grocery, why she keeps three by the door.

“Honestly, I never really thought about it,” she said. “Locals like sitting and sipping sodas … that’s how they relax, or in the case of my husband, spend an inordinate amount of time gabbling nonsense with local gringos about football.”

I felt chuffed.

Built to outlive your phone

That contrast — Rosa’s practical indifference versus the chair’s actual ubiquity — led me to the broader point.

We live in an age of flat-pack furniture and Allen wrenches. Luckily, the Mexican plastic throne rises above all that. It arrives fully formed and morally uncomplicated. Best of all, it’s ready to be abused. Leave it in the July sun until it fades to the color of old teeth? No problem. Stack it. Drop it. Drag it. It will probably outlive your phone and possibly your career. Take that, AI.

I grew up thinking chairs were supposed to earn their keep, but in Mexico, they run the place.

So next time you’re handed a slightly warped, suspiciously wobbly plastic throne, don’t test the legs.

Just sit.

Listen to the comal sizzle. Listen to the overlapping conversations. Mexico doesn’t need Roche Bobois or Poltrona Frau to hold its people together. It has cheap polypropylene, and against all economic and gravitational odds, it works.

Besides, if a 250-pound tío can balance on it like an Olympic gymnast, so can you.

Just skip the Hulk Hogan routine. The chair will survive, but your dignity might not.

Paolo Ferrari is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: How Oaxaca’s La Ventanilla turned tourism into conservation
World.content:
Standing on La Ventanilla beach is a breathtaking experience. In the distance, a rock formation shaped like a window frames 15 kilometers of pristine beach — one of the last protected areas on the Oaxaca coast. This area remains largely untouched thanks to the Zapotec community, which began transforming it into an oasis for local wildlife, particularly turtles and crocodiles, 30 years ago.

By the late 1990s, the crocodile and turtle populations in La Ventanilla, located in the municipality of Santa María Tonameca, were on the verge of extinction. Their skins were highly valued in trade, and turtle meat and eggs were part of a local culinary tradition, often prized for their supposed aphrodisiac properties.

National laws protecting crocodiles were enacted in the late 1970s, followed by turtle protection in the early 1990s. By 1998, Mexican authorities in La Ventanilla had imposed stricter penalties for poaching and strengthened the reserve’s overall protection. “It was then that the community, led by individuals like Agustín Reyes and Vicente García and guided by NGOs, began a revolutionary shift in both mentality and economics,” said Eulalio Cortés, a member of the cooperative.

This community effort led to the creation of the Ecotourism Cooperative La Ventanilla. Today, it is a global model for conservation, successfully balancing ecotourism with the protection and well-being of local flora and fauna.

The importance of La Ventanilla for conservation

La Ventanilla is renowned for its beauty, but it also hosts a unique ecological phenomenon. During the rainy season, saltwater from the sea and freshwater from the lagoon converge. This mixing supports rich biodiversity and creates an ideal breeding environment. This period is also optimal for crocodile mating, and these predators play a crucial role in the mangrove and lagoon ecosystems by controlling the populations of other species. Simultaneously, the healthy mangrove forests act as a natural barrier against hurricanes and are vital for carbon sequestration in the fight against climate change.

Furthermore, turtle nesting is essential to maintaining this ecological balance. La Ventanilla thrives thanks to the efforts of 30 families dedicated to protecting this equilibrium. The project is registered as a Wildlife Conservation Management Unit and operates under a management plan approved by the Department of the Environment and Natural Resources, known by its Spanish acronym Semarnat.

Conservation activities include protecting the lagoon and mangroves, managing crocodile populations on a small island, and conducting nightly monitoring for biometric research. These efforts provide valuable opportunities for university students and researchers, while responsible tourism supports the project’s sustainability.

Today, the cooperative protects at least 300 American crocodiles, along with species such as deer, iguanas and various birds, using a self-sustaining model. This is funded through silent, nonmotorized boat tours of the mangroves and visits to the small island where the animals are cared for.

Science, tourism and livelihoods

The cooperative organizes two activities for tourists that double as vital conservation efforts. During the turtle nesting season, members monitor the beach nightly to collect eggs, transferring them to a protected shelter to shield them from predators and poachers. A small group of tourists is welcome to assist in this process.

Additionally, around 6 p.m., cooperative members release thousands of hatchlings into the sea. Tourists can also participate in this experience, directly contributing to conservation. According to Rocío García, a member of the project, between 25,000 and 30,000 turtles are released here annually.

The island tour allows visitors to see crocodiles up close, with the fees from these tours used to feed the animals. Today, the community relies on tourism not only for its livelihood, but as a means to protect the lagoon, the mangroves and the thousands of creatures that call this area home.

Their work is increasingly vital, demonstrating that local communities are essential to mangrove conservation at a time when, according to the National Commission for the Knowledge and Use of Biodiversity (Conabio), Mexico has lost more than 27,000 hectares of mangrove forest in the last five years alone.

Ana Paula de la Torre is a Mexican journalist and collaborator for various outlets, including Milenio, Animal Político, Vice, Newsweek en Español, Televisa and Mexico News Daily.

World.title: From the archive: Sharing the planet means accepting scorpions and tarantulas
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in May 2021 — is a humorous and at times terrifying look at the creatures one can occasionally encounter in Mexico.

“¡Ya quítense, pinches moscas!” (“Go away, damn flies!”) shouts my friend as she desperately swats at the noisy black dots buzzing around her table where she’s just set the food out. She misses most of them that day, but I have another friend who’s gotten so good at catching them that she’s up to about a 50% kill rate.

Even with her strongly worded demands that certainly would have made my little fly-heart jump, they were unfazed and kept nose-diving toward the chicken like the crazy little kamikaze pilots they are.

Bugs are a big part of life in Mexico — to a greater extent, I think, than in further-north North America.

The bugs we love and the bugs we hate

There are the famous bugs that we love, of course: the beautiful monarch butterflies that tourists come from far and wide to observe and that are becoming increasingly more difficult to protect are one famous example. Another are the fireflies (actually beetles) of Tlaxcala, which I’m hoping to go see myself this summer.

And while they’re not an official attraction, I’ve been known to stop for half an hour at a time to observe ants as they march back and forth in their impossibly long and efficient lines that I’ve seen stretch for a kilometer or more.

Buggy beauty is truly in the eye of the beholder.

The bugs you can eat

There are the edible bugs too, of course, considered a delicacy in several regions of the country. While I’ve tried the famous chapulines (grasshoppers) and got the obligatory picture of myself looking simultaneously amazed and very dubious as I did so, I’ve yet to venture into the rest of the vast world of edible insects.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Gio Cruz (@elgiomx)

While I’ve traditionally been pretty chill about even icky bugs that make it into my house — I pride myself on not jumping up onto the sofa and waving my hands in front of my tear-streaked and horrified face when I see a six- or eight-legged critter — I draw the line at the ones that could potentially send me or my kid to the hospital.

Terrifying bugs

In Querétaro, it was scorpions, which my dog at the time (RIP, sweet She-ra) mercifully hunted and killed with a vigor I wouldn’t have expected from her calm, chill demeanor.

Querétaro was also the place where I watched in horror, after one particularly rainy day, as the patio of the school where I taught became covered with the biggest ants that I’d ever seen with wings. That’s right: giant ants that fly.

They might as well have been those flying monkeys from “The Wizard of Oz,” as far as I was concerned. But what choice did I have but to try to make space? We share the planet with adorable kittens and mutant flying ants alike.

Here in Xalapa, I recently found a tarantula. A TARANTULA, people. In my living room. I’d never even seen one not in a terrarium before.

Before it made it to the blanket draped over my napping child, I managed to trap it in a wide-rimmed empty peanut container (I tried with a big mayonnaise jar first, but it wasn’t big enough. Insert totally grossed out scream GIF here).

And then, I took it outside and threw it out into what the tarantula must have believed was a vast and endless forest, the wooded terreno in front of my house. I mean, I wasn’t going to kill something the size of a small mammal.

Home invasions

Bugs have been on my mind more lately as they’ve been invading my home in great quantities. I’ve got a mosquito net above my bed, but the rest of the house is fair game as long as I want my windows to stay open, and I do. It’s been raining a lot, so maybe they’re seeking shelter inside my home?

I’ve got everything from the tiny ants marching around my bathroom sink (what on earth are they finding to eat there?) to the occasional flying cockroach (please just don’t fly suddenly in front of my face, okay, thank you), to the random unidentified beetles lying suddenly dead on my stairs. Did they come to my house to die, or did they not find their way out?

I haven’t found many spiders in my home lately, but when I do, I usually leave them be if they’re just minding their own business in a corner we humans don’t usually occupy. Really, I appreciate the service they provide by eating other bugs.

Cultivating a live-and-let-live attitude

Nature isn’t all romantic. Just ask my friend who just found four little sparrows decapitated and eaten in her backyard by a rogue crow (or a perfectly predictable and natural crow).

But not seeing any bugs at all would be much more worrisome than the occasional unidentified buzzing objects in my home. They’re part of this ecosystem that we all belong to, and while they may bug us personally (get it?), we need them.

So, for now, I’ll keep doing my best to live and let live as I’m awakened each morning before sunrise by the pleasant sound of cicadas right outside my window and greeted each evening on the road to my house by lightning bugs guiding me home.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: A record hurricane, a population milestone and doubts over a ‘historic’ fuel bust
World.content:
Listen to this article

Hurricane Polo dominated headlines for much of the week, intensifying off Mexico’s Pacific coast at an unprecedented pace before oscillating between Category 4 and 5 as it pushed north. The storm dumped heavy rain and generated dangerous surf along Guerrero, Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco as it slowly moved up the coast, before curving north toward the Baja Peninsula.

Mexico also crossed a demographic milestone, with INEGI reporting the country’s population had surpassed 130 million even as the fertility rate continued its steep decline. Meanwhile, questions mounted over what officials had billed as Mexico’s largest-ever fuel-trafficking bust, after the firing of a federal prosecutor involved in the case.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Hurricane Polo threatens Pacific coast

Hurricane Polo formed Monday off the coast of Guerrero and intensified at a record pace, becoming the fastest system in the Western Hemisphere on record to go from a disorganized tropical depression to a Category 5 hurricane. By midweek it was described as “extremely dangerous,” with sustained winds of 165 mph as it moved slowly along the coast, prompting school closures in Guerrero and Michoacán. Polo’s peak winds of 180 mph made it the second-strongest eastern Pacific hurricane on record.

The storm oscillated between Category 4 and 5 through Thursday as its core remained offshore, sparing Mexico a direct hit while still delivering torrential rain to Michoacán and Guerrero. It moved out to sea later in the week, but is expected to turn back toward land. It is expected to approach the west coast of the Baja California peninsula on Monday as a hurricane.

Society: Phones banned in schools and a population milestone

Education authorities reached a deal to ban cell phones and tablets in primary and secondary schools nationwide starting in late October, with high schools left to set their own device policies. Separately, INEGI’s 2025 Intercensal Survey found Mexico’s population reached 130.9 million in late 2025, up 3.9% from the 2020 census, even as the fertility rate fell to 1.2 births per woman, dropping significantly below replacement rate.

On the healthcare front, IMSS and AmCham signed an agreement pledging $44 million toward bringing more pharmaceutical clinical trials into public hospitals through 2030.

This week also featured the debut of The MND Mexico Well-being Series, Part 1: Health and healthcare, the first in a new series of reports looking at well-being in Mexico.

Earlier this month, Congress opened the first ordinary session of the current legislative year. As the legislative agenda comes into focus, bills up for debate include:

The Digital Economy Law, which would expand digital payment tools like CoDi to reduce reliance on cash among small businesses and independent workers.

The so-called “Anti-Meme Bill,” an intellectual-property reform that critics say could criminalize satirical use of government logos, though the amended text exempts clearly unofficial parody and criticism.

A Senate bill to restore promotion and relegation in Mexican pro soccer, reversing a 2020 suspension that closed off Liga MX to second-division clubs.

Security and anti-corruption: Doubts grow over fuel bust as arrests continue

Anti-Corruption Minister Raquel Buenrostro reported that 4,193 public servants have been sanctioned since Sheinbaum took office, with corruption-prevention efforts credited with saving more than 80 billion pesos in government contracts. In Oaxaca, federal and state forces arrested the mayor of Juchitán on extortion charges over alleged ties to a group described as an operational arm of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, triggering road blockades in the city.

The week’s most consequential story on this front concerned the Sept. 17 announcement of what authorities called the biggest-ever single-site seizure of stolen fuel in Mexican history — 59 million liters at a Guanajuato storage facility. The case quickly unraveled after the facility’s owner presented documentation that it was operating legally, prompting the FGR to quietly reclassify the case from a seizure to an embargo. By Friday, the federal prosecutor who led the operation had been fired, and Guanajuato’s state security minister and attorney general were also under investigation. Meanwhile in Sinaloa, Sheinbaum pledged continued military support for the state amid an ongoing cartel turf war, repeating her view that U.S. interference contributed to the violence.

Mexico-U.S. relations: Sharp words at the UN, warmer ties elsewhere

At the U.N. General Assembly, Trump called Mexico the “epicenter” of cartel violence and said the country must “reclaim control of its soil,” while also praising the bilateral relationship. Sheinbaum offered a pointed but restrained response, suggesting she could just as easily criticize U.S. drug use and gun production, while announcing her first trip to Asia as president, for November’s APEC summit in China.

Mexico also deepened ties elsewhere, as Sheinbaum and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung signed 17 agreements spanning trade, AI, aerospace and defense cooperation.

Economy and trade: Peso weakens as Banxico holds steady

The peso depreciated more than 1%, passing 17.7 to the dollar, amid expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve isn’t done raising rates. Banxico held its benchmark rate at 6.50% for a third straight meeting, a decoupling from the Fed that analysts said could be tested if U.S. rates rise further. On trade, a top economy official said Mexico is pushing to raise the Mexican-made share of electronics exports from roughly 8% to as much as 40%, as talks with Washington continue amid the Trump administration’s decision not to renew USMCA in its current form.

In other business news from the week, Lego announced a $400 million investment in Nuevo León expected to create 1,300 jobs by 2029, Guanajuato drew $630 million in data center investment with a third facility under construction, and Mexico City, Querétaro and Nuevo León topped IMCO’s 2026 state competitiveness ranking, with Guerrero ranked least competitive for the second straight year.

Elsewhere in Mexico

Looking ahead

Hurricane Polo, having spared Mexico’s mainland Pacific coast a direct hit, is now forecast to approach Baja California Sur as a hurricane early next week, with life-threatening flooding, mudslides and dangerous surf possible along that coast. Unresolved questions remain over whether the fuel-trafficking investigation in Guanajuato will widen further, and the next round of Mexico-U.S. trade talks is tentatively expected in October after being postponed this week. Sheinbaum’s November trip to China for the APEC summit will also be a marker to watch as Mexico works to diversify its trade relationships ahead of further USMCA negotiations.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Britain Revises Its Cuba Travel Advice: Bring Cash, Expect Blackouts
World.content:

CUBA · TRAVEL

Key Facts — The country Cuba, a Caribbean island of under 10 million people, has long drawn British and European holidaymakers. Its foreign arrivals fell 64.4 percent in the first eight months of 2026.

— The background Since 11 February 2026, the UK Foreign Office has advised against all but essential travel to Cuba, as fuel shortages hit flights, power and water.

— Why now On Friday 25 September it published a full review, with changes throughout its Cuba pages.

— What happened The warning level is unchanged. The revised text covers frequent protests, likely further grid collapses, one working terminal at Havana airport and no foreign bank cards.

— The numbers Foreign currency above US$5,000 must be declared on arrival. An online arrival form must be filed within 72 hours before entry.

— What it means for you Bring cash for the whole stay plus emergencies, check your insurance covers Cuba, and avoid protests.

— Still open When suspended airlines return, and whether the advice eases or tightens at the next review.

Britain’s Foreign Office revised its Cuba travel advice on Friday, reviewing it “for accuracy with changes made throughout”. It still advises against all but essential travel to the island, the level it set in February.

The new text is a blunt guide to daily life in Cuba’s crisis. It warns of frequent protests, power cuts, one working airport terminal in Havana and a cash-only economy for visitors.
