“He is not able to move around much, but the greatest thing is that he is still with us,” she said. “So many persons who took ill after my husband are not with us. But to God be the glory, he is still in the land of the living.”

Mrs Laing said Lt. Stitchie’s GoFundMe page remains active and has helped ease the cost of his prolonged care, although donations are intermittent.

“It is still a bit of a struggle, but every now and then, people will donate so to God be the glory,” she said.

A former athlete and schoolteacher, Lieutenant Stitchie (real name Cleve Laing) cut his musical teeth on the competitive sound system circuit in Spanish Town, his hometown, during the early 1980s alongside other aspiring artistes such as Papa San, Wickerman, and Major Worries.

In 1986, he got his mainstream breakthrough with the hilarious Wear Yuh Size, followed by Natty Dread, another rib-tickling hit.

He signed to Atlantic Records in 1988 and released three albums for that label, including the well-received Wild Jamaican Romances.

In 1997, Lt Stitchie became a born-again Christian and has since recorded a number of inspirational albums and songs.

World.title: Between horror and hope
World.content:
Patients seated in Kingston Public Hospital’s morning clinic waiting area at 11:30 am last Tuesday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

HOSPITAL horror stories are all too familiar for Jamaicans, and though the age-old issues of long wait times, lack of resources, and poor service appear unyielding and have only led to more frustration when accessing the country’s public health-care system, there appears to be at least a glimmer of hope.

While Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton continues to highlight increased government spending in the public health sector, Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes has argued that there are major disparities in access and quality between the wealthy and the poor.

Last week, this Jamaica Observer reporter visited public health facilities in Kingston, St Andrew, and St Catherine — namely University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), Kingston Public Hospital (KPH), Spanish Town Hospital, and Linstead Public Hospital — to find out from patients whether public health care reliably serves them, who are the ones depending on it.

“I would like to see a total revamp of what is going on here, and the health-care system,” said Norman James, a patient at KPH who was sitting under a tent with people awaiting blood tests last Tuesday.

James said he got out of bed at 5:30 am to ensure he was on time for his 9:00 am appointment.

When the Sunday Observer arrived at the hospital at approximately 11:30 am, he had already been seen by a doctor and was waiting to leave the compound. But James said his experiences at KPH were often markedly different.

The 70-year-old recalled one admission to the hospital, which saw him waiting days before being properly accommodated on a ward.

“I’ve come to this hospital a couple times to be admitted, and let me tell you, that’s a whole other story. I came in here the Friday night, and Saturday passed and it was Sunday before I could get a bed,” he said.

His concerns also extended beyond waiting times. Pointing to the wheelchair in which he was sitting, James said its wheels lacked rubber, leaving only the metal rim to support him.

“Where are the funds going? They don’t have enough beds, they don’t have enough chairs, fans, and their wheelchairs don’t have rubber on them. They can do better,” he argued.

Across from him, a woman who asked not to be named, said she had been waiting since 7:00 am for medical attention and that her doctor had still not arrived.

She also complained about limited seating and the intense heat in the waiting area, while another woman said the lack of basic amenities needed for patient comfort often made hospital visits unpleasant.

This was also true for Kelly-Ann Dwyer, a patient at Spanish Town Hospital who was recently transferred from KPH, due to what she said was a three-year waiting list for a surgery on her leg that has been broken since February.

She told the Sunday Observer that, while she was more comfortable at the St Catherine hospital, it was not because of the facilities, but rather the dedication and compassion shown by the medical staff.

According to her, Spanish Town Hospital is still lacking in many critical areas.

“I find that there aren’t certain types of specialists here; there are no cardiologists, no neurosurgeons. I also find that the Drug Serv [pharmacy] doesn’t have much medication — no high blood pressure tablets, no sugar [diabetes] tablets. They just basically have the minimal stuff — cold medicine, itch cream, and stuff like that. There isn’t much to work with, and if you’re going to do surgery, more than likely you must buy some of the things. There aren’t many things for the doctors to work with,” she added.

But while Dwyer was fond of the service she received from medical practitioners, another client of the hospital was having “one of the worst experiences ever” at the facility.

The woman, who asked not to be named, was visibly upset as she told the Sunday Observer that she brought a family member experiencing a mild stroke to the hospital and he was left to sit in a wheelchair overnight.

“Tell you the truth, if I get sick, God forbid, I don’t want to come here. They should do better,” she said.

Speaking on the wider health-care system, she also highlighted high medication costs, though she noted that she does not have health insurance and is not the holder of a National Health Fund (NHF) card.

“Sometimes you have to just buy what you can afford, and in-between that, to make it serve you a little longer, you ease off of it and take your herbal medicine; boil your bush and drink it,” she said.

Her comments come against the backdrop of concerns raised by Tufton about the standard of care being delivered in the public health system.

The minister said last month that more than 1,000 complaints recorded through the Ministry of Health and Wellness’s Client Care Connect system pointed to problems involving communication, professional conduct, and patients’ overall experience.

He said the ministry would intensify efforts to expose system failures and hold negligent health workers accountable, while emphasising the need for patients to be treated with compassion, empathy, dignity, respect, and fairness.

Tufton also announced the rebuilding and modernisation of 101 health centres across five western parishes. Furthermore, he has spoken of major hospital redevelopments, including at Spanish Town Hospital and Cornwall Regional Hospital.

At Linstead Hospital, however, several patients were more than pleased with the facility and its staff.

They sang praises about the “always clean” compound, compassionate doctors and nurses, and the life-saving procedures they’ve received at the hospital.

“I’ve been admitted here more than six times. Last year I was admitted because of a blood clot in my chest. Two weeks after, I got a stroke and was stuck one place, and I’m telling you, they really took care of me. I couldn’t walk or talk, I couldn’t do anything. You see even the ladies who took care of me? Oh God man, they treat me so good,” said one woman.

Others agreed, noting that they’ve had similar experiences. While they expressed hope that the hospital’s capacity to handle specialised procedures would improve, it was their belief that the standard of care at the Type C facility is exemplary.

At UHWI, Errol Campbell sat among patients who had filled the hospital’s halls for their morning clinic visit, many having arrived before 8:30 am.

Campbell, who has been a patient at the hospital for more than three years and has undergone three surgeries there, had nothing but praise for the facility and its staff.

“It’s a bit expensive, but the care and the service I received with my surgeries were worth it. All my surgeries were life-threatening. One was cancer, and they stopped it in its track before it spread to my blood. The other was a brain surgery. So, I’m just really pleased with the service I’ve gotten here,” he said.

Campbell said clinic wait times vary, but he was not particularly bothered by delays, explaining that he expected a longer process on busier days.

“The health-care sector outside of the hospital is slack. To me, the treatment here is the best you’ll get. I don’t have any troubles sourcing the medication either; yes, it’s expensive, but I can access it. So I really and truly don’t have any problems,” he said.

Inside the hospital’s registration room, however, 86-year-old Herman Perkins offered another assessment.

“The University Hospital is not for the poor, it’s for the rich,” he said, pulling from his bag a list on which he had recorded the costs of medication and services from his previous visit. Perkins said he had paid $34,000 out of pocket.

“The Government not helping the poor. I’m telling you, it’s all just talk… So, the whole situation is bad,” he said.

The differing experiences described by patients paint a picture of the broader debate about the state of Jamaica’s public health-care system.

Last Sunday, Dr Dawes was scathing in his comments on the public health system.

“Under this Government, one Jamaica means having money [so] you get to live. In the other Jamaica, nobody listens to you unless you go on TikTok Live. Same flesh and blood, same country, same taxes — two different Jamaicas,” he said while addressing the public session of the People’s National Party’s 88th Annual Conference at Independence Park in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland.

He questioned whether increased Government spending on health was translating into better conditions for patients, saying, “They love to tell you that the budget has grown, but I ask them, show me the money! Walk into any hospital and show me the money that you have put into health, because we are seeing the same crowded emergency rooms, the same broken down theatres and elevators, the same broken down machines. The care went down when the funding went up,” he alleged.

“So don’t ask them what they spent, ask them what they built, and show me the money. Show me the [intensive care units] without the ventilators and show me the money. Show me the ambulances in the garages and show me the money. Show me the $28 million, 10 years later, no [Cornwall] Regional Hospital, still not functional, and show me the money,” he said.

World.title: Dry run
World.content:
According to the latest update from the National Water Commission, 99 of its 450 water supply systems are being affected by drought conditions.

WATER suppliers are struggling to keep pace with a surge in demand amid drought conditions, with one Manchester-based operator describing the current situation as the busiest he’s had in his 15 years of business.

Rohan Smith, owner of Rohan’s Water Truck in Mandeville, said the demand has become so intense that customers are calling at least once every day to refill.

“It’s really overwhelming. It’s the craziest I’ve ever seen it. It’s like everybody wants water every day. No matter how you give them water today, by tomorrow they [call] back. I’ve been in the business for 15 years, and this is the craziest I’ve ever seen it,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

His experience reflects the pressure placed on alternative water suppliers as Jamaica continues to grapple with drought conditions and restrictions on water use.

According to the latest update from the National Water Commission (NWC), 99 of its 450 water supply systems are being affected by drought conditions, representing approximately 22 per cent of systems nationally.

Additionally, water levels at two of the country’s main storage sources are also low. Hermitage Dam stood at 40.3 per cent as of September 25, while the Mona Reservoir stood at 34.1 per cent.

Smith said the situation in Mandeville is being compounded by the number of trucks competing for access to NWC loading bays.

“You find that when you go to get a load it takes forever. You have to wait an hour or hour and a half just to get one load of water, so you can’t move as fast as you want to, but the demand is very high so we can’t supply our customers. I am one of the truckers who supply our hospitals with water, and so I have to treat them as a priority. I have to make sure they get water on a regular basis, and that’s really hard to do,” said Smith.

He shared that he operates two trucks, each with a capacity of about 4,000 gallons of water. He said he often supplies hospitals with two loads per day, and is sometimes even on standby if supply becomes critical. According to Smith, on average, he refills his trucks 15 to 30 times a week.

He said the demand is so high that he sometimes has to defer customers when they request water. He said the surge has also forced him to concentrate his operations in Manchester.

“I get calls from out of parish, but I can’t leave Mandeville to go out of parish to do work when work is here…It’s a lot of trucks, and we still can’t keep up,” said Smith.

Although demand is high, Smith said fuel prices are eating into profits. He told the Sunday Observer that filling up on fuel for one of his trucks can cost more than $10,000 per day, depending on where he purchases fuel and how often the motor vehicles are used.

Smith said access to drivers is also a main concern that is affecting his ability to expand his business to meet the demand.

“The drivers are not reliable. I don’t know if it’s the generation or what, but these drivers nowadays, they start work this week, and they do good, next week they mess up, the other week they don’t want to work. They don’t try to care for the vehicle, and they always want to be speeding to prove to their friends that they can drive, and it’s just all kinds of stuff.

“It’s hard for you to buy a five- or seven-million-dollar vehicle just for them to try and prove to their friends that they can drive and mash up your vehicle; that doesn’t make sense for me,” he said, noting that other water trucking companies are having similar experiences.

Despite the mounting operating cost, Smith said he recognises the importance of the service and will continue to provide it to those in need.

“Water is life, and people need water. There is no substitute for water, and the people need the water, so we just have to price them as best as possible,” he said, expressing hope that fuel prices will eventually decline.

While the demand for trucked water is not as high in Montego Bay, St James, one water truck operator said the cost of fuel has changed how he operates his business.

“That [fuel cost] is the reason why I don’t really move on the house-to-house calls, because it nuh make no sense I drive to fill up $650 [worth of water] at this house and then do another $650 at another house. Fuel cost is too high to do that. We only drive out for requests for 2,000 gallons of water and up,” the operator told the Sunday Observer.

He noted that, currently, he mainly supplies hotels and health-care facilities with water, banking on contracts with government agencies to make the trips worthwhile.

The operator shared that his trucks can carry up to 4,000 gallons of water and are sterilised, in keeping with local regulations. However, he expressed concern that not all water trucking companies are compliant.

“They say they want us to sterilise our trucks and do all the necessary things to keep up with the specifications of the Government. You sterilise your truck, and then you have all four or five trucks just running freely without any sterilisation. It’s a double standard. It nuh make no sense they tell us to regulate our trucks and then we spend so much money to regulate the trucks and then you have other truckers just running free,” he said, expressing frustration.

He shared that he spends around $50,000 to sterilise his trucks so that he can utilise the NWC loading bays in the parish, a cost he said some truckers do not pay while still reaping the profits.

“The water system needs to be properly regulated,” he advocated.

Meanwhile, one water purification company in St Catherine is feeling the effects of inconsistent supply from the NWC.

Shaneil Brown, an employee at Kleen Water Purification Company, said the demand for water is higher than usual as customers seek to beat the heat.

“There is a huge demand with people wanting water. It’s higher than normal, but it is expected because we are in drought and heat conditions, so people run out of water quicker,” she told the Sunday

Observer.

Brown said the company normally obtains water from the NWC, but fluctuations in supply and water pressure can create challenges.

“From the other day, you have times when the water pressure will be low, so that impacts business, and so we have to find ways around it because we are a water company so we have to have water,” said Brown.

She said, in these instances, they have to rely on water from trucking companies, many of which are reliable, but it comes at an added expense to the company.

“We are hopeful that the conditions can improve, but we are grateful for the business that the drought brings,” she said.

World.title: ‘Legends never die’
World.content:
June Isaacs (right), widow of Gregory Isaacs, addresses the audience at the Excellence In Music Ceremony held at Courtleigh Auditorium in New Kingston on September 15. The singer earned some 10 awards posthumously on the night, some of which are seen on display in the background.

Sixteen years after his death, Gregory Isaacs’ legacy continues to grow.

At the September 15 Excellence In Music Ceremony at the Courtleigh Auditorium in New Kingston, the singer received 10 awards.

The accolades — which included a platinum disc from the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) for Simply Red’s cover of his song Night Nurse — were collected by his wife June.

That single, released in 1982, also earned a silver disc from the BPI for sales of over 200,000 in the UK. The album of the same name got similar recognition for selling over 60,000 copies in that country.

June Isaacs also received certificates for four of her husband’s albums which were nominated for Best Reggae Album Grammys. Those are Mr Cool, Private and Confidential, Brand New Me, and Gregory Isaacs and King Isaac — Isaacs Meets Isaac.

The ceremony, staged by London-based Back 2 Da Future Music Ltd, issued 95 discs and certificates to artistes, musicians, producers, and engineers.

Kennedy Mensah, head of that organisation, spoke of Isaacs’ enduring popularity in the UK, where he died in October 2010 at age 59.

“Gregory is a legend, and legends never die, their legends just grow,” he said.

In May 2025, The Cool Ruler: The Musical, a stage production based on Isaacs’ life, had a successful six-show run in the UK. Terrence Wallen, the British artiste who played him, performed several of Isaacs’ songs at the Excellence In Music Ceremony.

Known as The Cool Ruler, Gregory Isaacs was from Denham Town in West Kingston. He broke through in the 1970s with songs such as Love is Overdue, All I Have is Love, Slave Driver, Soon Forward, and Tune In.

— Howard Campbell

World.title: Jamaica wants its 8,000 artefacts back
World.content:
Dr Danny Zborover (foreground), provides context and details of artefacts seen in the Americas Section of the British Museum to Jamaica’s Culture Minister Olivia “Babsy” Grange and a Jamaican delegation during a visit to the museum on September 10, 2026. Dr Zborover is the curator and head of the Americas Section.

THE British Museum has approximately 8,000 artefacts of Jamaican origin that have been identified in its vast collection of objects, and Culture Minister Olivia “Babsy” Grange says the Government is working at having them returned to the island.

Of that number, 7,000 pieces are held in the Americas Section, including the carpenter’s Mountain collection, Grange told the Jamaica Observer on Saturday after updating Parliament last Tuesday on her trip to London earlier this month to file a petition to King Charles III on the legality of chattel enslavement of Jamaica’s African ancestors.

“The holdings encompass archaeological materials, including Taíno artefacts, animal bones and shells, as well as ethnographic and historical objects,” Grange explained.

She said the objects associated with Taíno culture include sculptures (cemis), stone and shell tools (axes, celts), shell work (jewellery), animal bones, beads, pots and cooking tools, other ceramics, two small pieces of gold, basketry, as well as prints and coins.

Asked if there was an indication when the pieces were taken from Jamaica, Grange said, “The materials were acquired largely during the colonial period, with most collected before Jamaica’s Independence in 1962.”

She pointed to a Cedar Valley carving that was donated to the British Museum in 1757 by James Theobald; the Carpenter’s Mountain collection of Taíno wooden sculptures, which is believed to have been taken in 1792, exhibited at the Society of Antiquaries of London on April 11, 1799 and acquired by the British Museum between 1799 and 1803; as well as a collection acquired by the British Museum in 1969 following archaeological investigations at Jamaican caves, middens, and rock art sites, including White Marl, Breadnut Gully, Jacks Hill, and Rio Nuevo. That collection includes ceramics, animal bones, stone tools, and other archaeological materials.

“These collections reflect different periods and circumstances of collecting and acquisition,” Grange told the Sunday Observer.

She added that the Jamaican artefacts — notably botanical specimens and natural history items — are also part of the Sir Hans Sloane collection, which are the founding core of the British Museum, the Natural History Museum, and the British Library.

“Sloane arrived in Port Royal, Jamaica, on December 19, 1687. Over 50 years his collection grew enormously and first spawned what we loosely reference as the Sloane’s Museum in his home — a major attraction of its time which [pulled] a stream of distinguished visitors from Britain and other countries,” Grange said, pointing out that the collection includes 2,000 coins and medals; 50,000 books, prints, and manuscripts; a herbarium of 334 volumes of dried plants from around the world; and many more antiquities.

Biographical information on Sir Hans states that by his death in 1753 he had collected more than 71,000 items.

“Ultimately, he offered the collection to Britain for the sum of £20,000, which was purchased by the Government with money raised by a lotter creating the British Museum at Bloomsbury and later its offspring, the Natural History Museum at South Kensington established in 1881,” Grange added.

Britain’s Department for Culture, Media, and Sport (DCMS) has reported that 6.5 million people visited the British Museum for the 2025/26 and 2024/25 financial years.

In April 2026 the DCMS reported that its 15 sponsored museums and galleries had together surpassed a £1-billion milestone in collective self-generated income in 2024/25, a first since it started keeping records.

The £1.3-billion total, it said, was an increase of almost 2.5 times that of the previous year, when adjusted for inflation. The department attributed much of the increase to the British Museum, which alone accounted for 81 per cent of the figure.

The museum, which is supported by government grants and self-generated commercial and fund-raising activities, documents the story of human culture from its beginnings to the present. Its permanent collection of eight million artefacts is said to be the largest in the world.

Last Tuesday, in her report to Parliament, Grange said the Jamaica delegation also used the trip to London to strengthen engagement with the British Museum, which has allowed local teams to inspect its inventory.

“The relationship has improved and we are making inroads. There is greater willingness to discuss plans for collaboration, which we believe will assist to get these priceless artefacts back home where they belong, to the Jamaica people,” Grange told the House.

Asked to expand on the effort to have the artefacts returned, Grange told the Sunday Observer that “the museum has cited the British Museum Act 1963 as a constraint to repatriation, as it prevents the museum from giving away, selling, or returning objects from its collection, except under the specific conditions set out in sections 3 and 5 of the Act.”

However, she disclosed that consideration is also being given to developing a memorandum of understanding between the United Kingdom and Jamaica to address access, visibility, and other areas to be agreed.

“The British Museum has also demonstrated openness to professional engagement and has extended invitations to participate in collaborative research,” she said.

Grange also said that following a visit to the UK in May this year of two Jamaican experts, which was funded by the British High Commission here, “the British Museum offered to facilitate a virtual viewing of selected Jamaican objects in its collection, including the Carpenter’s Mountain collection, several other Taíno objects, including celts, pestles, bowls, and two small pieces of gold”.

She said that a viewing held on September 16, 2026 brought together 47 participants from the Institute of Jamaica, Jamaica National Heritage Trust, The University of the West Indies, and the Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport, providing an opportunity for Jamaican experts to examine objects they had never previously seen.

“To date, including select officials from the delegation I led, only under 10 Jamaicans have had the opportunity to view these objects in person, all during 2026,” the minister told the Sunday Observer.

Asked where the Jamaican artefacts would be housed if the repatriation efforts prove successful, Grange said: “The space to house them would be the National Gallery of Jamaica, where another Taíno collection from Aboukir, St Ann, also resides and is on display.”

World.title: ‘#1 PRESIDENT’
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (left) greets interim Reggae Boyz Head Coach Rudolph Speid (right) while Jamaica Football Federation President Michael Ricketts looks on ahead of Jamaica’s Concacaf Nations League game against Guatemala at the National Stadium on Friday night. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

The Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) looks set to back Gianni Infantino at the FIFA Presidential Elections next year following positive talks during his one-day visit to the island.

Infantino’s trip was highlighted by his attendance at the Reggae Boyz’s 3-2 win over Guatemala in the Concacaf Nations League at the National Stadium on Friday.

Infantino’s brief visit comes just weeks after JFF President Michael Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer that he would personally support Infantino and criticised UEFA, which called for his resignation.

Infantino is under pressure following his unsuccessful plan to sell stakes in FIFA competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cup, to private investors.

Infantino, who left Kingston on Saturday morning, is expected to visit Antigua and Barbuda, the British Virgins Islands, and St Kitts and Nevis over the next few days as he reportedly seeks support for his bid to remain FIFA President, with nominations set to close in November and elections set for March.

It’s his second visit to the Caribbean in two months after attending the Caribbean Football Union Presidents’ Meeting in the Dominican Republic. Concacaf President Victor Montagliani (also a FIFA vice-president) had requested that he not attend the meeting.

The Guardian reported earlier this month that the Caribbean has been given a separate FIFA administrative arrangement under Infantino, which his critics view as an attempt to weaken the group opposing him.

Ricketts told the Sunday Observer that the decision to vote for Infantino would ultimately be made by the board, and it’s understood that there is no opposition to that position, particularly given the warm welcome he received.

Infantino arrived in Jamaica on Friday afternoon and made his way to the National Stadium following a brief stop at S Hotel in New Kingston.

He and his delegation from FIFA were accompanied by Ricketts. Infantino and Ricketts watched the Jamaica and Guatemala warm-up sessions ahead of kick-off and greeted several players and staff, including Reggae Boyz interim Head Coach Rudolph Speid.

During a photo and video session prior to match time, Infantino did not field questions about the reasons for his visit or FIFA matters, including his re-election.

However, he told the Observer that he “was enjoying Jamaica very much” and called Ricketts the “number one president”.

Ricketts told the Observer he was “excited” and it was a “great achievement to have the FIFA president here”.

Infantino spent the duration of the match in the Royal Box in the Grandstand, where he sat with Sports Minister Olivia Grange and engaged in several discussions.

It’s understood that one of those conversations centred on Jamaica’s bid to co-host the 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup, with the official announcement expected in November.

At the end of the match, Infantino continued making his rounds and had a short conversation with Reggae Boyz captain and goalkeeper Andre Blake. Congratulating Blake on the victory, Infantino said, “See you at the World Cup,” referring to Jamaica’s imminent push to qualify for 2030 edition after missing out on last summer’s World Cup in the USA, Mexico, and Canada.

Infantino and his delegation were then treated to a private dinner session at the One Park Restaurant and Lounge in Kingston, which included several JFF board members and staff.

Infantino, who has served as FIFA president since 2016, previously visited Jamaica in 2018 during a FIFA Executive Summit in Montego Bay.

World.title: Rum Tour
World.content:
This summer, 12 international journalists arrived in Jamaica with an unusual assignment: Drink rum, listen to music, eat extraordinarily well, and follow a story that began here more than half-a-century ago. They came for Crossfire Hurricane, the Jamaican rum created in celebration of the Rolling Stones’ relationship with the island. What they found, and subsequently told the world, was a much bigger story about Jamaica.

As the brand’s Jamaica-based consultants, our decision was clear. If journalists were flying here to understand Crossfire Hurricane, we would give them more than a bottle. We wanted them to understand why the rum had to be Jamaican. As summer draws to a close, their stories have appeared in Rolling Stone Germany, The Independent, Time Out, Clash, Wonderland and Maxim. Whilst each writer found a different angle, one protagonist kept appearing beside the rum and The Rolling Stones: Jamaica!

St Ann Had to Be Home



Kingston would have been easier. The Stones came here in 1972 to record Goats Head Soup at Dynamic Sounds, beginning a relationship with Jamaica that would stretch across decades. For Keith Richards especially, that relationship became personal. He established a home in the hills above Ocho Rios, where his friendship with the Rastafarian musicians of nearby Steer Town grew through years of reasoning, drumming and recording. Those relationships eventually produced the Wingless Angels recordings. Decades later, some of those same musicians would become part of the story we were bringing the journalists to St Ann to experience. Grammy-winning record producer Wayne Jobson recalls Richards describing their hypnotic Nyabinghi sound as “marrow music” — music you feel in your bones.

That history meant this couldn’t simply be a Jamaican rum trip. A meaningful part of the story belonged specifically to St Ann.

Jamaica Inn: More Than a Hotel



If St Ann had to be home, we needed the right home base, and Jamaica Inn was a natural fit. Opened in 1950, its private beach, discreet service and refusal of unnecessary spectacle have preserved something increasingly rare in luxury hospitality: Personality. For four days, it housed our journalists, the Crossfire Hurricane team and Global Rum Ambassador Ian Burrell. More importantly, it gave the experience a setting that felt connected to the story we were telling.

On the final evening, at a long table by the sea, Herbie Miller of the Jamaica Music Museum spoke about rum’s complicated history, including the people who cut the cane and drank the roughest part of what they produced while the refined spirit created wealth elsewhere. Then Eric Donaldson, whose

Cherry Oh Baby the Rolling Stones covered in 1976, stood and sang it unaccompanied. It was unpretentious, intimate and incredibly memorable. There was mannish water on the table, served alongside traditional elevated dishes, Crossfire Hurricane in the glasses and the Caribbean Sea a few feet away.

This was Jamaica!

A Jamaican Story Travelling Outward



What the journalists chose to write about matters more than the coverage itself. They wrote about Jamaica Inn, Stush in the Bush, Miss T’s Kitchen and Worthy Park. They wrote about Eric Donaldson, the Wingless Angels, Jamaican food, music, history and rum. Jamaica’s opportunity is considerably bigger than selling another bottle of rum or another hotel room. The value lies in connecting the rum to the people who make it, a hotel to the history surrounding it, a meal to the land it came from and a song to the community that created it.

That is where our work meets: At the intersection of spirits, hospitality, brands and culture. After all, the best Jamaican brand-building happens when Jamaica becomes the story.

World.title: ‘You must die!’
World.content:
Late pastor of Pathways International Restoration Ministries Kevin Smith

A police sergeant testified on Friday that he opened gunfire on a knife-wielding male attacker at Pathways International Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James, after the man, who hurled death threats, refused to comply with law enforcers’ orders to drop his weapon.

The cop, who was the fourth witness in the murder trial of Andre Ruddock at the Home Circuit Court in downtown Kingston, said that the knife-wielding man was rushing from the church towards the police and using threatening language.

Ruddock is being tried in relation to the October 17, 2021 killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner, whose throat was cut, allegedly by the accused, at the church in what has been described as a human sacrifice ritual. Ruddock was said to have been acting on the instructions of the pastor of the church, Kevin Smith.

Smith died a few days later in a motor vehicle crash in St Catherine while being transported to Kingston to be charged in relation to the incident.

On Thursday, another member of the constabulary testified that Smith had instructed members of the church to kill the police if they gained access to the compound.

On Friday, the second police witness told the court that he and members of his team were attacked by the male member of the church and because he feared for his life, he was forced to discharge multiple rounds into the upper body of the attacker. His colleague also fired at the man.

The witness said that the members of the police team did not enter the church compound via the gate at the front, but had to skilfully scale a wall, topped with barbed wire, at the back of the premises to gain access. The policeman said that it was while the members of the team were going over the wall, one after the other, that the man with the knife rushed to them.

“I was in the process of assisting members of the team to get past the barbed wires. He spoke to me, and I turned around and looked in the direction of the church.

“I looked to the left of a boardwalk where I saw a man of dark complexion, slim build, about 5 feet 7 inches in height. He was dressed in a red shirt and a pair of white and grey trousers. I saw this man with what appeared to be a silver-looking knife in his right hand and this man seemed to be disturbed by the presence of the police on the church compound,” the cop shared.

He said that the man was looking in the direction of the police who were coming over the wall and was pointing the knife furiously at them.

“It was as if he was trying to say something. He was agitated, moving from one side to the other. At the time when I saw this man, I did not see anyone else. I shouted out to the man, saying, ‘Police! Put down the knife!’ He did not put the knife down. The man then started to run towards me and shouted, ‘You must die!’ repeatedly,” the cop said.

He told the court that when he first shouted to the man, he was about 33 metres away from the him. The policeman said he made numerous attempts to get the man to stop advancing towards him.

“He did not obey the command. He continued to advance towards me with the knife and on reaching about three meters away, he put his right hand in the air with the knife in a stabbing position. I moved two steps backwards and then to the right. I then pointed my M16 rifle to the chest area of the man and I discharged three rounds because I was fearful for my life and the life of my colleagues who were beside me. I also heard loud explosions to my right. A constable was positioned to my right and the loud explosions sounded like gunshots. It came from the constable’s rifle. The man [the attacker] fell to the ground,” the witness testified.

He further said that following the shooting, all seven members of his team had got over the wall, through the barbed wire, after which the knife was removed from the man’s palm.

“We tried to assist him to the hospital but the front gate was locked and the service vehicle could not enter the premises. I saw a few people on the verandah section of the church and they went inside of the church. I then contacted the police emergency communications centre and I informed the monitor at the Area One control centre about the incident. I also requested from the monitor additional personnel to come to the scene,” he said.

The cop told the court that he then instructed two of his team members to cover the rear of the building and another set was sent to monitor the front.

“I, along with one member, went to the top of the church building to also give coverage. I walked towards the front of the building where I could see the gate and the roadway. I could see persons on the inside of the church premises. I saw someone close to the front gate, kneeling behind a column, covered with a white sheet and it seemed as if this person was hiding,” he said.

“Whilst on the top of the building I went to the right and I saw someone motionless lying face down and covered with white cloth. I also saw what appeared to be blood leaking from the neck area to the head. I saw more police arriving on the scene, as well as members of the Jamaica Defence Force. I shouted out to them and told them not to climb over the gate because I did not know if that person who was kneeling was armed,” he said, explaining that instructions were given to them on how to safely enter the compound.

World.title: Europe’s divided conservatives launch 2029 plan to beat far right
World.content:
“The main polarization across the continent in many national elections, and certainly in the European election 2029 … will be the anti-European populists against the EPP parties,” said EPP vice-chair and Romanian prime minister nominee Siegfried Mureșan.

Anything beyond the “battle” between EPP and the far right “will be of secondary importance,” echoed the conservative group’s spokesperson Pedro López de Pablo. “Because they are not in government, they can promise the earth. Faced with that kind of rhetoric, we need to think of which alternatives we can offer to the people.”

Siegfried Mureșan participates in a meeting in Brussels on June 26, 2025. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

With the European Parliament not yet halfway through its current term, the task force marks an unusually early start to the EPP’s 2029 election preparations — and underscores the urgency party leaders feel as far-right parties gain ground across the bloc.

Led by Spanish MEP Esteban González Pons, the task force will help draft the party’s final electoral program. Talks are due to start at an October retreat in Sicily and continue through next spring’s EPP congress in Rome.

EPP lawmakers are already wrestling with the choice ahead.

“This is the political history, the historical dilemma EPP needs to decide — it needs to be clear and it needs be truthful for the voters, are we center right or are we another right-wing party?” said Finnish EPP lawmaker Sirpa Pietikäinen.

World.title: EU is drawing up membership action plans for most promising candidates
World.content:
The roadmaps will make clearer exactly what’s expected of each candidate country, one of the officials said, as well as create obligations for current members, which need to give their blessing for the process to go ahead. The plans also set rough dates for when groups of reforms, known as negotiating “clusters,” will be formally completed — major milestones on the path to membership.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pledged targeted support for the candidate countries “that have made most progress” during her State of the Union speech earlier in September.

However, other candidate countries at an earlier stage in the process, like Kosovo, North Macedonia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina would not be offered the roadmaps at this stage, the officials confirmed. Nor would Georgia, Turkey or Serbia, which have seen their applications grind to a halt over concerns about democratic and judicial backsliding.

A spokesperson for the Commission confirmed that the new roadmaps “will provide a pathway toward the conclusion of the accession negotiations. They will set out a clear priority list: timelines and deliverables to help the most advanced candidates complete the necessary reforms.”

‘Geopolitical imperative’

EU leaders are increasingly looking to other pro-trade democracies, particularly in their neighborhood, amid tensions with partners like the U.S., hostile practices from China and threats from Russia. Officials are concerned that joining the EU takes too long, exposing would-be new members to disillusionment or pressure from rivals not to pursue membership.

The move comes as the EU’s “pre-enlargement” policies undergo a separate overhaul. Candidate countries need to be offered a better path toward “gradual integration” into the bloc, officials believe, one that would use economic benefits and access to joint projects to reward them for progress. That policy review, led by von der Leyen’s close adviser Alexandre Adam, is to be presented to top officials Oct. 6; it is designed to keep them on the path toward the EU while their applications unfold.

World.title: Independent wins Kraków mayorship first round, as far right sees setback for Tusk
World.content:
For Gibała, Sunday’s result gives him another shot at winning an office he came within a few thousand votes of securing in 2024, when he lost to Miszalski.

Miszalski subsequently faced mounting local opposition, including over Kraków’s clean-transport zone, before being recalled. Opposition parties, including Law and Justice (PiS) and parties on the far right, presented that result as evidence of weakening support for Tusk’s government ahead of the fall 2027 general election. An effort is underway to hold a similar referendum in the capital Warsaw, targeting Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, also from Tusk’s party

Sunday’s exit poll had the PiS candidate, Michał Drewnicki, in third with 19.6 percent, which would mean he misses the runoff. Nationally, however, the Tusk-led coalition may not hold onto power, with polls suggesting the PiS and the far right could form a majority.

Earlier statements from parties opposed to Tusk’s coalition indicated some could back Gibała against Piątkowska in the second round.

Turnout Sunday was 41.9%.

World.title: Britain to keep tariffs on Chinese EVs ‘under review,’ UK business chief says
World.content:
EU capitals are currently considering whether U.K. auto exports should qualify for preferential treatment under the Buy European program, as Brussels moves to protect its member economies from U.S. tariffs, China’s manufacturing might and an influx of cheap EVs subsidized by Beijing.

European Union lawmakers and officials are preparing new legislation to deny overseas manufacturers access to subsidies, tax incentives and public procurement deals. The bloc slapped double-digit tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024.

But Reynolds said the U.K. government’s calculation on whether to impose tariffs differed from that of the EU.

“We are an export-orientated sector. So clearly, you shouldn’t do anything that risks your export markets, and you always have to take heed of retaliatory action if you put tariffs in place,” he said Sunday, calling the U.K.’s position on Chinese EVs “finely balanced.”

Cutting the U.K. out of Brussels’ new industrial program “wouldn’t be to the benefit of Europe,” Reynolds added.

The Made in Europe push is supposed to be “about greater resilience, greater autonomy for European industry in the face of very significant pressures from both the U.S. and China,” Reynolds added. “Now, if that is the objective, it stands to reason that the U.K., that’s the second-biggest economy in Europe, should be a part of that.”

World.title: UK business minister warns potential US diesel export ban ‘significant concern’
World.content:
The U.K. receives around one-sixth of its diesel from the U.S. and would be one of the countries most exposed to an export ban. However, Reynolds cautioned that it is important to “make a distinction between the statements and what is actually being proposed by the U.S.”

Donald Trump has said he is in favor of proposals to bar American diesel exports against a backdrop of high prices for American drivers and farmers, and with midterm elections looming. A 90-day ban has been considered, along with more limited voluntary export restrictions.

“Clearly something like that … would be a significant concern to the U.K,” Reynolds said when asked about the prospect of a full ban. “Our resilience comes from a diverse supply in a whole range of areas and fuel is no different to that.”

Reynolds is the latest senior European politician to voice concern over potential diesel export restrictions. On Thursday French President Emmanuel Macron said he had urged Trump against it, warning it would be a bad idea “not just for the rest of the world, but for the U.S. economy as well.”

World.title: EU rejoin push risks causing uncertainty, warns business secretary
World.content:
He backed the U.K. government's current approach to the European Union, warning people would be "misplaced" to seek to return to a customs union. "Look at the arrangements we've already got," he said. "You don't add a lot more to it through a customs union ... and you'd be having to, you know, frankly, accept a whole range of alignment on regulatory issues," he added.

Reynolds comments come days after former Prime Minister Tony Blair published a paper calling for the U.K. to rejoin a "reformed" union within the next decade. Burnham left the door open to putting a rejoin pledge in Labour's next election manifesto when speaking to journalists during a trip to New York earlier this month.

Asked if the U.K. should rejoin the EU within his lifetime, Reynolds said: "What will Europe be in the future? I mean, there are clearly very challenging politics in Germany. It's very clear that the French presidential election could be different. I honestly don't know if you will evolve in one direction or the other. So I can't really give you an answer to that."

The business secretary added that the U.K. better regulates industries like the tech sector.

World.title: Burnham must be ‘selective’ in conference speech, says key ally
World.content:
Steve Rotheram speaks at the POLITICO Pub at the Labour Conference in Liverpool, England on Sept. 27, 2026. | Baldo Sciacca for POLITICO

Liverpool City Region Mayor Steve Rotheram, who has seen a draft of the PM’s address, said there is “no way” he can cover all his arguments in one hour.

LIVERPOOL, England — Andy Burnham must be “selective” in the story he tells when he delivers his first conference speech as prime minister and Labour leader later this week, one of his closest allies said Sunday.

In an interview in The POLITICO Pub, Steve Rotheram, mayor of the Liverpool City Region, said he’s seen a draft of Burnham’s speech, which he’ll deliver to Labour members Tuesday afternoon.

“He’s going to have to be selective about the types of things that he wants to outline as a way forward,” Rotheram said, adding “there’s no way that in that one hour you can encapsulate everything that you want to talk about.”

Rotheram said what the public will see is “somebody who will articulate their values and principles, and put them into a context of policy decisions that he will either announce or we will announce in the future around types of things that need to be done first.”

The Liverpool mayor, who has run the city since 2017, praised Burnham’s opening weeks as prime minister for creating “lots of good news for us as Labour politicians to go out and campaign about.”

World.title: EU Commission calls on countries to cut energy demands as costs surge
World.content:
In a letter seen by POLITICO, Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen asked ministers to introduce new measures “in the context of constrained global supply.”

The European Commission has told capitals to reduce demand for gas and electricity in a bid to tame prices amid a global energy crunch.

"In the context of constrained global supply and high price volatility, demand reduction can be an effective tool to contain prices," EU Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jørgensen wrote in a letter to EU ministers, dated Sept. 25 and seen by POLITICO.

In the letter, Jørgensen invites ministers to take measures to reduce demand for gas and electricity "for as long as necessary." He argues that while the situation is "challenging", there are "currently no immediate risks to security of supply."

World.title: Watch: mass Madrid protests over Maricarmen eviction and housing crisis
World.content:
Around 150 tents filled the square on Sunday, with families of several generations joining the sit-in. Demonstrators say they will remain there until at least Tuesday, when the Spanish government is due to meet.

 

Banners across the square called for “Affordable housing”, “Right to Housing at a fair price” and “Not one more Maricarmen”, reflecting wider demands for rent freezes, stronger tenant protections and an end to evictions without alternative accommodation.

Maricarmen had lived in the same Madrid flat for around 70 years, after her father rented it in 1956. The Madrid Tenants’ Union says the property was later acquired by an investment fund, which increased her rent from €500 to €2,650 a month before reducing it to €1,650. Police eventually evicted her on Wednesday, after several attempts. She was taken to hospital after becoming exhausted during the operation.

Her eviction has become a symbol of Spain’s wider housing crisis. The Bank of Spain estimated a shortage of around 550,000 homes last year, while public subsidised rental housing represents less than 2% of the country’s housing stock, compared with an EU average of 8%.

Saturday’s march drew around 25,000 people according to authorities, while the Madrid Tenants’ Union put the turnout at more than 300,000.

World.title: Northern Ireland: 2,000 protesters block disputed Portadown march
World.content:
Around 2,000 people gathered despite heavy rain, while police monitored the scene with vehicles and a helicopter. The 35 Orange Order members authorised to take part remained inside a nearby church as the route was blocked. The limited parade was due to pass along the road without bands or supporters, in what would have been the first such procession there since 1998.

 

The standoff followed a late-night legal battle. A High Court judge initially halted the parade on Saturday, saying the long-running dispute had the potential to escalate. But the Court of Appeal overturned the ruling shortly before midnight, with Chief Justice Siobhan Keegan saying the judge had “unfortunately erred in law”. A subsequent High Court challenge was dismissed in the early hours of Sunday.

The procession was scheduled to leave at 8am and finish by 9.30am, but the PSNI said the road was not clear, delaying the march.

The decision has triggered strong criticism from nationalist leaders. First Minister Michelle O’Neill questioned why the route had been reopened after 28 years, while Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald called for the British government and police to stop the parade.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham appealed for calm, saying the gains made since the Good Friday Agreement must not be undone.

The confrontation revives memories of the Drumcree dispute, when the Garvaghy Road became a major flashpoint during the Troubles.

World.title: Sánchez vows to pass housing decree on Tuesday amid outrage over Maricarmen eviction
World.content:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez responded to Maricarmen on Sunday, a day after the 87-year-old woman, who was evicted from her Madrid home earlier this week, appealed directly to him for action.

 

Speaking at a Socialist Party (PSOE) rally in Getafe, Sánchez promised that his government was working "against the clock" to bring a new housing decree before the Council of Ministers on Tuesday.

"Maricarmen, I have a message for you," he said, describing the housing crisis as "a matter of humanity" that transcends political differences. He also urged parliamentary groups to make "one last effort" to approve the decree in Congress.

His remarks came as protesters spent their first night camping in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square. Sánchez did not directly address the protest.

Maricarmen, who was evicted from the flat where she had lived for seven decades, had recorded a video on Saturday urging the prime minister to introduce legislation to prevent others from experiencing "what has happened to me".

The pensioner was removed from her home in Madrid's Retiro neighbourhood on a stretcher and remains in hospital.

Her case has become a focal point for growing protests over Spain's housing crisis.

Urbagestión, the investment fund that owns her former building, has faced criticism from neighbourhood campaigners. Madrid City Council has rejected the fund's offer concerning the flat and launched its own mediation efforts.

Meanwhile, divisions have emerged within Spain's governing coalition over how to resolve the case.

The left-wing Sumar party has called for the property to be expropriated so Maricarmen can return to her home. However, government minister Félix Bolaños rejected the proposal, arguing that it lacks a "clear fit" within Spain's Constitution.

Pablo Bustinduy, a minister representing Sumar, responded that his party would continue to support expropriation despite opposition from its Socialist coalition partner.

From street protests to a protest camp

Demonstrators set up around 100 tents in Madrid's busy Puerta del Sol square after tens of thousands took to the streets on Saturday to demand lower housing costs and stronger protections for tenants.

Inside the camp, protesters have organised banner-making workshops, yoga classes and communal meals, although it remains unclear how long they intend to stay.

Organisers say the camp emerged spontaneously, but solidarity gatherings have already been announced in other Spanish cities, including Burgos, León, Córdoba and Almería.

Oscar-winning Spanish filmmaker Pedro Almodóvar visited the camp on Sunday to express his support for the protesters, describing the country's housing crisis as "unbearable".

"Maricarmen is the last straw," Almodóvar, 76, told Spanish public broadcaster RTVE.

"It is absolutely unbearable for Spanish society to have this problem for another day. And politicians have to fix it because they are the ones who govern us," he added.

The protests have also exposed political divisions over the government's response.

Left-wing Podemos has warned against watering down the proposed housing measures during negotiations, while the opposition People's Party has accused the government of "using Maricarmen to do politics".

What happens next?

The government is aiming to approve the housing decree at Tuesday's Council of Ministers meeting, following weekend negotiations to secure sufficient parliamentary support.

Government sources have expressed optimism that an agreement can be reached.

Among the measures reportedly being discussed with Junts are restrictions on evicting tenants from properties owned by investment funds and proposals to prevent such funds from acquiring additional residential properties.

However, even if the government approves the decree, there is no guarantee that protesters will leave Puerta del Sol. The Tenants' Union has already warned that it will only accept an ambitious package of housing measures, rather than a watered-down version resulting from negotiations with Junts.

This weekend's demonstrations in the iconic Madrid square have drawn comparisons with Spain's historic 15-M protests, which began on 15 May 2011.

During those protests, members of the "indignados" movement camped in Puerta del Sol for 28 consecutive days, inspiring similar demonstrations across Spain and internationally.

The movement emerged amid widespread anger over the consequences of the global financial crisis, including evictions, unemployment, austerity measures and corruption.

Political scientist and columnist Estefanía Molina said the latest protests reflect the growing severity of Spain's housing crisis.

In 2011, "people protested because they couldn't buy an apartment", she told Spanish television.

"Today, the protest is about not being able to rent a room in someone else's home," she added.

World.title: How neutral should Switzerland be? Voters deliver decisive verdict
World.content:
Swiss voters overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to strengthen the country's neutrality in a referendum on Sunday, with around 70% voting against the measure.

 

According to final results published by the Swiss government, the proposal was rejected in all 26 Swiss cantons.

The initiative would have restricted Switzerland's ability to impose sanctions on other countries, allowing such measures only if they had been approved by the United Nations.

That would have limited Switzerland's ability to adopt sanctions against Russia, which holds veto power as one of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.

Supporters of the proposal, led by the far right Swiss People's Party (SVP), argued that Switzerland had moved too close to the European Union and NATO, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"This result is not a vote against neutrality," Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said at a press conference on Sunday as the referendum results were announced.

"Switzerland was neutral yesterday, it will be neutral today and it will remain neutral," he stressed.

A costly campaign ends in defeat

The initiative was championed by Christoph Blocher, the 85-year-old billionaire and influential figure within the SVP, with campaign posters promoting the so-called "neutrality initiative" carried the slogan "No to war".

Its defeat had been widely anticipated. According to Swiss media reports, the foreign ministry in Bern had privately forecast the outcome several weeks before the vote.

Despite the expected result, Blocher invested heavily in the campaign.

SVP veteran Christoph Blocher - archive image RONALD ZAK/AP

According to Swiss newspaper Berner Zeitung, he spent 3.8 million Swiss francs on the initiative, reportedly the largest amount ever contributed by a single individual to a Swiss referendum campaign.

The result prompted criticism from political opponents.

"The initiative would have set neutrality in stone and would no longer have allowed an adequate response to a given situation," argued said Susanne Vincenz-Stauffacher, a member of the Swiss National Council, referring to Russia's war against Ukraine.

She warned that defining neutrality in such rigid terms could prevent Switzerland from imposing sanctions on an aggressor.

"At the end of the day you are not neutral but on the aggressor's side," she said.

"Blocher has completely lost his way here," said Marianne Binder, a Centre Party member of the Council of States representing Aargau.

What does neutrality mean for Switzerland?

Switzerland has maintained a longstanding policy of neutrality and is not a member of any military alliance.

However, the interpretation of that neutrality has been the subject of political debate for years, particularly since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The Swiss government currently advocates a policy of "cooperative neutrality", under which the country remains militarily non-aligned while retaining the ability to impose sanctions when it considers them necessary to uphold international law.

Swiss Defence Minister Martin Pfister has also called for closer cooperation with NATO.

The rejected initiative sought to enshrine "perpetual and armed neutrality" in the Swiss constitution. It would also have restricted military cooperation with NATO to situations involving an imminent military attack.

While Swiss voters rejected the proposed restrictions, support for neutrality itself remains widespread.

According to the latest survey cited in the debate, 82% of respondents continue to support Switzerland's neutrality.

The referendum was part of Sunday's nationwide round of votes on national and local issues.

Under Switzerland's system of direct democracy, citizens typically vote four times a year on proposed legislation, constitutional amendments and other policy questions.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV urges French Church to continue fight against sexual abuse
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV called on the Catholic Church to acknowledge its failings and confront sexual abuse as he celebrated an open-air Mass in Lourdes on Sunday, the latest stop on his visit to France.

 

After drawing nearly 800,000 people in Paris on Saturday, the pontiff was greeted by further crowds in Lourdes, where around 150,000 people attended Sunday's Mass.

In his homily, Leo urged the Church to take responsibility for wrongdoing within its ranks.

"The Church must have the courage to be the first to undergo this conversion. To heal the deep wounds, the acts of infidelity and the painful deviations committed in its midst, we must stand humbly under the Lord's purifying gaze," he said.

"Acknowledging our own faults is essential to our spiritual progress," he added.

Pope meets French bishops amid scrutiny over abuse

Earlier on Sunday, Leo met privately with France's bishops, praising their efforts to address sexual abuse while urging them to remain vigilant.

"In recent years, you have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse against minors committed by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context," he told them, according to remarks published by the Vatican.

"You have taken courageous measures to respond, through listening, the search for truth, justice, forgiveness, reparation and a firm commitment to a culture of prevention and protection against these crimes."

The Pope urged the bishops to continue their efforts while also supporting members of the clergy.

"It is important to continue along this path while maintaining the greatest vigilance. At the same time, your clergy needs to be supported and encouraged; I know it is the focus of your fatherly concern," he said.

Survivors question selection process for papal meeting

The Pope was also scheduled to meet seven survivors of clerical sexual abuse on Sunday, including one person who was abused as an adult.

However, the meeting has drawn criticism from some survivors, who questioned how participants were selected.

In an open letter published by French newspaper Libération on the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of survivors called on him to acknowledge the Church's responsibility and criticised the decision to allow Church officials to select those attending the meeting rather than leaving the process to survivors' organisations.

"The Church must relinquish its position as both judge and party to the proceedings," they wrote.

Monsignor Pierre-Antoine Bozo, spokesperson for the French bishops' conference, said two of the seven participants had been proposed by survivors' organisations.

He explained that the Pope had deliberately chosen a small group to allow for a more personal discussion.

"When it comes to listening to them, you can't have 50 people in front of you," Bozo said.

"So I think that's really what the pope chose: to listen so that we can act and respond more effectively."

France's Catholic Church confronts its abuse legacy

The French Catholic Church has faced intense scrutiny over its handling of sexual abuse.

An independent investigation published in 2021 estimated that approximately 330,000 children had been sexually abused over a 70-year period by priests, other Church workers and people associated with Catholic institutions.

The report identified around 3,000 alleged perpetrators among priests and Church workers.

Despite criticism of the report's methodology and conclusions, French bishops established an independent compensation system for survivors.

To date, the system has recommended that the Church pay more than €20 million in compensation.
