World.title: Italy's fuel crisis: SOCAR announces price cap at IP stations
World.content:
SOCAR is introducing a cap on petrol and diesel prices across the Italiana Petroli (IP) network. The Azerbaijani state energy company, which took control of the Italian group last May, has decided to tackle soaring fuel costs by setting a limit on the prices charged by filling stations.

 

The mechanism will be rolled out gradually, starting with the IP-branded network. SOCAR has not yet specified what the maximum price at the pump will be: in a statement released on Sunday it explains that the level of the cap will be set taking into account different needs and the economic sustainability of the supply chain.

The company also plans to explore ways to extend the mechanism to Esso-branded stations and to other operators that purchase fuel from IP and distribute it under their own brands.

Pressure on prices and company action

SOCAR's measure comes against a backdrop of severe tensions over pump prices. The Ministry for Business and Made in Italy (MIMIT) publishes national averages every day, while the prices actually charged by individual filling stations are collected through the Fuel Prices Observatory.

The issue concerns diesel in particular, whose price has continued to be affected by tensions on energy markets and disruption along supply chains.

SOCAR is not the only major company to have announced action on prices: ENI has also introduced a price-cap mechanism on its own network, in a context in which the government has asked operators to help limit the impact of high fuel costs on households and businesses.

What makes SOCAR's move different is that it comes just a few months after the acquisition of IP and therefore also marks one of the first signs of the Azerbaijani group's new strategy in the Italian market.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has welcomed SOCAR's decision to introduce a price ceiling, recalling that he had asked the company to intervene on prices at the beginning of September.

SOCAR, Azerbaijan's state oil company

SOCAR is the State Oil Company of the Republic of Azerbaijan, the country's state-owned oil firm. The group operates across several stages of the energy chain, from oil and gas production to refining, logistics and marketing.

Its presence in Italy was strengthened in 2026 with the acquisition of Italiana Petroli, the group that owns the IP network. The deal was finalised on 8 May, when SOCAR bought 99.82 per cent of IP's share capital from API Holding.

IP has a widespread presence across Italian territory and operates an integrated system that includes refining, storage and distribution activities. SOCAR's entry has therefore brought one of Italy's main fuel retail networks under the Azerbaijani group's control.

Fuel prices on 27 September

The announcement from the Azerbaijani company comes as fuel prices remain at high levels. According to the latest figures from the Fuel Prices Observatory of the Ministry for Business and Made in Italy (MIMIT), today, Sunday 27 September, the national average price in self-service mode on the road network is 2.159 euros per litre for petrol and 2.377 euros for diesel.

On the motorway network the average rises to 2.254 euros per litre for petrol and 2.459 euros for diesel. MIMIT calculates the national averages on the basis of prices reported by retailers and updates the data daily.

The figure for diesel is particularly striking: on the motorway network the average price is now approaching 2.50 euros per litre.

The price cap will start on the IP network

The new mechanism announced by SOCAR will initially be applied to IP-branded filling stations. The company says it wants to support operators and network managers, in other words those who run the sites, while taking into account the need to keep the entire supply chain in balance.

The Azerbaijani company explains that the maximum price will be set according to different needs, with the stated aim of ensuring the continuity of the supply chain and supporting households and businesses at a time of particularly high prices.

The company will then examine how to extend the system to Esso stations and to other operators that source fuel from IP. Any extension could therefore cover a broader network than the sites directly linked to the IP brand.

SOCAR and its relationship with Italy

The intervention on fuel prices also comes as SOCAR strengthens its ties with Italy beyond the energy sector.

The Azerbaijani company has in fact formalised a strategic partnership with the Italian Football Federation (FIGC).

The decision to introduce a cap on petrol and diesel prices across the Italiana Petroli network "confirms SOCAR's closeness to Italy, at a time when the Azerbaijani company is formalising a strategic partnership with the Italian Football Federation (FIGC), becoming the global energy partner of the men's and women's national football teams from 1 January 2027 to 31 December 2030, with the possibility of an extension for a further two years", the company said in a statement.

World.title: Netanyahu battles October 7 warnings revelations with defiant UN speech
World.content:
The political storm engulfing Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu over reports of additional foreign warnings about Hamas’ 7 October attack expanded on Saturday and Sunday when more revelations surfaced amid the looming Israeli elections, with the Israeli premier countering with a fiery and defiant speech about Israel’s defence at the UN.

 

The New York Times on Saturday confirmed a previous Israeli daily newspaper Haaretz report that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed secretly warned Netanyahu of the Hamas’ 7 October attack and that Israel’s premier did not pass on the warning to his security officials.

Also on Saturday, the US news magazine The Atlantic reported that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel secretly visited Israel 11 days before 7 October attack to warn of a significant Hamas attack.

And on Sunday, former Israeli Defence minister Yoav Gallant told the Israeli Army Radio that Israel received a message from Hamas through Israeli internal national security agency Shin Bet channels weeks before the 7 October attack, in which the then Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar warned that he would "shake the prisons".

The revelations come at a time when Israel’s election campaign is in full swing for the vote next month and Netanyahu’s handling of the 7 October attack is a key issue in the campaign. The revelations also coincide with the prime minister's fiery speech at the UN General Assembly, widely considered asa message to the voters in Israel.

Israel’s opposition leaders have launched a series of scathing attacks on Netanyahu, calling for an investigation into the warnings that Israel’s prime minister allegedly received in the run-up to the attacks and whether he ignored them.

The prime minister’s office (PMO) repeatedly denied the media reports calling them false.

Haaretz previously reported that 10 days before the attack, the UAE president allegedly warned Netanyahu in a 45-minute-call that the leader of Hamas in Gaza at the time, Yahya Sinwar, was planning a major attack against Israel. The Haaretz report claimed Netanyahu "reacted with relative calm" and assured bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario.

At the time, Netanyahu's office called the report "an absolute lie" and denied he spoke to the Emirati leader. "The press reports are false. No warning was given to the prime minister from the United Arab Emirates before 7 October," the PMO said in a statement.

Netanyahu faces fresh scrutiny over alleged warnings before 7 October

But on Saturday, the New York Times published its own extensive investigation citing multiple officials matching the Haaretz revelations, alleging that Netanyahu was warned by the Emirati president before the Hamas attack and that the warning was not shared with Israel security chiefs.

In parallel with the New York Times report, the Atlantic published its own investigation alleging that on 26 September 2023, Egypt’s intelligence chief Abbas Kamel made a secret 67-minute visit to Israel to warn of a possible Hamas attack, but the warning did not include specific details.

The Atlantic report said Kamel urged Israel to reduce tensions in the Gaza Strip and that it was not clear whom he met during his 1-hour long stay in Israel.

According to The Atlantic, officials from seven countries told its journalists that such a short personal visit from Egypt’s intelligence chief himself should have been noticed by Israel’s political and security leadership and that Egyptian warnings allegedly continued until two days before the attack, but still without further specifics.

Just days after the 7 October attack, the PMO said that Netanyahu "has not spoken or met with the head of Egyptian intelligence since the establishment of the government, neither directly nor indirectly". Then on Saturday, the same office repeated that the report in The Atlantic "was denied at the time and is being recycled to manipulate the Israeli public," the Jerusalem Post reported on Sunday.

"On October 11, 2023, Egypt officially denied that it had warned Israel of the October 7 attack," the PMO said, adding that "in the months preceding 7 October, prime minister Netanyahu neither met nor spoke with Abbas Kamel, then head of Egypt’s General Intelligence Service. No Israeli intelligence official conveyed such a warning to the prime minister".

The US media reports were followed on Sunday by new revelations from former Israeli Defence minister Yoav Gallant who said that the Hamas leader at the time of the 7 October, Yahya Sinwar, warned Israel before the attacks that he would "shake the prisons".

In an interview with Israeli Army Radio, Galant said that Sinwar allegedly sent his message to Israel’s Shin Bet security agency through a former senior Fatah official during secret negotiations for a prisoner exchange deal before the Hamas attack.

Gallant also alleged that Netanyahu did not include him and senior security officials in sensitive conversations with the United Staes during the war.

"During the war, I learned many times about important conversations Netanyahu held with the Americans on the most sensitive issues, such as hostages and ammunition, only after the Americans called me and tried to verify what had been said in those conversations," Gallant told the Israeli Army Radio, adding that "their trust in the prime minister was low".

When asked about the foreign warnings’ allegations, Gallant said he was not informed of them during his time as defence minister.

"I first heard about these warnings from media reports," he said, adding that "assuming these things are true, such a warning that a prime minister receives from the leader of a country is not a political asset; it is a fundamental failure in the overall assessment of the situation".

Netanyahu attacks critics at UN as Israeli election looms

Israelis are due to head to the polls on 27 October for a national election to determine the 120-seat Knesset (parliament).

Despite a growing onslaught by the opposition, Netanyahu has so far rejected multiple calls for an official government inquiry into the events surrounding the 7 October attack following other accusations of his handling of the crisis.

As the Israeli election campaign is in full swing, Netanyahu used his speech at the United Nations General Assembly last Thursday to reaffirm his hardline stance on Israel’s protection to voters at home, but also as a series of messages to the world.

"You know any other country the size of New Jersey capable of fighting a seven front war? And for three years? They all ganged up on us to wipe us off the face of the Earth," Israel’s prime minister said in his speech outlining his doctrine against Israel’s enemies, but also its critics.

But as he walked to the podium to begin his speech, dozens of delegations walked out of the General Assembly hall in protest at Israel’s policies, but many others stayed, including the United States, Germany, France, Italy, the United Kingdom, Ukraine, Japan, India and others, prompting Netanyahu to say: "If there are any other moral cowards who haven’t yet left this hall, please do so now."

"Now, you want to hear the ultimate irony? Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall. In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran's nukes," Netanyahu reacted to the departures.

He then engaged in a series of fiery attacks on countries and leaders that he perceives as enemies of Israel or of himself.

On Iran, he predicted that "this evil regime will fall" because “the power of the people will overcome the people in power!” as the "murderous regime will be toppled by its lies, by its corruption, by its cruelty".

To showcase the danger of Iranian missiles, he explained to the assembly that a one-ton ballistic missile "would obliterate the entire compound," and that "two such missiles would obliterate the UN".

He mocked Hezbollah by taking out a pager and saying "you remember the beepers? Remember these things? Remember them? Well, I can tell you this, Hezbollah certainly remembers them."

He singled out "people" in the United Kingdom and France when talking about accusations of "colonialism" againt Israel, saying "who accuses us? Among them, people in the United Kingdom and France. But for the love of God, they are the ones who invented the term! Their colonies stretched across the entire planet. Colonialism? Leave us alone!"

He again accused Qatar repeatedly, saying that Qatar had spent millions to "brainwash young minds to hate Israel, hate America and hate the West," culminating with "this is the same Qatar that hosts the Hamas butchers of October 7th."

He also accused several countries, including Qatar and Turkey, of spending billions to spread lies in the media against Israel.

Qatar rejected the accusations saying that "this continuing rhetoric against Qatar is nothing more than an attempt to divert attention from the atrocities committed by his government in the occupied Palestinian territories and their grave humanitarian consequences".

But his strongest words went against President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan whom he accused of being "a tyrant who also hosts Hamas terror leaders," who "illegally occupies Northern Cyprus, an EU member," who "as a NATO member, regularly violates Greece’s borders," "who wants to take over Syria" and, most of all, who "calls for Israel's destruction and he says he will be the ruler of Jerusalem".

"No, sir, you won’t. It is our city," Israel’s prime minister said.

While Netanyahu maintained that accusing Israel of "genocide" is the "biggest lie of the century," Turkish president Erdoğan declared in his own UNGA speech that "we face a genocidal mindset that can never get enough of killing. No one with humanity, mercy or conscience can turn a blind eye," describing Gaza as "the most inhumane, most shameful concentration camp of our time".

World.title: Adieu, dear listeners!
World.content:
This week is the final Sound Kitchen program, and it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listeners Corner’s” with Paul Myers, plus a special musical choice from me to you. Just click the “Play” button above to join the feast!

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October, and today’s show is our last meal together. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 7 February: I asked you a question about the 68th annual Grammy Awards that took place on 1 February. You were to re-read our article “French DJ wins Grammy for Lady Gaga remix” and send in the answer to this question: Which six artists were given “Lifetime Achievement” awards?

The answer is, to quote our article: “On Saturday evening, Nigeria's Fela Kuti was posthumously awarded a lifetime achievement award, becoming the first African artist to receive the distinction.

The king of Afrobeat was one of several artists to receive the award, including Cher, Whitney Houston, Carlos Santana, Paul Simon and Chaka Khan.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question, suggested by RFI Listeners Club member Alan Holder from the English Isle of Wight. Alan’s question was: “What would be your ideal gift from your best friend or spouse? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Mohamed Elsayed Abd Elraheim from Elsharkya, Egypt. Mohamed Elsayed is also this week’s bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club members Hans Verner Lollike from Hedehusene, Denmark; Helmut Matt from Herbolzheim, Germany; Kashif Khalil from Faisalabad, Pakistan, and last but not least, gentle Debashis Gope from West Bengal, India.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 14 February: That week, I asked you a question about the Benin Bronzes, the trove of Nigerian sculptures and artifacts that were looted by colonial powers.

One of the most well-known organizations working for the return of these works is in Nigeria: it’s the National Commission for Museums and Monuments – the NCMM- which requested the return of bronzes from Britain that were looted from the Kingdom of Benin during the British Benin Expedition of 1897. Some of the sculptures date to the fourteenth century, but the bulk of the collection dates to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

And that week, the NCMM had a win, as my good colleague Melissa Chemam noted in her article: “Cambridge University museum set to return Benin bronzes to Nigeria”.

You were to re-read Melissa’s article and give the details of the artefacts to be returned. What did Melissa name in her article about the Benin Kingdom artworks that went home to Nigeria?

The answer is, to quote Melissa: “Among the returned bronzes that will travel in the coming months are wood and ivory sculptures, as well as commemorative heads of King Oba and Queen Mother Lyoba Idia.

The term ‘Benin bronzes’ refers to objects crafted from brass and ivory as well as bronze, which were seized during the colonial-era military expedition.”

The bonus question you answered that week was: “What do you know after all these years? What have you found are important life truths?

The winners are: Faithful RFI Listeners Club member Jayanta Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Jayanta is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club member Nasyr Muhammad from Katsina State in Nigeria, as well as RFI English listeners M. Ganesan from Goa, India, and three listeners from Bangladesh: Rafiq ul Islam from Naogaon, as well as Abdul Mannan and Mahfuza Akhter, both from Chapainawabganj.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Minor Swing” by Django Reinhardt and Stephane Grapelli, performed by the composers with Le Quintette Hot Club de France; "Water No Get Enemy" by Fela Kuti, performed by Fela Kuti and Africa ’70; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer; “L'hymne à l'amour” by Edith Piaf and Marguerite Monnot, sung by Edith Piaf, and “I Wish You Love” by Charles Trenet and Léo Chauliac, performed by Laufey with the Iceland Symphony Orchestra conducted by Hugh Brant.

With much affection from The Sound Kitchen team – Erwan Rome, Paul Myers, and yours truly, Susan Owensby - fare thee well!

World.title: Israel strips Dutch diplomats of status in West Bank
World.content:
The move by the Israeli Foreign Ministry is a response to Dutch sanctions targeting goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The Dutch Foreign Ministry is yet to comment.

The Israeli government said on Sunday that it was revoking the diplomatic status of Dutch diplomats representing The Netherlands at the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, the administrative capital of the Palestinian Territories.

Israeli ​Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the move was a response to Dutch sanctions targeting illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

"Israel will not ignore measures intended to harm it," Saar wrote on social media.

He ordered Dutch diplomats operating in Ramallah to ​return their Israeli-issued diplomatic documentation within seven days.

"After this period, the diplomatic privileges and immunities granted to them by the State of Israel will expire," he added.

Israeli settlement trade ban widens across Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dutch ban on settlement goods: what does it entail?

Dutch authorities announced earlier this month that they would begin enforcing a ban on settlement goods.

The ban, which applies to personal baggage as well as commercial shipments, came into force on September 22 and, in recent days, Dutch and Israeli media have reported that passengers arriving at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport from Israel had their luggage searched for banned goods.

Earlier in September, Israel also ordered the closure of ⁠the British Consulate ⁠in East Jerusalem, the United Kingdom's representative to the Palestinian Authority, after London announced similar sanctions banning the import of goods from illegal settlements.

"Any country that acts in a hostile and unilateral manner against Israel will lose influence and relevance in the region," said Saar.

France and Canada have also announced a ban on goods from settlements, but Israel has not yet taken any action against ​those two countries.

In August, Israel also banned Dutch diplomats from a Israeli-based, US-led coordination center for Gaza over what the foreign minister described as "anti-Israel measures."

World.title: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic announces resignation
World.content:
Aleksandar Vucic will now be running to be prime minister in the upcoming snap parliamentary elections slated for next month.

Serbia's long-time President Aleksandar Vucic announced on Sunday that he would resign from his post in order to run for prime minister in the upcoming October snap elections.

From the presidential palace in Belgrade, Vucic spoke to supporters: "I am resigning as president."

"Tomorrow morning I will hand over my duties to the parliament speaker," he added "This is the last evening for me in this building," Vucic declared.

"I served you faithfully. I served all of you, and our homeland Serbia, honourably and honestly throughout my presidential term," Vucic told supporters. "The fight is only beginning," he added.

Dominating Serbian politics

Vucic is banned by the Serbian Constitution from seeking a third term. He was serving his second term and would have left office in May of 2027.

The 56-year-old, who has ties to Serbian nationalism and had once served as minister under the administration of Slobodan Milosevic, has dominated Serbian politics for more over a decade.

Vucic supporters praise him for his stability, stated commitment to development projects in Serbia and his patriotism, in a country long overshadowed by war in the 1990s and subsequent international isolation.

Opponents, however, have decried what they see as increasingly authoritarian tendencies and leading a government accused of endemic corruption.

Abroad, Vucic has had to juggle the competing interests of his country's European Union aspirations and its close ties to Russia.

Opposition had sought snap elections

Earlier in September, Vucic called for snap elections for October. He cited "major turbulence on the domestic political scene," as the reason.

Vucic was referring to the political movement and major setback for his government that was triggered by a tragedy in Serbia's second-largest city of Novi Sad. In November 2024, an awning of a newly reconstructed railway station in Novi Sad collapsed, killing 16 people.

The disaster triggered nationwide ⁠protests by students and the opposition. They ​demanded accountability for those responsible for the disaster, transparency in public procurement, an end to systemic corruption, and an early parliamentary vote.

Vucic's government repeatedly denied accusations, but still, several officials, including two ministers, were arrested or resigned after the incident. The upcoming snap election will test Vucic's popularity and political survival.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru, Wesley Dockery

World.title: Yemen: Houthis report deadly Saudi strikes on Taiz market
World.content:
The Houthi-run health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," vowing to retaliate. The Houthis' account of the attack cannot be independently verified.

Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday accused the Saudi Arabian Air Force of having struck a shopping area around the central market of Taiz. The Iran-aligned Houthis said at least seven people had been killed and dozens injured.

What do we know so far?

The group's Al-Masirah TV channel showed footage of large plumes of smoke and a destroyed warehouse stacked with food in cardboard boxes. Al-Masirah TV also reported that children were among those wounded, citing the Houthis' health ministry.

Taiz is currently under the control of Yemeni government forces, but it has long been besieged by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in the country's civil war. Taiz is located in southwestern Yemen.

The escalation in fighting comes after a fragile truce between Yemeni government forces and Houthi rebels broke down months ago and new regional tensions sparked by the Iran war.

The Houthi health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," saying it was directly and deliberately targeting civilian sites in Taiz.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree accused Saudi Arabia of launching two air raids that hit the market, adding that blood was "unjustly and aggressively spilled" in a statement posted online.

The group has vowed to retaliate.

The claims made by the Houthis cannot be independently verified.

In response to the Houthi report, troops loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen confirmed that their air force had struck a Houthi depot and vehicles in the area.

France sends troops as Houthi attacks threaten Saudi oil To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Saudi-backed coalition ramps up attacks after new Houthi offensive

The civil war in Yemen began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the Saudi-backed government. They went on to take control of vast swaths of the country's north.

Saudi Arabia joined forces against the Houthis the following year, leading an international coalition against them. But so far, Yemen's government forces have not been able to effectively repel the latest Houthi offensive.

Fighting has spiked in September as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them seize Yemen's entire Red Sea coast. The rebels have also launched a blockade on Saudi energy exports to coincide with Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Renewed clashes are is under way in several parts of the country, with at least 125,000 people displaced by it.

The Yemeni government has meanwhile called for a general mobilization, urging Yemenis to join the army and security forces.

Yemen is one of the poorest in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.

World.title: Avalanche in Nepal leaves 2 dead, several missing
World.content:
An avalanche has struck the Himlung Himal base camp in Nepal after days of severe weather. Two guides are confirmed dead and at least 14 people remain missing in the remote region.

Two people have died when an avalanche struck the base camp of a mountain in Nepal with at least 14 others still missing.

The avalanche hit the 7,126-meter (23,380-foot) Himlung Himal after several days of heavy rain and snowfall across the region.

The dead and missing are all mountain guides and staff of Nepalese expedition companies who had been preparing the base camp for paying customers to climb the mountain.

"There were a total of 14 kitchen staff members and two climbing guides from different companies who were missing," the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association said. "The two climbing guides have been found, but sadly, both were found deceased."

Unclear how many are missing

There was conflicting information as to how many people were in the affected area near the border with Tibet at the time of disaster. Local police said there were at least 22 people at the base camp when the avalanche struck on Sunday morning.

Bibhuti Chand Thakur, head of trekking company Himalayan Holidays Nepal, told news agency DPA that search and rescue operations were under way. "The chance of survival remains high because of fresh snow," he said, adding that he did not yet have a definitive number of missing or survivors, as the area is remote and cut off from communication.

While Mount Everest (pictured) is Nepal's most famous peak, peaks like Himlung Himal are also popular with climbers [FILE: May 21, 2024] Image: Narendra Shahi Thakuri/dpa/picture alliance

Authorities had warned of severe weather across Nepal over the weekend. Rain has affected much of the country since Thursday, with snowfall reported in the higher northern regions. The conditions have disrupted roads and trekking routes and led authorities to suspend climbing and trekking activities on several mountains.

The Himalayan nation is home to eight of the world's 14 mountains higher than 8,000 meters, and trekking and mountaineering tourism is vital to the country's economy.

The latest avalanche comes as Nepal continues to recover from devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: UK: 5 arrested after 'major incident' near Fairford air base
World.content:
Scores of homes were evacuated in the UK town of Whelford, near an air base used by the US military, with bomb disposal teams checking "suspicious vehicles" at the scene. Police said five men had been arrested.

British authorities evacuated buildings and deployed military bomb disposal teams over a "major incident" in the town of Whelford on Sunday morning.

London's Metropolitan police said five men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a "terrorist act" and explosive-related offenses.

The town is located near the Fairford air base, which is used by the US military. Around 30 emergency vehicles were seen in the area, including police cars, ambulances, and fire engines. The authorities said they believed the incident to be "contained."

UK police blocked roads leading to the Fairford air base Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

Counter-terrorism police were leading the probe.

"We are in the early stages of an investigation," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said in an online statement , adding that the authorities were "working closely with our partners" to understand the circumstances of the incident.

The statement urged the public to share any information they may have related to the issue.

Praise from Trump and Burnham

US President Donald Trump praised those involved in the arrests. “It was an amazing job," he told reporters in the US.

"We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," Trump said.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he understood that the incident would be "deeply concerning" for many people.

In a social media post, Burnham thanked the police and armed forces for their response and expressed his gratitude to residents who had been evacuated from their homes "while precautionary checks are carried out."

Trump says RAF Fairford suspects known to US authorities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bomb disposal units examining three 'suspicious vehicles'

Local police said they had received a call overnight on Sunday about "three suspicious vehicles" heading to the base.

"Armed officers responded and subsequently arrested five men in the Whelford area," assistant chief constable Richard Ocone told reporters.

He added that a cordon of 400 meters, or approximately 1/4 of a mile, has been put in place around the vehicles "while the army's explosive ordinance disposal unit examine them."

"As a precaution, around 85 households have been advised to evacuate while these examinations take place," Ocone said.

He added that some of the evacuees were taken to a nearby leisure center.

The Gloucestershire police representative also asked the public "not to speculate" but follow official channels instead.

Officials stay tight-lipped

A spokesperson for ​the US Air Force refused to discuss specific steps when contacted by the Reuters news agency, saying only that both US and British forces "remain vigilant and will take ⁠appropriate ​actions to ensure the safety and security of our ​US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families."

This Fairford base gate was blocked by construction machinery Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

The background for the incident was not immediately clear.

The UK has allowed the US to use Fairford for its war against Iran, with Iran's Revolutionary Guards warning UK officials against the move this summer. The evacuations also come at a time of heightened tensions in Northern Ireland, and less than two months after Germany discovered an explosive-laden drone at the Leipzig airport, which its authorities attributed to Russia.

World.title: Two people killed as bus crashes on way to Oktoberfest
World.content:
The bus was traveling from Italy to Munich, carrying 33 Filipino tourists who wanted to visit the famous beer festival. One of the dozens injured remains in life-threatening condition.

Two people were killed and many more injured when a bus carrying a group of Filipino tourists overturned in southern Germany on Sunday en route to the Munich Oktoberfest.

The bus was coming from Milan, an Italian city with a large Filipino community.

According to German police, there were 33 tourists on the bus when, at 5:41 a.m. local time (03:41 a.m. GMT), the vehicle went off the side of the A96 highway and overturned. No other vehicles were involved in the crash.

Six of the injured were immediately rushed by helicopter to nearby hospitals, one of whom was thought to still be in a life-threatening condition. Two more were taken by ambulance to the hospital, while another 22 were first treated at the scene before several of those were also brought to the hospital.

Police so far have only identified one of the two people who died as a 58-year-old Filipino citizen.

"It is naturally very chaotic at first, and establishing the facts is difficult,” explained a spokesperson for the local police headquarters. It took police hours to confirm how many people actually were on the bus.

Bus driver charged with negligent homicide

In addition to the 33 tourists, there were the two Italian bus drivers on board, both of whom were not injured in the crash. The driver who was at the wheel at the time of the crash is now being investigated for negligent homicide, police said. "That is standard procedure,” a police spokeswoman explained.

The cause of the accident remained unclear, police said. "The public prosecutor's office has commissioned an accident reconstruction expert report to determine the cause of the crash. It is far too early to comment.”

More than 200 firefighters, medics and police were rushed to the scene of the crash. A section of the highway was completely blocked for some time before, but in the afternoon, traffic was allowed to resume.

There have been a string of bus accidents in recent weeks. Earlier in September, a Dutch coach crashed in Switzerland, killing five, while a bus crash on Germany's A3 highway left 30 people injured.

Oktoberfest draws millions of visitors

Munich’s Oktoberfest is the world’s largest beer festival, attracting millions of visitors to the Bavarian capital each year. Held over roughly two weeks, it combines giant beer tents, traditional Bavarian food, live music and fairground rides, drawing visitors from Germany and around the world.

This year, the Oktoberfest runs from September 19 to October 4. Organizers said that at the halfway point, around 3.8 million people had already visited the festival — about 300,000 more than at the same point last year.

The Oktoberfest is the world's biggest beer festival and draws millions of international tourists Image: Matthias Schrader/AP Photo/picture alliance

World.title: Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit
World.content:
French bishops took "courageous" steps when faced with "the painful scourge of abuse of minors," Pope Leo XIV told the high-ranking clerics before his scheduled meeting with survivors at the Catholic shrine of Lourdes.

Around 150,000 attended the Mass celebrated by Pope Leo at the shrine of Lourdes during the third day of his four-day visit to France.

The shrine, located near the Spanish border, is venerated by Catholics as a place of healing. Many victims of sexual abuse have also traveled to the site in recent years as they seek to recover from their trauma.

Pope celebrated Sunday Mass at Lourdes (pictured) in front of some 150,000 people, following a mass in Paris attended by 800,000 believers Image: Laurent Cipriani/AP Photo/picture alliance

On Sunday, Leo urged respect for life, including for the sick and frail, in what was seen as veiled criticism of euthanasia and abortion.

"Your crutches, your wheelchairs and your hidden tears are not obstacles; instead, they are the very place where you are fully respected and welcomed," Leo said. "Lourdes is blessed as a place for professing the beauty and sanctity of life, for life is welcomed here as a precious gift from God."

Later, the pope also said it was "impossible to regard causing death as something normal."

"What is legal is not necessarily moral," he added, in what could be seen as a reference to France's euthanasia and assisted suicide law which came into effect last month.

"We must reject the temptation to cause death under the guise of false compassion," said the 71-year-old pontiff.

Hundreds of thousands of children abused in France alone

The head of the Catholic Church was due to meet with seven adult survivors of sexual abuse on Sunday — part of Vatican's decadeslong reckoning with the widespread molestation of children at the hands of the clergy and the steps senior Church figures have taken to cover up the scandal in many countries around the world.

A 2021 report found that around 330,000 children had been abused by Catholic priests and lay leaders between 1950 and 2020 in France.

As pope visits France, sex abuse survivor hopes for healing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While not directly referencing the issue during his Mass in Lourdes, the religious leader called for humility among the clergy's ranks.

"The admission of our mistakes is indispensable for our spiritual growth," Leo told the crowd. "In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within (the Church), we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze."

But some survivors expressed doubt that the pope's visit would lead to quick changes within the church.

"Things are moving very slowly," Michele Le Reun-Gaigne, a co-leader of a French survivors' association, told the Reuters news agency. "It isn't going to happen overnight."

Pope urges 'vigilance' while meeting bishops

Earlier on Sunday, the pope met with French bishops and praised their "courageous" response to "the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context."

He thanked the bishops for "listening, the search for truth, justice, forgiveness and making amends" and praised their "firm commitment to a culture of prevention and protection against these crimes."

"You must continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance," the US-born pope said, according to the readout provided by the Vatican .

World.title: European cities seek ways of boosting affordable housing
World.content:
In many major urban centers of Europe, the housing shortage has become an explosive social issue. DW looks into various models that have been put in place across the continent.

In the European Union's most populous city, pressure on the housing market is so great that many of its residents are willing to undertake a historic experiment: Five years ago, Berliners voted in a referendum to instruct the Senate of the German capital to draft a law that would put an end to the power of large real estate companies. Those that owned more than 3,000 units should be expropriated, they said. The Senate did not act on the results of the referendum, which was non-binding. Meanwhile, the average cost of new leases has since risen by about half.

But in the Berlin elections on September 20, the socialist Left Party, which in its campaign had promised to act on the referendum, won the largest share of the vote. Whether it will be able to make good on its promises now depends on how negotiations to form a coalition shape up. But whatever happens, the election has drawn attention once again to the severity of the housing crisis in many cities across Europe.

Left Party candidate Elif Eralp has promised to be a mayor for all Berliners. Her campaign was largely about providing affordable housing. Image: Britta Pedersen/dpa/picture alliance

Here are some initiatives that have already been put in place:

Vienna: The city is the landlord

The Vienna model is a flagship solution to soaring rent prices in Europe. The ambitious social housing program as introduced after World War I when the Austrian capital experienced a severe housing crisis. Beds were so scarce that some workers had to sleep in shifts. Diseases such as tuberculosis spread in the cramped living conditions.

The model serves to stabilize the city's housing market to this day: According to the Vienna authorities, the city owns approximately 220,000 municipal apartments that it rents out as well as 200,000 subsidized dwellings. More than 60% of Vienna's residents live in one of these two types of housing. This also helps to stabilize prices on the private market.

Public funds in Vienna keep rents down To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Basel: Public land, private buildings

The fact that housing is becoming increasingly expensive in many cities is largely due to the fact that a city's attractiveness is reflected in land prices. In many places, people are considering how to decouple rents from the price of land. One means of doing this is not to sell municipal land but to lease it to cooperatives or socially-conscious investors. This benefits councils that do not have to bear construction costs and developers too, as they do not have to factor in exorbitant land costs that are ultimately passed on to tenants.

The Swiss city of Basel is one of the pioneers of this model. About 40% of all cooperative housing units are located on public land. The Spanish city of Barcelona and the Portuguese capital Lisbon have also stepped up efforts to put this model in place.

Paris: Buying back office buildings and converting them into homes

It is harder if land and buildings are in private hands. In 2014, the French capital Paris launched an anti-displacement plan giving the municipality a "first right of refusal" in gentrifying neighborhoods to increase the share of affordable housing in the city. The current target is 30% social housing for low-income residents by 2035

Earlier this year, the French government and the Paris regional authorities identified 61 projects that could convert empty office buildings into housing and create up to 8,200 homes in the inner suburbs of the French capital.

Certain office buildings in the Paris suburbs are being converted into affordable homes Image: Vincent Isore/IP3press/imago images

Prague: Apartments for public-sector workers

The Czech capital has found another way to keep those without whom the city could not function in Prague: caregivers, police officers, teachers and sanitation workers. Some 660 new energy-efficient apartments reserved specifically for public-sector employees have just been built.

The subsidiary of a Czech bank, which has received European loans, handled the development. The aim is to keep rents 20% below the market rate thanks to economies of scale, and it is not the bank who decides on the tenants but hospitals or public sector agencies, which draw up leases and can attract new employees with affordable rent options. More apartments are currently being planned.

Few people can afford to live in the center of Prague Image: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS

Dublin: Non-profit cost rental housing

It has also become difficult for people with low incomes to stay in the Irish capital Dublin. During and after Ireland's financial crisis of 2008, foreign investors bought up a lot of real estate and at the same time rents skyrocketed when several major tech companies chose Dublin as their EU headquarters because of favorable tax rates. There are now long waiting lists for public housing in the city whose supply remains too low.

In 2021, the Irish government introduced the Cost Rental Housing program to provide housing to those on middle incomes, i.e. those who earn too much to qualify for public housing but too little to have a chance on the private market. To qualify in Dublin, a household has to have a net income of below €66,000 ($75,000) per year. Non-profits or public agencies lease out the apartments and rents are below market levels, by an average of almost 30% according to a recent study by the Dublin-based Economic & Social Research Institute (ESRI).

The Irish government hopes to be able to deliver 18,000 low-cost rental homes by the end of the decade. Last year, there were more than 4,200 applicants for 104 apartments in a new community in a suburb of Dublin.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Madrid acusa de “absoluta negligencia” al Gobierno por permitir la acampada en Sol y el delegado responde que la policía no actúa si no hay disturbios
World.content:
El ayuntamiento de Madrid ha exigido este domingo a la Delegación del Gobierno “reponer cuanto antes” la normalidad en la Puerta del Sol, donde cientos de personas acamparon anoche al finalizar la manifestación por el derecho a la vivienda. “La Delegación del Gobierno no puede mirar para otro lado ni cargar a otra administración con los problemas que causa su incapacidad e incompetencia para realizar sus funciones”, ha sentenciado el consistorio en un comunicado, en el que exige que se aborden las consecuencias causadas por “su dejación de funciones y repongan la normalidad en la Puerta del Sol cuanto antes”. El delegado del Gobierno, Francisco Martín, responde: “Mientras no haya disturbios, a la Policía Nacional no le corresponde actuar”.

Desde el sábado por la noche dos centenares de tiendas permanecen instaladas en la Puerta del Sol de Madrid tras la manifestación de apoyo a Maricarmen, la anciana desahuciada de su casa esta semana y para exigir el derecho a la vivienda.

El ayuntamiento madrileño ha mostrado su “sorpresa” e “indignación”ante la acampada de la Puerta del Sol y ha acusado a la Delegación del Gobierno en Madrid de “permitir que eso ocurriera”, además de recordar que, en 2011, con la protesta del 15M, los desalojos “fueron organizados y coordinados por la Delegación del Gobierno”. Ha tildado la acampada de “ilegal” y ha señalado que la situación es “consecuencia directa de la dejación de funciones y la falta de diligencia de la Delegación del Gobierno y del Ministerio del Interior, o quizás de la deliberada decisión de permitir que esto ocurriera”.

La Delegación del Gobierno en Madrid ha señalado que no tiene ninguna información oficial y directa de que el Ayuntamiento de la capital o la Comunidad hayan reclamado el desalojo de la Puerta del Sol. No hay tampoco ninguna previsión de actuar por parte de la Policía Nacional mientras no se produzcan incidentes.

“Cuando comenzaron los asentamientos ilegales, la Policía Nacional se retiró de sus emplazamientos. Por ello, y para saber si este hechos e debió a una orden directa del delegado del Gobierno, el Ayuntamiento de Madrid exige a la Delegación y al Ministerio del Interior una explicación”,ha reclamado.

En ese sentido, el consistorio ha apuntado que “es a Delegación del Gobierno a quien le corresponde el control del orden público, especialmente cuando se refiere al derecho de manifestación”. “La misma, sin embargo,debe adecuarse a lo comunicado por los organizadores y a lo así autorizado,algo que no ha sucedido en esta ocasión”, ha puntualizado.

World.title: Acampada en Sol contra los desahucios, en directo | Miles de personas se reúnen en Sol durante el primer día de una acampada ya consolidada
World.content:
El secretario general de CCOO, ante la acampada: “Hay que elevar el tsunami social que exija a las Administraciones políticas ambiciosas en vivienda”

El secretario general de CCOO, Unai Sordo, ha acudido esta tarde a la Puerta del Sol para lanzar un mensaje de solidaridad y acompañamiento a los concentrados: “Gente de CCOO vendrá a reforzar la acampada, hay que elevar una especie de tsunami social que exija al conjunto de administraciones políticas muy ambiciosas en materia de vivienda. Los precios del alquiler y de las hipotecas ahora mismo se están comiendo los incrementos de los salarios de millones de españoles. La juventud trabajadora tiene unos problemas enormes para emanciparse, la edad media de juventud de emancipación es de 30 años; esto es un disparate...”

Sordo ha indicado que CCOO "no se cierra a ningún escenario de lucha y de movilización para situar la movilización social, y llegado el caso de la movilización laboral, en medidas mucho más amplias y mucho más estratégicas para abaratar el precio de la vivienda, para contar con un gran parque público de viviendas, que dé soluciones habitacionales a la gente y que rebaje los precios de mercado que son un disparate”.

El líder sindical ha abogado por articular posiciones y movilizaciones entre las asociaciones, los sindicatos de inquilinas y los sindicatos de clase: "Cuando se aprobó la ley de vivienda hace ya tres años, ya dijimos que tenía algunas insuficiencias y que iba a dar problemas, entre otras cosas, porque se iba a bloquear en las comunidades autónomas, como ha sucedido. A día de hoy ni siquiera se está utilizando todo el potencial de la ley de vivienda, por ejemplo, para topar los alquileres en las zonas tensionadas. Son necesarias medidas de mucho espectro”.

CCOO sostiene que el Gobierno “tiene que utilizar todas las palancas de la ley y todas las palancas de la política fiscal para evitar que nadie pueda hacer negocio del acaparamiento de viviendas” y para evitar que, como sucede ahora, los fondos de inversión estén “comprando comunidades de vecinos enteras, edificios enteros para luego utilizarlos como viviendas turísticas, como alquileres abusivos”. Sordo cree que eso se tiene que acabar.

World.title: Amalia Sánchez, de 76 años : “Los jóvenes han regresado, desde el 15-M solo escuchaba gritar a los fachas”
World.content:
No se puede decir que estuviste acampado en la Puerta del Sol por el desahucio de Maricarmen si Amalia Sánchez, de 76 años, no te entregó una mandarina.

Amalia Sánchez es, de entre todos los presentes durante la primera jornada de acampada en el ‘kilómetro 0’ de Madrid, una de las personas más cercanas a Maricarmen por edad. “Tiene narices que haya tenido que ser una octogenaria quien haya provocado esto”, comenta. “Todos sabemos que su caso ha sido uno entre miles, que esto no es solo por ella sino por todos. Es importante por quién estamos aquí, pero más importante es que hemos vuelto, que los jóvenes han regresado”, observa. “¿Dónde estaban desde el 15-M? Porque en este tiempo yo solo he escuchado gritar a los fachas. Pensaba que los jóvenes estaban jugando a la Play. Verles de nuevo aquí me da la vida. Hay que ayudarles para que sigan fuertes“, reconoce.

La perspectiva del tiempo coloca en apariencia a Amalia en otra esfera muy distinta a la de los más de 300 chicos y chicas que acampan en Sol, casi todos españoles entre los 18 y los 35 años. Sin embargo, durante la noche del sábado hubo algo que también se encendió en ella. Amalia acudió a celebrar el cumpleaños de su hija en el centro de Madrid y no se había enterado de que una nueva manifestación por el deshaucio de Maricarmen estaba teniendo lugar en la Puerta del Sol. Se percató de que algo estaba sucediendo cuando se topó con decenas de policías en el Paseo del Prado. Al regresar a casa e interesarse por lo sucedido, escuchó que cientos de personas estaban llegando con tiendas de campaña y se quedarían ahí toda la noche. “¿Un nuevo 15-M? Tengo que ir a verlo", se dijo a sí misma.

Acampada en Puerta del Sol en protesta contra el deshaucio de Maricarmen. JUAN BARBOSA

Amalia se levantó temprano el domingo y junto a un amigo puso rumbo a Sol desde el barrio de San Fermín donde vive. “No pertenezco a ninguna plataforma. Vengo igual que vine hace 15 años, como ciudadana. Vengo porque tengo dos oídos, dos ojos y sentido común”, asevera. Llegó a primera hora y pronto perdió de vista a su compañero porque ella empezó a moverse de acá para allá como un torbellino. En la carpa del Sindicato de Inquilinas le dijeron que no hacía falta que comprara comida. En realidad, comida es lo que les sobraba. Amalia decidió entonces ofrecerse de “chica para todo”. Primero agarró una bolsa llena de botellas de agua mineral y fue repartiéndolas entre los asistentes. Más tarde, por iniciativa propia se dedicó a recoger el plástico que había esparcido por el suelo. De tanto en tanto la mujer se dolía después de agacharse para coger las cosas con la mano. “He empezado taichí y tengo unas agujetas que me muero, por eso voy tan lenta”, se excusaba. Por último, Amalia se hizo con otra gran bolsa, esta vez llena de fruta, y volvió a pasearse, de una en una, por las casi 200 tiendas de campaña.

—¿Queréis potasio? ¿Un poco de vitamina C?—, preguntaba.

De algún modo, la escena de Amalia repartiendo plátanos bajo el calor evoca el momento en el que los corredores de relevos se entregan el testigo. Ella lo tiene claro. “Ahora los que tenéis las fuerzas sois vosotros. Nosotros, los mayores, solo somos una ayuda, por eso vengo a apoyaros. Ganas de acampar aquí no me faltan. Pero, ¿qué hace una señora de 76 años durmiendo en el suelo?“, dice. ”Vengo aquí para empaparme de la gente joven, que son los que tenéis el poder. Me dolería mucho ver que esto se queda en flor de un día. Eso significaría que no hemos entendido nada”, manifiesta delante de un grupo de veinteañeras universitarias de la Complutense.

Amalia recuerda que ella “perdió su juventud” al quedarse embarazada con 22 años. “No había métodos anticonceptivos”, lamenta. “Esto me ha hecho pensar. Hemos avanzado en muchas direcciones, por ejemplo en esta de la educación sexual. Pero hoy estamos aquí porque se ha vuelto a retroceder en otras muchas cosas”, reflexiona. “Mi ex marido y yo compramos en el bajo de un edificio una vivienda en San Fermín que terminamos convirtiendo casi por completo en una zapatería, el negocio que él tenía. Vivíamos al lado, apelotonados en una habitación diminuta con mis hijos. Cuesta creer que esta gente esté volviendo a vivir de esa manera”, observa. “Un derecho tardas 20 años en que te lo reconozcan y 20 minutos en perderlo”, opina.

Su primer trabajo fue en una compañía de seguros americana donde no tenían derecho a descansar los sábados. Dice que el “espíritu crítico” comenzó con esas movilizaciones de trabajadores para que se les concedieran los fines de semana. El resto de su carrera profesional la ejerció como celadora en el Hospital Ramón y Cajal. “Ahí me he dado cuenta de que, como ciudadanos, hemos asumido que se nos maltrate. Esperar un año para que te miren una pierna se ha normalizado, pero no es normal. Que la vivienda sea una cosa de privilegiados se ha normalizado, pero no es normal. Es que, es que... ¡Es que me hierve la sangre!”, se indigna.

Después de cuatro horas, cuando otra joven voluntaria le ofrece crema solar para protegerse del sol, Amalia llega a la conclusión de que tal vez haya llegado el momento de parar por hoy. “O paro o se me acaba llevando el Samur”, bromea. “Yo necesito esto, ver que la gente no está en su casa, indiferente. Si la excusa ha sido Maricarmen, bienvenida sea”, celebra. Antes de marcharse a casa, a Amalia le da tiempo a pensar en su epitafio. “Un día me encontré una tumba en el cementerio de San Isidro que ponía: ’Me voy porque no os aguanto’. Yo no quiero que me pase eso”, rememora. “El mío tiene que ser algo así como: ‘Di guerra hasta que se aburrieron de mí‘ ”, se despide. Mañana, dice, volverá.

World.title: Los Alonso no quieren ser llamados buitres
World.content:
Artículos estrictamente de opinión que responden al estilo propio del autor. Estos textos de opinión han de basarse en datos verificados y ser respetuosos con las personas aunque se critiquen sus actos. Todas las tribunas de opinión de personas ajenas a la Redacción de EL PAÍS llevarán, tras la última línea, un pie de autor —por conocido que éste sea— donde se indique el cargo, título, militancia política (en su caso) u ocupación principal, o la que esté o estuvo relacionada con el tema abordado

Ricardo Alonso Fernández y Fernando Alonso Fuentes, los administradores de Urbagestión, no quieren ser calificados como “fondo buitre”. Seguro que saben de quienes hablo, pero, por si acaso, les resumo que es la empresa inmobiliaria que lleva siete años intentando echar a Maricarmen (una octogenaria en silla de ruedas) del piso en el que vivía desde 1956. Proeza que Urbagestión por fin consiguió perpetrar hace cuatro días, con la armoniosa ayuda de las instituciones de este país, esto es, de la policía que acudió a tirar la puerta abajo y a zurrar a los manifestantes, y de la judicatura, en concreto de la magistrada Elena Cortina Blanco. Como señalaba acertadamente Pablo Ordaz el otro día, lo más formidable del asunto es que toda esta brutalidad es por completo legal.

Pues bien, Ricardo Alonso Fernández y Fernando Alonso Fuentes están empeñados en negar que son un fondo buitre, hasta el punto de querellarse por ello contra el Sindicato de Inquilinas (que intentó defender a Maricarmen) y de avisar a los medios de que ni se nos ocurra usar semejante expresión. En su comunicado aseguran: “No somos propietarios de ninguna otra vivienda. Como bien sabe la parte ejecutada, no se trata ni de un fondo de inversión ni de un fondo buitre, sino de una sencilla pyme”. Cómo me conmueve eso de “sencilla pyme”. Qué notable modestia empresarial. No tendrán ahora otra vivienda en esa empresa, pero con anterioridad han comprado y vendido inmuebles. Y por añadidura ambos son administradores solidarios de más de una docena de otras sociedades que van desde el sector inmobiliario al agroalimenticio, según leo en un informe de Jacobo García en EL PAÍS. Así que yo diría que es una sencillez algo compleja.

Pero, volviendo al tema, Ricardo Alonso Fernández y Fernando Alonso Fuentes no quieren ser llamados buitres, y yo estoy de acuerdo. Porque los buitres son unos animales majestuosos que sólo se alimentan de criaturas muertas y que, al hacerlo, están cumpliendo una labor esencial y beneficiosa para el ecosistema. Ahora díganme en qué se parece esto a la actuación de Ricardo Alonso Fernández y Fernando Alonso Fuentes, que se han abalanzado sobre Maricarmen mientras la pobre aún respira (aunque van a conseguir acabar con ella del disgusto) y con una actitud que, de entrada, se diría llena de avaricia (palabra que, según la RAE, significa afán desmedido de poseer y adquirir riquezas para atesorarlas).

Y es que el piso que compró Urbagestión por 240.000 euros en 2018 ha cuadruplicado su valor. Al parecer, primero le pidieron a Maricarmen (que pagaba y siguió pagando hasta el final su alquiler de 500 euros al mes) una renta de 2.650 euros, cantidad que considero alucinante y, como diría la RAE, muy desmedida, porque el piso de Maricarmen debe de estar en unas condiciones de mantenimiento bastante más sencillas que la pyme de Ricardo Alonso Fernández y Fernando Alonso Fuentes. Luego rebajaron el recibo a 1.650, también inalcanzable para Maricarmen, que cobra 1.450 de pensión. Y ahí comenzó este largo martirio.

Ahora hemos sabido que el pianista James Rhodes envió dos emails a Urbagestión ofreciéndose a comprar el piso; que la ministra de Vivienda intentó pagar la diferencia del alquiler o adquirir el inmueble, y, por último, me consta que, como se publicó en EL PAÍS, una persona que quiere mantener el anonimato se había ofrecido a completar la renta por el resto de la vida de Maricarmen. Pero Urbagestión no contestó. Un silencioso empeño en el desalojo que hacía sospechar que lo único que le importaba a Urbagestión era dar el pelotazo. Desalojar al bicho para poder revender el piso por un pastón, como en tantas otras rapiñas inmobiliarias. Por desgracia no es necesario registrar los costes humanos en la columna del debe de los libros contables.

Pero el escándalo y la movilización han sido tan grandes que, dos largos días después del desalojo, Ricardo Alonso Fernández y Fernando Alonso Fuentes se han descolgado con un extenso comunicado en el que se quejan de haber sido maltratados, aseguran que quieren llegar a un acuerdo y ofrecen el piso al ayuntamiento para el programa ReViVa (el ayuntamiento ya ha contestado que eso es inviable). Qué increíble que de golpe recuperen la voz. Siendo malpensada, se me ocurre que quizá se les haya venido abajo una posible venta. A ver quién va a comprar ahora esa patata caliente. O como ha dicho en Bluesky el ministro de Asuntos Sociales: “Ha sido hablar de expropiarles la vivienda y de pronto les ha entrado la conciencia social”.

La tragedia de Maricarmen ha sido especialmente escandalosa por sus agravantes, como la extrema vulnerabilidad de la víctima. Pero me pregunto cuántos otros casos semejantes hay que ni siquiera cuentan con un eco público. De hecho, Isabel Díaz Ayuso ha minimizado el desalojo de Maricarmen alardeando de los 25.000 desahucios anuales que hay en España; que lo haga mientras juega al Monopoly con su ático de seis millones de euros es una coincidencia simbólica tan rematadamente obvia y delirante que hasta da reparo mencionarla.

Pienso en esos miles de inquilinos, en esas Carmencitas y Paquitas y Lolitas y hasta algún Francisco a los que van a desahuciar este año. Eso no lo pueden arreglar Rhodes ni los donantes anónimos. La febril inflación del precio de los pisos, la pavorosa falta de alquileres accesibles, la facilidad con la que las empresas inmobiliarias se dedican a cazar y echar inquilinos indefensos para poder hacer los negocios del siglo es una realidad indecente, una situación insoportable que sin embargo soportamos. Y me temo que cada día hay más individuos para los que este comportamiento de corsarios, que yo veo como una especie de terrorismo habitacional, constituye una sana manifestación del libre comercio, la libre iniciativa y el libre triunfo del poderoso sobre el débil. Por eso a Ricardo Alonso Fernández y Fernando Alonso Fuentes lo que más les encocoró fue que los llamaran buitres (a ellos, avispados y exitosos empresarios): publicaron su protesta por el término un día antes de comunicar que están buscando una solución. Qué extraordinario que les urgiera más deslindarse de un nombre que del hecho de arrojar a las tinieblas a una anciana impedida.

Hace unas semanas me contaron que la furia devoradora de las empresas inmobiliarias es tal que andan ofreciendo hasta 50.000 euros de propina a los porteros para que les avisen del fallecimiento de un dueño. Mal asunto, pensó mi febril cabeza escribidora. Que me perdonen los porteros, unos profesionales estupendos (amo a mi maravilloso conserje, por ejemplo), pero en esta sociedad tan encallecida lo mismo podría aparecer algún portero decidido a adelantar la muerte de ese vecino tan viejecito y solo. En la selva del ladrillo vale todo.
