World.title: El hartazgo no cabe en un decreto
World.content:
La imagen de Maricarmen Abascal, de 87 años, acompañada por los antidisturbios mientras era desalojada en camilla de su casa en Madrid por una orden judicial, ha devuelto de golpe a la sociedad española a los momentos más duros de la crisis financiera de 2008, aquellos en los que se ejecutaron miles de desahucios de familias incapaces de pagar la hipoteca de su residencia habitual. Esa imagen ha catalizado el profundo malestar ante el problema de la vivienda, del que no escapan ni los mayores como Maricarmen ni los más jóvenes, ni tampoco una clase media cada vez más excluida de los beneficios de la economía que presume de ser la alumna aventajada de Europa.

No parece que las administraciones sean del todo conscientes del mar de fondo que ha impulsado las protestas por el desahucio de la anciana. Es un hartazgo que lleva tiempo gestándose y afecta a millones de personas. El principal desencadenante es la escasez de oferta. El déficit de viviendas, que el Banco de España cifraba hasta hace poco en unas 750.000, alcanzará en dos años el millón. Ese desfase ha disparado los precios y ha hecho que el mercado resulte inaccesible para buena parte de la población. Mientras la renta disponible de los hogares se multiplicaba por 1,8 desde los años ochenta, los precios inmobiliarios se han multiplicado por 3,5.

Durante años, los distintos niveles del Estado han fallado a la hora de paliar esa escasez y se han enredado en un reparto de competencias y de culpas que puede acabar pasando factura a los partidos en las urnas, para deleite de los extremos. El drama particular de Maricarmen exige una respuesta inmediata y adaptada a sus necesidades, pero el debate no puede quedar atrapado en este episodio concreto. Debe ir más allá.

El Gobierno ha presentado tres iniciativas en el Congreso para evitar situaciones similares, pero no ha sido capaz de armar una mayoría. Ahora trabaja contra el reloj para aprobar un decreto en el Consejo de Ministros de este martes. El decreto, que incluiría desde medidas que limitarían los desahucios a una simplificación de los trámites en las licencias para acelerar la construcción, supone una oportunidad, un primer paso para romper el bloqueo ante una crisis que no admite más retrasos y que merece el máximo consenso. Hoy, gracias a la presión ambiental, tiene más posibilidades de salir adelante.

Otra medida posible es la modificación de la regulación de los alquileres de renta antigua, como el de Maricarmen, que se rigen por una ley de 1994. Y, aunque puede resultar útil el escudo antidesahucios que proteja a las personas más vulnerables, los expertos advierten del riesgo de que lleve a muchos propietarios a evitar alquilar a estos inquilinos. Existen otras formas de darles la protección necesaria, como un aval del Estado a estos alquileres. Allí donde se han aplicado los topes al arrendamiento, como en Barcelona, se ha logrado moderar la subida de precios, pero también han reducido la oferta. Si se trata de disminuir la influencia de los fondos de inversión, una opción es retirarles los incentivos fiscales. Lo mismo vale para los pisos turísticos, cuyos alquileres están exentos de IVA o se les aplica un tipo reducido del 10%. En ambos casos es competencia de la Administración central.

Lo ineludible, a la hora de dar respuesta a la espiral de precios, tanto en el alquiler como en la compra, es la ampliación de la oferta. Sería necesario construir un mínimo de 200.000 viviendas anuales, casi el doble que ahora, para atender al crecimiento de la población y la creación de nuevos hogares. Y en este caso, las competencias son de las comunidades autónomas y de los ayuntamientos, de los que depende agilizar las trabas burocráticas para que una promoción no tarde hasta 15 años en salir al mercado. También es su responsabilidad crear un parque público de alquiler que saque a España del 3% que la sitúa a la cola de Europa.

Ninguna de estas medidas es posible sin la cooperación entre los partidos y las administraciones, aunque en este marco de mínimos ante lo que es un emergencia social parezca una quimera. No es que falte un diagnóstico: sobra cálculo electoral. Los obstáculos a la vivienda tocan justificadamente un nervio sensible y, cuando la democracia deja de servir a los ciudadanos, el malestar puede estallar en cualquier momento y dar alas a quienes cuestionan el mismo sistema y su legitimidad. Como ha mostrado el desahucio de Maricarmen Abascal, el precio de esta inacción siempre acaba siendo excesivo e inaceptable.

World.title: La idea de expropiar pisos en Berlín agita la política alemana
World.content:
La formación poscomunista Die Linke gana las elecciones de la capital con propuestas radicales para bajar los precios del alquiler que trastocan a la CDU y al SPD

Las estadísticas pueden ser una manera fría pero efectiva de entender grandes problemas. La crisis de la vivienda en Berlín es uno de estos casos: alquilar un apartamento en la capital de Alemania se encareció un 69% entre 2016 y 2026, según datos del Gobierno federal. Si hace 10 años alquilar un piso de 100 metros cuadrados costaba de media 900 euros, hoy son 1.525 euros. Al mismo tiempo, entre 2015 y 2025, según datos de la Administración de Estadística de Berlín, los ingresos per cápita en la ciudad habían aumentado un 33%, menos de la mitad de lo que se ha encarecido tener un hogar. El impacto social es mayúsculo porque se le añade que un 83% de los berlineses viven de alquiler.

Otra manera de explicar una crisis son las consecuencias políticas. La formación poscomunista Die Linke venció el pasado domingo por primera vez en unas elecciones regionales en Alemania. Pasó del 13% de los votos en 2023 al 25%. Los democristianos de la CDU quedaron por detrás con un 18%. Die Linke tiene opción de gobernar, también por primera vez, la capital de Alemania. Y lo ha conseguido con una campaña electoral centrada en su política de vivienda y, más en concreto, en la promesa de expropiar más de 200.000 pisos en manos de grandes empresas inmobiliarias o con la toma de control de estas por parte de la Administración.

“Si Die Linke gobierna en Berlín, nacionalizaremos”, aseguró la candidata principal del partido, Elif Eralp, la misma noche electoral tras conocerse su victoria.

Eralp luce un collar con la palabra en alemán Mietendeckel, que traducido significa “tope del alquiler”. En Berlín se aplican límites al aumento de un alquiler, un 15% en la renovación de un contrato de tres años y solo si no supera la media del barrio. Un nuevo contrato de arrendamiento no puede tener un precio superior al 10% de la media del barrio. Die Linke considera que esto no ha sido suficiente, hay múltiples maneras de saltarse los topes. Las estadísticas, de nuevo, le dan la razón.

Para gobernar necesitará el apoyo de Los Verdes y de los socialdemócratas, el SPD. Los Verdes están predispuestos a pactar, en la cuestión de la vivienda no están muy distanciados. El SPD, en cambio, tiene una posición muy alejada de Die Linke.

Los Verdes asumen que debe aplicarse el resultado del referéndum que celebró Berlín en 2021 convocado a partir de una iniciativa legislativa popular. La pregunta era clara: ¿debe el Gobierno de Berlín estatalizar (en alemán la denominación es “socializar”) empresas propietarias de más de 3.000 viviendas? El 58% de los votantes dijeron que sí. La consulta no era vinculante, pero el Ejecutivo de coalición del SPD y la CDU respondió formando una comisión que estableció las bases legales para hacerlo. Aunque no se llevó a cabo.

Los socialdemócratas y los democristianos son contrarios a estas medidas. Hay otras ideas de Die Linke que ponen los pelos de punta al centro político alemán. El programa de los poscomunistas establece, por ejemplo, que la Administración reconocerá el derecho a ocupar una vivienda que lleve más de un año vacía.

El canciller alemán, el democristiano Friedrich Merz, ha reiterado que el Gobierno federal actuará legalmente para impedir expropiaciones o nacionalizaciones de empresas. La Constitución alemana lo ampara, sea una nacionalización del Ejecutivo federal o de los gobiernos de los Estados federados, pero nunca hasta ahora se ha implementado.

Elif Eralp con un ramo de flores tras una asamblea del partido Die Linke en Berlín, el 25 de septiembre. Fabrizio Bensch (REUTERS)

La vivienda es un derecho reconocido en la ley fundamental, pero los expertos coinciden en que, al no haber precedentes, los jueces tendrán un amplio margen de interpretación. ¿Priorizará la justicia el derecho a la propiedad privada? ¿Considerará el juez que hay otras alternativas posibles antes que la expropiación? La CDU y las patronales consideran que el debate perjudica a la economía alemana porque pone en duda la estabilidad jurídica y la propiedad privada.

Deuda pública descontrolada

Otra dificultad mencionada por la CDU y el SPD es el coste económico de los planes de Die Linke. El Tribunal de Cuentas de Berlín estimó que el land debería desembolsar casi 40.000 millones de euros para indemnizar o nacionalizar a las empresas afectadas. El presupuesto del Estado de Berlín en 2026 es de 46.000 millones de euros; su endeudamiento actual es de 68.000 millones.

Las empresas en la diana son, en primer lugar, el grupo alemán Vonovia y su filial Deutsche Wohnen. Tienen más de 138.000 viviendas en Berlín y el precio de mercado de estos activos es superior a los 30.000 millones de euros, según las cuentas de ambas sociedades. Otras inmobiliarias que podrían verse afectadas son la alemana Adler Group, la luxemburguesa Grand City Properties y la sueca Heimstaden.

Los documentos académicos sobre los efectos de expropiar estas empresas difícilmente coinciden en sus conclusiones. Un estudio hecho público el 25 de septiembre por la Fundación Hans Böckler (dependiente del sindicato DGB) asegura que estas medidas tendrían beneficios claros en la contención del precio del alquiler, mientras que un informe reciente del instituto Empirica asegura que solo saldría ganando el 12% de la población.

En lo que coinciden unos y otros es que el principal problema es cómo financiar estas expropiaciones. La fundación Hans Böckler estima que el desembolso público mínimo serían 13.500 millones de euros. “Se supone que las expropiaciones permitirían aumentos del alquiler significativamente más moderados y precios más bajos en nuevos contratos”, explica Wibke Werner, directora general de la Berliner Mieterverein, la mayor asociación que representa en la ciudad los intereses de los inquilinos. “Aunque todo depende de la cuantía de las indemnizaciones que habría que pagar y las condiciones para la obtención de préstamos o bonos”, admite Werner.

Markus G. y Hauke Stiewe viven en el distrito de Friedrichshain, donde Die Linke obtuvo su mayor porcentaje de votos, un 40%. Stiewe regenta el bar del edificio en el que Markus reside como propietario. El edificio fue construido y es propiedad de la cooperativa en la que él su mujer son socios. Markus (prefiere no aportar su apellido) y Stiewe visitan con asiduidad España y conocen la crisis de la vivienda en sus grandes ciudades. Los precios del alquiler en Barcelona y Madrid son superiores a los de Berlín: el metro cuadrado de alquiler es un 71% más elevado en la ciudad condal, según datos comparados de los buscadores inmobiliarios Idealista e InmoScout, y un 64% más en la capital de España. A ello hay que añadir que el poder adquisitivo de sus ciudadanos es menor que en Berlín.

¿Qué hace diferente la problemática en la capital alemana? “Una particularidad importante de Berlín es que la situación ha cambiado rápido en poco tiempo, en los últimos 20 años”, opina Markus. Hasta inicio de siglo, prosigue este programador informático de 48 años, había más oferta que demanda porque muchos edificios y solares del antiguo Berlín oriental estaban vacíos y podían incorporarse al mercado inmobiliario. “Otra diferencia es que en el pasado no había un interés por especular, y ahora está a la orden del día que cualquiera invierta y especule, es lo que llamamos el oro de cemento”, añade Hauke.

Edificio en construcción en el centro de Berlín, el 25 de septiembre. FILIP SINGER (EFE)

“Berlín era considerada como la gran ciudad con los alquileres más asequibles, en comparación con otras, pero esto ha cambiado drásticamente en los últimos años”, confirma Wibke Werner.

Markus es escéptico sobre la efectividad de las propuestas de Die Linke y, sobre todo, de que puedan ser financiadas. “Los partidarios de las expropiaciones aseguran que podrán pagarse a un 40% de su precio de mercado, lo dudo”. Stiewe, por el contrario, sí cree que es viable: “La reducción de los alquileres dará más capacidad económica a los ciudadanos y eso repercutirá positivamente en las cuentas públicas”.

AfD pesca en aguas revueltas

Otro factor diferencial que destacan estos vecinos de Friedrichshain es que la capital ha recibido 500.000 nuevos vecinos en la última década (la población es de 3,9 millones). Muchos de estos nuevos berlineses son migrantes y de ello se aprovecha el discurso del otro partido que se ha disparado electoralmente, la extrema derecha de Alternativa para Alemania (AfD).

Los hasta ahora grandes partidos sobre los que se construyó la Alemania democrática, la CDU y el SPD, pierden apoyo electoral a marchas forzadas en favor de formaciones hasta ahora minoritarias y con propuestas alejadas del centro político.

El primer punto del programa electoral de AfD está dedicado a la vivienda y empieza así: “El crecimiento demográfico provocado por las políticas migratorias descontroladas, sumado a la creciente dificultad de construir nueva vivienda, ha disparado los precios de los alquileres a niveles récord y ha multiplicado la necesidad de viviendas sociales”.

“Esta afirmación es absurda y no tiene base”, dice Werner: “Si bien es cierto que Berlín tiene muy pocos apartamentos asequibles y muy poca vivienda social en general, casi la mitad de los residentes de Berlín, por sus ingresos bajos, podrían solicitar el certificado para acceder a una vivienda social. La demanda de vivienda social, que supera la oferta, existe independientemente de la llegada de nuevos residentes”.

“Además”, prosigue la directora de Berliner Mieterverein, “los extranjeros a menudo desconocen la legislación sobre alquiler y el idioma alemán, y algunos propietarios los consideran un público objetivo para viviendas con precios exorbitantes”.

World.title: Meerdink double gives Xavi first win as Oranje coach in Belgrade
World.content:
Mexx Meerdink’s first two international goals were enough for the Netherlands to edge past Serbia and earn Xavi Hernandez his first win as coach in a gritty encounter in Belgrade.

Meerdink scored from the penalty spot in the first half after Crysencio Summerville was brought down in the area, and slotted the winner midway through the second half in a period when Oranje were dominating.

But there was a blow for Xavi ahead when Cody Gakpo had to be replaced by Ruben van Bommel in the 17th minute after going down under a heavy challenge from Saša Lukici in the penalty area.

The coach said he satisfied with his first week of competitive fixtures, including the 1-1 draw with Germany in Amsterdam on Thursday, but saw plenty of room for improvement.

“I feel happy that we got three points, but we need to play better, especially in the first half,” Xavi said. “Second half we dominated more and attacked the spaces more.

“It’s important to get the three points, but the most important thing is we are generating lots of chances to score and the players feel comfortable with the structure that we have.”

Stodgy first half

Oranje had the better of a stodgy first 45 minutes of their second Nations League fixture, but only occasionally showed a cutting edge. Meerdink was unable to connect properly with Gakpo’s cross in the 15th minute, while a long spell of possession ended with Ryan Gravenberch dragging a shot wide.

The Dutch looked comfortable defending their lead and almost went further ahead when Serbia goalkeeper Vanja Milinkovic-Savic needed all of his 2.02m height to tip Joey Veerman’s inswinging corner over the crossbar.

The home side equalised right at the start of the second half as they poured into the Dutch penalty area, drawing two good saves from Bart Verbruggen. The Oranje defenders were unable to clear their lines and the ball fell to half-time substitute Luka Jovic, who gave Verbruggen no chance from close range.

Dumfries dangerous

The Dutch took a grip on the game with Denzel Dumfries repeatedly finding space down the right, first picking out Van Bommel, whose shot hit the outside of the post, before an even better cross was turned over the crossbar by Tijjani Reijnders.

Meerdink’s winner in the 69th minute was provided by Guus Til, who had just come on as a substitute, as the AZ striker held off the close attentions of his marker to steer the ball into in the far corner.

Jovic remained Serbia’s greatest threat as the hosts pushed for an equaliser, twice flashing headers narrowly wide, while Van Bommel should have put the game beyond reach with a late breakaway, but his tame shot failed to test Milinkovic-Savic.

The Netherlands next play Greece, who beat Serbia 2-1 in their opening match, in Thessaloniki on Thursday.

World.title: Would you read a book if it was printed like a newspaper?
World.content:
Typically, book formats are pretty standard. Hardback, paperback, e-book. But in the 1970s, a Dutch publisher tried a new configuration for novels: the newspaper.

Theo Knippenberg attributes his publishing career to his mother, who had for years nagged him to find a respectable trade.

“Totally by accident, I became a publisher,” Knippenberg told DutchNews.

The now 80-year-old stumbled on his success at an arts festival in Utrecht in the late 1960s. He sold a series of tiny books, bound together with an elastic band, by Dutch writers.

Knippenberg expalined that he ran into author Harry Mulisch at a road crossing and convinced the writer of The Discovery of Heaven to let him publish an excerpt of an essay. Once Mulisch was on board, Knippenberg used it as leverage to convince other famous Dutch writers, such as Jan Wolkers, to contribute.

A voracious reader, Knippenberg found books unaffordable during his student years. He took the proceeds from the mini book sales and invested them into publishing equipment – not a traditional printing press but one built to print newspapers.

Thinner newsprint was cheaper to produce and therefore cheaper to sell. Together with his wife, Patty Voorsmit, Knippenberg launched Bulkboek.

The first edition, published in 1970, was Schroot by Belgian writer Jef Geeraerts. It follows a former colonel in the Belgian military who is struggling to adapt to life in the Congo.

Over the following 26 years, Bulkboek would publish 250 novels in the newspaper format.

Readers could 

The editions were aimed at secondary students and included interviews, critical essays and explanatory texts to help readers understand the work.

The works were selected based on published availability and “my own tastes,” Knippenberg said.

He knew nothing about how publishing worked and had to learn how to create the text sheets, include illustrations and run the books off. He describes his early set-up as “so primitive.”

The initial print runs were all books from Dutch or Flemish authors but by the late 1970s, Knippenberg began branching out. “I got ambitious,” he says. Leo Tolstoy, Pablo Neruda and Iris Murdoch were a few of the authors whose works found their way into the Bulkboek format.

The publisher also moved beyond the Netherlands into Belgium, Germany and France, and began to publish books in languages other than Dutch.

In the early 1990s, the economics of publishing had changed, as cheap paperbacks came onto the market.

Last year, Bulkboek was taken over by educational publisher BruutTAAL, but Knippenberg continues to be involved with some aspects of the company. The new endeavour is working on a series of publications of short stories.

“Students have much shorter attention spans these days,” he says, explaining why short fiction is a better way to draw in young readers.

The publication format continues. On second-hand book websites, Bulkboeks are still available for sale. Leo Tolstoy’s Boyhood, Cees Nooteboom’s Half the World and Willem Frederik Hermans’s The Signet Ring can all be found, many for two or three euros. Less than you would have paid when they were first published by Bulkboek.

World.title: Opposition parties Pro and Volt team up to force budget deal
World.content:
Opposition parties Pro and Volt have joined forces for the next round of budget negotiations as they try to step up the pressure on the cabinet to make further concessions on social security.

Prime minister Rob Jetten said ministers had spent the last week drawing up “a new and attractive offer” addressing opposition parties’ concerns on welfare, the cost of living and replacing the “Box 3” asset tax mechanism.

Pro leader Jesse Klaver said the combined votes of his left-wing party and the pro-European Volt would give the government a “stable majority” in both houses of parliament.

An agreement with both Pro and Volt would give the coalition parties a comfortable majority in the lower house and the 16 seats it needs in the Senate, where Pro is the largest group but still needs Volt’s two seats to get over the line.

But the right-wing liberal VVD, the party of finance minister Eelco Heinen, is anxious not to make too many concessions to Pro, which would risk driving its voters away to its rivals such as JA21 and Geert Wilders’ far-right PVV.

Pick a side

“We are fighting for progress for ordinary people and a fair contribution from the super-rich,” Klaver said. “We believe in progressive co-operation.”

Volt leader Laurens Dassen said: “The world is changing rapidly. People expect politicians to work together towards a sustainable and innovative future.”

Jetten has been under pressure from the opposition on left and right to choose a side after all parties poured cold water on his hopes of finding a route through the middle.

The prime minister argued he would be “short-changing the country” if he excluded one side from the talks, but JA21 leader Joost Eerdmans said a broad approach “isn’t going to work” while Klaver warned his party would block the entire budget if the cabinet tried to do separate deals for each department.

Welfare cuts

Heinen has already agreed to postpone or cancel around half of the €6 billion cuts to welfare spending that were in the coalition agreement in February, but Pro wants the cabinet to go further.

Parties such as JA21, on the other hand, want to see even bigger welfare cuts, arguing that lower taxes are the best way to relieve the pressure on households and businesses.

Jetten and Heinen held talks on Saturday with Pro, Volt and the ChristenUnie, whose leader, Mirjam Bikker, said there had been “movement” from the coalition parties.

The ChristenUnie’s priorities are to ensure households are able to pay for essentials through the winter as energy and grocery bills rise. Bikker said it was “high time” that the coalition parties “feel the urgency” to make a deal.

BBB back on board

Later on Saturday the two ministers are due to talk to JA21 and the orthodox-protestant SGP, who have formed a right-wing alliance with 12 seats in the lower house.

Jetten and Heinen will also speak to Jan Struijs, leader of pensioners’ party 50Plus, and Henk Vermeer of the farmers’ party BBB, who are the second largest party in the Senate.

Jetten had initially said the BBB were no longer an option after the party backed a motion of no confidence during the budget debate, but he and Vermeer patched up their differences in a phone call last week.

World.title: Man shot dead in packed bar in Amsterdam was prison warden
World.content:
A man who was shot dead on a packed terrace in Amsterdam on Friday afternoon was a warden at a local prison, Dutch media have confirmed.

Marcel Blijd was killed at point-blank range as he sat outside De Baanderij restaurant on the NSDM quay, on the north bank of the IJ, in what initially appeared to be a row over a dog running off its leash.

Sources quoted by Het Parool and local crime news sites said the gunman had previously been detained in Zaandstad prison, where Blijd worked, but it is not clear if the two men knew each other.

The shooting at 3pm was witnessed by dozens of people who were enjoying a drink at the bar, and filmed by several people in the area.

Video footage showed the gunman, wearing a white shirt and red trousers, threw the weapon into the water but made no effort to flee and surrendered to police when they arrived a few minutes later.



One witness said the two men clashed initially over the shooter’s dog, which was running loose around the quayside and barking. “He walked up and down a few times. We thought they were going to come to blows, but then there were shots.”

An ambulance and air ambulance were called to the scene, but Blijd could not be saved. A child’s buggy was parked next to the spot where he lay.

Detectives are now investigating whether the shooting was linked to Blijd’s position at Zaanstad jail, where some of Amsterdam’s most dangerous criminals are housed, including members of the Top 600 – a list of repeat offenders, many with connections to the underworld.

“Father figure”

Blijd worked in the prison system for 30 years and was seen as a “father figure” by colleagues and the young criminals he worked with, one colleague told Het Parool.

“Marcel could get on with everybody,” the colleague said. “If you were working with him in the cell block, you knew it was going to be a good day.”

Police cordoned off the area around the terrace and ferries to and from Amsterdam Centraal Station, which dock beside the restaurant, were suspended for three hours while investigations were carried out at the scene.

Witnesses were taken in police vans to the local police station to have their statements taken. Anyone who was in the area at the time can contact Victim Support Netherlands (Slachtofferhulp) for advice and counselling.

World.title: New group home for psychiatric patients tried in Rotterdam
World.content:
Rotterdam is to set up a new type of supervised accommodation for homeless people with serious psychiatric problems and addiction issues.

Forty people will be brought together under one roof in Poortugaal, a village near Rotterdam that is also home to a forensic psychiatric clinic, in a supervised environment where they can receive more structured support.

The residents will be allowed to stay in the facility for up to eight years, receiving long-term and structured support that is often lacking in temporary accommodation.

Around 1,500 people in the Netherlands are classed as posing a high risk to public safety. They often have learning difficulties, suffer from psychiatric illness and struggle with addiction, which can lead to aggressive, disruptive or deranged behaviour in public.

Many of the patients have spent their lives alternating between living on the streets and being incarcerated in clinics or prisons, posing a danger to themselves and others.

Pillar to post

“They get passed from pillar to post when what they really need is intensive support for several years,” Laura van Goor, of Artes, the organisation running the facility, told Nieuwsuur. “But we don’t have that right now in the Netherlands.”

Psychiatric clinics are intended for short stays of around three months, but patients often end up staying longer to prevent them ending up back on the streets.

But the treatment is short-term and keeping patients in care for longer adds to waiting lists.

Van Goor said the patients would have more freedom to move around on the campus than in smaller-scale facilities, while also benefiting from a more structured regime. They will not be allowed out unsupervised.

Drink and drugs will be formally banned, unlike in temporary housing where usage is usually tolerated. “But it’s not a case of ‘if you use, you’re out,’ Van Good said. “That’s not possible: 95% of them have drug problems.”

World.title: Nearly half of people experience neighborhood nuisance
World.content:

Almost half of Dutch people say that have experience social nuisance in their neighborhood, from noisy neighbors to the drug trade, according to new figures from the Dutch statistics office.

The CBS released its biennial Safety Monitor on Friday, which found that 42% of adults say they dealt with some type of anti-social behaviour near their homes during 2025.

The report looks at crime and safety issues across the country.

The largest number of complaints stem from loitering youth, which make up 26% of the reported problems. Issues with neighbors account for 20% of the concerns.

Overall problems with nuisance have risen in the past few years. Some 14% of people say they have experienced significant social nuisance in their neighborhood, up from 12% in 2021.

Those living in urban areas have the most problems. City residents report nearly four times the number of issues than non-urban dwellers.

World.title: Cabinet wants private companies to pay more towards gas storage
World.content:
The Dutch government wants to make private companies responsible for storing gas for the winter to cut its liabilities as prices on the markets soar.

At the moment the cost of filling the four gas storage facilities in Norg, Grijpskerk, Bergermeer and Alkmaar is met by the government-funded operator Energie Beheer Nederland, but soaring gas prices mean they are facing a €1 billion loss.

Private companies have no commercial incentive to stock up on gas for the winter because prices are currently forecast to drop after the autumn.

Demand has been stoked by the need for European governments to meet EU-set targets to fill their gas reserves by the start of November. The Netherlands last week reduced its target figure from 74% to 64%. The current storage level is 57.5%.

Under EU rules the Dutch government is also not allowed to keep the stored gas it buys for itself, but must export it to other member states who need it, as well as the UK, which has limited gas storage facilities.

The Netherlands’ facilities date from the time when it exported gas from the Slochteren field in Groningen, but since it was forced to end production two years ago because of earthquakes in the northern province it has filled the chambers with imported gas.

LNG imports

The high cost of importing liquefied national gas from the United States, which is the main supplier, have added to the government’s costs.

It wants to pass on the cost to commercial companies such as Essent, Eneco and Vattenfall by making it mandatory for them to build up their own reserves. A similar obligation is in force in Austria.

“At the moment there is virtually no market in the Netherlands for storing gas in the seasonal storage facilities, even though seasonal storage is an essential element of supply guarantee in the portfolio of suppliers’ prospectuses,” the letter, sent from the ministry of economic affairs, said.

“The question is whether the bill should continue to be met by the Dutch taxpayer, or whether supply guarantee can be be ensured through a different mix of measures for a lower cost.”

World.title: Russia condemns Polish city’s “barbaric” removal of Monument of Gratitude to the Red Army
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Russia has criticised the removal of a monument in the Polish city of Rzeszów expressing “gratitude” to the Soviet Red Army. It called the move “barbaric” and “sacrilegious”. The monument – part of which will be moved to a nearby Soviet cemetery and another to a museum – has been the subject of a long-running legal and political battle, amid wider debate in Poland about “decommunising” public spaces, especially in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. ⚡️Komentarz Ambasady Rosji w Polsce 23 września 2026 r. w Rzeszowie (województwo podkarpackie), decyzją władz polskich i z naruszeniem dokumentów rosyjsko-polskich dotyczących ochrony obiektów dziedzictwa memorialnego, rozpoczęto proces demontażu pomnika wdzięczności żołnierzom… pic.twitter.com/HYuNeLG5dy — Russian Embassy, PL (@rusemb_pl) September 24, 2026 The Monument of Gratitude to the Red Army, standing 8.5 metres tall and weighing 6.6 tons, was erected in Rzeszów, southeast Poland, shortly after the end of World War Two, when the Soviets had pushed Nazi Germany out of Poland and then installed their own communist government. It is located on Ghetto Victims Square, a public space also created after the war on the grounds of the city’s former Jewish cemetery, which had been destroyed by the German occupiers in 1942. Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance, a state historical body, notes that the monument was erected just a few metres from where two Polish anti-communist resistance fighters who had been members of the wartime Home Army (AK) had been publicly hanged by the communists. The monument’s plinth featured bas-relief sculptures depicting Red Army Generals Ivan Konev and Karol Świerczewski, soldiers, and industrial and agricultural workers carrying a hammer and sickle. At the top of the 8.5-metre column was a statue of a woman and child. In 2016, the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government introduced a law requiring local authorities to “decommunise” public spaces by removing objects and names that “propagate communism”. That triggered a legal battle in over the monument in Rzeszów. The government-appointed provincial governor and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body, moved to have it dismantled, arguing that the monument glorified communism. But city hall – led by left-wing mayor Tadeusz Ferenc, who had been a member of the communist party before 1989 – challenged the decision. It argued that the monument did not promote communism and noted that its name, referring to gratitude to the Red Army, was not an official one. In 2019, the provincial administrative court sided with the city and overturned the decision to remove the monument. However, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 prompted many Polish municipalities that had not removed Soviet-era monuments to begin doing so. In April 2022, Rzeszów’s current mayor, Konrad Fijołek, announced that his city’s monument would be removed from its current location and placed in a Soviet soldiers’ cemetery elsewhere in the city. “In principle, I am not in favor of dismantling or demolishing monuments, as they are a testament to history,” said the mayor. “But in light of the current wartime reality, this monument should not remain in its current location. But we are not barbarians; we will not demolish the monument, but relocate it.” However, the IPN opposed the idea of relocating the monument and refused to cover the costs of doing so. It wanted it to be liquidated entirely. Another Soviet memorial has been demolished in Poland – the 43rd since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "We say ‘no’ to Russians who believe these lands somehow belong to their sphere of influence,” declared the Institute of National Remembrance https://t.co/aG9VQVlUQI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 12, 2025 As a result, the city is paying 156,000 zloty (€35,700) for the monument to be removed, reports news website Wirtualna Polska. The bas-reliefs will go to the Soviet cemetery while the statue of mother and child will go to the city’s Museum of Technology and the Military. Work to remove the monument began this week and is expected to last until November. Once the above-ground section has been removed, a special conservation committee, including a representative of Poland’s Rabbinical Commission for Cemeteries, will determine how to proceed with the monument’s foundation. The beginning of the removal work prompted anger from Moscow, with the Russian embassy in Warsaw issuing a statement that called it a “sacrilegious step”. It demanded “the immediate cessation of work” and restoration of the monument to its previous state. “With regret, we must state once again: the barbaric policy of the Polish authorities, consisting of destroying everything that serves as evidence of the invaluable feat of the soldiers and officers of the Red Army in liberating Poland from Nazi occupation, is being continued at an ever faster pace,” they continued. Russia regards the Soviet Union’s driving of Nazi Germany out of Central and Eastern Europe at the end of World War Two as a “liberation”. However, many in the region reject that term, given that it involved bringing their countries under brutal Soviet domination instead. In its statement, the Russian embassy also claimed that the actions in Rzeszów are a “violation of Russian-Polish documents concerning the protection of memorial heritage sites”. Moscow regularly claims that Poland’s removal of Soviet memorials violates a 1994 agreement between the two countries on respect for graves and other places of memory. It did so in August this year, when protesting the demolition of a monument in the town of Pyrzyce. However, Poland points out that the agreement relates to graves and war cemeteries, not separate monuments and symbols, which can be legally removed. Russia has criticised the "sacrilegious" demolition of a Soviet monument in Poland, calling it a “flagrant violation” of a bilateral agreement. But Poland's @ipngovpl says it was a "propaganda object" that had to be removed under a "decommunisation" law https://t.co/73T99ZlPqU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Rzeszów is also home to one of the famous – or infamous, depending on one’s perspective – communist-era monuments in Poland, the 38-metre-tall Monument to the Revolutionary Struggle. It has become a landmark of the city. In 2017, the IPN recommended that it be removed under the “decommunisation” law. The owners of the land upon which it sits also wanted to demolish it. However, mayors Ferenc and Fijołek sought to protect the monument, and their efforts succeeded last year, when it was added to Poland’s list of protected monuments, preventing it from being destroyed. World.title: Polish president “doesn’t like” Trump inviting Putin to G20 but will still attend summit
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish President Karol Nawrocki “does not like” the fact that the Trump administration has invited Vladimir Putin to this year’s G20 summit in the United States, says his chief foreign policy aide. However, Nawrocki, who is a close ally of Donald Trump, still plans to attend the event – which Poland has been invited to as a guest rather than a full G20 member – in order to represent Polish interests and push for full membership of the group. 🔴 "Nie podoba nam się to". Nawrocki ma problem po decyzji Trumpa Prezydent Karol Nawrocki weźmie udział w grudniowym szczycie G20 w Miami, na który zaproszono również Władimira Putina. Szef Biura Polityki Międzynarodowej Kancelarii Prezydenta Marcin Przydacz przyznał na antenie… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) September 26, 2026 The G20, a major intergovernmental forum, holds an annual summit whose location rotates among members. This year’s event will take place in December at a golf resort in Miami owned by Trump. On Wednesday this week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Trump has invited Putin to attend the summit, saying that “we think it’s an opportunity for him to engage…with other world leaders” and “we hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept”. “If you only meet with people that you agree with, then these are very nice meetings but nothing happens,” added Rubio. “In order to solve problems, you have to meet with people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with.” Marco Rubio on Russia: We’ve invited President Putin to the G20. We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with Trump, but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he will accept. pic.twitter.com/e0GSz7Y8gm — Clash Report (@clashreport) September 23, 2026 Last December, Rubio also announced Poland’s invitation to the summit as a guest, saying that it would be “assuming its rightful place in the G20”. In May this year, the US also “expressed its strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member”. Poland will be represented by Nawrocki, who is a vocal critic of Putin and Russia, and is himself on a Russian wanted list for his work leading efforts to demolish Soviet-era monuments in Poland. In an interview on Sunday with news website Wirtualna Polska, the head of Nawrocki’s international policy office, Marcin Przydacz, was asked if the US was right to invite Putin. “We don’t like it,” he replied. “But we were invited to the G20 summit as guests, and it’s not our role to tell the participants who should be part of it,” he added, noting that Russia is a founding member of the G20. However, “if it were up to us, Russia should be isolated in all international forums.” Nevertheless, “President [Nawrocki] is going to Miami and doesn’t intend to change his plans at this stage”, confirmed Przydacz. “Poland will be at the G20 summit because it’s in our interest…This isn’t the only format in which we sit with countries we disagree with.” However, he also added that, “if the Russian leader actually intends to come, and is not just invited, we will discuss this with our European and Euro-Atlantic allies”. Putin has not attended a G20 summit in person since 2019, initially due to the COVID-19 pandemic and later amid the fallout from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant against him. The US is not a member of the ICC, so the arrest warrant does not apply on its territory. Przydacz told Wirtualna Polska that Putin “should be held accountable for his crimes”. Asked if Nawrocki would shake hands with the Russian president at the G20, Przydacz said that he “doesn’t think any interactions will occur”. The United States has expressed "strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member" following talks in Warsaw, after which it also emphasised "strong and growing" Polish-American relations https://t.co/qTpCACnMfu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 2, 2026 He also emphasised that Poland’s invitation to the summit was a “major success, demonstrating our growing role”. He said that Nawrocki would use the event to push its ambition to become a full member of the group. He added that it would also seek to “bring a Central European perspective” to the event, representing its entire region, which has so far been excluded from the G20. Earlier this week, Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski said that, in his opinion, the US should make Putin’s invitation to the G20 conditional upon Russia implementing a ceasefire in Ukraine, reported news website Interia. However, he noted that, when a G20 meeting of finance ministers took place in the US earlier this year, Poland had attended alongside Russia. President @NawrockiKn says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump” https://t.co/uGGJSBe5nr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 23, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support to its eastern neighbour. Poland has also been one of the primary targets of Russia’s hybrid actions against European countries, including airspace violations, acts of sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation. World.title: Poland extends tax rights to same-sex couples with foreign marriages
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad and have had their wedding certificates transcribed into the Polish registry the same tax rights as other married couples. The decision follows a ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) requiring Poland – whose domestic law does not allow same-sex couples to form any type of legal union – to recognise same-sex marriages contracted in other EU member states. Podpisałem dziś interpretację ogólną, która zapewnia, że osoby, które uzyskały transkrypcję aktu małżeństwa będą miały w polskich urzędach skarbowych takie same prawa i obowiązki podatkowe jak wszyscy małżonkowie. — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) September 24, 2026 “Today, I signed a general interpretation ensuring that persons who have obtained a transcription of their marriage certificate will have the same tax rights and obligations in Polish tax offices as all other married couples,” announced finance minister Andrzej Domański in a social media post. A general interpretation is an official position taken by the finance ministry aiming to clarify the application of tax law in a specific area. Among the benefits that couples with a transcribed foreign marriage certificate can now receive include preferential treatment under inheritance and gift tax rules and the ability to file joint personal income tax returns. Couples may also pay tax on behalf of a spouse and refuse to testify as a witness in proceedings involving their spouse. “This is about basic equality, justice and fairness,” Domański told broadcaster TVN. “We want these rights to be enforceable in an effective way.” The finance minister said that the decision would have a “negligible” impact on the state budget. He also noted that such couples would be subject to the obligations that apply to other married couples in Poland, which include liability for their spouse’s tax obligations. Osoby, które uzyskały tak zwaną transkrypcję aktu małżeństwa, będą miały przed polskimi urzędami skarbowymi dokładnie takie same prawa i obowiązki jak pozostali małżonkowie – powiedział minister finansów Andrzej Domański w rozmowie z Grzegorzem Kajdanowiczem w @faktypofaktach w… pic.twitter.com/uVwDaD3ZDk — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 24, 2026 The finance minister’s decision has drawn criticism from right-wing politicians, who argue that recognition of same-sex marriage violates the constitution, which states that “marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland”. Paweł Szefernaker, chief of staff to President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, said Domański’s actions were “inconsistent with the constitution” and had been carried out “without legislation, without debate, without honestly telling Poles what is really happening”. “Everyone has the right to a private life,” he added. “However, the state has a duty to protect the legal order and provide tax support for marriage.” Patryk Jaki, a deputy leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition party, said that the finance minister’s actions “clearly violate Polish law and will have legal implications in the future” for Domański, who is “writing additional points in the indictment against himself”. Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) group, said the tax interpretation “will be revoked on the very first day” if his party comes to power. To jest niezgodna z Konstytucją próba faktycznego zrównania małżeństwa ze związkami jednopłciowymi. Bez zmiany Konstytucji, bez ustawy, bez debaty, bez uczciwego powiedzenia Polakom, co naprawdę się dzieje. Każdy ma prawo do prywatnego życia według własnych wyborów. Ale państwo… https://t.co/0CQ9Lnfl02 — Paweł Szefernaker 🇵🇱 (@szefernaker) September 24, 2026 The changes follow a ruling issued by the CJEU in November 2025 ordering Poland to recognise same-sex marriages contracted in other EU states. The court found that failing to do so infringes the freedom to move and reside within the EU as well as the right to respect for private and family life. In light of that ruling, in March this year, Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA) ordered Warsaw’s registry office to recognise a marriage conducted by two Polish men in Germany by transcribing it into the Polish civil registry. In May, the Polish government issued a regulation allowing such transcriptions of foreign same-sex marriages to take place nationwide. It went into force in August. However, even before then, some cities had begun transcribing marriage certificates, beginning with Warsaw and Wrocław in May. At the end of August, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski reported that 84 same-sex couples had already transcribed their foreign marriages under the government’s new regulation. Poland has begun paying benefits to same-sex couples who married abroad then entered their marriage into the Polish registry. The EU court ordered Poland to recognise such marriages, even though domestic law does not allow for any form of same-sex union https://t.co/svnRjyBO8Q — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 22, 2026 While foreign same-sex marriages can now be entered into Poland’s civil registry, questions have remained as to what that will mean in practice for such couples, especially as domestic law does not recognise same-sex relationships. In another development, labour minister Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk announced last week that the Social Insurance Institution (ZUS) has begun paying care allowances to qualifying same-sex couples who married abroad and have had their wedding certificates transcribed into the Polish registry. World.title: Prosecutors drop case in which Wałęsa was accused of lying about being communist collaborator
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prosecutors have ended a decade-long case in which former president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa was accused of falsely claiming not to have authored documents relating to his alleged cooperation with the communist authorities. Wałęsa, who led the Solidarity movement that helped bring down the communist regime in the 1980s, has always denied longstanding claims that, in the 1970s, he acted as an informant to the communist security services. The case has become highly politicised, with right-wing figures – especially from the Law and Justice (PiS) party that ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023 – critical of Wałęsa. By contrast, the former president, who turns 83 next week, enjoys good relations with the current ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Waldemar Żurek, Tusk’s justice minister and prosecutor general, welcomed the decision to drop the case against Wałęsa, saying that, under PiS, “a politicised state apparatus hounded the legend of Solidarity, deliberately ignoring facts and basic logic”. Now, “truth has triumphed over an attempt to rewrite history”. Prokuratura ostatecznie umorzyła śledztwo przeciwko Lechowi Wałęsie. Przez lata upolityczniony aparat państwa ścigał legendę „Solidarności”, celowo ignorując fakty i elementarną logikę. Zignorowano bezsporny fakt historyczny – SB masowo fałszowała dokumenty i podpisy Wałęsy w… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 24, 2026 The case in question stems from statements made by Wałęsa in 2016 during an investigation by the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body that also has prosecutorial powers. Those proceedings, in which the former Polish president testified as a witness, were launched after documents apparently carrying his signature were found in the home archives of former communist interior minister Czesław Kiszczak. The files indicated that Wałęsa, working under the code name TW Bolek, signed a commitment to collaborate with the communist Security Service (SB). They also included payslips and informant’s notes. The former president had told the media at the time when the documents were discovered that they had been forged. When speaking to IPN investigators, he also denied having drafted or signed all but one of the documents. However, prosecutors subsequently claimed that – after comparing the documents from Kiszczak’s file with others they said had been written and signed by Wałęsa, as well as consulting forensic handwriting experts – Wałęsa’s testimony was false in the case of over 50 of the documents. In 2021, the former president was charged with giving false testimony. Then, in 2023, he was indicted, meaning the case was sent to court. However, in 2024, after Tusk’s government had taken power from PiS, prosecutors asked that the case be returned to them by the court, which agreed to the request. Now, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw has announced that it is discontinuing the case entirely, after finding that there are no grounds for Wałęsa to be prosecuted. Lech Wałęsa will face trial accused of falsely testifying not to have signed documents of cooperation with the communist authorities. If convicted, he can be jailed for up to 3 years. He calls the claims against him "terrible insults and monstrous lies" https://t.co/X0eb4e5ahm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2023 In a statement explaining the decision, prosecutors claimed that there had been significant “methodological errors” made previously in attributing handwritten texts to Wałęsa and in handwriting comparisons between them. “There was no evidence to assume with 100% certainty that the comparative material actually came from Lech Wałęsa,” they wrote. In fact, “the evidence collected clearly indicated that Lech Wałęsa did not write long manuscripts during his life, and especially not in the 1970s”. “Some witnesses explicitly stated that, at that time, he was a secondary illiterate,” meaning someone who has lost their ability to read and write, said the prosecutors. “He was not able to write and could barely read.” This, along with other concerns over how the case was previously conducted, “led to the conclusion that there was no certain basis to assume that Lech Wałęsa was the author of the documents disclosed in the ‘Kiszczak files’, and therefore there was no evidence that he lied during the interrogation”. Hit! Ekipa Tuska ogłosiła Wałęsę analfabetą by wybronić go przed Bolkiem! To się nie dzieje! To niemożliwe! pic.twitter.com/PQnOn5XDb0 — Sławomir Cenckiewicz (@Cenckiewicz) September 24, 2026 Prosecutors also said that “the testimony of numerous witnesses proves that the files of TW Bolek, discovered in the possession of General Kiszczak’s widow, were most likely fabricated. Finally, they argued that, even if Wałęsa had given false testimony, he was protected by the constitutional right against self-incrimination while being interviewed as a witness. “The prosecution found that Lech Wałęsa could have feared that if he admitted to having prepared or signed the documents from the ‘Kiszczak files’…all his testimonies in which he denied being secret collaborator “Bolek” in previous proceedings…would be deemed false and would lead to his being held criminally liable.” Lech Wałęsa, Angela Merkel and Volodymyr Zelensky have been named the first distinguished members of the European Order of Merit. The award was created by the European Parliament to "honour those who did not simply believe in Europe, but helped build it" https://t.co/inosiiRQkW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 11, 2026 In response to the announcement, Wałęsa shared on his Facebook page the post by Żurek praising the prosecutors’ decision. Wałęsa then added a comment claiming that Jarosław and Lech Kaczyński, the founders of PiS, had ordered a right-wing historian, Sławomir Cenckiewicz, to fake the Kiszczak files. Cenckiewicz has written extensively about Wałęsa, including about his alleged collaboration with the communist security services. He also recently served as national security advisor to current Polish President Karol Nawrocki, who was elected last year with the support of PiS. In a series of social media posts on Thursday, Cenkiewicz said that he had “never read a bigger lie” than the prosecutors’ statement justifying dropping the case. He also ridiculed the idea that Wałęsa could have led the Solidarity movement in the 1980s and served as president in the 1990s if he was a “secondary illiterate”. Większego kłamstwa przebranego w wymiar sprawiedliwości RP nigdy nie czytałem! To większe kłamstwo niż skandaliczny wyrok Kapińskiego i spółki z 2000 r.! Reżim Tuska uznał, że Wałęsa nie był Bolkiem, a Instytut Sehna niczego kategorycznie nie ustalił! I powtórzyli brednie… — Sławomir Cenckiewicz (@Cenckiewicz) September 24, 2026 The accusations of communist collaboration have tarnished Wałęsa’s reputation among some Poles. In 2017, shortly after the Kiszczak files were uncovered, a poll by IBRiS for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 28% believed Wałęsa was not a national hero. However, 62% said that he was. Earlier this year, Wałęsa was named as one of the first three distinguished members of the European Order of Merit, a new initiative launched by the European Parliament, alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and former German Chancellor Angela Merkel. Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Polish government has launched an information campaign on how to respond in the event of an air strike. It has also announced that 85,000 shelters are to be marked with clear signs across Poland and an evacuation plan is being developed. The moves come amid growing concerns over Russia strikes in Ukraine near the Polish border. The prime minister and foreign minister have warned that Russia could be planning “something big” this year, without specifying what that might involve. 🟡 KOMUNIKAT | MSWiA publikuje instrukcję reagowania podczas zagrożenia atakiem z powietrza. 📄 Ministerstwo Spraw Wewnętrznych i Administracji udostępnia nową instrukcję postępowania na wypadek ataku z powietrza. To rozwinięcie treści zawartych w „Poradniku Bezpieczeństwa”,… pic.twitter.com/aw3h07mdeF — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 25, 2026 On Friday, Poland’s interior ministry published information on how to respond to the threat of an air attack, expanding on a safety handbook sent to all 17 million households in the country earlier this year. The new guidelines explain where to seek cover during an air raid, how to prepare homes and what to do if an attack occurs while people are at home, at work, outdoors or in a car. They advise people to seek a shelter point, take a prepared evacuation backpack and any necessary medication, and use only stairs. If reaching a shelter would require spending a long time outdoors, people are advised to remain inside and move to a central room without windows. Separately, the ministry has prepared guidelines for schools after some were criticised last week for evacuating children outside school buildings during alarms in the eastern province of Lublin. W całej Polsce mają pojawić się obowiązkowe oznaczenia Punktów Schronienia. Specjalna aplikacja pokaże ich lokalizacje, a nowe oznakowanie ma ułatwić mieszkańcom znalezienie bezpiecznego miejsca w sytuacji zagrożenia. Materiał 🎥 Michał Niewodowski pic.twitter.com/HVoo3ypETT — 19.30 TVP (@1930_tvp) September 21, 2026 To make shelter points easier to identify, the interior ministry has prepared a draft regulation requiring local authorities and managers of designated sites to mark them clearly by the end of the year with a blue triangle on an orange background, as well as a green sign saying “Punkt schronienia” (“Shelter point”). The locations can also be found using a mobile application launched last year. According to the ministry’s own data, Poland currently has about 85,000 shelter points, which could host 23.7 million people, or 64% of the country’s population. A national plan is also being developed to coordinate potential evacuation as a result of war, a threat of war or a natural disaster. The plan is intended to establish evacuation routes and reception areas in advance, including how many people may need to be moved and where they could be accommodated. “When a threat arises, we warn the Polish people and defend our security. It is only natural that we prepare for worst-case scenarios, while deeply believing that they will never come to pass,” interior minister Marcin Kierwiński told the Rzeczpospolita newspaper. “Evacuation plans are being prepared…These plans rely heavily on the strength of the entire crisis response system. The more we strengthen that system, the more precise the plans will be,” Kierwiński added. Poland has launched a mobile application and website that allows people to find their nearest shelter in times of war or other emergencies https://t.co/YE3rsltCj5 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 22, 2025 The evacuation plans have become the subject of false claims circulating on social media. These posts allege that the government is preparing to forcibly displace Poles and ultimately eliminate the Polish nation, with some linking the alleged plan to an agreement between Berlin and Kyiv, reports the Onet news service. They claim that evacuees would never be allowed to return, allegations the government quickly moved to debunk. 📢 STOP FAKE NEWS! W sieci krążą fałszywe informacje, jakoby przygotowywany Krajowy Plan Ewakuacji miał oznaczać masowe wysiedlenie mieszkańców Polski ‼️To nieprawda‼️ 🔎 FAKT: Krajowy Plan Ewakuacji określa procedury na wypadek wojny, zagrożenia wojną lub klęski żywiołowej.… pic.twitter.com/YNEqXF3StJ — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 18, 2026 The measures are part of a broader effort to strengthen Poland’s civil protection system. Last week, Kierwiński said Poland plans to triple the current number of warning sirens in Lublin province to more than 1,000 by the end of 2026. This follows a series of Russian attacks in western Ukraine, including a drone strike on a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw about 2 km from the Polish border. The recent escalation comes after several incidents in recent years involving violations of Polish airspace, including the entry of around 20 Russian drones on one night last year, as well as the explosion of a Russian missile in a field in eastern Poland earlier this year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned last week that Russia’s further plans could include attacks designed to test NATO’s response. Those warnings were echoed yesterday by Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, who said that multiple sources suggested that “Russia is planning something big this year.” “I think Putin needs a pretext for mobilisation, so they might carry out a false-flag attack to tell the Russians, ‘We are under attack, and that is why we must mobilise,’” he added. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has expressed his horror at an “evil” knife attack carried out today by a Ukrainian man at a Catholic abbey in Poland, which left one priest dead and others seriously injured. The incident has caused shock in Poland, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledging that the perpetrator, who is in police custody, will face the “full severity of Polish law”. W Opactwie Sióstr Benedyktynek w Jarosławiu obywatel Ukrainy dopuścił się straszliwej zbrodni. Jesteśmy wstrząśnięci tym złem. Według dotychczasowych informacji zginął ksiądz katolicki, a kilka innych osób zostało rannych. Składamy najgłębsze kondolencje rodzinie i bliskim… — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 24, 2026 The attack took place on Thursday morning on the grounds of a Benedictine abbey in the town of Jarosław in southeast Poland. Local police reported that a 31-year-old Ukrainian man had stabbed four male victims and one female. Three were members of the clergy and two laypeople. Authorities later confirmed that one of the men, a priest, had died of his injuries in hospital and that two others were in serious condition. The cathedral in the nearby city of Rzeszów named the deceased as Stanisław Zbojnowicz. The superior of the Benedictine Sisters Monastery, Barbara Dendor, told news website Interia that Zbojnowicz had been in a confessional when the attack began. He had rushed out to attempt to close the gates and protect other people, but was stabbed by the assailant before he could do so. In its initial social media post announcing Zbojnowicz’s death, the cathedral also said that a second priest, Marek Pieńkowski, had died. However, a few minutes later it deleted that claim, blaming the “enormous information chaos surrounding today’s tragic event”. One person was killed and four were injured in a knife attack at a Catholic convent in Poland this morning, with clergy among the victims. Police have detained a 31-year-old Ukrainian man on suspicion of carrying out the attack. The motive remains unknown https://t.co/93nbqpwnIA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 On Thursday afternoon, prosecutors revealed that the suspect, who has not been named, had entered Poland from Germany in the early hours of Thursday and “was heading to the border crossing [with Ukraine] in Korczowa”, which is around 30km (18.6 miles) from Jarosław. However, he ultimately did not cross the border and, for unknown reasons, ended up in Jarosław, where he entered the grounds of the abbey and began his attack, using a knife taken from the kitchen. Prosecutors said that doctors would assess the suspect’s condition before he was interrogated. Blood samples were also taken to be tested for the presence of narcotics and alcohol. The motive for the attack remains unknown. Dendor told news website Wirtualna Polska that the perpetrator was unknown to them. “He looked like a madman, in shorts and a T-shirt, even though it was cold today,” she said. Wirtualna Polska reports, based on the accounts of unnamed witnesses, that the Ukrainian man had earlier in the day knocked on the gates of the abbey and asked for financial assistance. However, he was turned away due to the suspicion that he was drunk or under the influence of drugs and was asked to come back later. That is standard practice for places that offer aid, reports the news service. The man “flew into a rage when he didn’t get help and allegedly threatened priests”, said one of the unnamed sources. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk expressed his sympathy for the loved ones of the victims of the attack and pledged that the perpetrator “will be punished with the full severity of Polish law”. President Karol Nawrocki likewise expressed his condolences and called on the authorities to “quickly and thoroughly clarify all the circumstances of this tragedy”. Later on Thursday afternoon, Zelensky also extended his condolences in a social media post published in Polish. “We are shocked by this evil,” he wrote. “The perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility in accordance with the applicable law.” Morderca z Jarosławia jest w rękach Polskiej Policji. Trwają czynności. Sprawca to obywatel Ukrainy. Będzie ukarany z całą surowością polskiego prawa. Łączę się w bólu z bliskimi ofiar tego brutalnego ataku. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 24, 2026 Earlier, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw had “condemned the brutal attack” in Jarosław. However, it also appealed for people “not to allow pain to turn into hatred or further violence”, saying that “accountability for the crime must be based solely on the law”. Polish-Ukrainian relations have been tense in recent months, amid rising anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland and anger at Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during World War Two. There has been a rise in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland this year. Marcin Piotrowski, a board member of the Folkowisko Foundation, which provides aid to Ukrainian refugees, told newspaper Rzeczpospolita today that the tragedy in Jarosław was already being exploited on social media. He expressed fear that “we are almost on the verge of lynchings”. 🔴Jesteśmy na granicy nastrojów linczowych. World.title: Polish constitutional court officials charged with preventing entry of new judges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further, after prosecutors charged two senior TK officials over their role in preventing new judges from taking up their positions on the court. Those judges were chosen by the government’s majority in parliament but rejected by President Karol Nawrocki and the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, both of whom are aligned with the right-wing opposition. Following news of the charges, Święczkowski announced that he has initiated proceedings of his own against three other new judges who were admitted to the court this year after being chosen by the ruling coalition. That could result in them being expelled from their positions. Zarzuty w śledztwie dotyczącym niedopuszczenia sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego do orzekania: ⬇️https://t.co/MPiKCEqGBs — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) September 23, 2026 After coming to power in December 2023, the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk refused to recognise the TK, which was stacked with judges appointed by the former Law and Justice administration. It argued that, because some of those judges were unlawfully appointed, the TK itself was illegitimate. Earlier this year, Tusk’s majority in parliament finally began the process of appointing new judges to the TK to fill the growing number of vacancies. Normally, 15 judges sit on the tribunal, but many seats were empty after incumbents’ nine-year terms had expired and the government had previously refused to fill them. However, under Polish law, new TK judges must take an oath “before the president” in order to take up their position. Nawrocki, who was elected last year with the support of PiS, has refused to swear in four of the six judges chosen by parliament in March. Nawrocki argues that there were legal doubts surrounding their election. The government rejects this, as do the judges themselves, who organised their own swearing-in ceremony before a notary and then submitted the documents to the presidential chancellery. Afterwards, the four judges attempted to take up their positions at the TK. However, Święczkowski, who served in the PiS government before becoming a TK judge, refused to admit them, arguing that they had not taken the necessary oath before the president. The judges took their case to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which in May issued an interim order requiring that they be allowed to take up their positions. But Święczkowski has refused to comply, arguing that the ECHR does not have the competence to make such a decision. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 While Święczkowski himself is protected from prosecution by legal immunity, two senior TK officials have now been charged over their role in refusing entry to the four judges. One of the two suspects, who can be named only as Zofia H. under Polish privacy law, is the director of the TK’s chancellery; the other, Piotr P., is the commander of the TK’s security service. They have been charged with abuse of power by a public official, which is punishable by up to three years in prison, and “maliciously and persistently” violating the employment rights of the judges, an offence that carries a sentence of up to two years. Prosecutors say that the officials’ actions were “to the detriment of the private interests of judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and the public interest in the proper functioning of the judiciary in Poland”. Both of the accused have been questioned and pleaded not guilty. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further after the tribunal ruled that the president is not obliged to swear in new TK judges appointed by parliament. President Nawrocki last month refused to swear in four new judges https://t.co/ycnweW9pSR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 13, 2026 The decision to bring charges was welcomed by Waldemar Żurek, who serves as justice minister in Tusk’s government as well as prosecutor general. “In a building that should stand guard over the constitution, unlawful blockades were organised, humiliating inspections were conducted, and malicious bullying was directed at legally elected judges,” he wrote on social media. “A state official has no right to place themselves above the law, and the gates of the tribunal are not the gates of a private fortress,” he continued. “Anyone who carries out unlawful political orders and destroys the foundations of the rule of law must reckon with criminal liability.” W budynku, który powinien stać na straży Konstytucji, urządzono bezprawne blokady, upokarzające kontrole i złośliwy mobbing wobec legalnie wybranych sędziów. Urzędnik państwowy nie ma prawa stawiać się ponad prawem, a bramy Trybunału nie są bramami prywatnej twierdzy.… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 23, 2026 The TK itself, however, condemned prosecutors’ actions, calling them “unlawful” and a “tool of personal pressure and a form of intimidation”. “The director of the chancellery and all other employees of the TK have performed and continue to perform their duties and official orders in accordance with the applicable law,” wrote the tribunal on its official X account. It argued that it would, in fact, have been a criminal abuse of power to have “allowed persons who have not taken the oath before the President to assume the office of a TK judge”. W dniu dzisiejszym @PK_GOV_PL przedstawiła Pani Dyrektor Kancelarii Trybunału Konstytucyjnego absurdalne zarzuty z art. 231 § 1 i 218 § 3 Kodeksu karnego, które od początku do końca są oparte na wymyślonych podstawach prawnych. Działanie to stanowi kolejną próbę wywarcia wpływu… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) September 23, 2026 On Thursday, the day after the charges were announced, the TK issued a further statement saying that Święczkowski had initiated proceedings against three new TK judges who were chosen by parliament this year and sworn in by Nawrocki (two in March, the other in June). The TK said that it was assessing complaints that two of those judges filed against tribunal employees, as well as their refusal to participate in sessions of the TK’s general assembly. Those three judges have shown solidarity with their four excluded colleagues by refusing to participate. “These proceedings may conclude with the most severe ruling of the disciplinary court in the form of removal from office of the aforementioned TK judges,” wrote the TK. Prezes @TK_GOV_PL Bogdan Święczkowski, działając na wniosek jednego z sędziów, wszczął dzisiaj postępowanie mogące się zakończyć zarzutami dyscyplinarnymi wobec trojga sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego: Magdaleny Bentkowskiej, Dariusza Szostka oraz Sławomira Patyry.… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) September 24, 2026 An eighth new TK judge chosen this year, Maciej Berek, who was elected by parliament earlier this month, has also not yet been sworn in by Nawrocki. Berek’s appointment has been particularly controversial, given that he served in the government until being nominated to the TK. Tusk described Berek as his “right-hand man”. Even some MPs from Tusk’s ruling coalition voted against Berek’s appointment, arguing that it contradicted the government’s own efforts to “depoliticise” the judiciary, including by banning recently serving politicians from sitting on the TK. The presidential chancellery has so far refused to swear in Berek based on a technicality, arguing that there is no evidence he has previously served for at least ten years as a legal counsel, which is a requirement to sit on the TK. Berek says that he has presented such evidence.
