A fire last night at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company, was caused deliberately, says digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which relies heavily on Starlink connections. Although the fire is still being investigated, “the modus operandi in this case is clearly Russian”, says Gawkowski. 🔴 Gawkowski o pożarze stacji Starlink. "Element wojny hybrydowej" Wicepremier Krzysztof Gawkowski ocenił pożar stacji Starlink na Mazowszu jako celową próbę zakłócenia łączności. – Wiele wskazuje na to, że pożar stacji Starlinków na Mazowszu to kolejny element wojny hybrydowej… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) September 24, 2026 Firefighters were called out at around 9 p.m. on Wednesday to the facility, which is located in the village of Wola Krobowska, just south of the capital Warsaw. Due to suspicions that the fire had been caused deliberately, police and officers from the Internal Security Agency (ABW) were also later dispatched to the scene. “We’re dealing with an arson attack that was intended to impact critical telecommunications infrastructure that influences internet operation,” Gawkowski, who also serves as deputy prime minister, told broadcaster TVN on Thursday morning. In a separate interview with TVP, the minister said that the facility is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel and “provides internet transmission through Poland, and also to Ukraine”. He noted that other internet providers use Exatel’s facility, including Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which is the owner of Starlink. Starlink terminals have been vital in Ukraine during Russia’s war against the country. Gawkowski told TVN that “the modus operandi in this case is clearly Russian” and “is another element of the hybrid warfare we are facing”. Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe, including a series of arson attacks. “The Russians want to paralyse critical infrastructure, cut off water, gas and electricity, paralyse the internet,” said the minister. “All these processes have one goal: to incite panic and stir up emotions.” However, in his remarks to TVP, Gawkowski acknowledged that, for now, “it is impossible to say” for sure whether Russia was behind the attack. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 The spokesman for Poland’s security services, Jacek Dobrzyński, likewise told TVN that “at this stage it is still too early to talk about the causes or motives of this fire”. However, he confirmed that “everything points to arson”. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek also told broadcaster RMF that “this could be an act of sabotage, and we are taking that into account, so nothing can be ruled out here, especially since these are sensitive elements that ensure satellite communications”. Polish news service Defence24 notes that ground stations are used by Starlink to connect its satellite constellation with terrestrial communications infrastructure. The facility in Poland, alongside one in Lithuania, serves the entire Central and Eastern Europe region, including Ukraine. Tu nieco więcej o roli stacji naziemnych w systemie Starlink. https://t.co/EYys481dSi — Mariusz Marszałkowski (@MJMarszalkowski) September 24, 2026 Earlier this month, a fire broke out at a drone plant in Poland belonging to WB Electronics, which supplies the armed forces of Ukraine and Poland, among others. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that there was “no doubt” the fire was caused deliberately, and that Russia was likely behind it. The Polish government has in recent months warned that Russia is planning to escalate its hybrid actions against Poland and other countries in the region, including through acts of sabotage, disinformation, and potential airspace and border violations. In July, a Russian missile entered Polish airspace before landing in a field in eastern Poland. On Wednesday this week, the same day as the fire in Wola Krobowska broke out, a Russian helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace. World.title: Czech Women Win Billie Jean King Cup Again After Eight Years
World.content:
Czech Republic eased past Ukraine to win the Billie Jean King Cup for the 12th time.

This year’s Wimbledon finalists Linda Noskova and Karolina Muchova breezed past their opponents to secure a 2-0 victory and deny the Ukrainians a first title in the competition.



Muchova, the runner-up at Wimbledon, comfortably beat Anhelina Kalinina 6-2 6-3 in the opening singles match before Noskova’s 6-3 ⁠7-6 (7-5) win over world number seven Elina Svitolina ‌secured the title.

It is the Czechs’ first win at the event since 2018, making them the second-most successful nation in its history after the United States, who have 18 titles.

In her first year as Czechia captain, Barbora Strycova has made history.

Former Grand Slam doubles champion Strycova is just the fourth woman to win the Billie Jean King Cup as both a player and a captain. Strycova joins a Hall of Fame cast of Margaret Court, Chrissie Evert and Billie Jean King in achieving that feat.

CZECHIA'S NEW ALL-STARS ARE WORLD CHAMPIONS 🇨🇿🏆#BJKCup pic.twitter.com/W8B2WucxI0 — Billie Jean King Cup (@BJKCup) September 27, 2026

She’s also the first player in event history to win the Billie Jean King Cup juniors title as a player and the Billie Jean King Cup title as a player and a captain. Strycova won the Billie Jean King Cup juniors title alongside Petra Cetkovska and Lucie Safarova in 2001.

The Czechs also knocked out Great Britain in the quarter-finals in Shenzhen, China, which led GB captain Anne Keothavong to describe them as “the strongest team here”.

World.title: Bolt and Lucid Plan 25,000 Autonomous Vehicles Across Europe
World.content:
Bolt and U.S. electric vehicle maker Lucid Group have announced a partnership to develop autonomous mobility services in Europe, with plans to deploy more than 25,000 fully autonomous vehicles across European cities over the coming years.

The vehicles will be based on Lucid’s upcoming Midsize platform and use NVIDIA Hyperion, a reference architecture and development platform for autonomous vehicles.



The companies plan to develop the vehicles for SAE Level 4 autonomous driving, which allows vehicles to operate without human control within defined conditions.

Bolt says the project is part of its wider ambition to have 100,000 autonomous vehicles operating on its platform by 2035.

The companies will work together from the early stages of vehicle development. Bolt will contribute traffic and mobility data, operational experience and knowledge of European markets, while Lucid will provide its software-defined vehicle platform and automotive technology.

Bolt will also define requirements covering the vehicle, software, safety and passenger experience. Its autonomous driving division will oversee the partnership and develop the infrastructure needed to operate the fleet.

This will include vehicle dispatch, charging, maintenance, remote assistance and customer support. Bolt also plans to own and operate the autonomous vehicles itself.

Rollout will depend on local regulations

The companies have not yet announced which European cities will receive the service first.

Bolt and Lucid said launches will take place city by city and depend on local regulations, official approvals and operational readiness. The companies also plan to work with autonomous driving technology providers, European regulators and policymakers before introducing the service.

For the foreseeable future, autonomous vehicles on the Bolt platform will operate alongside vehicles driven by human drivers.

Lucid’s side of the project will be led by Lucid Technologies, a newly established division bringing together artificial intelligence, advanced driver-assistance systems, autonomous driving and other digital technologies.

Bolt currently operates in more than 850 cities across 50 countries and says its platform serves more than 200 million customers. Its services include ride-hailing, car-sharing, electric scooters and food and grocery delivery.

Lucid Group, listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker LCID, develops electric vehicles and related technologies. The company operates manufacturing facilities in Arizona and Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Prague Airport Works to Speed Up Border Checks for Non-EU Travellers
World.content:
Prague Airport and the Czech Ministry of the Interior are preparing additional measures to reduce waiting times for passengers arriving from non-Schengen countries following the introduction of the EU Entry/Exit System (EES).

The new system has made border checks more complex, particularly for travellers from outside the EU. Prague Airport says it has already introduced several measures aimed at keeping passenger flows moving during busy periods.



Airport staff, known as the Red Team, are assisting passengers in the terminal, directing them through the new procedures and providing information where needed. The airport has also adjusted passenger flow corridors based on data collected since the system was introduced.

One of the main issues identified so far is the self-service registration process. According to the airport, a significant number of passengers do not complete their registration at the kiosks, which can lead to additional delays at passport control.

Prague Airport is therefore examining the entire journey from the registration kiosks to passport control and looking at ways to make the process easier, particularly for families and older passengers.

“Data has shown us that the most common delays occur when people interrupt the registration process at the terminals,” said Radomír Lašák, Chairman of the Board of Prague Airport. “Together with the Police of the Czech Republic, we are not merely putting together temporary stopgaps but are redesigning the entire process so that it remains resilient even during peak periods.”

Further measures are also being prepared at the European level, including the possibility of allowing passengers to complete parts of the EES registration before departure. Airlines could also provide passengers with information about the process during flights.

The Czech Ministry of the Interior and the Immigration Police are working with Prague Airport on the next steps and have committed additional resources to help manage the new system.

Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said the authorities’ priority was to maintain security standards while limiting the impact of the new procedures on passengers.

The airport said it will continue monitoring passenger flows and adjusting its procedures based on actual operations, particularly during peak travel periods.

World.title: Czech Statehood Day 2026: What Is Open and What to Do in Prague
World.content:
September 28 is a public holiday in the Czech Republic, marking Czech Statehood Day and the feast of St. Wenceslas. This year, the holiday falls on a Monday, giving many people a three-day weekend.

For anyone planning to spend the day in Prague, however, there are two practical questions: which shops will be open, and what can you do around the city?



Where you can shop on September 28

Under Czech legislation regulating retail opening hours, shops with a sales area of more than 200 square meters must close on September 28.

The restriction applies throughout the day and covers large supermarkets, hypermarkets and home improvement stores.

Smaller shops with sales areas of up to 200 square meters are exempt and can open at their owners’ discretion. Petrol stations and pharmacies can also operate.

Other exceptions include shops located at airports, railway stations and bus terminals, as well as retail outlets inside healthcare facilities.

Why September 28 is Czech Statehood Day

The holiday commemorates Prince Wenceslas, a member of the Přemyslid dynasty who became one of the central figures in Czech history.

Wenceslas was killed by his brother Boleslav I on September 28, 935, in Stará Boleslav. His death later became the foundation of a cult that developed around him from the late 10th century onward.

His remains were transferred to Prague in 938 on Boleslav’s orders and buried in the Rotunda of St. Vitus. The reasons behind the transfer are not known with certainty, but the move helped strengthen Wenceslas’s status as a religious figure while also reinforcing Prague’s position as the center of the emerging Czech state.

Over the following centuries, Wenceslas became the patron saint of the Czech lands and an important symbol of Czech statehood.

The connection between Wenceslas and Czech political tradition was further strengthened under Charles IV, who commissioned the Crown of Saint Wenceslas. The crown became one of the principal symbols of the Czech monarchy and remains part of the Czech Crown Jewels.

See the Czech Crown Jewels at Prague Castle

September 28 is also the final day of this year’s exhibition of the Czech Crown Jewels at Prague Castle.

The jewels are being displayed in Vladislav Hall as part of the exhibition Habsburgs 500. Admission is free, and the display also includes a coronation robe dating from 1653 and other historical objects.

The exhibition closes at the end of the day on September 28.

Government buildings open to visitors

Several normally restricted buildings will also be accessible to the public.

Straka Academy, the official seat of the Czech government, will open its doors on September 28. Visitors can see the government meeting room, ceremonial areas and the building’s garden.

The program also includes an interactive exhibition called Journey of the Republic. Tours are free and begin at 10 a.m., with the final group scheduled to leave at 5 p.m.

The Ministry of Finance on Letenská Street will also welcome visitors. Tours start at 9:30 a.m. and include the ministry’s historic premises and the former monastery.

Museums and other attractions

The National Technical Museum in Letná will remain open on September 28, giving visitors access to its permanent exhibitions.

The Postal Museum will also be open.

For those looking for a more traditional Prague attraction, September 28 will be the final chance this year to ride the historic Letná Carousel.

Another option is the National Museum, where the Přemyslids exhibition examines the history of the dynasty that ruled the Czech lands during the country’s early medieval period.

The exhibition runs until October 15, 2026, making the public holiday particularly relevant for visitors interested in the history behind Czech Statehood Day.

World.title: Bangkok Gears Up for the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings
World.content:
All eyes are on Thailand as the country prepares to host the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) Annual Meetings, also known as the 2026 Annual Meetings or AM2026 Thailand.

Running from 12-18 October 2026, at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok, the event will mark Thailand’s second time hosting the meetings, following its first in 1991. This will make Thailand one of only three nations to have hosted the IMF–WBG Annual Meetings twice.



The IMF–WBG Annual Meetings, held for two consecutive years in Washington D.C. and every third year in one of the 191 member countries, serve as a gathering of top economic figures from around the world. By covering a broad range of issues, the meetings aim to strengthen global financial stability, combat poverty, and ensure inclusive economic growth and job creation.

Thailand’s selection to host again in 2026 highlights how the country has advanced over the past three decades in terms of its institutional progress, economic resilience, and sustained engagement with international partners. As host, Thailand brings decades’ worth of experience in economic transformation and regional leadership to the table.

The “Olympics of Finance”

Often dubbed the “Olympics of Finance,” the meetings are set to attract more than 15,000 participants, including finance ministers, central bankers, economists, business leaders, civil society representatives, and journalists from the IMF and World Bank’s 191 member countries, including the Czech Republic.

The Annual Meetings will be held under the theme of “Thailand’s New Horizons: Empowering People, Building Resilience”. Therefore, the meetings will focus on enhancing people’s potential and creating opportunities, with the goal of fostering a financial and economic system that is safe, sustainable, and inclusive.

Under the theme, the government plans to showcase four policy priorities it believes are increasingly relevant in an era marked by geopolitical fragmentation, economic volatility, and demographic change. These are indeed the issues that warrant serious conversation and sincere collaboration among the global community and all stakeholders to address them in the most efficient way:

Digital Transformation: The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems.

The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems. Connected Economy: A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored.

A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored. Climate Finance: The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change.

The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change. Longevity Economy: The final priority seeks to turn the challenges of ageing populations into new sources of economic growth.

Alongside these focus areas, the Bank of Thailand plans to unveil the “Bangkok Blueprint,” an international framework developed jointly with the IMF and the World Bank aimed at combating digital financial fraud and strengthening trust in the digital economy.

Readiness in All Aspects

According to the Fiscal Policy Office, Thailand’s overall readiness has been assessed at “Grade A” following months of coordination between the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Thailand, and the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings Secretariat.

Preparations extend beyond the conference venue. Authorities have developed contingency plans for traffic management, emergency responses, and arrangements for high-level foreign officials. A working group has also been established to address cybersecurity matters.

Beyond Tourism: A Regional Economic Capital

Beyond its long-established reputation as a world-renowned tourist destination, the 2026 Annual Meetings offer Thailand an excellent opportunity to present another dimension of the Kingdom to the international community.

AM2026 reinforces Thailand’s standing as a trusted international partner while highlighting its growing role as a regional economic capital and a hub for finance, investment, policy innovation, and multilateral dialogue in Southeast Asia. Having said that, countries and companies vying for economic and business opportunities cannot overlook Thailand and its potential to become an important impetus for their long-term prosperity and growth.

(Source material and reporting courtesy of Thailand NOW)

World.title: Hotline for Foreigners in Czechia: Tips to Save Time and Frustration
World.content:
Reaching the Client Centre for residence-related questions in Czechia requires patience.

More than 2,000 calls are received every day, so some waiting time is unavoidable.

However, you can significantly reduce your waiting time by calling during less busy hours, which are published through the authority’s official channels.



It is also worth having your identification document number ready before calling. This can speed up the process, particularly if you are calling to book an appointment.

Those who do not want to wait on the phone can use other ways to get in touch. Answers to many common questions are available in the Frequently Asked Questions section of the Information Portal for Foreigners (ipc.gov.cz).

If your matter is not urgent or your question is more complicated, you can also contact the centre by email at [email protected].

The current status of your application can be checked online using the dedicated service on the same portal.

When it comes to appointments, most bookings can be made through your personal account on the Information Portal for Foreigners.

You only need to book by phone in three cases: to provide biometric data, to inspect your case file, or to collect a residence card as an EU citizen.

World.title: Czech President Warns NATO Allies May Need to Shoot Down Russian Aircraft
World.content:
Czech President Petr Pavel has warned that NATO may eventually need to shoot down Russian aircraft or drones that deliberately violate the alliance’s airspace.

Speaking to Fox News Digital in New York during the U.N. General Assembly, Pavel said Russia was testing NATO’s readiness and could interpret continued restraint as a sign of weakness.

“There might be the time when we will have to shoot down some of these planes or unmanned vehicles that are testing our readiness,” Pavel said.



Pavel said the alliance needs to distinguish between accidental airspace violations and deliberate incursions in which an aircraft ignores warnings to leave.

“If it is deliberate and the violator doesn’t respond to our measures, then we will have to act, because otherwise Russia simply would push further on,” he said.

His comments came after a series of incidents involving Russian aircraft and drones near NATO territory.

On Wednesday, a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace after crossing from the Kaliningrad region. According to Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command, the helicopter travelled around 300 metres into Polish territory and remained there for 42 seconds.

On Thursday, Romania also scrambled two F-16 fighter jets after an unidentified aerial target entered its airspace from the direction of Ukraine. The object later crashed near the country’s border with Ukraine, with no casualties reported.

Pavel said Russia’s actions reminded him of incidents during his time at NATO, when Russian aircraft repeatedly tested the responses of allied forces.

“They are, on one hand, provoking. On the other, testing what will our reaction be,” he said.

In a speech to the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, Pavel said Russia’s “aggressive posture poses a direct threat to European security” and warned that the risks were increasing.

The Czech president also questioned whether Russia was genuinely prepared to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine. He said Moscow would need to agree to a ceasefire before entering meaningful negotiations without conditions.

World.title: New Sports Complex Opens in Prague’s Riegrovy Sady
World.content:
A new sports complex has opened in Riegrovy Sady, giving residents of Prague 2 access to a refurbished court, parkour equipment, a climbing wall and an outdoor fitness area.

The facility, next to the TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady building, was officially opened Tuesday afternoon. The renovation and installation of new equipment cost CZK 8.7 million, excluding VAT.



The site is intended for people of different ages and can be used for several sports. The refurbished court is suitable for football and basketball, while the new equipment includes a parkour area, climbing wall and a small fitness zone.

The project forms part of the district’s longer-term plans for Riegrovy Sady. Officials said the upper section of the park has lacked sufficient space for outdoor sports and exercise.

The sports area occupies land that until last year was used by two unauthorized structures, the Ice Magic ice sculpture exhibition and the Containall sports and cultural center.

The district is also considering a much larger project for the site. A multifunctional hall for sports and cultural events could eventually replace the current outdoor facility.

Petr Janů, deputy chairman of TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady, previously said the goal was to create a building designed to remain in place for decades or longer.

The project is still at an early stage. Prague 2 plans to discuss the design with local residents, heritage authorities and Prague’s Institute of Planning and Development. An architectural competition is also expected to be held.

World.title: PM Magyar: Parliament to hand over two corrupt politicians to investigators on Monday
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Sunday evening that Hungary’s newly created National Asset Recovery and Protection Office will begin investigating several high-profile corruption cases on Monday, while parliament is expected to vote on lifting the immunity of two former ministers.

In a Facebook post published on Sunday evening, Magyar said the government’s “Operation Purgatory” would move into a new phase on Monday.

“On Monday, the landing begins as part of Operation Purgatory. The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office will begin investigating several high-profile corruption cases. Parliament will also hand over two corrupt politicians to investigators,” Magyar wrote.

The “two corrupt politicians” reference appears to concern former ministers Balázs Hankó and Miklós Seszták, whose immunity is due to be considered by parliament on Monday. Both face criminal allegations, but neither has been convicted, and both have denied wrongdoing. Parliament is also expected to consider the immunity of Prime Minister Péter Magyar and MP Mária Gurzó in separate cases.

What is the asset recovery office?

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) was established in 2026 as an independent state institution tasked with tracing, protecting and recovering public assets believed to have been unlawfully removed from public ownership.

Under the law establishing the body, it can examine transactions involving public procurement, state subsidies, concessions, EU funds, state-owned companies and other forms of public property. It also has investigative powers and can represent the public prosecution in court in cases falling within its remit.

The office was one of the central elements of Magyar’s “Operation Purgatory”, which he first announced in parliament in June as part of a broader anti-corruption and institutional reform programme.

For more on Monday’s high-profile immunity votes, see our earlier report: Hungarian immunity rights: Prosecutors seek suspension for PM Magyar and two former Fidesz ministers

Several corruption cases already in focus

Magyar did not specify in his Sunday post which cases the NVVH would formally open first. He has, however, repeatedly pointed to several high-profile cases involving public funds, state contracts and institutions linked to the former government.

Prosecutors are seeking to suspend Balázs Hankó’s immunity in connection with an investigation into the National Cultural Fund, while Miklós Seszták faces a separate corruption case linked to Volánbusz.

Monday’s extraordinary parliamentary session will add further political weight to the launch of the new office, with lawmakers expected to vote on several immunity cases involving senior politicians.

At the same time, the NVVH is expected to begin turning the government’s anti-corruption campaign into actual investigations and asset-recovery proceedings. That will make Monday an early test of how far the new authority is prepared to go — and which cases it chooses to prioritise first.

World.title: Hungary moves to cut hospital waiting times with weekend operations and extra pay
World.content:
Hungary is launching a new programme aimed at cutting hospital waiting times by expanding surgery into afternoons and weekends, while offering extra financial incentives to medical teams. The move comes as patients in some hospitals still face waits of several months for planned procedures.

Hospital waiting lists are one of the most visible pressure points in Hungary’s healthcare system.

According to the National Health Insurance Fund’s current waiting-list database, average waiting times for cataract surgery exceed 200 days at several hospitals. At the Markhot Ferenc Hospital in Heves County, the average waiting time over the previous six months stood at 310 days, while patients at the Nagykanizsa hospital waited an average of 246 days. In Zala County, the figure was 188 days.

Against this backdrop, Health Minister Zsolt Hegedűs announced on Sunday that the government is launching a new waiting-list reduction programme previously promised by Prime Minister Péter Magyar.

“There is a strong commitment from the medical profession. Our task now is to bring together the additional funding, professional expertise, the right incentives and the available capacity in a way that allows patients to feel the benefits as soon as possible,” Hegedűs Zsolt wrote.

In his announcement, the minister said the aim is not simply to perform more operations, but to make better use of existing surgical capacity and give healthcare workers a direct financial incentive to take on additional work.

More surgeries after normal hours

The programme will primarily expand operations into the afternoon hours after regular shifts, while hospitals with sufficient staffing and professional capacity will also be able to perform additional surgery at weekends. A new financing incentive will be introduced to support this extra workload.

Hegedűs said a significant share of the additional funding would go directly to the teams that make the extra procedures possible, including doctors, nurses and other hospital staff.

Part of the new funding would be linked to quality indicators, patient-reported outcomes and patient satisfaction. The model is intended to move closer to what Hegedűs described as a “best practice tariff” approach, in which financing rewards both efficiency and measurable clinical outcomes.

Hospitals to be assessed individually

Each hospital will receive its own “problem map” identifying the main bottlenecks limiting surgical capacity. These may include staff shortages, inefficient operating-room management, competition from private healthcare providers and limited personal incentives for additional work.

The ministry also plans to monitor operating-room utilisation, actual surgical time, the time needed to change patients between procedures and the efficiency of the entire process.

Hegedűs argued that operating theatres are among the most expensive parts of hospital infrastructure and that unused capacity represents a significant loss.

If you missed it: Construction projects in Hungary could be halted for six months over environmental violations

Semmelweis and Pécs expanding capacity

Semmelweis University and the University of Pécs are already working on expanding surgical capacity under the programme.

Foreign specialists experienced in ERAS, or Enhanced Recovery After Surgery protocols, are also expected to participate. These protocols are designed to shorten hospital stays where medically appropriate, speed up patient recovery and allow hospitals to admit the next patients sooner.

The programme will also include a review and “clean-up” of waiting lists, with the aim of identifying which patients are still genuinely waiting for surgery and removing outdated or inactive cases.

BMI rule also set to change

Another important change concerns orthopaedic surgery. A protocol introduced in April 2025 automatically placed temporary restrictions on certain patients with a BMI above 35. Hegedűs said this rule is now being reviewed.

Instead of an automatic threshold, future decisions would be based on individual patient risk, professional assessment and the judgment of the treating team.

Patients may also receive more comparable information about hospital performance, quality and outcomes, allowing them to make more informed choices about where to seek treatment.

World.title: Construction projects in Hungary could be halted for six months over environmental violations
World.content:
Hungary has tightened its construction rules, allowing authorities to suspend permitting procedures and block new construction or facility permits for at least six months if a project breaches environmental or nature protection requirements.

Hungary’s parliament has approved amendments to the country’s construction rules that significantly strengthen the consequences of environmental violations at major development projects.

Under the new framework, if authorities establish a breach of environmental or nature protection requirements, the relevant construction permitting procedure must be suspended. In addition, new construction or facility permits may be withheld until the unlawful situation is remedied — and for a minimum period of six months, according to Kormány.hu.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar presented the measure as a response to earlier cases in which major projects continued despite environmental concerns.

“We have seen the consequences in recent years when nothing happened after environmental rules were violated during a priority investment. We are putting an end to that now,” Magyar said in a video announcing the change.

The changes also affect major housing developments linked to the Otthon Start programme, where some priority projects may face temporary permitting restrictions while the government reshapes its wider housing construction policy.

Otthon Start projects also face new restrictions

The amendment specifically covers certain large-scale housing projects connected to the government’s fixed 3% Otthon Start housing loan programme.

Under the scheme, large housing projects can receive priority investment status if they meet specific conditions.

According to the government’s Otthon Start Programme Office, qualifying developments generally need to include at least 250 homes, with at least 70% of the units meeting the programme’s eligibility criteria. Priority status can significantly speed up administrative and permitting procedures.

The latest changes, however, introduce the possibility of temporarily halting permits even for projects that have already received priority status.

The government says this is necessary because some previously planned large-scale Otthon Start developments now need to be coordinated with a broader housing construction programme that is still being prepared. The amendment allows the government to set, by decree, a period during which authorities may not issue new permits for certain already-prioritised Otthon Start developments.

If you missed it: Budapest streets could change dramatically under new pedestrian plan

This is potentially significant for developers because priority status was originally designed to speed up these projects. In practice, the new framework means that a fast-track development could still face a pause if environmental rules are breached or if the project needs to be brought into line with the government’s revised housing policy.

New rules for construction material exports

The parliamentary package also removes an earlier restriction on exports of construction materials.

Since 2021, companies planning to export certain building materials have been required to notify the Hungarian state in advance. The state also had a pre-emption right over the products concerned.

That system will now be abolished. Exporters will no longer have to file the same notification, and the state will lose its right to intervene in those transactions or purchase the materials before they are exported.

The change follows a ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union, which found that the Hungarian mechanism restricted the free movement of goods and therefore conflicted with EU law. The European Commission subsequently launched infringement proceedings after the measure remained in force.

World.title: Cold mornings, warm afternoons: Hungary braces for huge temperature swings next week
World.content:
Hungary is heading into a mostly sunny and dry week, with afternoon temperatures climbing to around 25°C in many areas. The catch: mornings will be sharply colder.

A stretch of settled early autumn weather is expected across Hungary next week, with plenty of sunshine and little to no rain.

According to HungaroMet’s latest forecast, daytime highs will generally remain between 21 and 26°C, keeping conditions pleasantly warm for the end of September and start of October. At the same time, nights and early mornings will feel considerably colder, with minimum temperatures falling as low as 1–2°C in some areas.

The sharp contrast will be one of the defining features of the week.

Weather portal Időkép says daily temperature swings could exceed 20°C in places, particularly where clear skies and light winds allow temperatures to drop quickly overnight before sunshine drives rapid warming during the day.

In practical terms, that means a jacket or cardigan may be essential when leaving home in the morning, while a T-shirt could be enough by the afternoon.

Sunshine dominates the week

Monday is expected to bring largely uninterrupted sunshine across the country, with dry conditions and afternoon temperatures of around 22–26°C.

Tuesday is forecast to remain similarly bright and dry. Morning temperatures could fall to between 1 and 11°C, followed by highs of 22–26°C later in the day.

Wednesday will also be mostly sunny, although some high cloud may reach northern Hungary later in the day. Temperatures are expected to range from around 1–11°C at dawn to 22–25°C in the afternoon.

The dry pattern is then set to continue into Thursday and Friday, with filtered or uninterrupted sunshine and daytime highs mostly between 21 and 25°C.

Despite the warm afternoons, the colder nights mean autumn is becoming increasingly noticeable. Időkép notes that temperatures could fall close to 5°C in many places, while ground frost may still occur in some of the country’s more frost-prone locations.

If you missed it: Budapest streets could change dramatically under new pedestrian plan

Little sign of rain

HungaroMet expects mostly dry conditions throughout the working week, with sunshine dominating and only limited cloud cover at times. Winds should generally remain light or moderate, although stronger gusts may develop locally, particularly around Sopron and parts of eastern Hungary.

The result will be a classic early autumn pattern: cold starts, warm afternoons and large temperature swings throughout the day.

For anyone heading out early, layering will likely be the safest option — because what feels like jacket weather before breakfast may feel almost summery just a few hours later.

World.title: Banking costs in Hungary have surged far faster than the EU average
World.content:
The cost of financial services in Hungary has risen dramatically over the past decade and a half, far outpacing the European Union average. A new analysis suggests that inflation and a series of taxes imposed on the banking sector have both played a major role in pushing up household banking costs.

The price of financial services in Hungary is now more than two and a half times higher than it was in 2010, according to an analysis by Bankmonitor reported by 24.hu.

Data based on the EU’s harmonised consumer price index show that the cost of financial services increased by around 2.6 times in Hungary between 2010 and 2026. Across the European Union, the corresponding rise was considerably smaller, at roughly 1.5 times.

Hungary also stands out among nearby countries. Poland recorded one of the largest increases in the region after Hungary, but even there financial services became around 2.1 times more expensive over the same period.

The rise in banking costs has also exceeded Hungary’s broader increase in consumer prices. According to Bankmonitor’s calculations, overall prices rose by roughly 2.04 times between 2010 and July 2026, compared with a 2.62-fold increase in financial services.

In other words, general inflation explains only part of the difference.

Taxes also left their mark on banking fees

Bankmonitor identified several periods when major changes in banking charges coincided with new taxes or modifications to existing ones.

Hungary introduced its bank levy in 2010, while the financial transaction tax followed in January 2013. The latter was increased later the same year, and further changes to the transaction levy were introduced in the second half of 2024.

Also, Hungarian banks cannot simply change account fees whenever they choose. Their terms and conditions set out circumstances under which charges may be adjusted, and these typically include inflation, changes in taxation and amendments to the regulatory environment.

Inflation pushed costs higher as well

A noticeable increase in banking fees followed the 14.5% average inflation recorded in 2022, while another round of price increases came after inflation averaged 17.6% in 2023.

More recently, the effect was temporarily held back by a voluntary fee freeze. Banks agreed not to apply certain inflation-linked increases to retail account charges until 30 June 2026.

With the freeze now over, some financial institutions have begun adjusting prices again. The National Bank of Hungary has said that certain fees have risen since July, although the exact impact varies considerably depending on the bank, account package and how customers use their accounts.

Cheaper accounts are still available

The sharp long-term increase does not mean every bank customer in Hungary is paying high fees. In fact, the Hungarian banking market has a somewhat contradictory feature: while average financial-service prices have risen rapidly, customers can still find relatively cheap account packages if they actively compare offers.

For a typical mixed-use customer, even the 20 cheapest bank accounts can cost between HUF 8,880 and HUF 29,400 a year.

The MNB’s comparison data show substantial differences between banks and individual packages. Depending on payment habits, the difference in annual costs between two otherwise suitable accounts can amount to tens of thousands of forints.

Another measure reducing costs for households is Hungary’s statutory free cash-withdrawal scheme. From February 2026, the monthly limit was increased to HUF 300,000, subject to the relevant conditions.

If you missed it: Major change in banking in Hungary: You can now withdraw twice as much cash for free!

Hungary remains an outlier

Even with cheaper products available, the longer-term trend remains difficult to overlook. Bankmonitor’s analysis indicates that high inflation was an important factor, but changes in taxation and the regulatory environment also contributed to the difference.

For customers, however, the sharp rise in average banking costs does not necessarily mean there is nothing they can do about it. The MNB’s comparisons show that annual fees can differ by tens of thousands of forints between account packages, even for customers with similar banking habits.

That means someone who has stayed with the same account for years may be paying substantially more than necessary. Checking recent statements, reviewing the current fee schedule and comparing alternative packages — including offers from the same bank — could therefore translate into meaningful annual savings.

World.title: “A manhunt will begin next week” – Fidesz faction leader predicts political retaliation
World.content:
János Bóka, leader of Fidesz’s parliamentary group, said on Sunday that recent developments in Hungary amount to political retaliation, predicting that a manhunt targeting members and leaders of his political community could begin as early as next week.

In a video published on Facebook on Sunday, Bóka argued that institutions and figures he described as the intellectual workshops of the Fidesz community had been targeted first, and that party members and senior figures could be next.

His remarks referred to a series of recent developments involving organisations and figures associated with Hungary’s political right, including the now-defunct conservative media outlet Mandiner, the House of Terror Museum and its dismissed former director Mária Schmidt, as well as the Centre for Fundamental Rights, where police carried out searches.

According to Bóka, these cases form part of a broader political process rather than isolated incidents.

“What is happening in Hungary now is political retaliation,” Bóka said in the video.

He went on to predict that a “manhunt” would begin as early as next week, with the aim, in his view, of intimidating and weakening Fidesz and silencing people who support what he described as a sovereign Hungary.

Bóka added that his political community could not be “broken, silenced or intimidated”, and urged supporters not to be afraid.

Parliament to consider immunity cases

His comments come ahead of an extraordinary parliamentary session expected on Monday, when lawmakers may vote on requests to suspend the immunity of former ministers Balázs Hankó and Miklós Seszták, as well as Prime Minister Péter Magyar.

Prosecutors are seeking to question Hankó in connection with an investigation into the National Cultural Fund. According to the prosecution, funds were allegedly distributed through a system that caused HUF 17.3 billion in financial damage to the central budget.

Investigators say more than 1,000 grants were used for purposes outside those permitted by law. Hankó has rejected the allegations and said the decisions and use of the funds were lawful.

Seszták, a former national development minister, faces a separate corruption investigation linked to Volánbusz. Prosecutors allege that more than HUF 12 billion in bribes were involved, including more than HUF 11 billion in unlawful benefits allegedly received through an intermediary between 2015 and 2018. Seszták has denied committing any crime and said he is prepared to defend himself before the authorities.

If you missed it: Prosecutors seek suspension for PM Magyar and two former Fidesz ministers

Fidesz and Tisza offer sharply different accounts

Bóka’s latest remarks echo earlier statements in which he described the proceedings against Hankó as politically motivated. Last week, he called the case a “show trial” and an example of political arbitrariness.

The phrase “manhunt” also follows similar rhetoric used by former prime minister Viktor Orbán, who recently suggested that several senior Fidesz politicians could become targets following the change of government.

The governing Tisza Party, however, presents the situation very differently. As we reported yesterday, speaking in Szolnok, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said political responsibility should fall on a relatively small number of people rather than on ordinary Fidesz voters. He stressed that “we are all Hungarians” despite political differences and argued that voters should not be treated as enemies.

Magyar’s rally was itself marked by tension. Objects, including an egg, were thrown towards the stage, prompting him to ask protesters not to target members of the crowd. Addressing the incident, he said some frustrated Fidesz voters were now confronting the fact that the leaders they had trusted had misled them.

Monday’s parliamentary session could therefore become another focal point in the confrontation between the governing Tisza Party and Fidesz, particularly as lawmakers are expected to consider requests to suspend the immunity of former ministers and Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s.

World.title: 70 years after the Hungarian Revolution: What became of the ’56ers who fled to Australia?
World.content:
It has been estimated that 200,000 Hungarians fled the country following the 1956 Hungarian Revolution and its Soviet suppression. Of those, about 14,000, roughly one in fourteen, eventually made new lives in Australia, a country about as far from Hungary as you can get.

Author: Liam Saville

Behind these numbers are thousands of different stories of escape and starting again. My mother’s is just one of them.

My mum began life as a poor peasant girl, but the childhood she remembers is one of privilege. Adopted by a wealthy Hungarian couple, both doctors, she was nine years old when the Hungarian Revolution broke out in 1956. “I was very privileged,” she told me. “We lived in Buda…it was a massive old house, and we had the top storey.” But she remembers Christmas the most. “The beautiful fresh Christmas trees that were cut down just for us, and the presents. Everything was expensive. I mean, we had oranges…not many people could afford to buy oranges, particularly at Christmas.”

While my mum had the good fortune of being taken to the zoo, given swimming lessons and regularly treated to the opera, childhood looked different for John Garamszegi, whose family struggled financially in central Buda. His father, János, was originally from Zebegény but, by 1956, had settled in Budapest with his family.

John recalls the start of the Revolution. “My mother, even though she only had a primary school education, joined the initial protest march of mostly university students,” he said.

Things changed quickly, and the family were soon hiding in their basement as Soviet troops and Hungarian revolutionaries fought on the streets outside. Later, John recalls his father watching as Stalin’s statue in Budapest was pulled down. The next day, he returned to saw off a piece of Stalin’s boot, a fragment John still has today.

The fragment of Stalin’s statue cut from the remains by John Garamszegi’s father after the monument was pulled down in Budapest during the 1956 Hungarian Revolution. John still has the fragment in Australia today.

Credit: Photo courtesy of John Garamszegi.

Leaving Hungary

By 1956, third-generation teacher Otto Huszár was no stranger to conflict. Conscripted into the Hungarian military during the Second World War, he’d served in a mortar unit and fought the Russians on the Eastern Front before returning to his profession after the war. In his own words, “by 1956 it was obvious that the Hungarians had had enough of the so-called communism and especially the Russian occupation.”

In a memoir provided by his grandson, Ben Heydon, Otto wrote: “The American ‘free radio’ constantly encouraged the reactionary forces to act. In October it happened. The Russian forces left the country, but returned through Czechoslovakia and of course everything was lost.”

With just ten minutes of thought, Otto packed a few clothes, some nappies for his daughter, photographs and documents and headed towards Austria along the Vienna-Budapest Highway.

Otto Huszár with his daughter Kathy. A former Hungarian school principal, Otto fled Hungary with his young family in 1956 and eventually returned to teaching in Australia.

Photo courtesy of Ben Heydon.

For 92-year-old Anna Prevend, the Hungarian Revolution was a very different experience. Then 23 and living in Vác with her older sister, she too remembers the broadcasts. “It’s the wireless, Free Europe,” she told me. “It just started, ‘We’re coming, we’ll help,’ and they go to bloody Suez Canal.”

“When it all started, I told my sister I was going to go…there were no cars or anything running, no buses or nothing. So, I just started to walk.” And walk she did, right into the centre of Budapest, where, as she puts it, “the fun started.”

For the next six or seven days Anna played “cat and mouse” with the Russians, throwing Molotov cocktails at the troops, darting off and returning to do it again. For Anna, the Revolution ended abruptly in Parliament Square, when she was shot in the chest by a Russian soldier.

“The rest of them, well, whoever it was, they just took me, and I don’t know how, but I woke up in Salzburg…From there, they cleaned me up, and they sent me to Switzerland.”

My mother’s escape was very different from Anna’s, yet the memories have stayed with her to this day. “We all knew. Even I knew that people were dying. People were being killed everywhere,” she said. “I was told nothing. It had to be very harsh, because as kids, we opened our mouths, didn’t we? So, I was told nothing, only when we left that we were going on a trip.”

Her escape began with a late-night train ride towards the Austrian border with her mother, as her father chose to remain behind. It almost ended in disaster four hours later, when Russian troops boarded the train as they got off.

“We packed one small suitcase, and it was a long walk after we got off the train.” It was late December, and they trekked twenty-five kilometres across frozen fields, dodging Russian patrols with the help of paid guides. “Young guys took us over the border, and apparently their payment was gold watches and money.” At the border, they had to wait until after midnight, when the Hungarian border guards replaced the Russians.

John Garamszegi with his brother Vili and sisters Ági and Kati playing in the snow in Budapest. The family fled Hungary following the 1956 Revolution and eventually settled in Australia. Photo courtesy of John Garamszegi.

During my interviews, I heard variations of the same story again and again. A woodcutter led John Garamszegi’s family through the forest with pálinka to bribe the guards. Marie Hanzlik Brown’s parents escaped at night, while Simone Brigit’s mother, Brigitta Rati, crossed on foot at Christmas. Different routes, but remarkably similar stories of escape and leaving almost everything behind.

Onwards to Australia

Many of the ‘56ers bound for Australia spent months in Austrian refugee camps. Most eventually travelled by ship from various European ports, though some, like Anna, flew to Australia.

My mum spent six months in the Austrian mountains. “It was somewhere in the mountains, but I don’t know where,” my mum told me. “It was a big chalet right up in the mountains…there were a lot of Hungarians. It was like a camp.”

Eventually, they were cleared to travel to Australia. As my mother’s uncle was already here, they were accepted as sponsored migrants rather than refugees, though they almost didn’t come at all. “The biggest thing was that Mum got an offer in America from the Mayo Clinic…yet knocked it back because at that stage my uncle was still alive.”

They arrived in Sydney on 14 June 1957 aboard the US transport ship, USNS General Harry Taylor. But in a cruel twist of fate, my mother’s uncle died before they landed. They still avoided the migrant camps and moved into her uncle’s apartment with his partner in Sydney’s Bellevue Hill.

For many Hungarian refugees, the migrant camp at Bonegilla in northern Victoria became their first Australian home. John Garamszegi’s family lived there for months, as did Otto and his family. Originally a military camp, Bonegilla was basic and, for many, not necessarily the warm welcome they might have expected.

John remembers seemingly endless meals of mutton, and his father constructing an improvised heater to make life more comfortable. Marie Hanzlik Brown recalls her mother, Katalin, describing “corrugated iron sheds and basic cooking,” while “possums used to be on the roof, and she’d feed them bananas.”

Making a new home

As the Hungarian arrivals began building new lives, learning English and finding work often determined what came next. My grandmother already spoke English, but my mum didn’t. That changed when they moved to Brisbane after my grandmother found work with the Red Cross while waiting for her medical qualifications to be recognised. Away from Sydney’s Hungarian community, my mum had to learn English. “There were no Hungarian kids at Coorparoo State Public School,” she told me.

Other Hungarians spread across the country in search of work. Anna found herself catching sheep for shearers before heading to Mount Isa, where she met her husband and began building a life in Australia.

“We are Australians now,” she told me. “We made the best of it, and we did very well.” Otto, a former school principal, found his qualifications weren’t recognised and worked in factories before eventually returning to teaching. Marie’s mother, Katalin, needed to start again, becoming a dressmaker after being unable to find mechanical work.

Seventy years on, just what Hungary means to those ‘56ers and their families varies enormously. My mum is unequivocal: she’s Australian. Anna sees it differently. “You never lose that; you’re always Hungarian.” John is different again. He spent years distancing himself from the Hungarian community, but now that he’s retired, he describes himself as a “born-again Hungarian,” though he’s clear that Australia is his home.

As for me, I’m both Australian and Hungarian and hold both passports. I grew up knowing surprisingly little about Hungary and speaking almost none of the language, yet as I’ve gotten older, my connection to the country has grown. My mum, now in her late seventies, summed it up best when she told me, “I’m Aussie. You’re more Hungarian than me.”

What is clear, though, is that the generation who lived through the Hungarian Revolution is disappearing, taking their stories with them. So, if you are lucky enough to have a ‘56er in your family, talk to them. Ask them about Hungary, about leaving, what they left behind and the lives they built afterwards. Just do it now, before it’s too late.

To learn more about the uprising that shaped the lives of Hungary’s ’56ers, read our article on the outbreak of the 1956 Revolution: 1956, October 23 – Start of the Hungarian Revolution

World.title: 90-year-old driver may have caused fatal crash in Hungary, reigniting debate over elderly drivers
World.content:
Two people died in a serious crash on the M80 expressway near Rönök on Friday afternoon. The tragedy has once again raised questions over whether Hungary’s current medical fitness checks are sufficient for elderly drivers.

Fatal crash on the M80

Two motorists lost their lives in Friday’s crash near Rönök in Vas County. According to information reported by RTL, one of the vehicles was driven by a 90-year-old man, who may have caused the accident.

Reports say the Audi, driven by the 90-year-old man and travelling towards Szentgotthárd, first made contact with a Hungarian-registered Fiat motorhome. The Audi’s front-left wheel was damaged in the collision, after which the car crossed into the opposite lane and collided head-on with a Hyundai travelling behind the motorhome.

The Hyundai eventually came to a stop against the guardrail. Both the driver of the Audi and the driver of the Hyundai suffered fatal injuries, while the occupants of the motorhome were reportedly unharmed.

“One person was trapped in each of the two vehicles. They were freed using hydraulic rescue equipment, lifted from the vehicles and handed over to paramedics by professional firefighters from Körmend and Szentgotthárd,” Hungary’s disaster management authority said.

The exact circumstances of the crash are still being investigated. The case, however, has revived a long-running debate in Hungary over how authorities should determine whether elderly motorists are still fit to drive safely.

Drivers over 70 undergo medical checks every two years

In Hungary, the required medical fitness checks become more frequent with age. Drivers over 60 must renew their medical clearance every three years, while those over 70 are required to do so every two years.

Dr Péter Torzsa, head of the Department of Family Medicine at Semmelweis University, told RTL that these examinations are not merely administrative formalities.

Doctors may check a patient’s blood pressure, eyesight and hearing, while laboratory tests and ECG examinations can also be ordered when necessary. Chronic conditions that could affect a person’s ability to drive safely are also taken into account.

Torzsa stressed that doctors carry significant responsibility from a road-safety perspective. If a patient has serious problems with their eyesight or hearing, for example, continuing to drive could pose a danger and medical clearance should not be granted.

At the same time, he argued that age alone should not automatically disqualify someone from driving. According to Torzsa, there are people in their 90s who remain healthy enough to operate a vehicle safely.

If you missed it: Asbestos crisis deepens in western Hungary as dangerous levels detected in air

Could virtual reality improve driving fitness tests?

Road-safety expert Károly Lovas, however, believes Hungary’s current system could be modernised.

He told RTL that newer technologies could provide a more objective picture of how elderly drivers react to unexpected or difficult traffic situations.

One possible method would be the use of virtual reality. Simulated traffic scenarios could test reaction times, attention and a driver’s ability to recognise and respond to potential hazards.

The Rönök crash has therefore brought renewed attention not only to the circumstances of the fatal accident itself, but also to the wider question of how elderly motorists should be assessed.

The debate does not necessarily point towards introducing a fixed upper age limit for driving. Instead, experts have focused on whether medical and cognitive assessments could be made more precise and better adapted to the abilities required for safe driving.

World.title: Bosnia Court Blocks Republika Srpska From Funding Secessionist Lobbying
World.content:
Bosnian lawmaker Denis Zvizdic, who initiated teh legal challenge. Photo: EPA/FELIPE TRUEBA.

Bosnia’s Constitutional Court on Friday declared that budgetary funds used by Bosnia’s Serb-dominated Republika Srpska entity to pay foreign consulting firms to lobby for independence violate the state’s constitutional architecture.

The ruling targets a consulting agreement signed between the Republika Srpska Representative Office in Vienna and a Montreal-based firm, Dickens & Madson Canada Inc., which listed “the independence of Republika Srpska” as a core political objective.

The legal challenge was initiated in April by a state-level lawmaker, Denis Zvizdic, who argued that using taxpayers’ funds to lobby against Bosnia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity was unconstitutional.

A 2008 ruling allowed the entity to engage foreign firms for general economic promotion. However, the court has now established that funding campaigns explicitly promoting secession represents an assault on the constitutional order.

“The Constitutional Court hereby prohibits all payments from the budget of Republika Srpska regarding the consulting services contract concluded with Dickens & Madson Canada Inc.,” the court said. “Financing lobbying services for goals that run counter to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina is strictly incompatible with the constitutional order.”

The applicant, Zvizdic, welcomed the announcement, saying the entity had weaponised massive public funds for anti-state campaigns.

“Public money cannot be used to finance lobbying aimed against the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its territorial integrity, sovereignty and its institutions,” Zvizdic stated.

“This binding decision establishes a clear legal standard: citizens’ money must serve development and investment, not the undermining of the state,” he added.

Under Bosnia’s state-level laws, entities possess no constitutional right to unilateral secession. Furthermore, ignoring or violating a binding order of the Constitutional Court carries severe penalties.

The court said the full text of the judicial decision will be delivered to all parties and published on its official website within the month.
