World.title: Сost of childhood: why Azerbaijan has no universal child benefit
World.content:
Child benefits in Azerbaijan

AI-generated illustration. Meydan TV

Azerbaijan has no monthly child benefit paid for every child regardless of their family’s income. For nearly 20 years, the government has followed a different model: it provides support to low-income families and specific social groups instead of making universal payments.

Against a backdrop of persistently falling birth rates, the debate over so-called “child benefits” has returned to the public agenda. The discussion is no longer just about where to find the money. Other questions have also come to the fore: how much a universal child benefit would cost the state budget, how much it would actually help families, and what the long-term social cost of refusing such support might be.

In May 2026, a statement by Gunay Agamali, a member of Azerbaijan’s parliament, sparked a new wave of debate. Speaking on ARB TV, she said that child benefits could make parents “dependent and lazy”. In her view, such payments could reduce some people’s willingness to work.

However, the issue of child benefits is far from new in Azerbaijan. It returns to the public agenda almost every year, and the same questions arise each time. Should the state pay benefits for every child or only for families that genuinely need support? Can the state budget afford such payments? And could child benefits reverse the decline in birth rates?

To answer these questions, it is worth first examining how the current system came about. Read the full article by Meydan TV.

What changed in 2006?

Monthly payments commonly referred to as “child benefits” existed in Azerbaijan before 2006. However, contrary to a widespread misconception, they were not universal either.

● Social assistance is shrinking in Azerbaijan: Is poverty falling, or are low-income people losing support?

● Birth rates decline year by year in Azerbaijan

● Child allowance in Azerbaijan: why is it not paid?

Under the rules in force at the time, families with an average monthly income of less than 16,500 old manats per person (around $3.4–3.5 or €2.7–2.8 at the 2004–2005 exchange rates) received a monthly payment of 9,000 old manats per child (around $1.8–1.9 or €1.5). Payments continued from birth until the child turned 16. For schoolchildren who did not receive a scholarship, payments could continue until the age of 18. Following the redenomination, this amount was equivalent to 1 manat and 80 qəpiks.

In other words, the previous system also took family income into account.

A new phase in Azerbaijan’s social protection system began on 1 January 2006, when the Law on Targeted State Social Assistance came into force. The Law on Social Benefits also took effect on the same date. The new system did not retain a separate child benefit linked to family income.

The government therefore effectively changed its entire approach. Instead of providing a separate payment for each child, it made targeted assistance the main form of social support, with eligibility determined by family income.

In a 2009 interview with Radio Azadliq, Babek Huseynov, a representative of the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of the Population, said the authorities considered the new system more effective. The previous child benefit, he said, had “lost its economic rationale”. He explained that under the targeted assistance system, payments are calculated based on the difference between a family’s total income and the eligibility threshold.

The same principle remains: assistance for those in need, not everyone

In the following years, the government introduced new types of benefits for children and families and changed payment amounts. However, the underlying principle remained the same: Azerbaijan has no universal benefit paid for every child.

In 2022, Labour and Social Protection Minister Sahil Babayev stated this position explicitly while addressing parliament. According to him, around 600,000 children from socially vulnerable groups receive support through various mechanisms, and social assistance should be targeted rather than universal.

The system in place in 2026 follows the same principle.

Lawyer Fariz Namazly explains:

“We have various benefits for children. Most are designed for socially vulnerable families. There are also one-off payments, such as the benefit paid when a child is born. Low-income families with children under one receive financial assistance, as do parents caring for children under three. Women with more than five children are also eligible for benefits. Separate social payments are available for children with disabilities, children who have lost one of their parents, and other categories.”

Families currently receive a one-off payment of 600 manats (around $353 or €305) when a child is born. Low-income families with children under one receive 140 manats (around $82 or €71) per month. Women with more than five children receive 140 manats (around $82 or €71) per month for each child. The childcare benefit for children under three amounts to 44 manats (around $26 or €22) or 28 manats (around $16 or €14), depending on the child’s age.

In addition, separate payments are available for children with disabilities, those who have lost a breadwinner, children without parental care, and other social categories.

The issue, therefore, is not whether the state provides financial support to families with children at all. Such support already exists.

The main question is who is eligible for it.

Universal child benefits or targeted assistance?

Under a universal system, family income does not matter: if a child meets the eligibility criteria, the family receives a payment.

Under a targeted system, the government first assesses a family’s income, assets and social circumstances before deciding whether it needs assistance.

Fariz Namazly believes both models have advantages and disadvantages:

“There are currently proposals to introduce a universal child benefit — that is, to pay it to all children regardless of family income. Such a system is more transparent. Families would not have to declare their income, the process would be much simpler, and there would be no need to check their financial circumstances. All children would be treated equally.

But this would place a significantly greater burden on the budget. Wealthier families would also receive the benefit. If payments are limited to low-income families, public spending is lower, and the money goes to those who need it most. The problem is that determining a family’s actual income can be difficult, creating opportunities for abuse. Such cases have also occurred in the allocation of targeted social assistance: people have tried to formally give up their jobs or even arrange sham divorces to meet the eligibility criteria.”

The new Law on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 2026, explicitly enshrines a child’s right to social security. Under Article 24 of the law, every child has the right to material support at least equal to the subsistence minimum established by law. The same article states that the government provides social assistance to certain categories of citizens to protect children.

In 2026, the subsistence minimum for a child is 260 manats (around $153 or €132).

However, this provision does not in itself mean that the state is obliged to pay every child 260 manats in cash each month. It establishes a general right to material support, while direct social payments remain available only to specific categories.

Can child benefits make parents “lazy”?

It was against this backdrop that Gunay Agamali argued that parents should not expect financial assistance from the state when deciding to have a child, and that such benefits could supposedly foster dependency.

This argument shifts the debate away from social policy and towards the behaviour of parents themselves.

Yet Azerbaijan’s existing system already provides direct payments to families with children. The debate is therefore not about whether the state should support families financially at all, but whether payments should cover all children or only specific groups.

Earlier, Aygun Gumbatova, the wife of imprisoned opposition activist Agil Gumbatov, called for the introduction of child benefits. She cited her family’s difficult financial circumstances as the reason for her position.

“We have found ourselves in a difficult financial situation. My husband was arrested on false charges. He was the family’s sole breadwinner. Now I am left with three school-age children,” Gumbatova told a Caucasian Knot correspondent.

Her eldest child has autism and requires constant care, making it impossible for Gumbatova to work. According to her, the family’s only stable source of income is the 320-manat disability pension (around $188 or €162) paid for her child’s second-group disability status.

At the same time, supporting a universal child benefit does not necessarily mean that its proponents see it as a solution to all social and demographic problems.

Natig Jafarli, an economist and chairman of the REAL Party, believes the issue is too easily exploited for populist purposes:

“This is a very sensitive issue, and it is extremely convenient for populism. People who do not bear political responsibility can use it simply to score political points. Such promises easily resonate with the public. For example, someone comes out and says: let’s pay 500 manats [around $294 or €253] for every child. Someone with two or three children at home will naturally think: ‘Great, that’s 1,000–1,500 manats’ [around $588–882 or €507–760].”

“That is precisely why the issue often fails to become the subject of serious discussion. It would be far more useful to sit down with government representatives, examine the budget’s capabilities and do the calculations: how much the state can afford, in what form, and under which model such payments could be introduced.

Sometimes populism goes so far that child benefits are presented as almost a solution to every problem. That is also wrong and misleads people. Azerbaijan already faces demographic problems, and the birth rate is falling. But claiming that simply introducing child benefits tomorrow would immediately reverse the situation is also populism. We can see this in European countries. In Poland, for example, families receive 800 zlotys [around $214 or €185] per child — a fairly substantial amount. Yet the demographic situation continues to deteriorate, and the fertility rate has fallen from 1.7 to 1.4.”

According to the World Bank, Azerbaijan’s total fertility rate was 1.7 children per woman in 2020, falling to 1.4 by 2024. The downward trend has continued in more recent statistics. According to Azerbaijan’s State Statistical Committee, 40,798 children were born in the country between January and June 2026. The number of births per 1,000 residents fell from 9.0 in the same period of 2025 to 8.0.

Can the budget afford a universal child benefit?

One of the main arguments against universal payments is their cost.

Natig Jafarli believes that child benefits are economically feasible in Azerbaijan, but that they do not necessarily have to be introduced for all children at once. In his view, the system could be rolled out in stages.

“If the aim is to reverse the demographic situation through child benefits, a benefit alone will not be enough. But from an economic perspective, such payments are possible. We simply need to determine the amount and the stages.

Several years ago, we proposed starting from the assumption that Azerbaijan has around 2.7 million children aged 0 to 18, and approximately 920,000 of them are second-born children in their families. If it is impossible to cover all children under 18 immediately, the programme could at least start with second and subsequent children. If we paid around 100 manats [around $59 or €51] per child, the first stage would require about 1 billion manats a year [around $588 million or €507 million]. That is an amount Azerbaijan’s budget could sustain.

If, on the other hand, we paid 100 manats a month to all 2.7 million children — even if we consider 100 manats a very small amount — the cost would exceed 3 billion manats a year [more than $1.76 billion or €1.52 billion] and reach approximately 3.2–3.3 billion manats [around $1.88–1.94 billion or €1.62–1.67 billion]. Such a burden could create certain difficulties for the budget at the initial stage. So we could start with 1 billion and then expand the programme as the economy’s capacity grows.”

Azerbaijan’s state budget for 2026 has approved revenues of 38.609 billion manats (around $22.71 billion or €19.57 billion) and expenditures of 41.7036 billion manats (around $24.53 billion or €21.14 billion).

Against this backdrop, spending more than 3 billion manats (over $1.76 billion or €1.52 billion) on a universal child benefit would indeed be a substantial expense.

But the scale of the expenditure alone does not settle the debate. A universal payment for every child is not the only possible option. The amount could depend on the child’s age, birth order, or parental income, or the programme could be introduced gradually.

The question, therefore, is not simply whether “the money is available in the budget”. It is also about which model of social policy the government considers a priority.

Birth rates are falling, but benefits are not the only factor

One reason the issue of child benefits has returned to the public agenda is the sharp decline in the number of births.

According to the State Statistical Committee, 122,846 children were born in Azerbaijan in 2022. The figure fell to 112,620 in 2023 and declined further to 102,310 in 2024. In 2025, the country recorded 95,875 births.

This means the annual number of births fell by nearly 27,000 between 2022 and 2025.

In 2025, the number of births per 1,000 residents fell from 10 to 9.4.

The age structure of the population is also changing. At the beginning of 2023, children under four accounted for 6.3% of the population. By the beginning of 2025, their share had fallen to 5.6%. Meanwhile, the proportion of people aged 65–69 rose from 3.9% to 4.6%, while the share of those aged 70 and over increased from 4.6% to 5.3%.

Sociologist Sanubar Heydarli told Meydan TV that support for young families is particularly important in this situation:

“Living standards in Azerbaijan cannot be described as high, and there are many social difficulties. That is why I consider child benefits an important form of support for young families. The figures also point to this: the birth rate is falling sharply, and the population is beginning to age.”

“But child benefits alone cannot solve this problem. We cannot assume that the government will start making payments and the birth rate will automatically rise. Other measures are needed alongside them. The decision to have a child depends on more than a family’s financial situation. Access to the labour market for women, a sense of social security, and the state of healthcare, education and social support systems all matter.

Nevertheless, child benefits provide significant support for young families. After a child is born, one parent temporarily leaves the labour market, reducing the family’s income. The state should therefore support families during childbirth and child-rearing. Child benefits are important, but they are not the only solution to demographic problems.”

What difference would 100 manats make?

Another question is how much the benefit would be worth.

Suppose the government pays 100 manats (around $59 or €51) per child each month. A family with two children would receive an additional 200 manats (around $118 or €101).

Could such an amount solve a family’s main financial problems?

Natig Jafarli believes it could not:

“In Europe, of every €100 spent on food, the figure is around €20 at most. If we spend half our income on food, that points to low living standards in Azerbaijan.

But much depends on the size of the benefit. Imagine a completely unrealistic scenario: the government pays 1,000 manats per child. Such an amount could indeed have a significant impact on poverty. But is that possible? No. If, at best, families receive 100 manats per child and a family with two children gets an additional 200 manats, would that be enough to eliminate poverty? Of course not.”

At the same time, the purpose of a child benefit does not necessarily have to be for the state to provide for a family entirely.

It could also be seen as the government’s contribution towards the additional expenses that inevitably arise when raising a child.

In the long term, Jafarli believes a completely different model would be ideal:

“People should be able to earn a living and support their own families. Small businesses and family businesses should be developed. The economy should move in a direction where people do not need such payments at all. That is the ideal model for me.

In principle, I am sceptical of the idea of the state constantly giving people money, because the more the state finances you, the more it can restrict your rights. We need to build a system, a society and a country where there is no longer any need for such payments. But is there a need for them now? Of course there is.”

Sanubar Heydarli also points to changing attitudes among parents towards raising children. Modern families may consciously choose to have fewer children, preferring to provide one or two children with better education, healthcare and opportunities for development.

What models have neighbouring countries adopted?

The experience of neighbouring countries shows that there is no single model for child benefits. In some countries, payments depend on family income; in others, they depend on the child’s birth order.

In Armenia, from 1 September 2026, every newborn child will qualify for a one-off payment of 500,000 drams, regardless of their birth order. This is equivalent to around 2,341 manats ($1,374 or €1,187). The Armenian government approved the decision on 13 August 2026.

In addition, a monthly payment of 50,000 drams — approximately 235 manats ($137 or €119) — is paid for the third and each subsequent child until the child turns six.

In Turkey, a one-off payment of 5,000 lira is available for the first child born on or after 1 January 2025. This is equivalent to around 176 manats ($104 or €89). For a second child, families receive 1,500 lira per month — around 53 manats ($31 or €27) — until the child turns five. For the third and subsequent children, the monthly payment is 5,000 lira (approximately 176 manats, $104 or €89).

In Georgia, the system is closer to a targeted model. Families with a social rating below the established threshold receive 200 lari per month — around 130 manats ($77 or €66) — for each child under 16. A UN report on social protection in Georgia states that the programme covers children from families with a social rating below 120,001 points.

According to figures for November 2025, more than 250,000 children were receiving these payments.

In Russia, the main unified child benefit is also not universal. When determining eligibility, authorities assess a family’s per capita income and other criteria of need. The payment can amount to 50%, 75% or 100% of the regional subsistence minimum for a child.

These examples show that the choice is not simply between having child benefits and not having them.

A government can provide a one-off payment at birth, introduce monthly benefits until a certain age, offer greater support for second and subsequent children, or limit payments to low-income families.

Azerbaijan currently follows the last model for the most part: targeted assistance and benefits for specific categories.

Is a separate law needed to introduce a universal child benefit?

According to Fariz Namazly, the government would not need to pass a separate law to introduce a universal child benefit:

“There is already a Law on Social Benefits, which could be amended. In addition, a new Law on the Rights of the Child has been adopted, and it could also be supplemented with provisions on new payments and benefits for children. In other words, the necessary provisions could be incorporated into either the Law on the Rights of the Child or the Law on Social Benefits.”

The burden on the budget — what about future costs?

Since 2006, the government’s overall approach has remained largely unchanged: instead of providing the same monthly payment for every child, it offers assistance based on a family’s financial need or a child’s membership in a specific social category.

As noted above, this does not mean the government provides no support to families with children. There are payments at birth, benefits for low-income families, childcare benefits, assistance for women with large families, and support for children with disabilities and those without parental care.

A universal child benefit would mean a shift away from this model.

Clearly, it would require substantial additional spending. At the same time, experts stress that child benefits alone cannot eliminate poverty or automatically reverse the decline in birth rates.

However, the falling number of births and the gradual ageing of the population raise a different question: can social policy be assessed solely in terms of how much money it costs today?

Sanubar Heydarli believes that failing to support families now could leave the state facing much higher costs in the future:

“By refusing to introduce child benefits today, leaving families to cope with their difficulties alone and failing to take responsibility, the state is effectively increasing its future expenditure associated with an ageing population.

Child benefits are a highly visible item of expenditure: when money is paid directly to families and the authorities calculate the total cost, the figures can seem enormous. But this ignores the fact that failing to support children today will translate into unavoidable spending on an ageing population in the future.

The state will have to pay more in pensions and benefits and increase healthcare spending. The proportion of elderly people will grow. As a result, the balance between taxes paid by the younger working population and spending on pensioners will be disrupted. There will be more pension recipients and fewer taxpayers. Ultimately, the burden on the state will only increase.”

With the support of the Mediset

Child benefits in Azerbaijan

World.title: Opinion: ‘Signs of cult-like behaviour are becoming increasingly apparent in Georgia’s ruling Georgian Dream party’
World.content:
“It is absolutely inappropriate to call an institutionalised protest movement a cult,” sociologist Iago Kachkachishvili says, commenting on an open letter by Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili, published on the 666th day of continuous anti-government protests.

In his letter, the speaker refers to the protesters as a “cult”. Kachkachishvili, however, argues that the protest movement has no single prominent leader or figurehead whose will its participants blindly follow. He also says Papuashvili’s remarks suggest that the ongoing protests are clearly troubling the authorities.

“When the outcome no longer justifies the process, the process itself must begin to justify itself. Ritual is one of the mechanisms through which this happens, and when continuing the ritual itself becomes the goal, a political movement gradually turns into a closed pseudo-religious cult. Today, on the 666th day, we see a combination of these characteristics,” Papuashvili wrote.

Speaking on the Free Studio programme, Iago Kachkachishvili said authorities could, in the future, impose certain restrictions on the protest movement, including legal restrictions, similar to their attempts to ban opposition parties. However, the sociologist believes that even in such circumstances, public protests would find a way to continue.

Kachkachishvili also discussed the criteria for what constitutes a “cult”. He said that, when comparing a social movement with a political party in this context, he believed political parties showed more characteristics of a cult.

He singled out the ruling Georgian Dream party in particular. In his assessment, the party is effectively run according to the decisions of its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, while its other members follow his directives without question.

Iago Kachkachishvili: “The sheer length of Shalva Papuashvili’s letter confirms that the authorities are troubled by the daily, ongoing protests.

The rhetoric he uses about the protest movement shows that the protests are a thorn in their side. This is despite the fact that they are no longer as large as they once were. But it is impossible for a protest to maintain the same scale when it has been going on for two years.

Shalva Papuashvili cynically called this protest movement a sect, even though he knows very well what the word ‘sect’ means. But, as always, he has turned his attitude towards the opposition into a cynical propaganda campaign.

Of course, the protest movement has become routine, and it is accompanied by certain symbols that have taken root. For example, the Georgian and EU flags at these rallies are a tangible symbolic expression of the movement’s support for Georgia joining the European Union. Another established symbol is the fact that the protests have remained on Rustaveli Avenue in Tbilisi, despite the roadworks currently taking place there.

Of course, Rustaveli Avenue is a symbol of protest — a place associated with the spirit and energy of dissent. We can point to other symbols as well. This is perfectly normal when a phenomenon becomes institutionalised, in this case a protest movement. This movement has developed into an institution with its own participants, rules, symbols, values and so on.

It is absolutely inappropriate to call this institutionalised protest movement a sect. First and foremost, it has no single prominent leader or figurehead whose will the protesters follow unquestioningly.

The protest movement brings together a wide range of people from different parts of society. It includes people who are not affiliated with any political party, academics, civil society representatives, members of organisations, artists and representatives of various political parties, including opposition parties that do not get along particularly well with one another. The protest movement is highly diverse, whereas a sect is characterised by almost everything except such diversity of views and backgrounds.

A second important indicator that this is not a sect is that it is not a closed group: people join it and leave it. Movement within the protest movement, including joining or leaving it, is not controlled, and there are no strict rules governing participation.

Another feature that fundamentally contradicts the perception of the protest movement as a sect is that it is not isolated from the opposition-minded public, or the broader society that supports the protests. It is an important representative of the opposition electorate.”

“It is entirely possible that this stigma, this negative label that Georgian Dream has attached to the protest movement — portraying it as a sectarian, almost satanic movement — could lead to the movement being declared illegal, banned, and its participants held legally accountable.

But it is impossible to silence the protest voice of an opposition-minded society on such a scale. The authorities would then have to shut down social media as well. However, I do not expect things to go that far. There will be certain restrictions, including legal ones, but the protest movement will still find a way to continue.

In general, a political party is much more likely to resemble a sect because, compared with a social movement, a political party is a more closed institution.

Political parties allow less pluralism and diversity of opinion, although this depends on the type of party we are talking about — democratic or authoritarian. In a democratic party, different views are legitimised and have their own legitimate space. Members exchange opinions, and there is no single leader or figurehead whose will dictates the party’s direction. But what happens in Georgian Dream? Isn’t Georgian Dream effectively Bidzina Ivanishvili?

Georgian Dream is a party built around one person’s authority. It acts exclusively in the direction set by Bidzina Ivanishvili. The defining feature of a sect is the presence of a leader to whom followers show unquestioning, unconditional and uncritical loyalty, whose authority they never challenge, and whose directives determine the group’s actions and direction. This is precisely what Georgian Dream has become under Bidzina Ivanishvili, and it is the clearest indicator of its sect-like nature.

And the most important thing we have witnessed in recent years is that anyone who criticises Georgian Dream is punished — harshly and through various means. This is what sectarianism looks like: the absolute and unquestionable principle that ‘whoever is not with me is my enemy’.”

On the protests and Georgian Dream

World.title: Theologian jailed for 30 days as Azerbaijan hijab-in-schools row reignites
World.content:
Azerbaijan schools hijab row

Theologian Abgul Suleymanov was detained for 30 days. His family links his detention to social media posts in which he spoke out against new school uniform requirements concerning the wearing of the hijab.

It has not been reported under which article of the Code of Administrative Offences the court sentenced him. It is therefore not yet possible to establish how Suleymanov’s posts were used to justify the decision to detain him.

Suleymanov’s wife, Zahra Suleymanova, told Meydan TV that the theologian was taken away from outside his home on the evening of 22 September. The following day, his family was unable to establish where he was being held.

According to Suleymanova, her husband has severe diabetes and needs to take medication. His relatives said on 24 September that, following the court hearing, he was taken to a temporary detention facility in Baku’s Binagadi district.

Hijab post and previous arrest

Following the Cabinet of Ministers’ decision, Suleymanov spoke out against restrictions on schoolgirls wearing the hijab. He wrote that if such a ban were introduced, he would rather go to prison. His family links his detention to this stance. Neither the police nor the court have publicly disclosed the reasons for his arrest.

The hijab issue is not new for the theologian. He is known for taking part in protests against restrictions on religious head coverings in schools, and his supporters refer to him as a “hijab prisoner”.

Suleymanov was detained in 2011 and sentenced to 11 years in prison on charges including organising unrest, attempting to disrupt public security and inciting disobedience. Official reports also alleged that drugs had been found in his possession. Suleymanov denied the charges. He was released in September 2022 after serving his sentence.

Following his release, Suleymanov said his religious beliefs had not changed and that he would defend his rights again if he faced obstacles to practising his religion. Documents relating to the current administrative case have not yet been made public.

Does new decision outlaw hijab?

A Cabinet of Ministers decision dated 21 September amended dress requirements for pupils at state schools. Under the new rules, pupils are prohibited from wearing additional items of clothing that disrupt the uniformity of the prescribed school uniform or are inconsistent with the principle of secularism in general education.

The word “hijab” is not mentioned in the decision. However, because religious head coverings are not part of the school uniform, the changes have been interpreted as a ban on wearing the hijab. The document does not specify which items of clothing are considered inconsistent with the principle of secularism, raising questions about how the new rule will be applied in schools.

Under the decision, parents or legal guardians must ensure that their children comply with the dress requirements. Issues relating to compliance are to be decided by each school’s pedagogical council. Elements of national dress may be worn only at certain events with the council’s approval. The document does not specifically provide for girls wearing the hijab to be excluded from classes.

Before the decision was adopted, the principle of “national values and secularism” was added to the Law on General Education in July, while the requirement for pupils and teachers to comply with dress rules was enshrined in law.

Previous complaints and unanswered questions

There have been previous complaints about girls wearing hijabs being denied access to schools. In an article we published in April, we reported on a parent’s complaint about School No. 15 in Sumgayit. He said his daughter had been prevented from attending classes because of her head covering. The school uniform requirements in force at the time did not specifically mention the hijab.

At the heart of the dispute are, on the one hand, requirements for a standard school uniform and the principle that children should not be forced to wear religious clothing and, on the other, pupils’ rights to freedom of religion and education. The issue of wearing the hijab in schools also came to prominence in 2012 following a protest outside the Education Ministry and subsequent arrests.

It remains unclear how schools will apply the new rules to pupils who wear the hijab. A key question also remains unanswered in Suleymanov’s case: what specific action did the court consider grounds for sentencing him to 30 days of administrative detention?

World.title: ‘No security guarantees’: Why Georgia’s Kamara festival was cancelled
World.content:
Kamara festival cancelled in Georgia

The Kamara music festival, scheduled to take place in the Georgian city of Gori on 26 September and close with a performance by opposition-minded musician Kordz, has been postponed indefinitely. The festival’s organiser, the Danish Cultural Institute, said it considered it unsafe to hold the event.

Kordz (Aleksandre Kordzaia) said he had faced attacks and threats from local authorities, members of the ruling Georgian Dream party and pro-government media.

The EU Delegation to Georgia responded to the festival’s cancellation by expressing regret. It said the Kamara festival was held as part of the EU-funded Creative Compass Georgia project and stressed that it “firmly believes in freedom of artistic expression”.

The delegation also noted that the EU had supported Georgia’s cultural sector for 30 years, including efforts to preserve the country’s cultural heritage, develop its creative industries and build links between Georgian artists and cultural organisations and their European counterparts.

Georgian parliament speaker Shalva Papuashvili responded critically to the EU Delegation’s statement. He said he had initially hoped the EU ambassador would realise that supporting “hatred and violence” in Georgia was unacceptable, but argued that the delegation’s statement suggested otherwise.

Papuashvili was particularly critical of the EU’s reference to the importance of freedom of artistic expression. He said the EU Delegation did not understand Georgia or Georgian society.

“This statement by the delegation is a direct incitement to hate speech, insults against mothers, labelling people as slaves, fascism and radicalism. The EU embassy is encouraging this,” Papuashvili told journalists.

The Georgian Musicians’ Union, in turn, responded to Papuashvili’s comments and the cancellation of Kordz’s performance by expressing solidarity with the musician. It said freedom of expression for artists was not a political privilege but a fundamental right.

The union said direct attacks by public officials on an artist over his civic stance went beyond debate and became a tool of censorship.

“It is unacceptable to use official power and rhetoric to intimidate musicians or disrupt concerts,” the union said.

It described Kordz as one of the prominent figures on Georgia’s music scene and warned that restricting artists’ ability to perform in their own country because of political pressure could have a serious impact on the cultural environment.

“Art cannot exist in an atmosphere of censorship and fear,” the statement said.

World.title: Russian tourists pelt Abkhaz Supreme Court judge with stones
World.content:
Russian tourists pelt Abkhaz Supreme Court judge

In Abkhazia, Russian tourists pelted a Supreme Court judge with stones. A criminal case was opened only several days later, and only after public pressure.

The incident took place in Sukhum on the evening of 20 September. According to official information, two Russian nationals, Yury Chudin and Sergey Bessonov, became involved in an altercation with a local woman in the street, threatened to kill her and then threw stones at her.

The woman was taken to hospital with a closed head injury, a laceration and bruising to her eyelid, and a haematoma.

The victim was later identified as a judge of the Supreme Court of Abkhazia, although neither investigators nor the media have named her. The cause of the altercation also remains unknown.

The incident was included in the official police report only after the Telegram channel Aiashara reported it a day later. The channel highlighted the fact that no criminal case had been opened, prompting a strong reaction on social media.

It was only after this that, on 23 September, the investigative department of the Sukhum police classified the attack on the judge as a criminal offence. Initially, the actions of the two Russian tourists had been treated as an administrative offence. Chudin and Bessonov refused to undergo medical tests for drug and psychotropic substance use, and a court subsequently sentenced them to 15 days in administrative detention.

The case has been transferred from the police to the Sukhum prosecutor’s office for further investigation. The ruling states that the decision was made in view of the public attention surrounding the case and the status of the victim.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan’s customs revenue soars to $1.8B
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 28. Customs revenue collected in Kyrgyzstan more than tripled from 2021 through 2025, totaling 157 billion som ($1.8 billion).

This was announced in a statement published by the Cabinet of Ministers of Kyrgyzstan, following the 8th meeting of the Interagency Commission on Countering the Financing of Criminal Activities and Legalization (Laundering) of Criminal Proceeds.

According to the information, the meeting attended by Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers and Head of the Presidential Administration of the Kyrgyz Republic Adylbek Kasymaliev.

The statement noted that the volume of customs payments increased from 47 billion soms ($537.45 million) in 2021 to 157 billion soms ($1.8 billion) in 2025.

Furthermore, the meeting was attended by experts from the Eurasian Group on Combating Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism (EAG), members of the Interagency Commission, and representatives of state bodies.

In the course of the meeting, it was noted that real GDP growth in Kyrgyzstan amounted to 11.1% in 2025, while GDP reached approximately 2 trillion soms ($22.87 billion).

To ensure the country’s further dynamic and comprehensive development, the National Development Program of the Kyrgyz Republic until 2030 has been approved.

Trend’s analysis indicates that the sharp increase in customs payments in Kyrgyzstan has been accompanied by broader growth in the country’s fiscal revenues and trade activity. Official data from the State Customs Service show that customs payments reached 157.4 billion soms ($1.80 billion) in 2025, exceeding the adjusted forecast by 5.8 billion soms ($66.32 million) and representing 127.9% of the 2024 level. The Customs Service attributed the result in part to improvements in customs administration and the digitalization of customs processes, including the Smart Customs platform.

In addition, Trend’s calculations show that the increase in customs duty revenue also occurred against the backdrop of a significant rise in total state budget revenue. According to the National Statistical Committee, state budget revenues rose from 209.9 billion soms ($2.40 billion) in 2021 to 673.2 billion soms ($7.70 billion) in 2025. This indicates that stronger customs collections form part of a wider expansion of the domestic revenue base.

World.title: Greece increases natural gas imports from Azerbaijan by 16% in 7M2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 28. Greece has increased natural gas imports from Azerbaijan by 16% during the first 7 months of this year.

This was reflected in the report "Foreign trade relations of Azerbaijan in January-July 2026", published by the State Statistics Committee.

According to the report, during this period, 603.9 billion cubic meters of natural gas in gaseous state worth $321.6 million were exported from Azerbaijan to Greece.

Trend's calculations based on the committee's data show that compared to the same period last year, gas exports to Greece rose by $43.5 million in terms of value, and by 83.4 million cubic meters in terms of volume.

According to the committee’s data, from January through July 2025, 520.5 million cubic meters of gas worth $278.1 million were exported from Azerbaijan to Greece.

According to data from the State Statistical Committee, the volume of natural gas exports from Azerbaijan to Greece in 2024–2025 changed as follows:

Year Export volume Export value 2024 927.1 million cubic meters $397.6 million 2025 910.5 million cubic meters 461.2 million

According to the data of the Azerbaijani State Statistics Committee, in 2025, the export of natural gas from Azerbaijan to Greece has slightly decreased in physical terms compared to 2024 - from 927.1 million to 910.5 million cubic meters, that is, by approximately 1.8%. At the same time, the value of exports, on the contrary, increased - from 397.6 million to $461.2 million, or approximately 16%.

Thus, in 2025, with a slight decrease in the physical volume of gas exports from Azerbaijan to Greece, its value increased significantly.

World.title: Italy's PM thanks President Ilham Aliyev for fuel price cap gesture
World.content:
Photo: Press service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 28. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has thanked President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev for the decision to cap fuel prices across Italy.

She made the remarks in a post on her official page on X.

“Following Eni, IP has also chosen to cap fuel prices across the entire national territory. This is an important signal of attention to Italian families, confirming that it is possible to make a concrete contribution to containing the rising cost of fuel. I wish to thank the President of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, for this gesture of attention that strengthens our cooperation, and the president of Socar, Rovshan Najaf,” she wroted.

Meloni said the Italian government would continue working to support families and protect their purchasing power amid the current international situation.

Meanwhile, recently State Oil Company of Azerbaijan (SOCAR) and Italian company Eni S.p.A. have exchanged a Protocol on the completion of the transaction under which SOCAR acquired a 10% stake in the Baleine oil and gas field development project in Côte d’Ivoire.

According to SOCAR, following the completion of the transaction, the project partners' stakes are distributed as follows: Eni — 37.25%, Vitol — 30%, Côte d’Ivoire’s national oil and gas company Petroci — 22.75%, and SOCAR — 10%.

"The acquisition of the stake will provide SOCAR with access to Africa's upstream sector and will become part of the company's long-term strategy to expand its global exploration and production activities," the company said.

World.title: Ex-Gidarjil CEO Kerry Blackman jailed over 'persistent' sexual assaults
World.content:
A woman who was sexually assaulted by Kerry Blackman has told a Queensland court she no longer felt safe and had lost her sense of belonging in the community.

Blackman, the former chief executive of the Gidarjil Development Corporation, was last week convicted in the District Court at Bundaberg of four sexual assault charges that involved aggressive and "persistent" physical advancements on the woman, who cannot be named for legal reasons.

The two-day trial heard the offending occurred between 2017 and 2023 and on the first occasion, when she was 23 years old, Blackman confronted her outside a toilet and whispered in her ear before he bit it and grabbed her bottom.

The trial was told that was the start of his sexual advancements, which saw him buying her a gift of lingerie and sending an inappropriate text referring to her bottom in native language.

The court heard the most aggressive and violent interaction involved Blackman locking a door then grabbing the woman by the head and kissing her.

On Monday, the woman sat in the District Court at Bundaberg to deliver her victim impact statement during the sentencing hearing.

She said her life had been "profoundly" changed by the ordeal.

"It has taken away a sense of stability … my sense of trust, dignity and belonging in my whole community," she said.

" I no longer recognise the woman I was. "

She said she turned to alcohol to deal with "silent battles with my mental health".

"I used to be a happy, free-spirited woman. That person feels very far from me now, " she said.

In her submissions, crown prosecutor Kate Thamm described Blackman's offending as "opportunistic" and said he showed no remorse for his actions.

Kerry Blackman has been jailed for up to 18 months. (ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside)

Blackman was awarded an honorary doctorate from CQ University in 2017 for his commitment to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, but the court heard it was revoked after the criminal charges were laid in 2024.

Defence lawyer Jordan Ahlstrand told the court Blackman's employment at Gidarjil, where he was a founding member, was terminated after the charges.

In handing down the sentence, Judge John Allen said Blackman's offending was "persistent and protracted".

"Your offending was an abuse of power."

He said Blackman had no other criminal history and was "otherwise a person of good character" who made "significant contributions to the community over decades".

The 69-year-old was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment and would be eligible for parole after serving 50 per cent of the sentence.

World.title: Government delays Upfield line upgrades until 2033 with duplication promise
World.content:
The Carroll government will duplicate Melbourne's Upfield line if re-elected, but will delay scheduled works to remove level crossings for seven years.

The railway line travels through the northern suburbs and still has a section of single-line track between Gowrie and Upfield stations, limiting the amount of services that can be run on the line at any one time.

Premier Ben Carroll said the duplication would be crucial for Melbourne's north and improve reliability of rail services to the area.

"I'm from Melbourne's north-western suburbs; this has been spoken about for generations," Mr Carroll said.

Ben Carroll says residents on the Upfield Line have complained about long waits between services on the single-track line. (Flickr: Philip Mallis)

The premier estimated the duplication would cost between $650 million and $1.4 billion, but stopped short of guaranteeing funding for the project.

Instead, the government is financially committing tens of millions of dollars to a study of the potential duplication, if it's re-elected in November's state election.

"$80 million to do a detailed study on what the duplication will require, those four kilometres of track," Mr Carroll said.

"We will expect the planning and duplication study to be completed by 2028."

The premier says the Upfield Line will be duplicated by 2033 if he is re-elected this November. (ABC News)

When asked about the decision to spend $80 million on a study conducted by government departments and agencies, Minister for Public Transport Vicki Ward said it was a financially prudent investment in the future of Melbourne's north.

"The government is giving the money to the Victorian people and the people who live on this line," Ms Ward said.

The announcement is the latest in a protracted series of promised business cases and plans to duplicate the Upfield line.

In February 2025, the Albanese government announced $7.05 million towards delivery of a business case to develop and prioritise options for upgrades to Melbourne’s northern metropolitan railway lines.

In this year's 2026/27 Victorian state budget, the government allocated $3.6 million to "complete a final program business case" on improvements including duplicating the Upfield line.

Last year, the government's Big Build website had promised 110 crossings would be removed by 2030, a date which has now been delayed by a further three years. (Victoria's Big Build)

Now, the Carroll government's announcement has increased the spending on planning the duplication by nearly twenty-fold.

As part of the announcement, the government said it would also delay the removal of eight level crossings on the Upfield line.

Mr Carroll said the delays would align the work with the duplication of the line in 2033, saving $686 million.

The delays will further stretch out the timeline of the level crossing removal project, with the Labor government promising after its 2022 election victory that 110 removals would be completed by 2030.

Delays on Upfield line upgrades criticised by Coaliton, Greens

Shadow Minister for Transport Infrastructure Evan Mulholland lashed the government over the announcement, saying the government had now delayed the level crossing removal for two more elections.

"Not into the next term of parliament, but into the following term of parliament," Mr Mulholland said.

" Whenever this government needs somewhere to cut, it picks the Upfield line, and it picks the northern suburbs. "

Mr Mulholland accused the government of delaying the level crossing removals repeatedly as a political strategy.

"Why have they been delayed? Because this government needs to get them outside of the forward estimates, to not account for them," he said.

The Victorian Greens also criticised the announcement, saying the government had not committed to actually building the project and was delaying much-needed works on the line.

"Labor promised these level crossings would be gone by 2027. Then it was 2030. Now it's 2033 — while communities across the north continue to grow and wait for the infrastructure they were promised," Greens MP Anasina Gray-Barberio said.

"Communities in the north deserve so much better than empty pre-election announcements that just disappear over the horizon."

The Greens are calling on the government to commit $246 million to duplicate the Upfield line.

World.title: Sandon Smith leads Newcastle out of an Immortal shadow
World.content:
It's rare that anybody in Newcastle shares an accolade with Andrew Johns, but Sandon Smith has managed it.

Fresh off his electric double in the Knights' 22-14 win over Penrith on Sunday, Smith will join Johns as the only men to play halfback for Newcastle in a grand final.

"It's pretty cool to hear. I don't think I'm anywhere near that [Johns]," Smith said.

"But it's an honour."

Talking about Johns is part of the deal when you play halfback for Newcastle but it's wrong to compare the two because it's wrong to compare anyone to Johns, who stands alone as the club and the city's ultimate legend and hero.

Johns was more than just a player to the Knights, even if he's the best player they have ever had or will ever know.

The 1997 and 2001 premierships made Johns a Newcastle folk hero and the personification of the Novocastrian dream, larger than life through his greatness and profoundly human at the same time, like if they found a demigod in the front bar of a Cessnock pub.

Every Newcastle halfback since his retirement in 2007 exists, to one extent or another, in his enormous shadow which has a gravitational pull from which some players never escaped.

Andrew Johns remains Newcastle's greatest ever player. (Getty Images via All Sports: Chris McGrath)

You'd have an easier time replacing Christ in Christianity, because at least then there's supposed to be a second coming.

The only way to do it is to opt out of that framing altogether, because it's a game that cannot be won and therefore shouldn't be played.

Smith doesn't need to be Andrew Johns for Newcastle to make a grand final, the prelim is proof that being himself is enough.

His first try was a clever effort backed by his speed but his second, a length of the field intercept in the dying seconds that sealed the club's first grand final berth in a quarter century, was something else entirely.

It brought Johns himself to tears and for the post-Johns generation, many of whom are seeing the Knights in a grand final for the first time, it was the greatest moment of their supporting lives.

"The first one I was just trying to stay in the game and I saw an opportunity. Those don't always come off, but it worked well," Smith said.

"The second one, I didn't know if I could make it. My little legs were hanging on for dear life. But I was happy to make it, I'm ecstatic.

"It's hard to put into words. There's so much emotion going on.

"I think there was a few tears coming out. I was happy, I was tired, I can't really explain it.

"When I came to the club, I heard a lot about the town and how our football affects the town.

"It's hard to put into words when you're a part of it, but it's so true and it's so special, to be a part of something like this that is bigger than ourselves."

One of those supporters was Johns himself, who wept openly and spoke with a voice clouded with emotion on Channel Nine commentary in the aftermath of Smith's last score.

It was a gift of a moment, a slice of heaven wrapped in red and blue, the kind that Johns gave his team and his town back in those olden days, but until Smith went all the way the Immortal had never received it himself.

That alone would be a high honour, but Smith stood up multiple times on his team's biggest game since the Johns age, creating the break that led to Dominic Young's try early in the second half and forcing a key error from Lindsay Smith late on.

It sets up a grand final berth against the Roosters, where Smith played from 2023 to 2025 before he travelled to Newcastle in an effort for more starting NRL after the Bondi club signed Daly Cherry-Evans.

He insists there's no bad blood with the Tricolours as he tries to pilot the Knights to a premiership at their expense.

"It won't change anything for me. I'll enjoy it, I'll embrace this whole week. I'll stay in the moment. It's just another team and it doesn't change anything for myself or the team," Smith said.

"If we win a grand final, I don't think it matters who it'd be against.

"They were transparent with me [around Cherry-Evans]. I've got no remorse, I loved the club and loved my time there, but I'm a Knight now."

Like many of his teammates, Smith's been trusted to do more than one job this season.

He's at halfback now, in relief of the injured Dylan Brown, but has also spent time at five-eighth and as the bench utility.

Sandon Smith joined Newcastle this year from the Roosters. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

But he's played them all well and it's added up to the best season of his young career with Smith thriving under the coaching of Justin Holbrook, who he'd worked with as an assistant at the Roosters.

"Justo's been such a rock for me over the past few years, [especially] coming to the club with him when I was unsure about what this year would look like for me," Smith said.

"He constantly reassured me to keep my head down, keep enjoying myself and keep getting better.

"The NRL season is a long season and your moment will come. He kept saying you need to be ready when that moment comes."

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

All halfbacks wear pressure on their shoulders in grand finals and Smith does so with the added spectre of Johns's legacy.

But having already earned one opportunity that has eluded all other Knights halfbacks since Johns, Smith has a chance to win an even greater prize.

Newcastle's most glorious times are inextricably tied with Johns but now Smith and his teammates can write a new legend with victory on Sunday.

It is one which, for the first time in Knights history, can exist beyond Johns and his titanic legacy.

His shadow will always be longest, but now Smith and these Knights have stepped outside it they have the chance to cast one of their own.

World.title: Six youths arrested over alleged assaults in Hobart CBD
World.content:
Six youths aged between 12 and 13 years have been arrested after members of the public were allegedly assaulted in central Hobart on Saturday.

Tasmania Police said it received reports shortly before 4:30pm that a "group of youths" was involved in a disturbance, and several members of the public had been assaulted.

Police went to the scene and arrested the six young people. They said no one was physically injured in the incident.

The youths were taken to the Hobart Police Station and were released into the care of parents or guardians.

"Tasmania Police would like to thank the members of the public who intervened and assisted the victims during the incident," police said.

Anyone with further information or mobile phone footage of the incident is encouraged to contact Hobart police or report anonymously to Crime Stoppers.

World.title: Breaking: Multiple shark warnings issued as whale carcass washes up on City Beach
World.content:
A whale carcass has washed up on Perth's City Beach, with authorities issuing multiple shark warnings for the popular swimming spot.

Several sharks have already been spotted circling in the area.

Local surf lifesavers found the carcass this morning and sounded the alarm.

Authorities are yet to confirm what species the whale is. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

"It is possible the carcass will continue to act as an attractant that could lead to sharks coming in close to shore along this stretch of coast," the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) warned.

The SharkSmart website has since issued several alerts for sharks seen at City Beach.

Sharks circling

The website said two white sharks, one measuring 5 metres and another 4 metres, were seen 10 metres offshore at City Beach, about one hour after the carcass was spotted.

A 3.5-metre unknown species of shark was also reported by the Surf Life Saving helicopter, and a 2.5-metre shark of unknown species was seen circling 10 metres offshore.

Local surf lifesavers found the carcass this morning and sounded the alarm as people came to look. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

DPIRD said people should exercise additional caution and follow any beach closures.

The department did not know the size of the whale carcass or the species.

The Town of Cambridge, which is managing the carcass, has been contacted for comment.

Swimmer killed

The warnings come just 10 days after a fatal shark attack at Sorrento beach, about 15 kilometres further north.

Swimmer Greg O'Neill was swimming close to the shore when he was attacked by a large great white, prompting Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis to issue a catch-and-kill order for the animal.

But the shark was not found.

World.title: SA hospital among growing list of measles exposures sites
World.content:
Contact tracing is underway at a major South Australian hospital after a confirmed case of measles spent more than 24 hours in the emergency department, among dozens of other newly-listed exposure sites.

SA Health said the latest case was a person in their forties linked to the growing cluster of cases at Brighton Secondary School.

Three students contracted the highly-infectious disease from an initial case who had returned from overseas and tested positive on September 14.

The latest infection brings the school cluster to five and the state's total to nine so far this year.

The measles cluster linked to the Brighton Secondary School has risen to five cases. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

SA Chief Public Health Officer Nicola Spurrier said the latest patient had a known exposure to the first case and has been hospitalised in a stable condition.

According to the SA Health, the patient was in the Queen Elizabeth Hospital emergency department's waiting area on September 23 from 5:15pm for about five hours.

Then the person was at the emergency department's "fast-track" area — which SA Health said was for patients who do not require urgent or life-saving care — from 9:45pm on Wednesday to 8:15pm the following day.

Professor Spurrier said it was "concerning" the Queen Elizabeth Hospital emergency department was among dozens of exposure sites, the full list of which can be found here.

The sites also included a pharmacy in Fulham Gardens, two SA Pathology Collection Centres, Westfield Marion, Harbour Town outlets and Morphett Vale Stadium.

"We haven't seen a cluster with this amount of spread for some time but it is in a way inevitable because there is so much measles overseas," Professor Spurrier said.

"They [contact tracers] are meticulously going through their records to look for the contact details of anybody who was in the emergency department or the area they call the fast track area and being able to send out messages directly to those people."

"They are also working through staff who might have been exposed during the time that the person was there, fortunately we do have a policy to make sure our staff are vaccinated against these sorts of infectious diseases."

Nicola Spurrier says SA Health was notified about the additional measles case on the weekend. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Professor Spurrier is urging anyone who may have come into contact with the infected person to monitor for symptoms, which include a fever, cough, blocked or runny nose, conjunctivitis and a red rash which spreads across the body.

"The average incubation period from the date that you might have exposed is around about 10 days, but it can go anywhere from seven days up to 18 days," she said.

"If you do develop any symptoms at all, please get yourself tested but we do ask for you to ring ahead to the doctor or the hospital so they know you may have been exposed so we can put precautions in place."

Professor Spurrier said anyone born from 1966 onwards may have only had one dose of the measles vaccine, which may not appear on the Australian immunisation register.

"If you don't have definitive evidence of those two doses then it's not harmful to have another dose just to be on the safe side," she said.

Health authorities are urging people to check their measles vaccination status amid an outbreak in SA. (Reuters: Annie Rice)

Alert but not alarmed

Australian Medical Association SA president Professor Peter Subramaniam said the latest outbreak was concerning but people should not be alarmed.

He said measles spread quickly and urged people to check their vaccination status.

"The normal course of events if you get two vaccines as a child at twelve months and eighteen months ... those two doses protect about 99 per cent of people for life," he said.

"To protect the people who are most at risk, the rest of us have to make sure we get vaccinated."

World.title: Baird quits as CA chair as Big Bash sell-off fallout continues
World.content:
Mike Baird has sensationally quit as Cricket Australia chair, after his own state association refused to back its representative in the fallout over the privatisation of Big Bash League clubs.

The former NSW premier informed fellow board members on Monday he would not seek re-election at next month's annual general meeting, with David Boon to take over as interim chair.

The decision comes after Baird lost the support of Cricket NSW, with the country's most powerful state unhappy with the decision to allow private investment.

Baird had served as NSW's representative on the board, and approached it recently to confirm it would not support him in the current circumstances.

David Boon will step in as the interim chair. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

He did have the option of moving into an independent role, but AAP was told he did not wish to continue without the support of all states.

Cricket Australia (CA) officials maintain they continue to back the call for the privatisation of clubs, which was confirmed earlier this month.

"After much consideration I have decided to stand down as CA chair and director," Baird said in a statement.

"I am delighted that David Boon has agreed to undertake the interim chair role while we complete the formal chair process, and I will undertake a transition process with David over coming weeks."

Baird had been on the CA board for six years and had served as chair since February 2023.

Alongside Todd Greenberg, he formed one of the most powerful duos in Australian sport.

In a statement on Monday, he again referenced the privatisation of the BBL as a positive move for the sport.

"This year CA will report record revenue, profit, attendance and viewership, and most importantly a 40 per cent increase in participation over the past four years," Baird said.

"With recent decisions on the Big Bash I also believe the long-term sustainability is assured.

"I believe Australian cricket continues to be well lead by the CA board."

Baird's exit comes after Cricket NSW slammed the decision to allow privatisation earlier this month.

"This decision risks leaving cricket in NSW and Australia strategically and financially worse off, with direct consequences for our ability to invest in grassroots cricket," a Cricket NSW statement said.

World.title: Eyre Highway marks 50 years since final section was sealed
World.content:
Fifty years ago, crossing the Nullarbor was not simply a matter of filling the tank, pointing the car east or west and settling in for a long drive.

Cars broke down. Tyres blew. Corrugations shook travellers for hours.

Heavy rain could turn the road into mud and sometimes the smoothest route was not the highway at all, but the firebreak running beside it.

This was life on the Eyre Highway, a more than 1,600-kilometre stretch of road connecting Norseman in Western Australia to Port Augusta in South Australia.

Efforts to seal the route began in the 1960s, with the West Australian section finished first and work continuing across South Australia into the 1970s.

The Eyre Highway in 1964, before the route was fully sealed. (Supplied: National Archives of Australia)

The last unsealed section of the highway was finished in the spring of 1976.

Half a century on and the crossing remains one of Australia's best-known road trips, taking travellers through remote outback country and past the cliffs of the Great Australian Bight.

The highway includes the 146-kilometre "90 Mile Straight", Australia's longest straight stretch of road.

Earlier this month, people with strong connections to the highway gathered at the Nullarbor Roadhouse to mark the 50-year milestone.

A road transformed

Among those who have watched the road change is Lance Sturtzel, from the Eyre Highway and Beyond group, who first crossed the Nullarbor in June 1964 while driving to Perth on his honeymoon.

Lance Sturtzel at the Western Australia border during a Nullarbor crossing. The photo is believed to have been taken in the 1950s or 1960s. (Supplied: Lance Sturtzel)

By the time he reached Port Augusta, heavy rain had fallen and travellers coming from the opposite direction warned him not to continue.

He went anyway.

"I had a Volkswagen then, which were renowned for being OK in wet weather and we got through OK," he said.

The trip took about three to three-and-a-half days.

"There was a lot of water on the road which was supposed to be the road," he said.

" It was more like the Eyre River than the Eyre Highway. "

Lance Sturtzel drove across the Eyre Highway for the first time in his turquoise Beetle in 1964. (Supplied: Lance Sturtzel)

Mr Sturtzel has since crossed the Nullarbor close to 100 times, but said the experience bears little resemblance to his first journeys.

"You might see 20 to 30 people in a whole day back then. Now, you see 20 to 30 people in 20 minutes," he said.

"It's a whole different ball game now."

For Mr Sturtzel, the modern journey may be faster, but it has lost some of the character of the old road.

"It's a very fast highway now," he said.

"It wasn't fast in the old days."

Lance Sturtzel says the Eyre Highway isn't as much fun as it used to be, but he still loves the road. (Supplied: Lance Sturtzel)

From endurance test to interstate link

For former regional engineer Peter Ryan, who helped oversee construction of the South Australian section, the difference was immediate.

"When I first got involved, in about 1973 or 1974, it would take all day to drive from Ceduna to Eucla," he said.

"By the time you got there, you had ruined two tyres or have two flats, and you felt completely worn-out."

By the time the work was finished, the same journey could be completed far more easily.

"When we finished, you could drive from Ceduna to Eucla and back in one day … no drama," he said.

An aerial view of the Eyre Highway looking east across the Nullarbor Plain in South Australia. (Supplied: National Library of Australia/Dave Tacon)

Mr Ryan said the new road changed more than travel times.

Freight could move more reliably between states, tourism increased and additional roadside facilities developed along a route that remained extremely remote.

Today, the Eyre Highway also forms part of a major interstate freight network used by heavy vehicles travelling between South Australia and Western Australia.

Life along the highway

For people living along the highway, the dirt road created different challenges.

Katherine O'Dea grew up with close family connections to Eucla and Border Village, just inside South Australia.

Before the road was sealed, she said the constant damage to vehicles created enough work to support two mechanics in Border Village.

A roadside fuel sign on the Nullarbor, beside the unsealed road. (Supplied: State Library of NSW)

The poor road conditions also affected where aircraft could safely land.

Today, designated sections of the highway can be closed and used as emergency landing strips by the Royal Flying Doctor Service.

Back then, Ms O'Dea said short strips near the highway were used because the road itself was often too rough.

"We had to use them because the Eyre Highway just had so many potholes with all the traffic going along it," she said.

But for Ms O'Dea, the Nullarbor was never simply about the challenge of getting across it.

She still returns to Eucla and describes the landscape as somewhere she feels at peace.

"Especially at night-time, just driving, looking at the stars, also the animals and the different types of seasons and the topography of the land," she said.

"It's just so amazing."

Peter Ellis and John Meredith on the Nullarbor Plain during their coast-to-coast field trip in 1991, travelling in an FJ Holden. (Supplied: National Library of Australia/John Meredith)

Crossing the old Nullarbor

For families moving across Australia before the highway was sealed, the drive could become an expedition in itself.

Gerard Cameron was one of 10 children when his family left a farm near Mount Gambier in the final days of 1966 to start a new life in Western Australia.

The family travelled in convoy with a ute, a Chevrolet Bel Air and a truck loaded with their furniture and farming equipment.

Mr Cameron remembers the crossing taking about two weeks.

James "Jamie" Wilmot driving across the Nullarbor in 1969. (Supplied: Mosman Local Studies)

Fifty years after the final dirt section disappeared, the Eyre Highway has become a safer and more reliable interstate route.

But for many travellers, crossing the Nullarbor remains something more than simply getting from one state to another.

World.title: V’landys intervenes to save thousands of Knights fans from trackwork drama as grand final sells out
World.content:
ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys has thanked NSW Premier Chris Minns for scrapping planned trackwork that threatened to cause grand final chaos for tens of thousands of Newcastle fans as the NRL decider sold out on Monday morning. V’landys rang Minns early on Monday morning when the prospect of buses replacing trains between Newcastle and Wyong on Sunday was raised with NRL officials. There was heavy traffic as fans travelled to Accor Stadium on Sunday. Sitthixay Ditthavong The Knights’ grand final run after claiming the wooden spoon in 2025 ranks as one of the unlikeliest stories in rugby league history, and has left transport officials scrambling. Plans are set to be finalised on Monday for trains to run between Newcastle and Sydney, with V’landys forecasting an influx of more than 30,000 Knights fans as ticket sales for Sunday’s decider were exhausted shortly before midday.



“Chris Minns is one of the most can-do people you’ll ever see,” V’landys said. “If it’s possible, he’ll get it done. And he wasn’t going to let 30,000-plus Newcastle fans down, so he immediately rearranged the trackwork. Kalyn Ponga, Francis Manuleleua and Jermaine McEwen celebrate with Newcastle fans on Sunday. Getty Images “The NRL and Newcastle fans cannot be more appreciative of that action.” Transport NSW officials have indicated that the scheduled works for Sunday are set to be moved to another day to accommodate increased commuter demand from the Hunter.



Knights fans already experienced drama getting to their team’s preliminary final on Sunday after an issue with a freight train at Warnervale led to delays and cancellations. But those who reached Accor Stadium made their voices heard as the Knights beat Penrith 22-14 despite playing more than half the game with only 12 men on the field. Two-time premiership winning Knight Mark Hughes said the team’s fans had stuck by them as they collected wooden spoons during the past decade. “The team this year have shown so much resilience, and our supporters have shown just as much,” Hughes told 2GB on Monday. Related Article NRL 2026 Shocking details of Nathan Cleary’s shattered ankle revealed



“And even yesterday, the trains were failing, it was raining, there were queues, but it didn’t worry us. We got there, and we got it done.” He predicted a similarly sizeable turnout this weekend when the Knights take on the Sydney Roosters. “There’ll be a red and blue army takeover of the stadium and our boys will give it their all,” Hughes said.
