World.title: Level crossings on hold as Labor vows to fix Melbourne’s most unreliable train line
World.content:
Labor has promised to duplicate Melbourne’s least reliable rail line and save taxpayers more than $600 million in major infrastructure works, while further delaying a signature policy of former premier Daniel Andrews. Premier Ben Carroll will on Monday announce a funding commitment of $80 million over two years to kickstart work on building a second track on the Upfield line, which will slash wait times for commuters in suburbs including Broadmeadows, Dallas, Campbellfield and Fawkner. The government has promised if re-elected, it will duplicate the Upfield line past Gowrie station to boost train frequency. Chris Hopkins Currently, the four-kilometre stretch of track between Gowrie and Upfield stations is a single line, creating bottlenecks, preventing more trains from being run and leaving passengers experiencing substantial delays during peak periods. Labor estimates duplicating the track will increase capacity by 50 per cent. The promise will attempt to shore up support for Labor in its heartland northern suburbs seats, including Pascoe Vale, where the Greens believe they can win in November for the first time ever.



The initial $80 million election pledge will be used to undertake site investigations, finalise project design and acquire relevant planning and environmental approvals. The government has not committed to a completion date for the project and said it will become clear after the initial development work is finished in 2028. Treasurer Colin Brooks will also announce on Monday the delay of eight level crossing removals along the Upfield line to coincide with the track duplication and minimise costs and disruption. Brooks said the decision to delay the removals was about “commonsense and timing” that would ultimately spare the state budget bottom line $686 million.



The delay is another blow for residents in Melbourne’s north, who have been waiting for the level crossing removals since 2022 when Andrews promised the works would be completed by 2027. Though the government later issued a new deadline of 2030, Labor now predicts the completion date to be in 2033 to coincide with the train line duplication works. “We are making commonsense decisions to save money and minimise disruption along the Upfield Line,” Brooks said. “Labor will remove every one of the 110 level crossings we promised.”



Carroll said: “Doing it in one go reduces costs and minimises disruption for passengers. It’s common sense.” The premier will also say that increasing frequency by duplicating the train line would have a substantial impact for commuters. “50 per cent more capacity on the line for turn-up-and-go services – that’s a huge change for the northern suburbs.” Although the $80 million will only be used for planning development, Carroll said “duplication has been spoken about for decades” and a re-elected Labor government would see the project built. “As a premier that spends taxpayer money wisely, I want to get the certainty on what duplication will cost. So we will delay several level crossings, then give Victorians certainty … and then we’ll get on, remove level crossings and duplicate the railway line at the same time,” he told reporters on Monday morning.



While passengers on other metropolitan lines such as the Mernda, Sandringham, Glen Waverley, Cranbourne, Pakenham and Sunbury lines wait less than 10 minutes in peak hour, commuters on the Upfield line still face waits of 15 to 20 minutes during morning and afternoon peak periods. A train “turn-back” at Gowrie station, which would have made 10-minute frequencies possible, was planned as part of the Metro Tunnel project so Upfield trains could utilise new capacity in the City Loop, but it was cut from the $15 billion project to reduce costs. The Parliamentary Budget Office has costed the turn-back facility at $54.4 million. Geordie Barker, from the residents group Elevating Brunswick, said it was disappointing that the level crossing removals had been delayed. However, he said the delay would allow time to improve designs of the new skyrail through the rapidly densifying section of Brunswick. Barker’s group has been pushing for one of two new elevated stations to be built next to a vacant block of land, south of Hope Street, rather than north of Hope Street, where the platforms would be metres away from existing apartments.



“Duplication is the key to an increase in frequency along the line. Tying them together is great, however, this is our third delay. Daniel Andrews said this would be built by 2027,” he said. “We’ve had announcements like this before and really they need to commit to doing it properly.” Improvements on the Upfield line have been considered long overdue by some public transport experts. Infrastructure Victoria last year called on the government to duplicate the line, and Merri-bek Council has long campaigned for the government to commit to the upgrades. Duplicating the line would cost about $245 million, according to Parliamentary Budget Office costings commissioned by the Greens in 2025, and provided to The Age at the time. That does not include about $50 million over a decade in operating and maintenance expenses.



Infrastructure Victoria estimated duplicating the track and upgrading power and signalling along the entire line would cost $650 million to $1.4 billion, Carroll said on Monday. Labor’s promise to upgrade the line may also shore up support in heartland northern-suburb seats. The Greens believe they can unseat Labor in Pascoe Vale, which the government holds on a slim 2 per cent margin. The duplicated train line will also benefit commuters closer to the city in the seat of Brunswick, which Labor hopes to win back from the Greens. Greens candidate for Pascoe Vale Angelica Panopoulos said it was time the northern suburbs were given the same quality of public transport as commuters in other parts of the city. “It shouldn’t take decades of advocacy from the community and Labor staring down the barrel of losing marginal seats to the Greens to finally move on this,” she said.

World.title: MTV VMAs 2026: Full list of winners and nominees

The blue carpet has officially been rolled up for the wildest awards show in entertainment, but the best is yet to come from the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs).

The VMAs earned their chaotic reputation long before the artist formerly known as Kanye West interrupted Taylor Swift’s acceptance speech in 2009, and that’s in large part thanks to Madonna. And on Sunday night at Los Angeles’ Peacock Theatre (Monday morning AEST), the queen of pop graced the stage and performed at the VMAs for the first time in 23 years, with the help of Sabrina Carpenter and Charli xcx.

Madonna enlisted Sabrina Carpenter for her first MTV VMAs performance in 23 years. The duo then picked up the best collaboration gong. Stewart Cook/CBS

Charli xcx was also tapped for an opening performance cameo. Stewart Cook/CBS

A quick refresher for the uninitiated: Madonna’s first performance at the VMAs was in 1984, an edgy rendition of Like A Virgin some critics dubbed obscene. She upped the edgy ante in 2003, when she performed the opening medley with Britney Spears and Christina Aguilera … and locked lips with them.

World.title: Wall Street’s multi-trillion-dollar question: Could bonds end the AI boom?
World.content:
BusinessMarketsBonds Opinion Wall Street’s multi-trillion-dollar question: Could bonds end the AI boom? Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 28, 2026 — 12:10pm

September 28, 2026 — 12:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The sudden spike in US bond yields over the past week to near 20-year highs raises a multi-trillion dollar question: Will those higher debt returns crash the sharemarket, and in the process derail the boom in artificial intelligence-related investment? Having edged up for most of the year – since the war in the Middle East caused oil prices to soar – the yield on US 10-year Treasury bonds has jumped from 4.95 per cent to 5.16 per cent in the space of a week, with similar moves across the yield curve. The spike in bond yields doesn’t bode well for the sharemarket, and its AI-investment boom. AP That’s the highest yield on the 10-year bond – the global reference point for most interest-bearing securities – since 2007, when it rallied in the lead-up to the global financial crisis. Bond yields and sharemarkets generally (there are exceptions) have an inverse correlation.



Bonds are “risk-free” assets. If you can get more than 5 per cent from investing in bonds, the dividend yield on the US stock market – currently about 1 per cent – starts to look unappealing when the risks of a sharemarket inflated by the hype around artificial intelligence stocks and trading at near-record levels are factored into decision-making. Higher yields push up borrowing costs, lowering company profits and dampening economic activity. They also lift the discount rates used to calculate the value of companies’ forecast future cashflows in today’s dollars, which is a particular threat to an AI sector increasingly reliant on access to the debt market to fund the extraordinary levels of investment in chips and data centres, and the energy and water infrastructure to support those centres. There’s a lot riding on a continuation of the AI investment binge and the promises of transformative productivity gains being realised – for investors, and the global economy. The scale of the AI investments being made – in the US, it is more than $US700 billion ($990 billion) this year and could top a trillion dollars next year – and the rates of revenue growth that would be required to justify the investments are mind-boggling. They make the AI sector and the “hyperscalers” dominating the digital infrastructure, and accounting for about 35 per cent of the US market’s value, exceptionally vulnerable to an increase in discount rates.



So far, there’s been no material impact on the sharemarket from the spikes in yields and, apart from a brief sell-off when the US and Israel launched their attack on Iran in February, it has traded largely unaffected by the surge in oil prices above $US100 a barrel, the stubbornly high inflation rate and the US Federal Reserve’s decision this month to raise its policy rate for the first time in more than three years. Related Article Opinion

Global economy The four horsemen of the apocalypse are coming for the global economy That may be because of the continuing conviction that AI will change the world, and those companies leading the revolution will profit immeasurably. It may also be because the US economy is growing strongly, buoyed by the investment in AI, by fiscal stimulus – the US government deficit is running at almost 6 per cent of GDP - and the strength of spending by higher income households, and by booming corporate profitability. The AI investment boom may, however, taper or burst.



The resort to debt by even the hyperscalers – companies like Amazon and Alphabet – is an indication of the stresses even the biggest and most profitable companies are experiencing in funding their ever-escalating AI investments. Spending on AI has absorbed their vast legacy cashflows and is stretching the equity market’s capacity to support them with new equity. The rise in yields makes the cost of AI debt – which already has a risk premium – more expensive, while the rise in interest rates being driven by the bond market and the Fed will start to squeeze consumers’ finances. The spending by wealthier households has been held up, so far, by the Republicans’ tax cuts and by the wealth effects of the sharemarket boom. The rise in yields makes the cost of AI debt more expensive, while the rise in interest rates being driven by the bond market and the Fed will start to squeeze consumers’ finances. Corporate earnings growth has been exceptionally strong. Third-quarter earnings estimates put it at about 25 per cent of the same period last year. The earnings numbers are, however, inflated to some degree by the hundreds of billions of profits AI companies are reporting that flow from the markups in the value of their holdings in each other in what’s been described as the “circular” AI economy. There’s a lot of paper profit and revenue within the sector.



At a macro level, the current US settings – the 6 per cent government deficit and more than $US40 trillion of government debt – are unsustainable in a rising interest rate environment. Related Article Opinion

Gold What the price of gold tells us about Trump and the future Peter Hartcher Political and international editor With the Fed having just started a rate-rising cycle, with the market pricing in at least three more 25 basis point increases over the next year, the threat posed to government and corporate finances posed by a significant increase in interest costs will only intensify. The US could grow its way out of the looming debt trap as low-cost debt issued in the post-financial crisis and pandemic eras continues to mature and be refinanced with higher-cost debt. But, more likely, it will have to try to inflate its way out, which will probably agitate the bond vigilantes even more. The risk to the sharemarket is heightened because today’s bond market is not what it once was.



Donald Trump’s trade wars and US sanctions have made the foreign central banks and institutions that were once the major buyers of US bonds more wary. They’ve been diversifying away from the US, into gold and other assets. The market is now peopled by hedge funds and other traders, pursuing carry trades by either borrowing cheaply in other markets (Japan used to be the primary source of low-cost funding) or by running leveraged arbitrages between US physical bonds and their policing in futures markets. The risk to the sharemarket is heightened because the bond market during Donald Trump’s presidency is not what it once was. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson That makes the market more volatile and potentially vulnerable if an “event” causes the funds to suddenly unwind their trades. The bond market’s equivalent of the VIX index (often referred to as the “fear” index), which measures volatility in the sharemarket, is the MOVE (Merrill Option Volatility Estimate) index. It leapt over the past week from 78.56, which is roughly its average level of the past decade, to 96. Presumably some of those leveraged bondholders became spooked by the pace of the run-up in yields.



With stocks trading at pricey levels – the cyclically adjusted profit-to-earnings or CAPE ratio is at levels last seen in 1999, in the lead-up to the bursting of the dot-com bubble – a sustained rise in interest rates is an obvious threat. It’s also a threat to both the real economy and the financial sector, where there’s been massive increases in non-bank, or “shadow banking” activity since the regulatory response to the 2008 crisis forced regulated institutions out of a lot of financial market activities. Related Article Global economy The world economy is becoming wary of America There is perceived increased risk to the corporate sector and the economy being priced into markets, with the credit default swaps for investment trade companies blowing out and the yield curve in the bond market flattening. An index for insuring against defaults on US investment grade debt started the year at 51 basis points and is now at 58 basis points – where it would have cost $US510,000 to buy insurance against a default on $US100 million of loans, it now costs $US580,000. For some of the hyperscalers, the cost is above 90 basis points, or more than $US900,00 per $US100 million.



The flattening of the yield curve – the difference between the yields on two and 10-year bonds has shrunk from about 85 basis points at the start of the year to about 30 basis points – points to an expectation that the US economy will slow as the Fed, and the market, respond to the risk of sustained high inflation levels. It is, of course, conceivable that a sharemarket that has shrugged off Trump’s tariffs, the war in the Middle East and $US100-a-barrel-plus oil prices, $US40 trillion of government debt and the administration’s erratic policymaking can ignore the myriad of latent threats, buoyed by the transformative potential of AI. There’s a lot riding on a continuation of the AI investment binge and the promises of transformative productivity gains being realised - for investors, and the global economy. World.title: Lamarre-Condon told friend how he would dispose of a body, court told
World.content:
NationalNSWLamarre-Condon trial Lamarre-Condon told friend how he would dispose of a body, court told Michaela Whitbourn September 28, 2026 — 12:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A former NSW police officer accused of murdering Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies told a friend at a dinner how he would dispose of the body if he killed someone, a court has heard. Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, is standing trial in the NSW Supreme Court on two counts of murder over the shooting deaths of Baird, 26, his former casual romantic partner, and Davies, 29, in Paddington on February 19, 2024. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Georgia Cook outside the NSW Supreme Court on Friday. Her evidence continued on Monday. George Chan Georgia Cook, a former friend of Lamarre-Condon, told the court on Monday she distanced herself from the then-police officer after he asked her over a dinner in Kirribilli in May 2023: “What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?” She said she froze and replied: “No, because I don’t want their ghost to haunt me.”



Cook said he asked her later in the dinner, “So, if you did kill someone what would you do with their bodies?” Lamarre-Condon said he would “take their stuff, I would put it in a dumpster, and I would take their bodies to bushland where no one would ever find them”, Cook told the court. A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon in the NSW Supreme Court. Rocco Fazzari “It felt very surreal,” she said. “I didn’t know whether to believe anything I’d heard. I really couldn’t continue a friendship after hearing these things.” She said she had told Lamarre-Condon before the dinner about a confidential medical diagnosis, and he had said at the restaurant that “what I’m about to tell you, if you tell anyone else, I know about you”.



He was using the information “to hold over me, so I wouldn’t go and tell … what he had told me”, Cook said. She said she was “really scared” after the dinner, and distanced herself from him permanently in December 2023. Cook gave a statement to police in June 2024, four months after Lamarre-Condon was arrested in February. She rejected a suggestion by one of the accused’s barristers, James Lang, that Lamarre-Condon did not have this conversation with her, and that she had repeated details about the alleged location of the bodies and other items from media reports. “When someone says something that scary or shocking, it’s not something that leaves your mind,” Cook said. “I can remember it like it was yesterday. It was jarring. I could never forget these words being said to me.”



Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial Three shots, a shopping trip and 14,000 hours of CCTV: The case against Beau Lamarre-Condon Asked about the delay in coming forward to police, Cook said she was “absolutely terrified”. “After the news had come out, I was scared,” she said. “I didn’t know what to do with what I knew. I didn’t know if I wanted to be involved. “If he wasn’t put away, what would happen to me? That puts me in a scary position.” Cook testified on Friday that Lamarre-Condon had told her during the same dinner that he had been watching Baird from outside his house, using his mother’s car and wearing a black hoodie.



“In that time he’d seen Jesse have sex with other men,” she said he told her. She said the accused also claimed that he saw Baird over the back fence taking photos with friends with a Polaroid camera he had given him. Lamarre-Condon told her he kept watching until Baird left the home and saw where he left his key. “He [said he] went and got the key and unlocked the door, broke into the house, he stole the Polaroid camera, he ate Jesse’s Easter egg, and he said that there was something else that he did, but he wouldn’t tell me what it was, which concerned me,” she said. The court has heard that Baird broke up with Lamarre-Condon for the first time in April 2023. The two men resumed seeing each other briefly in late 2023 before Baird ended it permanently in November.



Lamarre-Condon is charged with breaking into Baird’s home in August 2023 and stealing Baird’s wallet and phone. He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated break and enter. The defence case is that he used a key Baird had given him to enter the home. The prosecution alleges Lamarre-Condon murdered Baird, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, after developing an “obsessive and jealous infatuation” with him. Davies, Baird’s new boyfriend, was killed to eliminate a witness to the crime, the Crown alleges. There is no dispute that Lamarre-Condon was at Baird’s Paddington share house when Baird and Davies died, that they died of gunshot wounds from his police-issued pistol, and that he was disguised as a delivery rider. However, the defence case is that Lamarre-Condon was there to pick up some of his belongings and did not expect anybody to be home. A struggle ensued in which his gun accidentally went off twice, killing Baird, and Davies accidentally shot himself in a second struggle after grabbing the gun, the defence says. The trial continues.

World.title: Ten minutes of madness: How the Wallabies beat the Boks with 11 men
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies Ten minutes of madness: How the Wallabies beat the Boks with 11 men Jonathan Drennan September 28, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wallabies coach Les Kiss prides himself on having every detail covered when preparing his teams. Ahead of facing the Springboks in Perth on Sunday night, Kiss had challenged his side to work on contingency plans, such as losing five-eighth Ben Donaldson while not having an experienced playmaker in reserve. That would have been a simple scenario to deal with compared to what actually took place. Loading Ultimately, nothing could have prepared Kiss or his team for the 10 minutes and 30 seconds of madness that ended the Test match against South Africa. The Wallabies led by 25 points before yellow cards to Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Hunter Paisami left the team with 11 players against the world champions. Here’s how the Wallabies hung on and won the Test.



69th and 70th minutes: 18-point lead. Wilson and Lonergan yellow cards Wilson had enjoyed one of his best Test performances until referee Andrea Piardi gave him a yellow card for a high tackle on South African hooker Malcolm Marx. Wilson was his team’s top tackler, making 13 and not missing one. Marx dipped late, and Wilson made glancing high contact. He left the field with just over 10 minutes left on the clock. With Wilson absent and the Wallabies pack weakened, South Africa took full advantage a minute later.



The Springbok scrum was metres away from the Australian line with centre Hunter Paisami packing down in Wilson’s place. Lonergan dives at the ball illegally while South African back-rower Jasper Wiese has it at his feet. A penalty try is awarded, and Lonergan is off the field for 10 minutes. Kiss later said the team remained calm amid these scenes. “We were asking a lot of questions about what was happening; we were trying to get messages down the sideline and just get an idea of where things were,” Kiss said. “The pleasing thing for me was that the group out there on the pitch there was a nice calmness and focus about what they had to do next. Hearing that back and seeing how they looked and felt in those tough moments, that’s incredibly pleasing.” 71st and 72nd minutes: 11-point lead. Suaalii yellow card



The Wallabies are tired, with spaces opening up all over their defensive line. Springboks playmaker Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu charges through a gap and passes to centre Canan Moodie, who looks certain to score a try. Fullback Tom Wright yells for cover, and it comes. Donaldson and Max Jorgensen manage to mow down Moodie. Wright believes that the team was playing completely on instinct. “We were just trying to bust ass,” Wright said. “I think when you’re down, and there is no real plan, it’s about how hard can you hustle and make it as difficult for the opposition to score as possible. That’s what we were talking about and trying to execute when we didn’t have the ball.” Loading



Suaalii is yellow-carded for offside, leaving the Wallabies with 12 men on the field. Piardi is having to use a mobile phone to speak to television match official Matteo Liparini due to communication problems. He explains to Wallabies stand-in captain Jeremy Williams and South Africa skipper Andre Esterhuizen the difficulties he is having with the technology, pleading that he is doing his best. After the game, Williams had every sympathy for the officials. “The refs had a really tough job; they obviously had problems with the radios and things like that, so they did the best they could while they were out there, and I don’t envy that job at all, they did an awesome job,” Williams said. Two minutes later, Morne van den Berg scores a converted try for South Africa, pulling the score back to 42-31.



75th minute: Down to 11 players, leading by 11. Paisami yellow card. With just 12 teammates, Wright took a gamble, shooting out of the line and catching a pass from Esterhuizen. The fullback finishes under the posts, thinking he has sealed the game for the Wallabies, but Piardi’s blue mobile phone comes back out. After a quick review, the try is rubbed out after a high tackle from centre Hunter Paisami, leaving the Wallabies with 11 players on the field. View post on X



“That’s how it goes, isn’t it? We said we wanted to make it difficult for them. We knew that they needed to score points and wanted to run,” Wright said. “We said if we were to concede a little bit of space anywhere, they were going to have to go around us. “We were hustling, showing that care and connection that we talked about during the week. The ball fell favourably for me; sadly, a high shot was the call that we came back to, and we had to go from there.” Minutes 76-79: Desperate times call for desperate measures. Four-point lead Down to 11 men, the Wallabies are forced to defend desperately. The Springboks have a luxury of space, but for three minutes the Wallabies hold them off, shaving precious time off the clock.



“I haven’t played with 11 before. That’s the game. You can have a plan until you get punched in the face. We didn’t get punched in the face, so to speak, but certainly we weren’t expecting to play with 11,” Wright said. “You don’t expect to play with 14 or 13 or 12, but you certainly don’t expect to play with 11 ... we certainly can’t fault our effort and how much we put into defending our tryline.” In the 79th minute, South Africa prop Ox Nche crashes over for a converted try to reduce the Wallabies’ lead to four points. There is time for one more play, and for South Africa to win the Test. Wallabies captain Harry Wilson celebrates after taking down the Springboks. Getty Images Last two minutes: Lonergan and Wilson return to help seal victory



Wilson has been sitting on the sideline for 10 minutes, unable to help his team and desperate to come on. After getting on the field, the captain’s message is simple: try to get the ball back. With the clock on 81 minutes, 13 Wallabies hang on for a famous victory after South African playmaker Quan Horn is penalised for an accidental offside. “I had fresh legs then, so I was going to chase after everything, because when you let your team down, it always hurts, especially when we’re in such a strong position when I did that [high tackle for the yellow card]. “So I was hurting there on the sideline, but I just loved the way the boys scrapped for each other and the care for the jersey.”

World.title: V’landys intervenes to save thousands of Knights fans from trackwork drama as grand final sells out
World.content:
ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys has thanked NSW Premier Chris Minns for scrapping planned trackwork that threatened to cause grand final chaos for tens of thousands of Newcastle fans as the NRL decider sold out on Monday morning. V’landys rang Minns early on Monday morning when the prospect of buses replacing trains between Newcastle and Wyong on Sunday was raised with NRL officials. There was heavy traffic as fans travelled to Accor Stadium on Sunday. Sitthixay Ditthavong The Knights’ grand final run after claiming the wooden spoon in 2025 ranks as one of the unlikeliest stories in rugby league history, and has left transport officials scrambling. Plans are set to be finalised on Monday for trains to run between Newcastle and Sydney, with V’landys forecasting an influx of more than 30,000 Knights fans as ticket sales for Sunday’s decider were exhausted shortly before midday.



“Chris Minns is one of the most can-do people you’ll ever see,” V’landys said. “If it’s possible, he’ll get it done. And he wasn’t going to let 30,000-plus Newcastle fans down, so he immediately rearranged the trackwork. Kalyn Ponga, Francis Manuleleua and Jermaine McEwen celebrate with Newcastle fans on Sunday. Getty Images “The NRL and Newcastle fans cannot be more appreciative of that action.” Transport NSW officials have indicated that the scheduled works for Sunday are set to be moved to another day to accommodate increased commuter demand from the Hunter.



Knights fans already experienced drama getting to their team’s preliminary final on Sunday after an issue with a freight train at Warnervale led to delays and cancellations. But those who reached Accor Stadium made their voices heard as the Knights beat Penrith 22-14 despite playing more than half the game with only 12 men on the field. Two-time premiership winning Knight Mark Hughes said the team’s fans had stuck by them as they collected wooden spoons during the past decade. “The team this year have shown so much resilience, and our supporters have shown just as much,” Hughes told 2GB on Monday. Related Article NRL 2026 Shocking details of Nathan Cleary’s shattered ankle revealed



“And even yesterday, the trains were failing, it was raining, there were queues, but it didn’t worry us. We got there, and we got it done.” He predicted a similarly sizeable turnout this weekend when the Knights take on the Sydney Roosters. “There’ll be a red and blue army takeover of the stadium and our boys will give it their all,” Hughes said. World.title: Level crossings on hold as Labor vows to fix Melbourne’s most unreliable train line
World.content:
Labor has promised to duplicate Melbourne’s least reliable rail line and save taxpayers more than $600 million in major infrastructure works, while further delaying a signature policy of former premier Daniel Andrews. Premier Ben Carroll will on Monday announce a funding commitment of $80 million over two years to kickstart work on building a second track on the Upfield line, which will slash wait times for commuters in suburbs including Broadmeadows, Dallas, Campbellfield and Fawkner. The government has promised if re-elected, it will duplicate the Upfield line past Gowrie station to boost train frequency. Chris Hopkins Currently, the four-kilometre stretch of track between Gowrie and Upfield stations is a single line, creating bottlenecks, preventing more trains from being run and leaving passengers experiencing substantial delays during peak periods. Labor estimates duplicating the track will increase capacity by 50 per cent. The promise will attempt to shore up support for Labor in its heartland northern suburbs seats, including Pascoe Vale, where the Greens believe they can win in November for the first time ever.



The initial $80 million election pledge will be used to undertake site investigations, finalise project design and acquire relevant planning and environmental approvals. The government has not committed to a completion date for the project and said it will become clear after the initial development work is finished in 2028. Treasurer Colin Brooks will also announce on Monday the delay of eight level crossing removals along the Upfield line to coincide with the track duplication and minimise costs and disruption. Brooks said the decision to delay the removals was about “commonsense and timing” that would ultimately spare the state budget bottom line $686 million.



The delay is another blow for residents in Melbourne’s north, who have been waiting for the level crossing removals since 2022 when Andrews promised the works would be completed by 2027. Though the government later issued a new deadline of 2030, Labor now predicts the completion date to be in 2033 to coincide with the train line duplication works. “We are making commonsense decisions to save money and minimise disruption along the Upfield Line,” Brooks said. “Labor will remove every one of the 110 level crossings we promised.”



Carroll said: “Doing it in one go reduces costs and minimises disruption for passengers. It’s common sense.” The premier will also say that increasing frequency by duplicating the train line would have a substantial impact for commuters. “50 per cent more capacity on the line for turn-up-and-go services – that’s a huge change for the northern suburbs.” Although the $80 million will only be used for planning development, Carroll said “duplication has been spoken about for decades” and a re-elected Labor government would see the project built. “As a premier that spends taxpayer money wisely, I want to get the certainty on what duplication will cost. So we will delay several level crossings, then give Victorians certainty … and then we’ll get on, remove level crossings and duplicate the railway line at the same time,” he told reporters on Monday morning.



While passengers on other metropolitan lines such as the Mernda, Sandringham, Glen Waverley, Cranbourne, Pakenham and Sunbury lines wait less than 10 minutes in peak hour, commuters on the Upfield line still face waits of 15 to 20 minutes during morning and afternoon peak periods. A train “turn-back” at Gowrie station, which would have made 10-minute frequencies possible, was planned as part of the Metro Tunnel project so Upfield trains could utilise new capacity in the City Loop, but it was cut from the $15 billion project to reduce costs. The Parliamentary Budget Office has costed the turn-back facility at $54.4 million. Geordie Barker, from the residents group Elevating Brunswick, said it was disappointing that the level crossing removals had been delayed. However, he said the delay would allow time to improve designs of the new skyrail through the rapidly densifying section of Brunswick. Barker’s group has been pushing for one of two new elevated stations to be built next to a vacant block of land, south of Hope Street, rather than north of Hope Street, where the platforms would be metres away from existing apartments.



“Duplication is the key to an increase in frequency along the line. Tying them together is great, however, this is our third delay. Daniel Andrews said this would be built by 2027,” he said. “We’ve had announcements like this before and really they need to commit to doing it properly.” Improvements on the Upfield line have been considered long overdue by some public transport experts. Infrastructure Victoria last year called on the government to duplicate the line, and Merri-bek Council has long campaigned for the government to commit to the upgrades. Duplicating the line would cost about $245 million, according to Parliamentary Budget Office costings commissioned by the Greens in 2025, and provided to The Age at the time. That does not include about $50 million over a decade in operating and maintenance expenses.



Infrastructure Victoria estimated duplicating the track and upgrading power and signalling along the entire line would cost $650 million to $1.4 billion, Carroll said on Monday. Labor’s promise to upgrade the line may also shore up support in heartland northern-suburb seats. The Greens believe they can unseat Labor in Pascoe Vale, which the government holds on a slim 2 per cent margin. The duplicated train line will also benefit commuters closer to the city in the seat of Brunswick, which Labor hopes to win back from the Greens. Greens candidate for Pascoe Vale Angelica Panopoulos said it was time the northern suburbs were given the same quality of public transport as commuters in other parts of the city. “It shouldn’t take decades of advocacy from the community and Labor staring down the barrel of losing marginal seats to the Greens to finally move on this,” she said.

World.title: MTV VMAs 2026: Full list of winners and nominees
World.content:
The blue carpet has officially been rolled up for the wildest awards show in entertainment, but the best is yet to come from the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs).

The VMAs earned their chaotic reputation long before the artist formerly known as Kanye West interrupted Taylor Swift’s acceptance speech in 2009, and that’s in large part thanks to Madonna. And on Sunday night at Los Angeles’ Peacock Theatre (Monday morning AEST), the queen of pop graced the stage and performed at the VMAs for the first time in 23 years, with the help of Sabrina Carpenter and Charli xcx.

Madonna enlisted Sabrina Carpenter for her first MTV VMAs performance in 23 years. The duo then picked up the best collaboration gong. Stewart Cook/CBS

Charli xcx was also tapped for an opening performance cameo. Stewart Cook/CBS

A quick refresher for the uninitiated: Madonna’s first performance at the VMAs was in 1984, an edgy rendition of Like A Virgin some critics dubbed obscene. She upped the edgy ante in 2003, when she performed the opening medley with Britney Spears and Christina Aguilera … and locked lips with them.

World.title: Wall Street’s multi-trillion-dollar question: Could bonds end the AI boom?
World.content:
BusinessMarketsBonds Opinion Wall Street’s multi-trillion-dollar question: Could bonds end the AI boom? Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 28, 2026 — 12:10pm

September 28, 2026 — 12:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The sudden spike in US bond yields over the past week to near 20-year highs raises a multi-trillion dollar question: Will those higher debt returns crash the sharemarket, and in the process derail the boom in artificial intelligence-related investment? Having edged up for most of the year – since the war in the Middle East caused oil prices to soar – the yield on US 10-year Treasury bonds has jumped from 4.95 per cent to 5.16 per cent in the space of a week, with similar moves across the yield curve. The spike in bond yields doesn’t bode well for the sharemarket, and its AI-investment boom. AP That’s the highest yield on the 10-year bond – the global reference point for most interest-bearing securities – since 2007, when it rallied in the lead-up to the global financial crisis. Bond yields and sharemarkets generally (there are exceptions) have an inverse correlation.



Bonds are “risk-free” assets. If you can get more than 5 per cent from investing in bonds, the dividend yield on the US stock market – currently about 1 per cent – starts to look unappealing when the risks of a sharemarket inflated by the hype around artificial intelligence stocks and trading at near-record levels are factored into decision-making. Higher yields push up borrowing costs, lowering company profits and dampening economic activity. They also lift the discount rates used to calculate the value of companies’ forecast future cashflows in today’s dollars, which is a particular threat to an AI sector increasingly reliant on access to the debt market to fund the extraordinary levels of investment in chips and data centres, and the energy and water infrastructure to support those centres. There’s a lot riding on a continuation of the AI investment binge and the promises of transformative productivity gains being realised – for investors, and the global economy. The scale of the AI investments being made – in the US, it is more than $US700 billion ($990 billion) this year and could top a trillion dollars next year – and the rates of revenue growth that would be required to justify the investments are mind-boggling. They make the AI sector and the “hyperscalers” dominating the digital infrastructure, and accounting for about 35 per cent of the US market’s value, exceptionally vulnerable to an increase in discount rates.



So far, there’s been no material impact on the sharemarket from the spikes in yields and, apart from a brief sell-off when the US and Israel launched their attack on Iran in February, it has traded largely unaffected by the surge in oil prices above $US100 a barrel, the stubbornly high inflation rate and the US Federal Reserve’s decision this month to raise its policy rate for the first time in more than three years. Related Article Opinion

Global economy The four horsemen of the apocalypse are coming for the global economy That may be because of the continuing conviction that AI will change the world, and those companies leading the revolution will profit immeasurably. It may also be because the US economy is growing strongly, buoyed by the investment in AI, by fiscal stimulus – the US government deficit is running at almost 6 per cent of GDP - and the strength of spending by higher income households, and by booming corporate profitability. The AI investment boom may, however, taper or burst.



The resort to debt by even the hyperscalers – companies like Amazon and Alphabet – is an indication of the stresses even the biggest and most profitable companies are experiencing in funding their ever-escalating AI investments. Spending on AI has absorbed their vast legacy cashflows and is stretching the equity market’s capacity to support them with new equity. The rise in yields makes the cost of AI debt – which already has a risk premium – more expensive, while the rise in interest rates being driven by the bond market and the Fed will start to squeeze consumers’ finances. The spending by wealthier households has been held up, so far, by the Republicans’ tax cuts and by the wealth effects of the sharemarket boom. The rise in yields makes the cost of AI debt more expensive, while the rise in interest rates being driven by the bond market and the Fed will start to squeeze consumers’ finances. Corporate earnings growth has been exceptionally strong. Third-quarter earnings estimates put it at about 25 per cent of the same period last year. The earnings numbers are, however, inflated to some degree by the hundreds of billions of profits AI companies are reporting that flow from the markups in the value of their holdings in each other in what’s been described as the “circular” AI economy. There’s a lot of paper profit and revenue within the sector.



At a macro level, the current US settings – the 6 per cent government deficit and more than $US40 trillion of government debt – are unsustainable in a rising interest rate environment. Related Article Opinion

Gold What the price of gold tells us about Trump and the future Peter Hartcher Political and international editor With the Fed having just started a rate-rising cycle, with the market pricing in at least three more 25 basis point increases over the next year, the threat posed to government and corporate finances posed by a significant increase in interest costs will only intensify. The US could grow its way out of the looming debt trap as low-cost debt issued in the post-financial crisis and pandemic eras continues to mature and be refinanced with higher-cost debt. But, more likely, it will have to try to inflate its way out, which will probably agitate the bond vigilantes even more. The risk to the sharemarket is heightened because today’s bond market is not what it once was.



Donald Trump’s trade wars and US sanctions have made the foreign central banks and institutions that were once the major buyers of US bonds more wary. They’ve been diversifying away from the US, into gold and other assets. The market is now peopled by hedge funds and other traders, pursuing carry trades by either borrowing cheaply in other markets (Japan used to be the primary source of low-cost funding) or by running leveraged arbitrages between US physical bonds and their policing in futures markets. The risk to the sharemarket is heightened because the bond market during Donald Trump’s presidency is not what it once was. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson That makes the market more volatile and potentially vulnerable if an “event” causes the funds to suddenly unwind their trades. The bond market’s equivalent of the VIX index (often referred to as the “fear” index), which measures volatility in the sharemarket, is the MOVE (Merrill Option Volatility Estimate) index. It leapt over the past week from 78.56, which is roughly its average level of the past decade, to 96. Presumably some of those leveraged bondholders became spooked by the pace of the run-up in yields.



With stocks trading at pricey levels – the cyclically adjusted profit-to-earnings or CAPE ratio is at levels last seen in 1999, in the lead-up to the bursting of the dot-com bubble – a sustained rise in interest rates is an obvious threat. It’s also a threat to both the real economy and the financial sector, where there’s been massive increases in non-bank, or “shadow banking” activity since the regulatory response to the 2008 crisis forced regulated institutions out of a lot of financial market activities. Related Article Global economy The world economy is becoming wary of America There is perceived increased risk to the corporate sector and the economy being priced into markets, with the credit default swaps for investment trade companies blowing out and the yield curve in the bond market flattening. An index for insuring against defaults on US investment grade debt started the year at 51 basis points and is now at 58 basis points – where it would have cost $US510,000 to buy insurance against a default on $US100 million of loans, it now costs $US580,000. For some of the hyperscalers, the cost is above 90 basis points, or more than $US900,00 per $US100 million.



The flattening of the yield curve – the difference between the yields on two and 10-year bonds has shrunk from about 85 basis points at the start of the year to about 30 basis points – points to an expectation that the US economy will slow as the Fed, and the market, respond to the risk of sustained high inflation levels. It is, of course, conceivable that a sharemarket that has shrugged off Trump’s tariffs, the war in the Middle East and $US100-a-barrel-plus oil prices, $US40 trillion of government debt and the administration’s erratic policymaking can ignore the myriad of latent threats, buoyed by the transformative potential of AI. There’s a lot riding on a continuation of the AI investment binge and the promises of transformative productivity gains being realised - for investors, and the global economy. World.title: Lamarre-Condon told friend how he would dispose of a body, court told
World.content:
NationalNSWLamarre-Condon trial Lamarre-Condon told friend how he would dispose of a body, court told Michaela Whitbourn September 28, 2026 — 12:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A former NSW police officer accused of murdering Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies told a friend at a dinner how he would dispose of the body if he killed someone, a court has heard. Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, is standing trial in the NSW Supreme Court on two counts of murder over the shooting deaths of Baird, 26, his former casual romantic partner, and Davies, 29, in Paddington on February 19, 2024. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Georgia Cook outside the NSW Supreme Court on Friday. Her evidence continued on Monday. George Chan Georgia Cook, a former friend of Lamarre-Condon, told the court on Monday she distanced herself from the then-police officer after he asked her over a dinner in Kirribilli in May 2023: “What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?” She said she froze and replied: “No, because I don’t want their ghost to haunt me.”



Cook said he asked her later in the dinner, “So, if you did kill someone what would you do with their bodies?” Lamarre-Condon said he would “take their stuff, I would put it in a dumpster, and I would take their bodies to bushland where no one would ever find them”, Cook told the court. A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon in the NSW Supreme Court. Rocco Fazzari “It felt very surreal,” she said. “I didn’t know whether to believe anything I’d heard. I really couldn’t continue a friendship after hearing these things.” She said she had told Lamarre-Condon before the dinner about a confidential medical diagnosis, and he had said at the restaurant that “what I’m about to tell you, if you tell anyone else, I know about you”.



He was using the information “to hold over me, so I wouldn’t go and tell … what he had told me”, Cook said. She said she was “really scared” after the dinner, and distanced herself from him permanently in December 2023. Cook gave a statement to police in June 2024, four months after Lamarre-Condon was arrested in February. She rejected a suggestion by one of the accused’s barristers, James Lang, that Lamarre-Condon did not have this conversation with her, and that she had repeated details about the alleged location of the bodies and other items from media reports. “When someone says something that scary or shocking, it’s not something that leaves your mind,” Cook said. “I can remember it like it was yesterday. It was jarring. I could never forget these words being said to me.”



Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial Three shots, a shopping trip and 14,000 hours of CCTV: The case against Beau Lamarre-Condon Asked about the delay in coming forward to police, Cook said she was “absolutely terrified”. “After the news had come out, I was scared,” she said. “I didn’t know what to do with what I knew. I didn’t know if I wanted to be involved. “If he wasn’t put away, what would happen to me? That puts me in a scary position.” Cook testified on Friday that Lamarre-Condon had told her during the same dinner that he had been watching Baird from outside his house, using his mother’s car and wearing a black hoodie.



“In that time he’d seen Jesse have sex with other men,” she said he told her. She said the accused also claimed that he saw Baird over the back fence taking photos with friends with a Polaroid camera he had given him. Lamarre-Condon told her he kept watching until Baird left the home and saw where he left his key. “He [said he] went and got the key and unlocked the door, broke into the house, he stole the Polaroid camera, he ate Jesse’s Easter egg, and he said that there was something else that he did, but he wouldn’t tell me what it was, which concerned me,” she said. The court has heard that Baird broke up with Lamarre-Condon for the first time in April 2023. The two men resumed seeing each other briefly in late 2023 before Baird ended it permanently in November.



Lamarre-Condon is charged with breaking into Baird’s home in August 2023 and stealing Baird’s wallet and phone. He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated break and enter. The defence case is that he used a key Baird had given him to enter the home. The prosecution alleges Lamarre-Condon murdered Baird, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, after developing an “obsessive and jealous infatuation” with him. Davies, Baird’s new boyfriend, was killed to eliminate a witness to the crime, the Crown alleges. There is no dispute that Lamarre-Condon was at Baird’s Paddington share house when Baird and Davies died, that they died of gunshot wounds from his police-issued pistol, and that he was disguised as a delivery rider. However, the defence case is that Lamarre-Condon was there to pick up some of his belongings and did not expect anybody to be home. A struggle ensued in which his gun accidentally went off twice, killing Baird, and Davies accidentally shot himself in a second struggle after grabbing the gun, the defence says. The trial continues.

World.title: Ten minutes of madness: How the Wallabies beat the Boks with 11 men
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies Ten minutes of madness: How the Wallabies beat the Boks with 11 men Jonathan Drennan September 28, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wallabies coach Les Kiss prides himself on having every detail covered when preparing his teams. Ahead of facing the Springboks in Perth on Sunday night, Kiss had challenged his side to work on contingency plans, such as losing five-eighth Ben Donaldson while not having an experienced playmaker in reserve. That would have been a simple scenario to deal with compared to what actually took place. Loading Ultimately, nothing could have prepared Kiss or his team for the 10 minutes and 30 seconds of madness that ended the Test match against South Africa. The Wallabies led by 25 points before yellow cards to Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Hunter Paisami left the team with 11 players against the world champions. Here’s how the Wallabies hung on and won the Test.



69th and 70th minutes: 18-point lead. Wilson and Lonergan yellow cards Wilson had enjoyed one of his best Test performances until referee Andrea Piardi gave him a yellow card for a high tackle on South African hooker Malcolm Marx. Wilson was his team’s top tackler, making 13 and not missing one. Marx dipped late, and Wilson made glancing high contact. He left the field with just over 10 minutes left on the clock. With Wilson absent and the Wallabies pack weakened, South Africa took full advantage a minute later.



The Springbok scrum was metres away from the Australian line with centre Hunter Paisami packing down in Wilson’s place. Lonergan dives at the ball illegally while South African back-rower Jasper Wiese has it at his feet. A penalty try is awarded, and Lonergan is off the field for 10 minutes. Kiss later said the team remained calm amid these scenes. “We were asking a lot of questions about what was happening; we were trying to get messages down the sideline and just get an idea of where things were,” Kiss said. “The pleasing thing for me was that the group out there on the pitch there was a nice calmness and focus about what they had to do next. Hearing that back and seeing how they looked and felt in those tough moments, that’s incredibly pleasing.” 71st and 72nd minutes: 11-point lead. Suaalii yellow card



The Wallabies are tired, with spaces opening up all over their defensive line. Springboks playmaker Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu charges through a gap and passes to centre Canan Moodie, who looks certain to score a try. Fullback Tom Wright yells for cover, and it comes. Donaldson and Max Jorgensen manage to mow down Moodie. Wright believes that the team was playing completely on instinct. “We were just trying to bust ass,” Wright said. “I think when you’re down, and there is no real plan, it’s about how hard can you hustle and make it as difficult for the opposition to score as possible. That’s what we were talking about and trying to execute when we didn’t have the ball.” Loading



Suaalii is yellow-carded for offside, leaving the Wallabies with 12 men on the field. Piardi is having to use a mobile phone to speak to television match official Matteo Liparini due to communication problems. He explains to Wallabies stand-in captain Jeremy Williams and South Africa skipper Andre Esterhuizen the difficulties he is having with the technology, pleading that he is doing his best. After the game, Williams had every sympathy for the officials. “The refs had a really tough job; they obviously had problems with the radios and things like that, so they did the best they could while they were out there, and I don’t envy that job at all, they did an awesome job,” Williams said. Two minutes later, Morne van den Berg scores a converted try for South Africa, pulling the score back to 42-31.



75th minute: Down to 11 players, leading by 11. Paisami yellow card. With just 12 teammates, Wright took a gamble, shooting out of the line and catching a pass from Esterhuizen. The fullback finishes under the posts, thinking he has sealed the game for the Wallabies, but Piardi’s blue mobile phone comes back out. After a quick review, the try is rubbed out after a high tackle from centre Hunter Paisami, leaving the Wallabies with 11 players on the field. View post on X



“That’s how it goes, isn’t it? We said we wanted to make it difficult for them. We knew that they needed to score points and wanted to run,” Wright said. “We said if we were to concede a little bit of space anywhere, they were going to have to go around us. “We were hustling, showing that care and connection that we talked about during the week. The ball fell favourably for me; sadly, a high shot was the call that we came back to, and we had to go from there.” Minutes 76-79: Desperate times call for desperate measures. Four-point lead Down to 11 men, the Wallabies are forced to defend desperately. The Springboks have a luxury of space, but for three minutes the Wallabies hold them off, shaving precious time off the clock.



“I haven’t played with 11 before. That’s the game. You can have a plan until you get punched in the face. We didn’t get punched in the face, so to speak, but certainly we weren’t expecting to play with 11,” Wright said. “You don’t expect to play with 14 or 13 or 12, but you certainly don’t expect to play with 11 ... we certainly can’t fault our effort and how much we put into defending our tryline.” In the 79th minute, South Africa prop Ox Nche crashes over for a converted try to reduce the Wallabies’ lead to four points. There is time for one more play, and for South Africa to win the Test. Wallabies captain Harry Wilson celebrates after taking down the Springboks. Getty Images Last two minutes: Lonergan and Wilson return to help seal victory



Wilson has been sitting on the sideline for 10 minutes, unable to help his team and desperate to come on. After getting on the field, the captain’s message is simple: try to get the ball back. With the clock on 81 minutes, 13 Wallabies hang on for a famous victory after South African playmaker Quan Horn is penalised for an accidental offside. “I had fresh legs then, so I was going to chase after everything, because when you let your team down, it always hurts, especially when we’re in such a strong position when I did that [high tackle for the yellow card]. “So I was hurting there on the sideline, but I just loved the way the boys scrapped for each other and the care for the jersey.”

Follow RNZ's live election updates above.

It's day two of the election campaign, with politicians out and about around the country.

On Sunday, the two major parties kicked off their campaigns in Auckland with promises about taxes, student debt and the cost of living.

National's campaign launch featured a significant focus on Labour and another pledge card rather than any new policy, along with conspicuously empty seats.

While Labour leader Chris Hipkins promised "plenty more fire" this election, and to cut student debt if elected.

Both Hipkins and National leader Christopher Luxon came across as fed-up on Sunday - but for different reasons.

World.title: National sharpens spending pledge on eve of Treasury update
World.content:
National appears to have sharpened its promise to shrink government spending, drawing a starker comparison with Labour, a day before Treasury opens the books.

The party unveiled an 11-page "economic plan" on Monday afternoon, underscoring National's pledge to introduce "no new taxes" and return the books to surplus in 2028/29.

It also highlighted its commitment to "right-sizing government" and "public sector reform", promising to reduce core Crown spending below 30 percent of GDP.

National's previous fiscal policy was to drive down spending towards 30 percent.

The change - while very slight - widens the gap between National's prescription and Labour's. Last month, Labour set its spending cap at 33 percent of GDP in the medium term.

Neither National nor Labour have set a firm date for reaching their respective targets.

At the May Budget, Treasury's forecast put core Crown spending at 32.6 percent of GDP in both 2025/26 and 2026/27.

Treasury will release its pre-election economic and fiscal update (PREFU) on Tuesday.

In a statement, National's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said the only way to keep momentum was with a National-led government.

"We need to continue with the plan that is working, especially as the world remains volatile," she said.

"Now is not the time to dramatically change course by loading on more spending, more taxes and more borrowing as Labour is proposing."

World.title: Ellerslie double homicide: Lok Fung Lorrence Li found guilty of murder
World.content:
The man accused of murdering an Auckland couple and plotting to murder his former landlord has been found guilty.

Lok Fung Lorrence Li has been on trial in the High Court at Auckland, charged with the murder of Fuk Fu Joseph Kwok and his wife Mei Han Chong at their Ellerslie home in 2023.

Li had pleaded not guilty to their murders, but admitted to the manslaughter of the pair, which meant Crown lawyers had to prove murderous intent.

Over the past four weeks, jurors heard how Li plotted with his churchmate, Shu Man Poon, to kill Li's former landlord.

Poon pleaded guilty to all charges last year, and gave evidence against Li during the trial.

When their plan for Li's landlord fell through, the duo shifted focus to the Kwoks.

Kwok and Li had been in a minor traffic accident nearly a year earlier.

The matter was taken to the Disputes Tribunal, who were asked by Kwok to keep his address confidential.

Fuk Fu Joseph Kwok asked for his address to be kept from Li during a Disputes Tribunal case. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

The police officer who investigated the Disputes Tribunal process, Robert Lawrence, told the court "he didn't ask for Mr Li's address so he didn't see why Mr Li should have his address."

Jurors in Li's trial heard from the service manager for the Auckland Disputes Tribunal at the time, Glenn Adkin, who said that request had been refused on a lack of evidence.

Lawrence said the reason recorded for denying Kwok's request was a lack of real safety reasons or concerns.

As a result, Kwok's address was sent to Li in an email along with other documents on 1 November, four days before the murders.

Jurors reach a verdict

After four hours deliberating on Monday, jurors returned with their verdicts.

They found Li guilty on all charges.

Li stood stone-faced in the dock as Justice Jane Anderson convicted him.

Lok Fung Lorrence Li during the trial. Nick Monro

Jurors had a number of different pathways to find Li guilty or not guilty, which delved into his level of involvement in the killings and his intention behind it.

"You don't have to agree unanimously about which pathway applies," Justice Anderson had said in summing up the trial.

"But each of you must be sure that every ingredient of one full pathway is proven beyond reasonable doubt."

Li will appear for sentencing in December.

A murder planned, and a murder committed

Days before the murders, Poon and Li had visited Li's former landlord's house, which Poon said they had found by using a GPS tracker, and spray painted over the security camera's outside the property.

Poon had told the court they were there to rob and kill the landlord and anyone else inside the home.

Before they could continue, the pair spotted another camera and retreated.

After yet another unsuccessful attempt, Li and Poon set their sights on the Kwoks, breaking into their home and attacking the couple using an air pistol and tomahawk.

Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and Mei Han Chong. NZ Police

Once the Kwok's were dead, Poon and Li cleaned the crime scene, leaving Fuk Fu Joseph Kwok's body in their home.

He was later found by their son Chi-Ho Ricky Kwok.

Chong's body was taken in the couple's blue Kia car and dumped in Greenhithe on the city's North Shore.

Poon and Li were arrested in the days after.

A large part of the trial was focused on Shu Man Poon, who had said he was pressured to take part in the murder plot and Kwok killings to pay off a $7000 debt to Li.

Poon had gone to the police over the murder conspiracy against Li's landlord, telling them about a plot to "make them disappear forever".

But jurors were told that report was filed away by police, and would not be looked at until two months later after the Kwok's were murdered.

World.title: ACT, NZ First hit back at National's warning against 'strategic voting'
World.content:
ACT and New Zealand First have hit back at National's warning against 'strategic voting', with David Seymour saying "both votes belong to the voter" and Winston Peters saying the comments were "very, very ill-informed".

At National's campaign launch on Sunday, Sir John Key used his speech to caution voters against splitting their vote, saying voters shouldn't try do something "you think is clever" that is the "opposite of clever."

It referenced a suggestion voters on the right give their party vote to a minor party, and electorate vote to the National candidate, with the intention of creating an overhang.

Seymour suggested the warning was talking down to voters, and that it was "important to respect that both votes belong to the voter."

David Seymour. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

"In my experience, voters are often busy, but they're not stupid, and it's never wise to talk down to them."

He suggested people should use the party vote to reflect their values, and vote for the candidate that would answer their call at 5pm on a Friday.

Peters said that it was "rather desperate" to have a former prime minister on stage with nobody behind him "giving out the wrong message."

He explained it was the wrong message because the "very manipulation of the electoral system" Te Pāti Māori and those on the left were engaging in "has to have a response."

"The response that Mr Key set out was simply just not appropriate and not right, and was very, very ill-informed in my view.

World.title: Lodestone aims to raise up to $100m in NZX’s first major float since 2021
World.content:
Solar energy company Lodestone is seeking to raise between $75 million and $100m through an initial public offering - the NZX's first major float since property developer Winton Land listed in 2021.

The company plans to sell shares at $2.25 each, valuing it at between $440m and $465m.

Lodestone said the money would help fund more solar farms and expand its electricity retail business.

Lodestone's customers have predominantly been commercial and industrial businesses, including The Warehouse Group, Inghams, Halls, Pink Batts, Open Country Dairy and Briscoes, although it has begun selling electricity to households and small businesses in Hawke's Bay.

Managing director Gary Holden said: "We founded Lodestone Energy in 2019 with a vision to build a solar farm in every community."

"The IPO allows us to continue doing what we have been doing, but at greater scale," he said.

The company builds and operates solar farms, as well as selling the electricity they generate. It currently operates five farms, with a sixth under construction at Ongaonga Road in Hawke's Bay, and is aiming to have up to 18 operating by the 2032 financial year.

Its existing solar farms generate enough electricity to power the equivalent of more than 33,000 average homes a year.

Holden said its standardised approach to designing, procuring and building solar farms was reducing costs over time, with Ongaonga Road expected to cost 11 percent less to build than the average construction cost of its first five farms.

"The IPO is one part of how we are proposing to fund growth. We also use project-level debt financing, strategic partnerships and cash generated by the business, which means the capital we're raising can support a much larger build programme," Holden said.

The company said no existing shareholders would sell shares through the IPO, meaning all the capital raised would go towards additional solar farms, expanding its customer base and general corporate purposes.

The offer opens on 29 September and closes on 14 October 2026, with Forsyth Barr and Jarden appointed to manage the pre-float bookbuild.

World.title: Seal pup who crossed busy Wellington road receives police escort back to water
World.content:
A seal pup caught crossing a busy Wellington street over the weekend received a police escort back to the water.

Police were called out after the seal was spotted crossing Hutt Road just after 1pm on Sunday.

A seal puppy is stopped by police after it crossed a busy Wellington road. Supplied / NZ Police

Senior Sergeant Miriam Bentley said the seal appeared to be heading back for the water when it was found near the Wellington train station, which would have seen it cross the road again.

Bentley said police and Department of Conservation (DOC) staff worked together to help the pup.

"With guidance from DOC, our staff were able to uplift the seal and drive it to a safe place where it was released into the water.

"This was collaborative problem solving which prevented any further issues for the young seal and for road users."

Constables Taylor and Leitch helped take the seal to the beach for safe release, and Taylor said they were happy to help.

"When I joined police 15 months ago they said to be ready for anything, so I guess this demonstrates that's true."

World.title: All Blacks veteran Beauden Barrett to make rare appearance for Taranaki
World.content:
All Blacks veteran Beauden Barrett will play his first game for Taranaki since 2020 on Sunday when the Amber and Blacks take on Wellington in New Plymouth.

Barrett, 35, is one of 14 players released by the All Blacks for the NPC this weekend. Other All Blacks who toured South Africa for the recent test series available for Taranaki include first-five Josh Jacomb and hooker Bradley Slater.

Barrett played only one test during the "Greatest Rivalry" series won 3-1 by the Springboks - the final match in Baltimore in the United States.

His brother, Scott, the former All Blacks captain, made a successful return for Taranaki in their 50-14 victory over Hawke's Bay on Sunday. Scott was making his comeback from back surgery.

Beauden, who has played 145 tests, is also hoping to be in the frame for the 34-man All Blacks squad for the upcoming Bledisloe Cup series, which will be named on Tuesday.

The All Blacks play Australia at Eden Park on 10 October and in Sydney a week later.

With Jacomb also in the mix for Taranaki on Sunday, it is likely that Barrett will start at fullback.
